en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Nidāna Vagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
1. Nidāna Saṃyutta 1.
Buddhavagga 1.
Commentary on the Paṭiccasamuppāda Sutta (Discourse on Dependent Origination)
1. Since the second sutta and the others were also taught by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) alone, he said, "The first is the Sutta on Dependent Origination.
Regarding the word *tatra* (there), showing that it indicates those places and times which were stated as qualifiers for the action of dwelling here, he said, "At whatever time...
[etc. ...it indicates. For the word *taṃ* (that) is a restatement of the meaning already mentioned.
Therefore, in this context, it is appropriate for the word *tatra* to refer to either the place or the time, and nothing else.

This, then, is the explanation of the meaning regarding the function of *tatra* as a demonstrative pronoun. However, since in such instances the word *tatra* indicates a place or time distinguished by the teaching of the Dhamma, it is said: "or to the place and time suitable for speaking."
"In that place" (*tena tattha*) means in such a location where the Blessed One addressed and spoke to the bhikkhus for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma;
"at such a time" (*kāle vā*) is the meaning. With the words beginning "for it is not," he supports that very point.
But was it not the case that while standing there, the Blessed One refused to teach the Dhamma to Bāhiya, saying, "It is not yet the right time"?
“Did he teach him the Dhamma while standing right there in the middle of the street?”—this is true.
For this is an example of not teaching at a time when it should not be taught. Therefore he said, “It was indeed the wrong time.
As for what was said there, “We had entered among the houses,” that too was spoken by way of indicating the fact that it was the wrong time for him. Of that...
For at that time, there was unworkability (*akammaññatā*) in the physical body (*rūpakāya*) due to the fatigue of the journey, and in the mental body (*nāmakāya*) due to the force of intense joy.
As both of these subsided, the Blessed One rejected [the request] by way of a formal refusal, saying, "It is not the right time," for the purpose of avoiding conceptual proliferation (*papañca*).
Furthermore, as an example of not teaching what should not be taught, [it is said]: "Then the Blessed One, having descended from the road..."

“...he sat at the foot of a certain tree; having emerged from the monastery, he sat on a seat prepared in the shade of the monastery”—such passages as these are included here by the word *ādi* (“and so forth”).

In phrases such as “That fool, bhikkhus, having performed evil deeds here,” the particle *kho* serves merely to fill out the meter. [And in the phrase] “One who lacks respect dwells in suffering... [the same applies].

In passages such as “appatisso,” it has the sense of emphasis; in passages such as “Kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekaṃ nānusikkhanti,” it has the sense of the beginning of time, meaning the commencement of a sentence.

Therein, by the sense of filling out the meter, a mere ornamentation of speech is effected; by the sense of the beginning of time, there is merely the introduction of the sentence; and by the sense of emphasis—
However, this is a demonstration of restriction. By the words “therefore he addressed [him] indeed,” the restriction regarding the act of addressing is shown.
As for the statement, “‘The Blessed One’ is an indication of his being revered by the world,” one might ask: was not the word “the Blessed One” already stated previously?
Even though it was stated previously, that was intended to show the specific agent of the action of dwelling in the place as previously described.
It is not for the purpose of addressing [the assembly], but here it is for the purpose of addressing; therefore, the word "Bhagavā" is stated again in the text for that reason.
To show its meaning, he said: "‘Bhagavā’ is a designation indicating one who is revered by the world.

It is a term for a person fit to hear the discourse—that is, a term for a person capable of hearing the teaching on dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) which is about to be spoken. Among the four assemblies...

Having shown that the term "bhikkhu" is used here to demonstrate that monks are especially worthy vessels for such teachings and thus preeminent recipients of the Dispensation, he now says "apica" (furthermore) in order to show the etymological meaning of the word.
In this context, "bhikkhu" means one who begs; the sense is that he is called a "bhikkhu" because his nature is to beg and his duty is to beg. He has entered upon the practice of begging.
He is called a *bhikkhu* because he has entered upon the wandering for alms (*bhikkhācariyā*), the practice of gleaning (*uñchācariyā*), which was adopted even by the Buddha and others;

and because he has undertaken and established it. For anyone who, having abandoned a small or large mass of wealth, goes forth from the home life into homelessness, abandons the means of livelihood such as plowing and cattle-tending, and enters upon the wandering for alms merely by accepting the [monastic] emblem, is a *bhikkhu*.

He is a *bhikkhu* because he has entered upon [the life of a mendicant]. Alternatively, even while eating solid food in the middle of a monastery, he is a *bhikkhu* because he has entered upon the practice of alms-gathering due to his livelihood being dependent on others;
or, he is a *bhikkhu* because he has entered upon the practice of alms-gathering due to having conceived the aspiration for the going-forth by relying on the eating of morsels of alms-food.
In this context, the meaning should be understood in this way.

“By way of the method beginning with ‘Ādinā nayena’” means by the method found in the *Vibhaṅga*: “He is a bhikkhu because he wears torn robes; he is a bhikkhu because he breaks evil, unwholesome states; he is a bhikkhu because of his having broken evil, unwholesome states,” and so forth.

“Ñāpane” means in making known, that is to say, in causing understanding; the meaning is “in proclaiming. It is the nature of begging for alms, not the nature of making a living through agriculture, trade, and so forth.

The nature of mendicancy (*bhikkhanadhammatā*) is the inherent character of begging as described by the phrase, "The Noble Ones stand depending on others," and not the character of being a beggar or a petitioner.
Skillfulness in begging (*bhikkhane sādhukāritā*) is the state of non-negligence therein, having recollected the teaching: "One should rise up and not be negligent.
Alternatively, "virtue" (*sīla*) refers to one's natural disposition; here, however, it refers to a formal resolve. "Dharma" (*dhamma*) refers to the practice (*vata*). Others [say...]
However, they describe it thus: "Virtue (*sīla*) is undertaking by way of a vow; the Dhamma is conduct handed down through tradition;
and 'acting well' is acting with diligence and performing with reverence.

Regarding the mode of life practiced by those of inferior and superior character: those who, even while established in the state of a bhikkhu, are arrogant and conceited due to pride in their birth and so forth...
And for those who, even while in the state of a householder, consider the practice of alms-gathering to be the height of miserliness because they do not even approach others with a sense of need—
for both of these groups, respectively, the word "bhikkhus" refers to that mode of livelihood practiced by low-born people,
the poor, and those who have reached the height of miserliness, who maintain their existence by wandering for alms among other families.

It should be understood that by explaining [this], he refutes arrogance; and by explaining the mode of livelihood practiced for the sake of purifying one's way of life by the Buddha and others—who had gone forth from distinguished families of great wealth and nobility among many people—he refutes dejection.
Since the word "monks" (*bhikkhave*) is an address, it serves to bring [the listeners] face-to-face; from the context...
And by means of its power, it produces a desire to listen and enjoins one toward careful listening and attention;
therefore, in order to demonstrate that meaning, he said, "By this [phrase], 'Bhikkhus,'" and so forth.
In that context, "even when attending carefully" refers to both careful listening and careful attention. How does it proceed?

“Are the hearings and so forth being carried out properly? [The answer is: “Certainly, by means of this practice, the entirety of the success of the Dispensation will come into one’s hands,” through the application of reverence and respect, and by not disparaging others in discussions and the like. For it is said:
“Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, one who hears the true Dhamma is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness.”
Rightness regarding wholesome states. By what five? He does not despise the discourse; he does not despise the speaker; he does not despise himself;
he listens to the Dhamma with an undistracted mind and a one-pointed mind; and he attends to it wisely.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, one who listens to the true Dhamma is capable [of understanding it].
“...for the sake of entering into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states. Therefore he said: “For the success of the Dispensation depends upon careful attention.
Success in the Dispensation means the accomplishment of virtue and the other [qualities]. This is by way of attainment because it arises first;

and by way of practicing the virtues of virtue and so forth, because it conforms to the Teacher’s conduct; and because the practice in accordance with the Dhamma becomes possible through the three vehicles.
Because he was the receiver of the entire dispensation (*sāsana*).
"From his presence" (*santikā*) means from being in close proximity. "From his constant attendance" (*santikāvacarattā*) means because of the state of living together with him at all times.
"According to the instruction" (*yathānusiṭṭhaṃ*) means in accordance with the teaching; the meaning is that they received the instruction in its entirety. "Some monks" (*ekacce bhikkhūti*)...
Those who are intent on hearing the teaching on the phenomena of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) are [the ones addressed].
Previously, by stating, "The Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma is common to all assemblies," and so forth, the reason for addressing the bhikkhus alone was shown;
now, having addressed the bhikkhus, he raises the objection, "But for what purpose did the Blessed One [teach this? in order to show the purpose of the teaching of the Dhamma.
In this context, "thinking of something else" means being preoccupied with another matter. "With distracted mind" means having an unconcentrated mind.
"Reflecting on the Dhamma" means mentally reviewing the Dhamma heard on the previous day or on subsequent days.

By way of contrast, [the Buddha] stated that one who is capable of observing the teaching from the very beginning when the Dhamma is being taught after addressing the bhikkhus—this is the very point [of the preceding passage].
In order to show this, the passage beginning with “without having taken leave of them” was stated.
Regarding the word *bhikkhavo*, the elision of the vowel *i* should be understood as occurring through euphonic combination (*sandhi*), as in “*bhikkhavo iti*.
For this particle *iti* has many distinct meanings, such as indicating a cause, the conclusion of a section, the reversal of a word’s meaning, specification, illustration, and so forth. Likewise...
In such passages as, “Bhikkhus, it is because it is afflicted (*ruppati*) that it is called ‘form’ (*rūpa*),” it is seen in the sense of a cause;
in such passages as, “Therefore, bhikkhus, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things,” it is used for the purpose of concluding;
and in such passages as, “Thus, he abstains from visiting displays of such a kind,” it is used in the sense of ‘beginning. [In the phrase] “Māgaṇḍiya,” it refers to that brahmin...
In such passages as "convention, designation, description, common usage, name, naming, denomination, expression, phrasing, and utterance," it refers to the variation of word-meanings;
in such passages as "Thus, monks, the fool is full of fear, while the wise man is fearless; the fool is beset by calamity, while the wise man is free from calamity," it refers to a manner or mode;
and in "With this as condition, there is aging and death," [it refers to a causal condition].
In such passages as, "Being asked thus, Ānanda, one should say, 'It exists. If it should be asked, 'With what as condition is aging-and-death?
one should say, 'With birth as condition is aging-and-death,'" it has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
In such passages as, "Kaccāna, 'everything exists' is one extreme; 'nothing exists' is the second extreme," it has the sense of illustration (*nidassana*). Here too, [it has the same sense].
It should be understood as indicating [the preceding word]. The word *iti* indicates the manner of address, "Bhikkhus," in the phrase "he addressed them, saying, 'Bhikkhus.
Following this method, the meaning of the word *iti* should be understood accordingly in cases such as "Venerable Sir" (*bhaddante*) and so forth.
Since it was previously stated that "the Blessed One addressed them," the genitive case "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavato*) is used here in the phrase "they replied to the Blessed One."
With the intention that "the addressing itself requires another related party," it is said: "They heard the addressing of the Blessed One.
Furthermore, the word "of the Blessed One" (bhagavato) is a dative case used in connection with the act of responding.
At this point, the connection is that the Nidāna has been spoken, adorned as it is by the factors of time, place, teacher, assembly, and location.

Here it is asked: For what purpose is the introductory statement (nidāna) included when the compendium of the Dhamma and Vinaya is being made? Is it not the case that only the words spoken by the Blessed One should be compiled?
It is replied: It is for the sake of ensuring the stability, non-confusion, and credibility of the teaching.
For a teaching established by being bound together with the indications of time, place, teacher, cause, and audience remains stable for a long time.
It is of a nature that is not subject to forgetfulness and is worthy of trust, like a legal decision established by means of place, time, person, and audience. For this very reason,
when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked questions regarding the location and other details— beginning with, "Friend Ānanda, where was the *Paṭiccasamuppāda-sutta* spoken?"—
the Dharma-keeper (Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika) provided the answer to those questions by saying, "Thus have I heard."
The venerable Ānanda spoke this introduction (nidāna) for this sutta.

Furthermore, the introductory statement is for the purpose of manifesting the excellence of the Teacher. For the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the establishment of his status as a Perfectly Enlightened One (sammāsambuddha) follows from the absence of prior composition, inference, scripture, or ratiocination.
Indeed, there is no need for prior composition and the like for one who is a Perfectly Enlightened One, in every respect.

Because his range of knowledge is unimpeded and because he is of one measure regarding all knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*), and likewise because he lacks the "teacher’s fist" (the withholding of doctrine), stinginess with the Dhamma, and any favoritism toward disciples, the state of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is established;
for those [faults] do not occur at all in one whose taints are utterly destroyed.
Thus, his activity of benefiting others is perfectly pure, as are his ignorance and craving—which constitute the defilement of the teacher and corrupt the perfection of view and virtue.
The Blessed One’s possession of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*) constitutes his practice for the benefit of himself and others:

the accomplishment of the first two grounds of self-confidence is due to the qualities of a Perfectly Enlightened One that indicate absolute non-existence [of faults] and manifest the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of abandonment;

and from that very fact, the accomplishment of the latter two grounds of self-confidence follows, because of the established absence of delusion regarding the things that are obstacles and the things that lead to liberation.

And it is revealed by the statement of the cause (*nidāna*), because the teaching of the Dhamma is illustrated there through spontaneous eloquence (*ṭhānuppattika-paṭibhāna*) according to the disposition of the assembled audience in each instance; here, however,

[it is revealed] by way of the two roots of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), which is free from the two extremes, bound by three links of time, endowed with the fourfold method, and characterized by brevity and profundity.

And it should be construed as “because of the indication of enlightenment. Therefore it was said: “The introductory statement (nidāna) is for the purpose of manifesting the perfections of the Teacher.
Likewise, the introductory statement is for the purpose of manifesting the perfections of the Dispensation.

For since all the activities of the Blessed One are embraced by wisdom and compassion, there is no engagement that is purposeless, nor is there any for his own benefit; therefore, it is solely for the benefit of others.

The entire bodily, verbal, and mental action of the Perfectly Enlightened One, who performs all activities, as it occurs and is being described, is called the "Teaching" (*sāsana*) in the sense that it instructs beings appropriately according to the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal;
it is not a mere literary composition. This conduct of the Teacher, together with its time, place, teacher, and audience...

In various places, it is elucidated by means of introductory statements (*nidāna*) as appropriate; here, however, it is done by way of the exposition of the twelvefold dependent origination (*paccayākāra*).
Therefore it is said: "The introductory statement is for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
Furthermore, the introductory statement is for the purpose of showing that the Dispensation possesses authority by demonstrating that the Teacher possesses authority.
And that demonstration of his authoritative status (pamāṇabhāva) should be understood as being elucidated by the word "Bhagavā" according to the method explained below.

By this word "Bhagavā," there is an illumination of the Tathāgata’s abandonment of all stains of defilement, misconduct, and faults such as lust, hatred, and delusion; and by the illumination of his possession of extraordinary, perfectly pure qualities such as knowledge and compassion, which are not shared by others, for that very reason...

By illuminating the state of being the supreme among all beings, this meaning is explained in every respect. This is the demonstration of the purpose regarding the introductory statement (*nidāna*). "Of that which has been set forth" means of that which has been taught.
For even teaching is called "setting forth" (*nikkhepa*) because it places the subject matter to be taught—such as virtue (*sīla*) and so on—within the mental continuums of those to be trained;
thus, when explained after first investigating the "setting forth of the Sutta," it becomes clear.

Having shown the classification of the origin of the Blessed One’s teaching in general by saying, "It occurs thus," and having demonstrated the origin of the teaching by saying, "In this case, this teaching has such an origin," it was stated [in the commentary] because the Sutta is easy to understand through the correct comprehension of its introduction (*nidāna*) once the origin of the teaching has been shown.
Below that, [it asks]: "Why did the Blessed One [teach] specifically by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*)?"...
When a challenge has been raised by someone saying, "The teaching has begun," the rebuttal— "This presentation of the Sutta is based on another's inclination"—

is well-stated. In this regard, just as the Suttantas, though divided into many hundreds and thousands of types, do not exceed sixteenfoldness according to the primary method beginning with those dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya),
so too [the Suttas] possess a fourfold nature by way of the presentation of the Sutta based on one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya) and so forth.
He said: "For there are four ways of introducing a discourse (suttanikkhepa).

And here, just as a distinction through combination occurs between what originates from one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya) and what arises from a specific occasion (aṭṭhuppatti), together with questions arising from another's inclination (parajjhāsayapucchā)—namely, "that which originates from one's own inclination and that which originates from another's inclination," "that which originates from one's own inclination and is dependent on a question," and "that which originates from one's own inclination, originates from another's inclination, and is dependent on a question"—[so too does it occur in other cases].
"...the occasion-arisen and that which accords with another's inclination; the occasion-arisen and that which arises from a question;
and the occasion-arisen, that which accords with another's inclination, and that which arises from a question"—this is because of the possibility of a sequence based on inclination and questioning.
Thus, although a distinction through combination may occur between the occasion-arisen and the inclination, it is [treated] first by means of one's own inclination and so forth.
Since there is no connection with the "occasion for the arising" (aṭṭhuppatti) among those [other methods] that remain, the detailed method (vitthāranaya) is not possible here in its entirety;

therefore, it was said, "There are four ways of laying down the Suttas. Alternatively, because all other possible ways of laying down are included within these, only four are shown by way of the primary modes of laying down.
And in this context, this distinction of combination (saṃsaggabheda) should be understood as the manner in which they are thus presented.

Herein, this is the etymological explanation (*vacanattha*): it is deposited (*nikkhipīyati*), thus it is a "deposition" (*nikkhepa*); the discourse itself is the deposition, hence "discourse-deposition" (*suttanikkhepa*).
Alternatively, the act of depositing is "deposition"; the deposition of a discourse is "discourse-deposition," meaning the teaching of a discourse.
One's own inclination is "self-inclination" (*attajjhāsaya*); that which has this as its cause is "motivated by self-inclination. One's own inclination...
"Of this" (*etassa*) refers to one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*). The same method applies to the inclination of another (*parajjhāsaya*).

That which occurs by way of a question possesses that quality; thus, it is "dependent on a question" (*pucchāvasika*). The arising of the meaning (*attha*) which serves as the basis for the teaching of the Sutta is "arising of meaning" (*atthuppatti*);
*atthuppatti* itself is *aṭṭhuppatti*. That which possesses this is "dependent on an occasion" (*aṭṭhuppattika*). Alternatively, it is that which is set forth (*nikkhipīyati*).

"Suttanikkhepa" means "the laying down of a discourse," which refers precisely to [discourses] arising from one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) and so forth. In this interpretation of the meaning, however, "one's own inclination" is *attajjhāsaya*;
"the inclination of others" is *parajjhāsaya*. That which is questioned is "inquiry" (*pucchā*), and the matter to be known is that which is to be understood after having inquired.
The speech of those who receive the Dhamma, which proceeds by way of such inquiry, is "occasioned by inquiry" (*pucchāvasika*).
That very term is stated as "dependent on a question" (*pucchāvasika*) by virtue of its masculine gender, in consideration of the word *nikkhepa* (the laying down of a discourse).
Similarly, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "dependent on an occasion" (*aṭṭhuppattika*) means that which arises from an occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*).

Furthermore, in this context, because it is independent of external causes such as the ripening of the faculties of others, the laying down of a discourse according to one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) constitutes a distinct category of sutta.
This is because [the former] was delivered solely by his own inclination for the purpose of establishing the framework of the Dhamma.

However, how could there be no inclusion within the category of "occasional" (aṭṭhuppatti) discourses for those delivered on the occasion of questions arising from the inclinations of others—which serve as the cause for the delivery of the teaching—or for those occasional discourses that arose in accordance with the inclinations of others? Or rather, [how could they not be included] when they were delivered due to the inclination of others?
How is there no restriction regarding the inclinations of others (*parajjhāsaya*) in the case of discourses already set in motion? This need not be questioned.

For, since the occasion for the teaching of a discourse—when it arises independently of a formal request or inquiry from others—is taken as being an "occasion-arising" (*aṭṭhuppatti*), those [discourses] dependent on the inquiries of others' inclinations are mentioned separately.
Thus, in the *Brahmajāla*, *Dhammadāyāda*, and other suttas, the causes for the teaching—the praise or blame of others, the acquisition of material gifts, and so forth—are distinct.

This is called "the origin of the discourse" (*aṭṭhuppatti*). That which is taught by taking as its motive solely the inclination of others, without their having asked a question, is "based on another's inclination" (*parajjhāsayika*);
that which is taught specifically by means of a question is "based on a question" (*pucchāvasika*)—this meaning is well known.

It should be understood that he speaks according to his own inclination for the purpose of establishing the system of the Dhamma (*dhammatantiṭhapanattha*). "A bearer of the Suttantas of the Ten-Powered One" refers to the *Dasabalavagga*.
A series of suttas arranged in successive order; likewise [the sections on] the simile of the moon, the great raft, and so forth.

Factors conducive to the ripening of liberation are the faculties of faith and the rest. Inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) means resolution (*adhimutti*). Acceptance (*khanti*) means acceptance through the contemplation of views (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*).

Mind (*mana*) means consciousness (*citta*). Application (*abhinīhāra*) means aspiration (*paṇidhāna*). The state of awakening (*bujjhanabhāva*) means the nature of awakening, or the mode of penetration.
*Ugghaṭitaññū*: "Ugghaṭana" means the breaking open by knowledge; the meaning is that one knows the Dhamma at the very moment it is broken open by knowledge.
*Vipañcitaññū*: one who knows the meaning only when it is elaborated and explained in detail. *Neyyo*: one who is to be led by means of brief indications and so forth.
*Padaparamo*: one for whom the literal expression of the words is paramount. *Saha udāhaṭavelāya*: at the very time the teaching is uttered... [of the teaching].
At the very moment the summary (uddesa) is uttered: "The realization of the Dhamma" (dhammābhisamaya) means the convergence with knowledge regarding the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.

"This is called" refers to the person capable of attaining Arahatship by directing their knowledge according to the teaching when the matrix (mātikā) is established in brief by way of the method beginning with "the four foundations of mindfulness. Such a person is called "one who understands through a condensed statement" (ugghaṭitaññū).

It is said: "This one is called... This means that when the meaning is analyzed in detail after establishing the brief outline (mātikā), the person capable of attaining arahantship is called "one who gains knowledge through elaboration" (*vipañcitaññū*).

"From exposition" (*uddesato*) means for the sake of exposition; the sense is "for one who is reciting or causing to be recited. There is also the reading *uddisato*, which has the same meaning. "From interrogation" (*paripucchatoti*)...
"For one who asks questions. "The realization of the Dhamma occurs gradually" means that the attainment of Arahatship occurs step by step.

"The realization of the Dhamma does not occur in that very birth" means that by means of that particular individual existence (attabhāva), one is unable to produce either the Path or the Fruit, or at least the meditative absorption (jhāna) or insight (vipassanā). "This is called... refers to this person [who is merely a master of] the words and phrases.
Because he stands having made [the teaching] supreme, he is called "one for whom the word is supreme" (*padaparama*).

"Wandering alone" means dwelling solitary due to delighting in seclusion. "Wandering in pairs" means wandering by way of the practice of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*) and so forth, after two have come to share a single aspiration.

This same method applies to the remaining terms. It is "emptiness" (*suññata*) because it reveals the emptiness of the seven [types of persons]. For that very reason, it is "gentle" (*saṇha*) and "subtle" (*sukhuma*).
Having stated, "The Blessed One began this discourse on account of the inclinations of others," those persons referred to as "others" are of two kinds:
those who have not undergone preparatory work and those whose practice of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*) has been thoroughly purified.
To clarify the Teacher’s conduct toward both of these types by way of a simile, he said, "Just as... and so forth. [He does not produce a form] by way of writing.

He causes [them] to arise. "Those who have not practiced" means those who have not applied themselves to the cultivation of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā). Regarding "endowment with virtue" (*sīla-sampadā*) and so forth:

the construction is as follows—he joins those who have not undertaken the precepts to the endowment of virtue; those whose virtue is perfectly purified to the endowment of concentration (*samādhi-sampadā*);
and those whose view is straightened through rectification to the endowment of right view (*diṭṭhi-sampadā*).

This refers to the practice belonging to the prior stage. "Virtue" (sīla) means the virtue of the fourfold purification. "And view" (diṭṭhi) means both the view of self-agency (kammassakatā-diṭṭhi) and the right view of the courses of action (kammapatha-sammādiṭṭhi).
"In three ways" means in a threefold manner according to the nature of its objects: internally, externally, and both internally and externally.
This serves as a specific condition for the aforementioned purification of view.
It is said that virtue itself is the foundation for development, as expressed in the words: "relying on virtue, established in virtue.
It is like pure gold from which all dross has been removed; it is like a four-cornered gem-cluster that has been polished and well-wiped.

The "conditioning mode" refers to the state of being a cause-condition and so forth, belonging to conditions such as ignorance and the rest, with respect to each respective dependently arisen phenomenon.

However, since in its actual meaning it is precisely ignorance (*avijjā*), he says: "Dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) means the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). Therefore, he says: "For the mode of conditions," and so forth.

Granted that the particle *vo* stands after a word and expresses a specific contrasting meaning, yet when it follows a noun, it awakens [the understanding] of that very thing as distinguished by various factors such as the agent, the object, or the instrument;
however, when it follows the indeclinable *hi*, it serves merely as an ornament for the statement.
He said: “‘Vā’... [etc] ...is seen. “That teaching” means the teaching of that dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
For it is referred to here by the word *ta-* (that). Because of the statement “Listen! which indicates that it is to be understood by the auditory consciousness, it is not only dependent origination.
This word has the same meaning; the addition of the word *ka-* is made merely for the sake of increasing the syllables of the phrase, therefore it is formed from the word *sādhu*.
The intention is that the extraction of the meaning (*atthuddhāra*) has already been properly performed even for the word *sādhu*.

Regarding "Sādhu, bhante," he says "in the sense of a request" (*āyācane*), because the meaning here is "I entreat you, bhante. Again, regarding "Sādhu, bhante," he says "in the sense of acceptance" (*sampaṭicchane*), because the meaning here is "So be it, bhante.
Regarding "Sādhu, sādhu," he says "in the sense of encouragement" (*sampahaṃsane*), because the meaning here is "Ah! Ah! (an expression of praise).
“Sādhu dhammarucī” means one who delights in the Dhamma; the sense is that he is beautiful because he desires merit. “Paññāṇavā” means possessed of wisdom. “Addubbho” means one who is not malevolent.
“Daḷhīkamme” refers to making firm, that is, in the performance of a task with thoroughness. “Āṇattiyaṃ” refers to commanding.

For when it is said, “Listen well and attend closely,” the word “well” (sādhuka) implies the thoroughness of both listening and mental attention, just as in the case of performing a task with thoroughness.
Thus, it is also stated as a command. Its nature as a command should be understood in the same way as its nature as a request.
Here, the connection should be understood as follows: "Now, the application [of the meaning] here is to be known thus.

The prevention of distraction of the ear-faculty is by way of enjoining one to listen, because it functions to prohibit other activities; for the meaning is "lend your ear. The prevention of distraction of the mind-faculty...
Because it precludes thinking of other things. "The former" refers to the word "Listen. "In this" refers to the pair of words "Listen, attend," or to this section.
The prevention of grasping at a distortion of the phrasing (*byañjana*) is due to its warding off distraction at the ear-door;
for one who listens according to the facts, there is no distorted grasping of the sound itself. The prevention of grasping at a distortion of the meaning (*attha*)...
Because it wards off the distraction of the mind-faculty. For one who carefully reflects upon the Dhamma, there is no grasping at a distorted meaning.
It enjoins one to listen to the Dhamma by arranging it thus: "Listen! Regarding the terms "retention" (*dhāraṇā*) and "investigation" (*upaparikkhā*):
here, by the inclusion of "investigation," it encompasses weighing, scrutinizing, and so forth, as well as the thorough penetration of the view (*diṭṭhi*). "With the phrasing" (*sabyañjana*)...
In this context, it is called *byañjana* (the letter) because it makes manifest the intended meaning; it is the conventional terminology (*sabhāvanirutti*).

That which is "with letters" (*sabyañjana*) means endowed with letters; the sense is that it is perfected in its phrasing. It is called *attha* (the meaning) because it is to be approached and entered into; it refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) and so forth.

That which is "with meaning" (*sāttha*) means endowed with meaning; the sense is that it is perfected in its significance. Regarding the phrases "profound in the Dhamma" (*dhammagambhīra*) and so on, "Dhamma" refers to the textual tradition (*tanti*).
"Teaching" (desanā) means the exposition and verbal expression of that textual tradition (tanti) which has been determined by the mind. "Meaning" (attha) means the meaning of the textual tradition.
"Penetration" (paṭivedha) means the realization, in accordance with reality, of both the textual tradition and the meaning of the textual tradition.
Since these—teaching, meaning, and penetration—are difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom and provide no foothold, just as the great ocean is for fish and other aquatic creatures, therefore:
It is profound. Therefore it was said: "Because this Dhamma... [as before] ...you should attend to it well.
And herein, because penetration is difficult to achieve and because the knowledge of teaching is difficult to master regarding the meaning of the Dhamma, the teaching is difficult to fathom;
furthermore, because penetration cannot be produced [by mere study], and because of the arising of the knowledge whose object is that penetration—

It should be understood that its state of being difficult [to penetrate] is due to its depth of suffering (*dukkha*). "Teaching" (*desanā*) refers to reciting [the text], which is similar to providing a brief indication.
For instance, in the *Vibhaṅga-sutta*, after saying "I shall teach," it is further stated, "I shall speak.
Its detailed exposition is what is intended here by "speaking"; thus he said, "it is meant that 'I shall speak it even in detail. It is well-known.
“Speaking” means uttering. “Like the warbling of a myna bird” means as sweet as the call of a myna bird—pleasant to the ear and lovely.
“Eloquence” means sound. “He uttered” means it was pronounced; the sense is that it was spoken. When this had been said, they were filled with zeal, thinking: “Listen!”
When he said, "Pay close attention; I shall speak," they became joyful and elated, thinking, "It seems the Teacher will not teach only in brief, but will also speak in detail.
As for the word "Which" (*katamo*), it is understood from its general form to be a question, but not as a specific one; therefore, [the commentary] explains its nature as a specific question.

Having stated that "the inquiry arising from a desire to speak" (*kathetukamyatā-pucchā*) occurs when one is speaking, [the author] demonstrates, by way of that very context, all the inquiries found in the *Mahāniddesa* according to the method of extracting the meaning (*atthuddhāra-naya*), beginning with the words "for the inquiry is fivefold.
Therein, it is called "illumination of the unseen" (*adiṭṭha-jotana*) because by means of it, what has not been seen is illuminated.
It is called "corroboration of the seen" (*diṭṭha-saṃsandana*) because by means of it, what has been seen is corroborated. And here, "corroboration" (*saṃsandana*)...

Making a determination by means of discussion. It is called "the cutting off of doubt" because it cuts through doubt by means of this. "Inquiry for consent" is an inquiry made with the purpose of obtaining consent;

for when there is an inquiry such as, "What do you think, monks?", the consent is being asked for by the question, "What is your approval? "The desire to speak" refers to the state of wishing to speak.
"Characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) refers to any intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) when asked to be known. "Unknown" (*aññāta*) expresses the state of being unknown by any kind of knowledge.

"Unseen" (*adiṭṭha*) means not seen by means of the eye-like knowledge that functions as seeing. "Untasted" (*atula*) means not weighed by means of the knowledge that functions as weighing, such that one could say, "This is so much.
"Unrealized" (*atīrita*) means the completion of the cognitive act has not been performed by means of the knowledge that functions as investigating.
“Unmanifested” (*avibhūta*) means the state of being not evident to knowledge. “Uncultivated” (*avibhāvita*) means the state of not having been made evident by knowledge.

Having shown that among the five types of questions there are none that do not exist for the Buddhas in every respect, the passage beginning with “In that regard” (*tattha*) was stated in order to conclude the question intended here.
That is indeed easy to understand. If dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*), then...
Why did the Blessed One, in his teaching on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), speak of formations (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth as "dependently arisen"? To this he says: “And here,” etc.
He speaks of the dependently arisen because, by showing what is dependently arisen, the state of being a condition for the conditioning phenomena is thereby shown.
The passage beginning with “of the Chapter on Nutriment” [refers to] the fact that “dependent origination is the mode of conditions.”
This was stated for the purpose of showing [the sequence]. One should connect it by bringing forward the verbal form "arising" (*sambhavanti*) which is stated later in the text;

otherwise, it would not be understood whether the formations (*saṅkhārā*) do something or perform an action. From the perspective of the forward progression of existence, there is the discourse on dependent origination in direct order, beginning with "with ignorance as condition" (*avijjāpaccayā*).

The passage beginning with “But as for ignorance... is a reverse exposition, the inverse of that [forward sequence]. It is called *virāga* (dispassion) because by means of it one becomes utterly dispassionate toward volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
*Aseṣanirodha* means cessation without remainder, that is, eradication.
“Thus, of those ceased” means of those volitional formations that have been ceased through the cessation of non-arising. Thus, by the statement regarding the cessation of ignorance and the rest—
He speaks of arahantship. "Of the whole" means of that which is without remainder. "Devoid of a being" means devoid of a soul (jīva) as imagined by others.
"Having turned back" means having reversed [the perception] by way of showing non-arising and cessation.
"With uplifted minds" means their hearts were seized by joy and gladness; and being thus, they are said to have "gladdened minds," hence he said this.
“With joyful hearts”: regarding the phrase “his words should be rejoiced in,” the word *abhinandana* here has the sense of rejoicing (*anumodana*).
Regarding the phrase “having rejoiced,” it has the sense of acceptance (*sampaṭicchana*). However, since both senses are appropriate here, he said:
“they both rejoiced and accepted.”
The commentary on the *Paṭiccasamuppāda Sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Vibhaṅga Sutta*.
Regarding "In the second as well": this means in the second sutta; by the word "also" (*pi*), it is implied that this applies to other suttas as well. [As stated] in the *Visuddhimagga*:
Having said, “It has indeed been stated,” the passage beginning with “Just as... was spoken to show that a portion of it is suitable for application here.
“That” refers to the root text. “Detailed teaching” refers to the teaching of the *Vibhaṅga* (Analysis), which proceeds by way of demonstrating the meaning of the phrase “I shall analyze.

The teaching of the summary (*uddesa*) is exactly like the teaching in accordance with the sequence found in the first sutta. Again, [it concerns] the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its reversal (*vivaṭṭa*).
"Dassento" means showing both the process of occurrence (*pavatti*) and the process of cessation (*nivatti*) by way of the passage beginning with "Thus, monks.

First, the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*) was shown by way of a summary and by way of analysis; therefore, since the turning away from the round has already been shown by way of the method of contrast (*byatirekanaya*), it is mentioned again.

Regarding the phrase "of this and that being," this is said to be a description "in brief... pe ...by way of a generalization," because it encompasses all beings collectively without specifying any particular mode.

"By way of destiny and birth" means by way of the five destinies (*gati*), and within each of those destinies, further by way of birth such as *khattiya* and so forth, or earth-dwelling deities and so forth, or elephants and so forth. [This applies] in cases such as "mind (*citta*), intellect (*mano*)" and so on.
It is like a specific function, as in the case of "mental" (*mānasa*) and so forth; it is like a specific term for an identical meaning, as in the case of "white" (*paṇḍara*) and so forth;

it is like a specific quality, as in the case of "mental factor" (*cetasika*) and "heart" (*hadaya*) and so forth; it is like a specific state or mode of another, as in the case of "stability of consciousness" (*cittassa ṭhiti*) and so forth;
and it is like a specific state of activity of another, as in the case of "non-greed" (*alubbhanā*) and so forth.

In such cases as “non-greediness” (*alubbhitatta*), the description of individual essence (*sabhāvaniddesa*) is the illumination of the mere phenomenon (*dhammamatta*), without regard for distinctions such as the absence of something else.
As for aging, it is the mode of occurrence by way of the process of growing old; thus he says, “a description of mode” (*ākāraniddesa*).

A “description of function” (*kiccaniddesa*) refers to the time of transgression; that is, those [aging-factors] which arise at the moment when the preceding material forms reach the state of decay, starting from the stage of the *kalala*.
The "final material phenomena" arise in conformity with fully matured material phenomena, becoming increasingly transformed;
thus, at the time of maturation of those material phenomena that have become well-transformed through gradual succession, the intrinsic natures such as brokenness (*khaṇḍicca*) arise.

Therefore, "brokenness" and so forth are descriptions of the function of aging (*jarā*) when the [period of] time has elapsed. They are "descriptions of the nature" (*pakatiniddesa*), meaning they are descriptions of the nature by which the fruit undergoes ripening.
Or rather, the very fruit that is to be reached by aging is its natural state; this is the exposition of it.

Furthermore, "aging" does not consist merely of brokenness and so forth. Just as the breaking of grass and trees on paths leading through water and other places is distinct from the path itself, so too, brokenness and the like—which are found in fully developed forms that constitute the path of maturation—should be understood as the "paths traversed by aging," and not as aging itself.

Because for one who has reached old age, life-span diminishes and the faculties become worn out, the terms "diminution of life-span" and so forth are natural descriptions; therefore it is said, "the last two are natural descriptions. For this reason he says, "But by these," and so on.

It is called "uninterrupted aging" (*avīcijarā*) because its immediate succession is not clearly perceived, and because the signs of decay occurring moment by moment in gems and the like, or in each of the ten-day periods of a lifespan, are difficult to discern.
"In others than those" means in things other than gems and the like, such as mushrooms (*ahicchattaka*) and so forth.

The meaning is: among living beings, throughout an entire lifespan included within a single existence—during the stages of infancy, youth, and old age—and after the passing of one, two, or three days regarding flowers and so forth.
For in that context, because the specific distinctions of aging are easily discernible, it is called "aging with intervals" (*savīcijarā*).

"By way of the process of falling away" means by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) that are subject to falling away. It is simply the falling away through death consisting of one, four, or five aggregates.

He says, "By means of a term denoting a state, there is an indication of the characteristic," meaning that it is a demonstration of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of death, which is called "falling away" (*cuti*) in the Pāḷi.
"The arising of dissolution" (*bhaṅguppatti*) is the state of being dissolving.

By this term "dissolution" (*bhedo*), he shows that the state of the aggregates' dissolving and their possession of dissolution are expressed. It is an illumination of the absence of any station (*ṭhānābhāvaparidīpana*) by way of any mode whatsoever.
This is an illustration of the absence of persistence. The phrase "just as in the case of a jar" is a dissimilar example.

It is said "disappearance" (*antaradhāna*) to show that when the aggregates of death break up, no remnant of any kind remains, unlike a jar which, when broken, still has remnants such as shards left behind.
"Death known as death" (*maccusaṅkhātaṃ maraṇaṃ*) means death designated as "death. They call it "timely death" (*kālamaraṇa*).
The death of those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), which consists in the absolute cutting off of the continuum, is "death as cutting off" (*samucchedamaraṇa*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), momentary death (*khaṇikamaraṇa*) is included. Its "activity" (*kiriyā*) is the activity of the Ender; that which is called "Death" (*maccu*) in the world—this is the meaning of "death.
Or rather, the very time of passing away is specifically called "time" because it cannot be transcended. Of that...
In terms of its actual meaning, *kiriyā* (action) is simply the occurrence of the dissolution of the aggregates (*khandha*) at death.

Alternatively, without forming a compound here as "death is Māra" (*maccu maraṇaṃ*), one should understand the meaning in this context as follows: that which is called "Māra" is the dissolution itself, and that very dissolution is "the relinquishing of life" (*pāṇacāga*).

"By way of the fourfold existence" (*catuvokāravasena*) means by way of the fourfold existence (*catuvokārabhava*). For in that [fourfold existence], there is no physical body (*kaḷevara*) known as the form-aggregate (*rūpakāya*).

"Whatever one might cast off. Although there is no casting off of a physical carcass even in the single-aggregate existence (*ekavokāra-bhava*), the phrase "the casting off of a carcass by way of the single-aggregate existence" is stated by taking merely the presence of the material body (*rūpakāya*) therein.

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the expression "and by way of the four-aggregate existence," he shows this meaning: "the breaking up of the aggregates by way of the remaining two [existences]. This applies in all cases.

Because of the existence of the breaking up of the aggregates (*khandhabheda*). "By way of the remaining two" means that the casting off of the body occurs precisely by way of the other two states of existence (*bhava*).
Although the material body (*rūpakāya*) exists in the realm of one-aggregate beings (*ekavokārabhava*), there is no casting off of the corpse;
therefore, it is stated specifically as "because of the existence of the corpse. Since the casting off of the corpse exists among humans and others, [it is said] among humans and so forth.
The construction is: “the casting off of the body. That by which the body (*kaḷevara*) is cast off is death; thus, it is the casting off of the body.
“Having made into one” means having brought together into a single whole, merely by way of grasping them as one.
“In the sense of being born,” and so forth, refers to encompassing all sentient beings by means of two terms: by way of the bases (*āyatana*) and by way of the wombs (*yoni*).
This was said in order to show birth (*jāti*) by means of its full extent. Some, however, say that the two terms were stated according to the sense of the agent.

But because the genitive case is used for the agent in the phrase "the birth, the arising (*sañjāti*), of this and that being," the designation of the abstract state (*bhāva*) applies to both meanings as well.
Birth that is complete is "arising" (*sañjāti*). Manifest production is "manifest arising" (*abhinibbatti*). Of these...
"Of those beings... [the phrase] 'rebirth' (abhinibbatti) is a teaching by way of conventional designation because it occurs by way of beings.
In each respective case," refers to the five [factors] arising at the moment of rebirth-linking in the one- and four-aggregate existences;
and in the remaining fine-material element, to the seven, nine, or ten [factors] by way of those with deficient or complete faculties in the sense-sphere element.
Furthermore, the synthesis should be understood by way of ten and eleven bases (*āyatana*).

"In continuity" means in the continuity conditioned by that karma through which the manifestation of the aggregates occurs; this, moreover, should be understood by way of the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

Karma itself is "existence as karma" (*kammabhava*), because existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) comes into being from it. This is by way of the manifestation of a personal existence (*attabhāva*) bestowed by karma.
It is called *bhava* because it "comes to be" (*bhavati*); thus, it refers to the resultant [existence] produced in such and such a way, as well as the matter of past deeds (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).

However, in the Commentary, it is stated that "it is called *bhava* by taking the sense of 'it comes to be,'" because the existence of rebirth (*upapatti-bhava*) is what will be explained; therefore, it is said that "kamma is called *bhava* by way of a metaphorical designation for its fruit.
Sentient beings "cling" (*upādiyanti*) by means of this defiled desire, grasping with a firm grip. Here, the term is not used solely in the instrumental sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*).
Furthermore, it is said that the term may also function as an agentive noun, hence the phrase "or oneself. "That" refers to the object of desire (*vatthukāma*).
It is called *kāmupādāna* (clinging to sensual pleasures) because it is both *kāma* in the sense of desiring and *upādāna* in the sense of intense grasping. "This" refers to the word *kāmupādāna*.
Again, "this" refers to that which is designated as *kāmupādāna*.
The statement "the self is eternal" is spoken in order to show a subsequent view while adhering to a preceding one;
just as this [subsequent] view adheres to the preceding one by way of strengthening it, so too do views such as "there is no giving.
However, the inclusion of the term "self" in the phrase "clinging to the doctrine of self" (attavādupādāna) should be understood not as a demonstration of the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna).

And the phrase "the world" (loko) should be understood here as a reference distinct from the grasping of a self, which constitutes the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna), as expressed by the preceding and subsequent statements regarding views.

That wrong adherence by which one undertakes and practices such things as the cow-virtue and cow-observance is what is intended by "cow-virtue, cow-observance, etc. Therefore he said: "The cow-virtue... [etc. ...are themselves the clingings. From "abhinivesato" means "from adherence" (abhinivesanato).

“Grasping at the doctrine of self” (*attavādupādāna*) means: views that serve as the cause for the proclamation, the manifestation, or the grasping of the statement “self. “Merely the doctrine of self” means: because of the non-existence of a self, this is merely a verbal expression of “self.

“They grasp” means they seize firmly. “Occurring in the eye-door, etc. is a statement of the cause for craving’s state as craving for forms (*rūpataṇhā*), etc.; it is because the phenomena having the six doors as their objects have specific, determined objects.
“Occurring in the cognitive series” (*javanavīthi*) is a demonstration of the place where that [craving] occurs.

For one who is unable to arise by his own nature, existence—acting not as a support like a bamboo cane but through its state of clinging—is said to be similar to that [existence] because it serves as a condition for grasping;
thus it is called the "object" (ārammaṇa). In the phrase "in form" (rūpe), the locative case refers to the object.
"That is threefold" is the syntactical connection. Craving for sensual pleasure (kāmataṇhā) occurs by way of the state of relishing sensual pleasures. Thus they gratify.

Because it is associated with the eternalist view—which serves as its co-nascent, support, conjoined, presence, and non-disappearance conditions—it relishes [existence] by way of the adherence to what is permanent, stable, and eternal.
Craving accompanied by existence is "craving for existence" (*bhava-taṇhā*).

For the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) is called "existence" (*bhava*) through the elision of the latter part of the compound, meaning that which "exists" or "persists at all times"; [craving for existence] functions by way of the relishing of such existence.
In this manner, the meaning of "craving for non-existence" (*vibhavataṇhā*) should be understood here.

"Non-existence" (*vibhava*) refers to the view that occurs in the sense that "one ceases," "is cut off," or "perishes," with the elision of the latter member of the compound. Thus, those eighteen are as follows:
the six cravings for sensual pleasure, the six cravings for existence, and the six cravings for non-existence that have been mentioned; these eighteen modes of craving are the condition of craving.
“Internal” means within one’s own continuity (*santati*). “External” means outside of that.

Whether they have past objects or other [present or future] objects, there are thirty-six craving-modes (*taṇhā-vicarita*) that are themselves past. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well.
This connects with the passage beginning, “one hundred and eight craving-modes. Now, by another way as well, the one hundred and eight craving-modes [are explained].
To show this, he said, "Of the internal," and so forth. Therein, "of the internal" (*ajjhattikassa*) refers to the fivefold aggregate of the internal;
for this genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. "Having taken as basis" (*upādāya*) means having grasped. "The conceit 'I am' arises" (*asmīti hoti*):
when one grasps that same fivefold internal aggregate as a whole by way of craving, conceit, and views, there arises the conceit "I am. In that regard—
The meaning is "it exists. Here, however, the meaning should be understood by way of objects such as visible forms and so forth.
"The thought 'I am this' occurs" means that among the classes of khattiyas and so on, it occurs by way of craving, conceit, and views, thinking, "I am of such a kind.
This, first of all, is grasping without comparison.
“Such as these” means that by the word “etcetera,” the following are included: “I am thus, I am otherwise;

I shall be, I shall be such, I shall be thus, I shall be otherwise; I might be, I might exist, I might be, I might be such, I might be thus, I might be otherwise; may I not be, may I not be such, may I not be thus, may I not be otherwise.”

The inclusion of these [conceits] is expressed as "it might be otherwise. To show that grasping by comparison is also twofold—namely, from a standpoint of equality and from a standpoint of inequality—it is said: "I am thus" and "I am otherwise. Therein, "I am thus" is grasping by comparison from a standpoint of equality;
the meaning is: "Just as this khattiya is, so am I. However, "I am otherwise" is [grasping] from a standpoint of inequality.
“Grasping” means: “This khattiya is such-and-such, whereas I am different from him—either inferior or superior”; this is the meaning.
These, first of all, are the four modes of craving’s movement (taṇhāvicarita) with respect to the present. Furthermore, the four beginning with “I shall be” are stated with respect to the future;
their meaning should be understood in the same manner as that explained for the preceding tetrad. “Asasmī” means “I am eternal.”
This is a designation for the permanent. "I am" means "I am impermanent"; this is a designation for the impermanent.
Thus, these two are stated by way of eternalism and annihilationism. The four following [views], beginning with "I might be," are stated by way of speculative doubt;
they should be understood in meaning according to the method explained for the preceding tetrad. "I might not be," and so forth...

However, the four [remaining types] are stated by way of aspiration and mental construction, thinking, "May I indeed become [this]," and these too should be understood according to the method already explained for the preceding tetrad. Thus, among these:
Two have views as their head, four have purity as their head, and [the rest] have the head as their root.
One should discern these eighteen [views] as "three by three.
For these are called two heads of views, expressed by way of eternalism and annihilationism;
the four beginning with "I am," "I shall be," "I might be," and "may I not be" are called the pure heads; and the twelve beginning with "thus I am" are the heads based on the roots.
The name should be understood thus. Since craving is presented here in the text by way of visible-form objects and so forth, he says, “based on internal form and so forth.
The connection is made by supplying the phrase “the eighteen modes of craving’s wandering.

By this [thought] “I am,” through such [modes] as being anointed, a general, or a minister, one comes to have the thought “I am a khattiya” due to its being the fundamental state; the rest should be understood according to the method already explained.

“Collecting” (*saṅgaha*) refers to the act of collecting by way of condensing the craving that has been analyzed as previously stated. The exposition beginning with, “Bhikkhus, these six are groups of craving,” is the definition (*niddesa*).

The meaning of the definition beginning with, “Craving for forms is craving-for-forms,” is the detailed explanation (*niddesavitthāra*) starting with, “By way of the nature of sensual lust,” and so forth, as well as that starting with, “Having taken up the internal [bases],” and so forth.
The summary (*saṅgaha*) is that which begins with, “Only six in relation to the objects such as form,” and so forth.

Because there are indeed many feelings arising at each individual door, such as the eye-door and so forth—just like the various consciousnesses that arise at those doors—they are spoken of collectively as "the six groups of feeling" by taking them as a whole; thus he says, "aggregates of feeling.
The eye-element and so forth serve as diverse conditions by way of being the support and by way of being the doors of arising; these [doors] are contained within the belly...
Because they are as if bearing [them] and as if nourishing [them], their similarity to mothers is stated.

"Due to eye-contact" means by way of the conditions for eye-contact, such as its support (nissaya). This—namely, this feeling—is stated in a general sense as "feeling born of eye-contact," and so forth.
"In this" refers to this term "feeling. "Comprehensive" means [it includes] wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional [feelings].

By way of this [classification], it is inclusive of all. Having thus spoken generally according to the method presented in the *Vibhaṅga*, he said, "But by way of result," and so forth, in order to show specifically the feeling intended here.
"Contact in the eye" means contact arisen with the eye as its support;

the same method applies to the rest. Since the eye and the other [faculties] have been analyzed according to their characteristics and so on in the *Visuddhimagga* within the exposition of the aggregates (*khandhaniddesa*), [the text proceeds].
In the exposition of the sense-bases (āyatana), they have been analyzed by way of their specific and general meanings, as well as through the functions of seeing sounds and so forth;
therefore, he said: "That which ought to be stated... has already been stated.
"Having the characteristic of bending" means having the nature of bending toward the object, because it does not function without that [bending].
The characteristic of being subject to change (*ruppanalakkhaṇa*) has already been explained above. As for the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), it is simply feeling itself.

The five sense-consciousnesses (*pañcaviññāṇa*) are indeed called the weakest of all minds. One might ask: "Are there not also moments of life-sustaining consciousness (*jīvitacittaṭṭhiti*) therein? True;

however, their function is not as manifest as that of volition (*cetanā*) and the other mental factors. Therefore, only those [factors] are extracted here in the text. By means of which [factor], such as the great manifestation and so forth...

"By way of cause. "In this" means in this exposition of the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*). "Another method of analysis" means another method of analysis than the determination of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth by way of "the meaning of the words" and "the group" (*kalāpa*), etc.
[Objection: But was that not already stated in the *Catudhātuvavatthāna* (The Determination of the Four Elements), and not in the exposition of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*)?

[Response: Even though it was stated there, because it is stated here by way of extension (*atidesa*) as "stated in the *Catudhātuvavatthāna*," it is included in the exposition of the aggregate of form.

It is said: "It has been stated. "Dependent upon" (*upādāya*) means "in reliance upon" (*paṭicca*). For derived matter (*upādārūpa*), which arises in dependence upon the primary elements (*bhūtāni*), is said to be "having taken them," because it does not exist apart from them.
Some also say "supported by" (*nissāya*), because of its status as a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*). He explains the meaning by supplying the remainder of the text:
"An action occurring at a prior time is necessarily in relation to an action occurring at a subsequent time. [This is done] by means of a transposition of case-endings (*vibhatti-vipallāsa*).
In order to show the meaning even without [explicitly stating] "the aggregate," the phrase "or in the sense of an aggregate" (*samūhatthe vā*) and so forth was stated.

Since the sense of an aggregate is indicated by the designation of the owner (*sāminiddesa*) in relation to the aggregate, he said "having taken the aggregate" (*samūhaṃ upādāya*) to demonstrate that. It is stated as "twenty-three-fold" according to the method found in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*;
for there, the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) is not specifically mentioned in the formula "that matter depending on which... (*yaṃ rūpaṃ nissāya*).

Or, because it is included in the *Paṭṭhāna*, the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*) is also taken; having combined the accumulative and continuative [materiality] with the materiality of birth, it is stated as "twenty-threefold.

Or, "consciousness of the eye" (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) means consciousness belonging to the eye. This designation is made by way of the specific cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*). "With volitional formations as condition... [and so forth].

Regarding the phrase "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*), since all worldly resultant consciousness (*vipākaviññāṇa*) is to be included here, it is stated that "this is a designation for the resultant mind of the three planes.

"Characterized by volitional formation" (*abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇo*) means having the nature of accumulation (*āyūhanasabhāvo*). "By way of impelling" (*copanavasena*) means by way of the impelling of intimation (*viññatti*).
The meaning is: "by way of originating bodily intimation. "By way of verbal differentiation" means by way of the arising of verbal differentiation;
the meaning is: "by way of originating verbal intimation. To show that there would be no such instigation (*copana*) [in this case], it is said:
"of one sitting in secret and reflecting. Regarding the number "twenty-nine," here only those excluding the volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*) amount to twenty-nine.
Volition (cetanā) should be understood [as suffering] because it lacks the status of being a condition for that resultant consciousness (vipākaviññāṇa).

Regarding the term "dukkha," even this single locative expression undergoes a specific application by dividing itself according to its functions as a conjunction, a support, an object, and a pervader;
thus, it is said, "by four reasons," and so forth. For even a single grammatical case-indication (vibhattiniddesa) [can have multiple meanings].
It undergoes manifold application, as in the case of the *taddhita* suffixes and the formation of compound words (*uttarapada-samāhāra*). "That" refers to ignorance.

"The truth of suffering" refers to the truth of suffering characterized by the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). "Of that" means of ignorance. "By way of being a support-condition" means by way of being a pre-arisen support-condition (*purejāta-nissaya-paccaya*);
however, by way of being a co-arisen support-condition (*sahajāta-nissaya-paccaya*), the contact and other factors co-arising with it [are meant].
It should be stated thus. The construction is: "The truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) is its object" by way of being the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya).
"Dukkhasacca" is the singular accusative case. "Etam" refers to ignorance (aññāṇa). "Tassa" refers to the truth of suffering.

To show the mode of concealment mentioned here in the word "paṭicchādeti" (it conceals), the phrase beginning with "yāthāvato" (as it really is) was stated. [This occurs] even by means of a consciousness dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta-citta).

They say that because penetration of the characteristics as they truly are occurs even by way of a single part, it was stated, "by way of obstructing the penetration of the characteristics as they truly are," and then added, "and by not granting the occurrence of knowledge herein.

However, the former is shown as a statement prohibiting the arising of penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*), while the latter refers to the arising of subsequent knowledge (*anubodha-ñāṇa*). Thus should the meaning here be understood.
"Herein" means in the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
It is said "by way of basis" because the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*) serves as the basis for co-nascent ignorance by way of being its supporting condition (*nissayapaccaya*).
"By way of object" means by way of being its objective condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), since the truth of origination is the object of ignorance.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is stated as "ignorance regarding the origin of suffering.

The concealment [of the truth] is exactly as explained in the case of the truth of suffering, because for the other three truths it is impossible for the same reason. But what is that single reason? He says:
"because of concealment" (*paṭicchādanato*). To explain this in detail, he says: "Of cessation and the way leading thereto," and so forth. *Tadārabbhā* means "starting from that."
"Having taken that as the object" means having made that the focal point. For the "last two truths" are cessation and the path.

Because they are profound in their method, they are "difficult to see"—that is, because they consist of subtle and delicate phenomena, and by virtue of their inherent profundity, they are difficult to see, difficult to understand, and difficult to grasp.
"Therein" refers to the first two truths. "Become blind" means become like darkness; [the knowledge] does not proceed with respect to that object.

It is not able to do so. "By way of being expressible" means by way of its state as a designator, because it appears in that manner. "Because the characteristic of intrinsic nature is difficult to see":

since the characteristic of intrinsic nature—namely, "this is suffering" and "this is the origin"—is difficult to see and difficult to discern according to its true mode through the aspects of oppression and so forth, or accumulation and so forth, the first two [truths] are profound. "Therein" refers to the first two truths.
"It occurs by way of seizing through perversion" means that ignorance occurs by way of being the condition for the seizing of the opposite of beauty and so forth.
Now, in order to show the meaning of "ignorance regarding suffering" and so on by another method, the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apicā*) was stated.
Therein, "to this extent regarding suffering" means by the phrase "ignorance is said to be [present] regarding suffering. "By way of inclusion" (*saṅgahato*)...
"From the standpoint of convergence. "From the standpoint of function" means from the standpoint of the function of non-penetration.
"As if it were ignorance" means as if its function were to fail to provide penetration of the true nature of the object as it really is.

Having considered that by the words "regarding suffering," etc., ignorance is shown there in a specific sense, [the author] now shows this to be a demonstration of its undifferentiated nature in all respects.
The passage beginning with “But without distinction,” etc., is stated.

Since momentary cessation is not intended here, and because it would be inappropriate [in this context] and because of the mention of fading away (*virāga*), what is intended here as “cessation” is the warding off of ignorance and the rest by means of their opposites; and that is simply their absolute non-arising.
He said: "Cessation occurs; non-arising occurs. "Ignorance ceases herein, thus it is the cessation of ignorance;
formations cease herein, thus it is the cessation of formations"—thus it should be understood that Nibbāna is taught by all these terms for cessation.
Therefore he said, "Nibbāna indeed," and so forth. "The cycle and the turning away from the cycle" means both the cycle (*vaṭṭa*) and the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*).

“By twelve”: this should be applied individually, meaning “here the round [of existence] is shown by twelve terms in forward order, and the turning away from the round by twelve terms in reverse order.
The commentary on the Vibhaṅga Sutta is finished.

3. Commentary on the *Paṭipadāsutta* One proceeds wrongly by means of this, thus it is the "wrong way of practice" (*micchāpaṭipadā*). It is the path leading to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), because it brings about suffering.
That is the wrong way of practice. Therefore he said: "the way of practice that does not lead out. How is that formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) a wrong way of practice?

The intention is that it brings happiness in the state of prosperity (*sampattibhava*). "The pinnacle of the round" (*vaṭṭasīsa*) means because it is the supreme limb among those belonging to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"At least" (*antamaso*) is said with reference to the upper limit, not the lower limit.
It was performed having aspired for Nibbāna, thinking: "May this merit of mine be a condition for the attainment of Nibbāna. "Merely the gift of a handful of leaves" (*paṇṇamuṭṭhidānamatta*)...
It is merely the gift of a handful of vegetables and leaves. "Without having reached" (*appattā*) is an expression that includes the cause within it; the meaning is "without having brought about.
Alternatively, just as one is said to have "reached" (*patta*) Arahantship by virtue of practicing [the path], so too the practice (*paṭipadā*) that brings about that [fruit] is called "reached";
thus it is said "without having reached. "By way of conformity" (*anulomavasena*) means by way of the conformable dependent origination (*anuloma-paṭiccasamuppāda*).

"In the reverse order" (paṭilomavasena): here too, the same method applies. By the phrase "the way [of practice] was asked about," the sense that the teaching on the way has been commenced is also included;
for the inquiry arises here out of a desire to explain the meaning of what has already been begun.
Even in the teaching on dependent origination in direct order, it is by way of contrast that [it is shown]: "But through the cessation of ignorance, etc., there is knowledge..."

When there is [craving], there is the non-arising of volitional formations; thus it is said, "Nirvana has been apportioned. However, by its very nature, it is the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) itself that is revealed.
For he will say at the conclusion: "Only the round and its unraveling have been explained.
By "the fruit" means because the path, which is the cause for attaining it, has been shown along with the fruit to be attained. Just as...
For there are three kinds of causes: the indicative, the productive, and the accomplishing; likewise, there are three kinds of fruits:

that which is to be indicated, that which is to be produced, and that which is to be accomplished. Therefore, the meaning is: because the path, which serves as the cause for accomplishing it, has been shown by means of *nibbāna*, the fruit to be attained. Hence he said, "By the fruit below," and so forth. This is called... thus.

This "right practice" is said to have Nibbāna as its fruit. The phrases "without remainder of fading away" and "without remainder of cessation" refer to the complete fading away and the complete cessation of ignorance by way of its utter eradication;

with these two terms, he speaks specifically of non-arising cessation, for that indeed is Nibbāna. In the second interpretation, this is the intended meaning: by means of which path acting as the instrument...
"It is the complete cessation of ignorance; it is to show that path by depending upon which the complete cessation of ignorance occurs. "If this were so" means:
if the meaning of the term *nibbāna* were present in this word-analysis (*padabhājana*). "The practice with its power is analyzed" means:

the practice which is the cause for the complete cessation of ignorance is "with its power" (*sānubhāvā*) because of its association with an especially eminent efficacy (*sātisaya-sāmatthiya*) therein.

It is analyzed. Because the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is also analyzed here by means of the inclusion of the wrong way of practice (*micchāpaṭipadā*), it is said: "The round and the unrounding have been explained.
The commentary on the *Paṭipadā-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Vipassī-sutta*.
4. "Vipphandanti" means by way of blinking. "Animisehi" means with eyes that are free from blinking, [eyes] that are simply open.
Therefore it was said in the *Mahāpadāna*: "In this"—that is, in this word "Vipassī," or in this Sutta passage as it has come down beginning with "with unblinking eyes.
The reason for the Great Being’s acquisition of the name "Vipassī" due to his unblinking eyes has been stated; that...
Regarding the objection that the state of having unblinking eyes is not the sole reason for other Great Beings (mahāsatta) in their final existence, the text says "And here...
and so forth; then, in order to show another reason, it says "Moreover... and so forth. *Palāḷayamānassa* means "of one who is pleasing.
This genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used in the sense of disregard. *Aṭṭassa* means "of the meaning."

Because he possesses (*atthi*) a portion (*bhaga*)—consisting of accumulated merit (*puññussaya*)—in an eminent degree, he is called the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*); thus it is said, “one endowed with fortune.

Regarding the word *sammā*, it means “properly,” that is, according to reality (*yāthāvato*), by way of method (*ñāyena*), or by reason (*kāraṇena*); thus he says, “by way (*nayena*) and by cause (*hetunā*).

The prefix *sam-* has the same meaning as *sāma-*, so he says, “personally (*sāmaṃ*), by one’s own individual effort (*paccattapurisakārena*), [that is,] by self-enlightened knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇena*).”
