The meaning is as follows: It is called *sambodha* (awakening) because one perfectly awakens by means of it; that is, path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*). By taking the sense "one awakens by means of this," the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) is also included here.
A being possessing awakening is a *bodhisatta*; this is a case of eliding the latter member of the compound, as in the term *sākapatthava*.
Here, [the term] "awakening being" (*bujjhanaka-satta*) refers to one who awakens by means of the practice of the Great Vehicle of Awakening (*mahābodhi-yāna*).
Because he possesses a distinction among beings and is a being, he is called a *bodhisatta*. He proceeds while aspiring, meaning he practices having conceived the desire:
"When indeed shall I attain great enlightenment? Suffering (*dukkha*) is suffering rooted in birth and the rest.
Granted that falling away and rebirth are also death and birth; yet, after stating "is born, dies," [the text] says "falls away, is reborn."

This statement is not intended to include those comprised within a single existence (*ekabhavapariyāpanna*), but rather to show that there is a collective inclusion of those comprised within various existences (*nānābhavapariyāpanna*);
thus he said, "This... was said. "Its escape" means it is called the escape from that aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Since the Great Being went forth after seeing the aged, the sick, and the dead, therefore aging and death alone appeared to him first.
"By means of wise attention" (*upāya-manasikārena*) means that attention proceeds by way of skillful means, method, principle, and path.

"There was a conjunction" (*samāyogo ahosi*) means there was a coming together through the mode of penetrating reality as it truly is. Regarding "wise attention" (*yoniso manasikāra*), the ablative case is used in the sense of a cause;
thus he spoke with the instrumental case in the phrase "by means of wise attention" to express that cause.
When there is birth, there is aging-and-death. As the Bodhisatta was investigating the cause of aging-and-death—thinking, "Now, when what exists does aging-and-death come to be?
With what as condition does aging-and-death arise?"—he grasped the reason for aging-and-death by means of an unerring investigation into the causal relationship of birth, [realizing]:
"That which, when it exists, something else comes to be, and when it is absent, that other does not come to be—that is the cause of the latter. Thus, with respect to birth...
"When there is birth, aging-and-death comes to be; with birth as condition, aging-and-death":
the meaning is that when the wisdom which grasps the cause of aging-and-death arose, through its arising, there was for him the "clear comprehension" (*abhisamaya*), which is to say, penetration.
"Iti" is a reference to the manner already described. "Hi" is a mere particle. "Idaṃ" refers to the round [of existence] (*vaṭṭa*) as it has been stated, directly before one's eyes.
[This is] a grasping. Therefore he said, "Thus this. Here, because the origin of ignorance has been presented, it is stated as "in eleven instances.
"Having condensed the origin" means having taken the origin of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth together.
Since knowledge proceeds by way of seeing the origin many times, there is the reduplicated expression "origin, origin. Now...
Or rather, the statement "thus there is an origination" (evam samudayo hoti) is not merely intended to show the process of arising;
for here, just as with the term *paṭiccasamuppāda*, the word "origination" (*samudaya*) refers to the state of being a condition by way of origination.
And as many conditioning factors as have been specified here, such as consciousness and the rest, they are [treated] in their general form according to the desire for detailed analysis.
While grasping it, he said, "The origin, the origin. Therefore he said: "With ignorance as condition, there is the origin of volitional formations.
In the sense of seeing, it is the eye; the state of directly seeing the origin is the eye. In the sense of being known means by way of its state of being known.
In the sense of understanding means: "Through this occurrence of various conditioned phenomena, beginning with ignorance and volitional formations..."
"Or it is [the knowledge] in the sense of knowing by way of the prefix *pa-* as "the origin of the mass of suffering. In the sense of penetration (*paṭivedhana*):
in the sense of penetrating that "this condition-dhamma, beginning with ignorance, is the origin because of its state of being a condition for this [result], beginning with volitional formations.
In the sense of illumination (*obhāsana*): by way of dispelling the darkness of delusion and the darkness of defilements which conceal the state of being the origin.
By way of illumination. This knowledge, moreover, is that which was stated by the words "the eye," and so forth.

In the section on cessation—that is, in the reverse order—for it has come down in the manner of proclaiming cessation, beginning with: "Through the cessation of what does the cessation of aging-and-death occur?
The commentary on the Vipassī Sutta is finished.
5–10. Commentary on the *Sikhīsutta* and others.
“Without connecting it in this way”: this means not connecting it by way of conjunction (samuccaya) with the words beginning “of Sikhī as well.
He states the reason for this with the words beginning “Why? To make the aforementioned point clear, he says: “Because it was not taught in a single sitting; [rather,] in various places...”
"‘Hī’ and so forth was said. Even though those [qualities] were taught as being stated individually, their commentary (*atthavaṇṇanā*) is identical, because their meaning is not different.
The construction is: "No one else declares that ‘the Buddhas are born.
For there is no need for the Great Bodhisattvas in their final existence to rely on the instruction of another. "By the very path already traversed..."
It is the natural law (*dhammatā*) that subsequent Great Bodhisattvas proceed by the very path traversed through the practice of the way.

"They proceed" means that with minds established in the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), they proceed by way of awakening to perfect enlightenment after having developed the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) according to reality. As for their initial application of insight (*vipassanābhinivesa*):

In order to demonstrate that [it is not only the Buddha], it is said: "All Bodhisattvas," and so forth. *Buddhavipassanā* refers to the insight leading to Buddhahood, or insight for the sake of Buddhahood.
The commentary on the *Sikhīsutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Buddhavagga is finished.
2. The Chapter on Nutriment (Āhāravagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Nutriment (Āhārasutta).
11. “They bring” means they lead forth, they cause to arise; the meaning is that they support. “Born” (nibbattā) means those who have been delivered.

They are called “beings” (bhūtā) because from that point onward there is the worldly convention of being “born. However, from the moment of seizing rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) until the time of emerging from the mother’s womb, they are “seekers of existence” (sambhavesino).
This, then, is the distinction between “beings” and “seekers of existence” regarding those in the womb; as for others...

However, it is stated by way of the first moment of consciousness and so forth. Here, the word *sambhava* (arising) signifies birth for those born from a womb, while for others it signifies origination.

For at the moments of the first consciousness and the first posture, they are said to "seek" (*esanti*) or "approach" (*upagacchanti*) arising—that is, origination—because they have not yet become [fully] beings due to their lack of firm establishment in rebirth.
They have indeed become [extinguished] because all craving for existence has been utterly cut off. By the restrictive phrase "they will not exist again," he shows the meaning that has been excluded.
Furthermore, in such expressions as "one who has become a consumer of time" (*kālaghaso bhūto*), the word *bhūta* should be understood as referring to one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
And here, the particle *vā* has the sense of conjunction, as in "by fire or by water."
With the intention that the assistance to be provided by the nutriments here consists simply in the maintenance of the individual existence through their respective conditions, he said:
"The difference in expression... [is] only one. "Of the phenomena arisen in a being" means of the phenomena arisen in the continuum of a being.
Just as when it is said, "He remains for a hundred years," [it refers to] by way of continuous succession.
"It occurs" is what is meant; thus, "for the sake of stability" means for the sake of occurrence by way of continuous succession.

Furthermore, because that [stability] is non-interruption, he said "for the sake of non-interruption. Since the continuity of beings is said to be "assisted" through the arising of phenomena in continuous succession, he said "for the arising of the unarisen. These are the terms "stability" and "assistance. In both cases...
These are not to be understood according to their literal connection.
Since the nutritive essence (*ojā*) residing in the physical basis (*vatthu*) goes along with that basis into the state of being swallowed, it is said, "edible food is that which is swallowed.
However, with reference to the nutritive essence that has been produced, it is said, "edible food brings in the material qualities consisting of the eightfold nutritive essence."
It will be explained. Coarseness (*oḷārikatā*) refers to the lack of nutritive essence (*ojā*), not to the bulkiness or hardness of the physical object;
therefore, that object in which the nutritive essence is slight is "coarse. Snakes and other such creatures should be understood as coarse because they produce suffering.
They say that the horns and so forth, when discarded after three years and having become putrid, are "soft" because they have been softened by the saliva of hyenas.
But for those who have become thus, there is softness; for this is the very nature of things (*dhammasabhāva*). The food of snakes is subtle because they consume tender grass and crops.
The food of birds is subtle because they consume seeds of grass and so forth. The food of border-dwellers is subtle because their diet consists of meat, mung beans, radishes, and the like.
"Of them" refers to the Paranimmitavasavatti devas. "It is indeed subtle" means that it is subtle in and of itself, and not merely in comparison to something else.
He has reached the ultimate because of the absence of anything more subtle than that.
However, the grossness and subtlety of nutriment here have been stated by way of its physical basis;
in order to show that this should be understood through its moisture, heat, and lightness, he said, "And here," and so forth. "Parissaya" refers to the affliction arising from hunger.
"Disperses bodily distress": this means it performs the mere act of dispersing that [distress].
"But it cannot sustain" means it is not capable of maintaining the body because it is devoid of nutritive essence (*ojā*). "It cannot dispel danger" because it does not fill the stomach.
By the phrase "even the sixfold," he indicates that no contact whatsoever is to be left out. Here, the sequence of contact and so forth follows the order of the teaching itself.
"It is because it is a second [instance] and so forth, not for any other reason," thus he said, "And this is simply the method of teaching," and so on.

The mention of "mind" (mano) is for the purpose of showing that volition belongs to the mind and not to a "being" (satta), as in the expressions "stability of mind" (cittassa ṭhiti) and "liberation of mind" (cetovimutti);

hence he said, "mental volition (manosañcetanā) means volition (cetanā). "Mind" (citta) refers to any kind of consciousness whatsoever. "Having made into a single heap" means having brought together into one place.

The meaning is that they were taken collectively without making a distinction. In that context, the statement beginning with “edible food” was said in order to show the distinctions among those things that are obtainable, such as *upādiṇṇaka* (clung-to) and so forth. They do not accomplish the purpose of nutriment because such nutriment is not being brought in.
“Even then” means even at the time when it has been broken down and has disappeared. Some say that [the elements] are called “nutriment that is clung-to. This...
However, this is not accepted by some teachers because, at that time, there is an absence of even derived materiality (*upādinnaka-rūpa*).

The statement "arising simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness" is merely a definition; its purpose is to demonstrate the existence, uninterrupted occurrence, and arising of the nutritive essence (*ojā*) included within all kamma-born materiality.
"Up to the seventh day" means from the day of birth until the seventh day.
It protects the continuity of material form by way of maintaining the lineage. "This very [nutriment]" refers to the nutriment born of kamma.

However, the nutriment that arises dependent upon the nutriment born of kamma is to be understood as "nutriment not grasped at" (anupādiṇṇa-āhāra) because it is not itself born of kamma. The connection is made by supplying the words: "the contact and so forth that are not grasped at are to be understood.
To the question, "How are the supramundane contact and so forth explained? he says: "But the supramundane ones are spoken of by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī)."

Since there is no way of speaking of those wholesome states as "clung-to" (*upeta*), it should be understood that the way of speaking of their results as "clung-to" (*upādiṇṇa*) does not exist either;
thus, the expression "not clung-to" (*anupādiṇṇa*) is also stated by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*).
Since it was previously stated that "nutriments are conditions," if one objects by saying, "If the meaning of nutriment is the meaning of condition," and so forth, then...
"Why are only these four stated?"—this means: "Why are only four stated? And why are these very ones stated? This is the construction.

Regarding the phrase "because they are specific conditions": by this it is shown that while other conditioning phenomena (*paccaya-dhamma*) function solely as conditions for their own conditionally arisen effects, these [four], however, function both in that way and otherwise; thus, although their status as conditions is equal, they are "additional" or "specific" conditions.
Therefore, this shows the meaning of the phrase “they are called ‘nutriments’. Now, in order to show that they are superior conditions, it is said:
“For they are specific conditions,” and so forth. The physical nutriment (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) is a specific condition for the material body because of its state of providing support.
Thus, it is said in the Commentary: “The four nutriments are the nutriment-condition by way of being beneficial through their state of supporting both the material and the immaterial.”
For even though mindfulness possesses the quality of being a producer, it belongs to the immaterial nutriments and to the nutriment that produces the materiality born of nutriment;
however, in the absence of the quality of support, the nutriments lack the quality of production. Thus, the quality of support is primary.
For even while producing, a nutriment produces only by way of supporting through non-interruption; therefore, the state of being a supporter is [the essential factor].
Such is the nature of nutriment. Contact is the specific condition for feeling, for it is said: "With contact as condition, there is feeling.
From the statement "with volitional formations as condition, consciousness," mental volition is the condition for consciousness, for it is said: "Volition produces threefold existence.
And from the statement "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form," [mental volition is the condition] for name-and-form.
Consciousness is the specific condition. For in the absence of the consciousness that enters [the womb], there is no possibility for the existence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). As it is said:
"If, Ānanda, consciousness were not to descend into the mother’s womb, would name-and-form coagulate in the mother’s womb?
and so forth. The phrase "as it is said" (*yathāha*) and so on was stated in order to establish this very point by means of the Sutta.
Thus, although the meaning of "condition" (*paccaya*) is the same as the meaning of "nutriment" (*āhāra*), these alone are called "nutriments" because they are specific conditions;
having shown their status as specific conditions without distinction, [the text] now begins with the words "But what here... in order to show them by way of distinction.
Even when merely placed in the mouth and not yet chewed, by that much alone [it serves] for the nutriment of the interior.
It is indeed a condition. Therefore he said: "It arouses eight kinds of material phenomena. "Favorable to pleasant feeling" means conducive to pleasant feeling.

"In every way" means by way of eye-contact and so forth. According to however many varieties of contact there are, in all those modes, the nutriment of contact brings about the three feelings as appropriate; there is no mode that does not provide nutriment.

"In all cases" (*sabbathāpi*): here too, the meaning should be understood according to the method explained regarding the nutriment of contact (*phassāhāra*). "By way of the threefold continuity" (*tisantativasena*):

by way of the threefold continuity consisting of the body-decad (*kāyadasaka*), the state-decad (*bhāvadasaka*), and the base-decad (*vatthudasaka*). "By way of the method of co-nascent and other conditions" (*sahajātādipaccayanayena*): by the system of co-nascent and other types of conditions.

For rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*) [acts] as a condition for the name (*nāma*) co-nascent with itself through the conditions of co-nascence, mutuality, result, faculty, association, presence, and non-disappearance.

It is said that "it consumes that" precisely because it is a condition by way of being a nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*). However, regarding co-nascent material phenomena (*sahajata-rūpa*), one should apply the analysis by way of other conditions, setting aside the basis-condition (*vatthu-paccaya*) for the physical base and the dissociation-condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*) for the remaining material phenomena, while also setting aside the mutuality-condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*) for those others.
The use of the neuter demonstrative "tāni" is an elliptical expression that includes non-neuter terms as well.

[The term "nutriment" (*āhāra*) is used] because it is spoken of together with neuter [terms]. Only wholesome and unwholesome volitions associated with the taints (*sāsava*) are mentioned here, as this is intended to show their status as specific conditions;

therefore, he said, "But without distinction," and so forth. The same principle applies here as well regarding the statement that "only rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) is mentioned.
Just as these possess the sense of nutriment due to being specific conditions for their respective fruits, so too do they have that sense without distinction.
In order to show this, the phrase beginning with "without distinction" (avisesena) was stated.
Therein, "of those phenomena associated with them and originated by them" means both of those phenomena associated with contact and so forth, as well as of the material phenomena originated by them.
In that context, the inclusion of "associated" should be understood according to what is appropriate, whereas the inclusion of "originated" is without such distinction.

"Supporting, it accomplishes the function of nutriment": thus, while supporting, it produces matter; indeed, its accomplishment of the function of support is achieved solely through the production of the "nutriment-octad.
"Only while touching": performing the very function of touching. "While exerting themselves":
only while intending and only while striving. "Only while cognizing": only while cognizing by way of conceiving rebirth.

The construction is: "It accomplishes the function of nutriment. And in all cases, the accomplishment of the function of nutriment consists precisely in the continued occurrence of the personal existence (attabhāva) by way of being the cause for the arising of feeling and so forth.
Regarding the question, "Why was it said 'by means of establishing the body'?", he says, "Even though produced by kamma," and so on, in response to the objection:
"Is it not the case that matter born of kamma and so forth occurs solely through kamma and the like?"

Since the maintenance of the temperature-born and mind-born material continuities is accomplished precisely through the support of the appropriated material continuity, it is said, "of the two material continuities.
And with reference specifically to this support, it is said, "acting as a protector.

For maintenance (*yāpanā*) and protection (*anupālanā*) consist in being the cause for the persistence of the material body. "Serving as the basis for pleasure and so forth" means [the basis] of pleasure and so on.
It is that which serves as the locus of occurrence. For even an object (*ārammaṇa*) is called a "basis" (*vatthu*) because consciousness dwells therein by way of making it its object;
thus they are called "states with that as their object. The phrase "only while touching" is said because contact has the intrinsic nature of touching.
Indeed, there is no occurrence of mental states apart from their own intrinsic nature, and for sentient beings, there is no wandering about without the occurrence of feeling.

He said, "There is no [existence]," [concluding] with "there is pleasant feeling, etc. And here, in this discussion of non-percipient existence (*asaññībhava*), non-percipient existence itself need not be demonstrated;
for even that [non-percipient existence] exists only by way of the occurrence of feeling which serves as its cause, and thus the reason for its persistence is not all-pervasive.
For it has been stated: "Mental volition (*manosañcetanā*)... leads to the persistence of beings by way of producing the root of existence. Precisely for that reason—
"Consciousness cognizes only" means that it is said to "cognize only" by way of conceiving [itself as] reborn.
The four fears should be seen through the discernment of their danger (*ādīnava*). "Craving" (*nikanti*) means longing; he speaks with reference to craving for flavor (*rasataṇhā*).
For that [craving] is powerful regarding edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*); therefore, a restriction is made here. "One fears because of this" means...

Fear is indeed attachment, because it is the cause of great harm. "Approaching" refers to the occurrence of the sense faculties, objects, and consciousnesses, and of the objects and consciousnesses, by way of association;
that is called "fear" because it is the cause for the arising of feeling and the other [mental factors].

The purpose of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is exactly as stated in the previous method. This same method applies to the remaining two [terms] as well. "Exertion" (*āyūhana*) means connecting together, or arranging.

They say this. It is called "fear" because it is the cause for the arising of existence (*bhava*). "Impact" (*abhinipāta*) is the production of consciousness by way of seizing rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in various states of existence.
That is called "fear" because it is the root cause of all misfortunes that have the arising of existence as their cause.
Now, [the text proceeds] to explain in detail the fearful nature of attachment (*nikanti*) and so forth.

The passage beginning with “For what reason? is commenced in order to demonstrate this. Therein, “having formed an attachment” means having produced a settling (ālaya), which is to say, having generated craving (taṇhā).
“Preceded by cold and so forth” means standing before cold and so forth; the meaning is that one is being afflicted by cold and so forth.
“Approaching contact” means causing the occurrence of contact divided into eye-contact and the rest. “Delighting in contact” means...
They have the nature of relishing that which is reckoned as the tangible by way of body-contact.

Indeed, in order to show that craving for the tangible arises in beings by way of body-contact, the object of tangibles was singled out in the demonstration of the danger of the nutriment of contact, beginning with the words, "in those things protected and guarded by others," and so forth.
Alternatively, *phassassādino* means "those who relish contact," that is to say, "those who relish the nutriment of contact."

For when there is contact as nutriment, there is gratification for beings in the object of that contact, but not when it is absent; therefore he said, "rooted in the gratification of contact," and so forth.
It is called "rooted in that" because fear regarding the sign of birth is grasped by way of its nature as an impact;
the meaning is that it is the sign for the accumulation of kamma. All fear—namely, the twenty-five kinds, the three great fears, and whatever other fears exist—is indeed included.
It exists because it brings about a personal existence (attabhāva) characterized by fear.
"Abhinipatati" means "is produced" (abhinibbattati). For the first production of beings in various existences that resemble pits of glowing coals is similar to a falling down.
"Because it is rooted in that" means because it is rooted in the production of name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Indeed, the very falling [into suffering] is the root of all fears.
It is called *bhaya* because one fears it.
It is as if it were handing over the cause, for the fruit approaches as if by way of its own acquisition; thus, it is like a cause. "That" refers to the fruit.
"From that" means from the cause. "Of these" refers to the nutriments (*āhāra*). "In the manner described" refers to the mode of expression stated in the passage beginning with "the fruit indicates."
"By way of meaning. "In all instances" means in all the phrases such as "by the cessation of feeling," and so forth.

"Beginning with rebirth-linking" means taking the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) as the starting point. With reference to the types of nutriment that are clung-to (*upādiṇṇaka*), it is said:
"of the nutriments comprised within the personal existence (*attabhāva*). For these, in the primary sense, have craving as their source. [This refers to] beings whose sense bases are complete.

"By way of the continuity of beings" means by way of the seven continuities of those possessing complete sense bases and normal faculties—namely, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, existence, and physical basis.
"Of the rest," meaning those with incomplete sense bases who are blind, deaf, or lacking normal faculties.
"By way of deficient continuities" means by way of the deficiency of the eye, the ear, both together, or the lack of existence.

“Born at rebirth” means born at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in the phrase “the first moment of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*), etc.,” the inclusion of the object-receiving consciousness (*tadārammaṇa-citta*) should be understood.
The construction is: “he knows the cause even of craving. There is also a reading: *taṇhānidānaṃ pi*.

Having shown the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*)—that is, having shown the entire round both in its specific form and by way of its underlying method—he now explains that matter in detail: “In this [round]...”
He said, “But in this place,” and so forth. “Having given a teaching directed toward the past” means:
having given a teaching concerning objects of the past, starting from the present existence, by means of that manner [of instruction]. “He shows the round of existence by means of the past” means:
he shows the round of kamma, defilements, and kamma-result by means of past existence. “Selfhood” (attabhāva) refers to the present selfhood.
If this is so, why is it said that "the round is shown by means of the past"? This is not a fault, because the phrase "by the past alone" (*atīteneva*) is not intended as a restrictive definition.

By taking it in this way, the grasping directed toward the past includes the productive karma; for craving is taken under the heading of "craving" (*taṇhā*), since it does not exist without the state of immediate succession (*ānantariya-bhāva*).
Indeed, craving cannot logically be the conduit to existence (*bhava-nettī*) without karma.
"Taṃ kammaṃ" (that karma) refers to the karma spoken of under the heading of craving (*taṇhā*). "Dassetuṃ" (to show) means to show that past personal existence (*attabhāva*).
"Tassattabhāvassa janakaṃ kammaṃ" (the karma that produces that personal existence) means the karma that produces the aforementioned personal existence.
Furthermore, it is stated in order to show the karma accumulated for subsequent personal existences as well. And ignorance (*avijjā*), like craving, is indeed a form of karma.
It is the grasping of karma alone. "In two places" means in two instances: by the grasping of nutriment and by the grasping of feeling and so forth.

"Individual existence" (attabhāva) refers to both present-time and past-time individual existence. Again, "in two" means in two instances: by the grasping of craving and by the grasping of ignorance and volitional formations (saṅkhāra).
"Its producer" refers to that which produces both the present and the past [existence].
And the construction is: "the karma that produces the individual existence (attabhāva) has been stated.

By the mention of "karma" here, that past birth in which that karma was accumulated is shown by way of its actual meaning. By this, he illustrates the beginninglessness of the cycle of existence (saṃsāravaṭṭa).
As for "in brief": even the inclusion of the five causes and five fruits is indeed a summary.
Because the phenomena to be included by way of the relation of cause and fruit are of many kinds.
If the round of existence has been shown by means of the past, then, showing that in such a case the teaching on the factors of dependent origination would be partial, he said, "In this regard...
and so forth. Therefore, even though the round of existence has not been shown here in its own form by means of the future, [it is nonetheless shown].
However, because it is shown even for that [person] by way of direction, he shows that the teaching on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is indeed complete in its scope.

Now, in order to clarify this meaning by means of a simile, the passage beginning with "Just as" (*yathā hi*) was stated. "Lying on the surface of the water" means lying upon the water by way of floating.
"The further part" (*parabhāga*) means the highest or uppermost part. "From this side" (*orato*) means from the other, lower part.
"Looking at it. "Incomplete" means having deficient parts. The passage beginning with "Possessed of such [qualities]" and so forth is a correlation with the simile.

For just as the neck is the root location for the tendons that support the body, so too craving is the root of the formations that support the personal existence (*attabhāva*); thus it is said, "the time when [it] was seen on the neck. Just as [the body] is a collection of many parts such as feeling and so forth...
The personal body (*attabhāva*) is thus called "the back" because it is a collection of many parts such as the ribs and vertebrae;
therefore it is said: "the time when his back was seen... [and so on]... the time when that was seen. "Designated by craving" means described by craving.
Here, in this teaching, ignorance and formations should be understood as the conditions; therefore it is said: "like the time when the base of the tail was seen. For it is thus:
At the conclusion, the simile “one would see the base of the tail” is presented. This should be understood as grasping the state of completeness by way of the method (*naya*).
Although the cycle of conditions (*paccayavaṭṭa*) is not explicitly mentioned in the text, its state of completeness—whether by way of cause or by way of fruit—is shown merely by way of its headings:
thus, there is a connection of fruit and cause at the beginning, a connection of cause and fruit in the middle, and a connection of fruit and cause at the end.
Thus, because it possesses three links, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is shown as having exactly four groups.
The commentary on the *Āhāra-sutta* is concluded.
2. Commentary on the *Moḷiyaphaggunasutta*.
12. "In this very place" means: having shown the four kinds of nutriment by way of their specific characteristics in the passage beginning, "Bhikkhus, there are these four...
nutriments," and then showing them again by way of a conclusion in the passage beginning, "These, bhikkhus, ...

for the maintenance and support," it is in this very place that he brought the teaching to its end. He brought the teaching—which elucidates the classification of the four nutriments—to its conclusion by way of a summary alone.
Having reflected upon this, he sat in silence. "One who has gone to a wrong view" (*diṭṭhigatika*) means one who has gone to a wrong view by way of the view of a self (*attadiṭṭhi*).
"Perfumed with excellent fragrance" (*varagandhavāsita*) means it was perfumed because it was saturated with both the naturally inherent fragrance of sandalwood and various other fragrances.
"With an excellent jeweled spittoon" (*ratanacaṅkoṭavarena*) means with a supreme spittoon made of jewels. "Connecting the sequence of the teaching" (*desanānusandhiṃ ghaṭento*) means...
Connecting the sequence according to the teaching as it was taught, and exerting himself so that the subsequent teaching might increase, he said:
"He who eats this... and so forth, thereby uprooting that speculative view in response to the question stated regarding the act of consuming the nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*).
When the nutriment of consciousness (viññāṇāhāra) is desired, there must also be one who experiences it;

this is the intended meaning of the question, "Who indeed? "At the time of the season" means at the time of emerging from the womb, for that is said because it is the period of the [appropriate] season.
"Lest the eggs be destroyed by water," [the birds] emerged from the great ocean. The young vultures...
Just as those tortoises are sustained by the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanā*) through the nutriment of edible food (*āhārasañcetanā*), such is the doctrine of that elder.
Although this doctrine—regarding whether it is appropriate or inappropriate for the elder—is concerned with the nutriments of contact and mental volition;
[it refers to] this question: "Venerable sir, who indeed consumes the nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*)?"
The intention is that he does not ask this question based on the aforementioned tenet (*laddhi*), but rather asks it out of a belief in the existence of a sentient being (*sattupaladdhi*).
"He" refers to the proponent of a wrong view (*diṭṭhigatika*). He is not to be rebuked because, like one who is insane, he has asked the question without understanding the underlying intention.
Therefore, [the Buddha] said: "I do not say that he 'brings forth' [the next existence]," and so forth.
"When I had spoken thus" means when I had said "he consumes," regarding that statement.
"This question" refers to the question, "Venerable sir, who is it that consumes the nutriment of consciousness?"—this would be a fitting question.

When the question is asked in this way, without grasping at the notion of a "being," [the answer] proceeds solely by way of the occurrence of phenomena (dhamma), as follows: "Of which phenomenon is it the condition? and so forth.

When the question was asked: "By that very consciousness," it means that together with that very rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*), the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that arose is intended here as the production of renewed existence in the future for one who holds wrong views in the past life.
"When name-and-form has arisen" means that when name-and-form has been produced, the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) come into being by breaking through that which served as their condition.
In this regard, the analysis of conditions is as follows: by "name" (nāma) is intended here the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling;

"form" (rūpa), however, comprises that which is included within the continuity of the sevenfold personal existence, namely, by necessity, the four primary elements, the six bases, the life-faculty, and nutriment.
Therein, at the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant name acts as an associate to the heart-base for the sixth mind-base.
It is a condition in seven ways: by way of the conditions of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, result, presence, and non-disappearance.

However, one should understand the maximum and minimum [of its conditioning] here as follows: some [mental aggregates] act as a condition through the root-condition, while others do so through the nutriment-condition.
As for the other five bases and the four great elements, acting as companions, they function by way of co-nascence, support, result, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.
It is a condition in six ways. However, some [of these] are conditions by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and some by way of the nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*);

all of this is the same as previously stated. In the course of existence (*pavatta*), that which is called "resultant" (*vipāka*) is a condition in seven ways for the resultant sixth base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*) according to the method already explained.
But that which is non-resultant (*avipāka*) is a condition for the non-resultant sixth [base] by removing the resultant-condition from that [list]. This applies to the eye-base and so forth.

Furthermore, both the present [nāma] based on the eye-sensitivity and so forth, as well as the other [non-resultant nāma], act as a condition for resultant nāma in four ways: by way of postnascent dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions;

the same should be understood for non-resultant [nāma] as well. As for material phenomena, however, the physical basis (vatthurūpa) acts as a sixfold condition for the sixth [consciousness] at rebirth-linking:
by way of conascence, mutuality, support, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.
However, the four primary elements (bhūta) act as a condition for the five bases, such as the eye-base, in four ways: by way of conascence, presence, non-disappearance, and support conditions.
Physical life-force acts as a condition in three ways: by way of presence, non-disappearance, and faculty conditions.
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga*.

"Providing an opportunity for the question" means providing an opportunity for this speculative question, "Who, venerable sir, experiences [contact]?"—the intention being that he wishes to separate [the interlocutor] from it thereafter.
"In all instances" refers to the statements uttered by both the speculative theorist and the Blessed One.
"A being" (satta) refers to the self (attā); moreover, even for the annihilationist, as long as it has not yet been annihilated, it still exists.
This is the tenet, let alone for those who hold to eternalism. "Bhūta" means existing. "Nipphatti" means accomplished.
Their tenet is that there is nothing further to be accomplished for it now. "From this condition, this [arises]" means:

from this condition of consciousness as nutriment, this name-and-form [arises]. Again, "from this condition, this [arises]" means: from this condition of name-and-form, this sixfold sense base [arises].
Because this has been stated by the Blessed One in many places, one arrives at the understanding that it is merely a conditioned formation produced from conditions.

"By him too" means even by that person who has arrived at such an understanding. "Having made it a single unit" means having joined it into one so that there is no opportunity for a further question. "Entered upon the teaching" means starting from the section on the six sense bases.
The teaching beginning with “with the six sense bases as condition, contact,” and so forth, has indeed entered the path of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
“Taking that very same [term]” means taking only the term “six sense bases. “Avoiding” means turning away from it.

“He spoke thus” means that when the teaching was given in the manner beginning with “but of the six [sense bases],” the person to be trained (*vineyyajana*) penetrates [the meaning]; thus he spoke. Consciousness-nutriment (*viññāṇāhāra*) leads to the production of renewed existence in the future.

Thus, because it has been taught as the condition for a future existence from a previous existence, and as the fundamental cause, it is said that "there is one junction between consciousness and name-and-form.
By this mention of "consciousness," it should be understood that the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*) is also included.
The commentary on the Moḷiyaphaggunasutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta 13.

Those who, through the convergence of the requisite conditions, are capable of penetrating the Truths by means of that very individual existence—even if they abide in external marks—are indeed regarded as ascetics (samaṇa), having regard for their future state of having stilled and cast out evil, due to their possession of that very capability therein.
It was said that they are unable to penetrate the truths because they are considered by the brahmins to be incapable of turning back [from their views].
"By way of the truth of suffering" means by way of the Noble Truth of Suffering. Otherwise, how could even outsiders not know that aging and death are suffering?
Some say it is stated as "together with craving" because of the absence of a teaching on the truths; however, that is not correct, because in various places...

In this context, "existence" (bhava) refers to the first manifestation [of rebirth], which is intended here as "birth" (jāti). And that [existence] is craving itself through its continuity; thus, craving is indeed that birth.
Furthermore, "aging-and-death" (jarāmaraṇa) intended here is clearly the conventional one, not the momentary. Therefore, this should be understood as a statement of fact:
craving alone is the origin of birth, aging, and death. This is not [the case] by way of the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*).
The construction is "they know. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "In all instances" means in all those instances where craving is to be expressed as a qualifying attribute.

He says, "the state of a recluse... and the state of a brahmin," because it is by being endowed with these that a person is called, in the ultimate sense, a recluse (*śramaṇa*) or a brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*). For, by whatever causal characteristic [it functions],...

The terms *samaṇa* (ascetic) and *brāhmaṇa* (brahmin) are established in their own specific senses; however, although they are not distinct [in meaning], it is appropriate to speak of them as two-fold according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
Thus it is said, "in both cases. In eleven places he taught the four truths, because the origin of ignorance (*avijjā-samudaya*) was not explicitly mentioned.
The commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇasutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Second Samaṇabrāhmaṇasutta: 14.
Regarding the phrase "What are these states? Which states?", here the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning. By this, [it refers to] "of these states..."
“Of which phenomena?”—this is the summary of these words. For these words were spoken as common to aging, death, and so forth, and thus they constitute an elaboration (*papañca*) for this teaching;
therefore he said: “Having made such an elaboration, it was taught... [the teaching]... by way of [the Buddha’s] intention (*ajjhāsaya*).
By this, having taken up those very things—aging, death, and so forth—he first [said] “these,” according to the intention of the person (*puggala*).

The teaching was commenced by means of the words beginning with "in the Dhamma," as these apply to all the terms [of the verse]. For the Suttanta teaching is an instruction according to the sequence [of practice], not an instruction according to the abstract nature of the phenomena (dhamma).
The commentary on the second *Samaṇabrāhmaṇa-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Kaccānagotta Sutta 15.

Since here both those who know and those who do not know—whether outsiders or members of the Dispensation—call one "possessing right view" (sammādiṭṭhi) either by way of hearsay and so forth or through their own direct experience, therefore, taking into account the speech of many, [the Buddha speaks] by way of repetition.
“Venerable sir, it is said, ‘right view, right view. He used this repetition (*āmeḍita-payoga*) for the purpose of showing that it has been defined in such a manner.
This is the intended meaning here: “It is called ‘right view’ by others as well;
but when it is so called, does it do so by way of its purpose and its characteristic? To what extent, venerable sir, is it called ‘right view’?”

"there is right view. However, in the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), regarding the expression "one of right view," since only the wise are the authority and not the ignorant, it says "that which the wise [hold]," and so forth.
That which has two parts is "two-fold" (*dvaya*); it is the twofold basis for grasping views.
Because one relies upon and looks toward the two-fold basis for grasping views, it is "dependent on the two" (*dvayanissita*). Therefore, he said: "dependent on two portions."
The view by which a theorist grasps that "this entire world exists, it is found, and it is apprehended at all times"—that view is "existence" (*atthitā*);
and because it proceeds with the grasp that "the world exists always, at all times," it is eternalism (*sassata*), and that is eternalism.
The view by which a theorist [grasps] that "this entire world does not exist, it does not come to be, it is annihilated"—that view...
One grasps; that view is non-existent, and it is precisely that which is cut off—thus, because of the grasping that has arisen, there is annihilation, and that is "annihilation.
"The world" refers to the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), because it is to be grasped therein. "By right wisdom" means by non-perverted wisdom, by wisdom according to reality.
Therefore he said: "Path-wisdom together with insight. "In phenomena that have arisen" means, for example, in material and immaterial phenomena produced by conditions.
“Only when they are being perceived” means only when they are being perceived by way of their continuity. “That which does not exist” refers to the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*);
because beings are cut off and destroyed right there and then, some being or phenomenon that could be said to “persist” would not exist within the world of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāraloka*).
Even the wrong view occurring in the form, “There are no spontaneously born beings,” [is included here].

Likewise, it has only the formations as they have arisen as its object. "That does not exist" means that for one who sees with right wisdom the arising and manifestation of the world of formations in dependence upon conditions such as karma, ignorance, and craving, that annihilationist view does not exist;
it does not occur, because of seeing the production of formations without interruption. "The cessation of the world" refers to the world of formations.
Momentary cessation. Therefore, it is said: "the dissolution of formations.

That which is called "existence" would arise as the eternalist view (*sassataditthi*)—the grasping of unity through the non-interruption of the continuum of what proceeds by way of the connection between cause and fruit—thinking, "The world exists for all time.
That [view] does not exist, because of the cessation of each and every thing that arises and the constant renewal of new things.
Because it shows the arising [of the world], that view of eternalism does not occur.
"The world arises from this" is *lokasamudaya*; thus he said, "the mode of conditions in direct order" (*anulomapaccayākāra*).

For the state of being a condition for one's own fruit among the conditioned phenomena is the mode of conditions in direct order. Having brought in "the mode of conditions in reverse order" (*paṭilomampaccayākāra*),...
The relationship: for the cessation of this or that fruit through the cessation of this or that cause is the mode of conditions in reverse order (*paṭilomapaccayākāra*).
That which is the state of being a cause-condition and so forth of the conditioning factors such as ignorance is, in the primary sense, the origin of the world.
[This refers] to the formations and so forth that have arisen from conditions. "Seeing non-annihilation" is the cause for the vision of non-annihilation. "This too" means not only...
There is the method of determining arising and passing away by way of moments; however, there is also the method of determining arising and passing away by way of conditions.
Craving (*taṇhā*) is the "approach" (*upaya*) in the sense of approaching [the object]; likewise is the approach of views (*diṭṭhi-upaya*).

By the phrase "this is the same method," he extends [the analysis] to show that clinging (*upādāna*) and the other factors are not different in meaning from these approaches. Nevertheless, a twofold nature is grasped among them. But are they not four?
Are the *upādānas* mentioned elsewhere? True, they are mentioned; however, since they amount to only two in meaning, they are stated here in this way.
Although "I" and "mine" are stated out of sequence, their meaning should nevertheless be understood according to the proper sequence.
By the word "etcetera," the inclusion of such things as "the beauty and ugliness of oneself and others" should also be understood.
"Those phenomena" refers to the phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence (*tebhūmaka-dhamma*). "They settle down" means they settle down in a distorted way;

the meaning is that they adhere to them (*abhinivisanti*). "By those" refers to craving and views. "Bound" means bound by being restricted, either through the inability to be released in a distorted manner or by the act of not granting release.
Regarding the statement "Adherence," it is said that this refers to a specific mode of occurrence for clinging and grasping (*upāyupādāna*); thus he says, "And that is this clinging and grasping."
“Of the mind” means of the unwholesome mind (*akusalacitta*). “Becoming a foundation” means becoming a support (*ādhāra*).

Since the occurrence of the unwholesome mind by way of hatred and delusion is also dependent upon craving and views as its proximate causes, craving and views are said to be the “basis” (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the unwholesome mind. “In that” refers to the unwholesome mind.
“Adhere” means adhering by way of such [notions] as “this is mine,” “this is my self,” and so forth.
They cause [them] to proceed. They persist means that, having become firmly established, they persist by way of non-abandonment.
Both of these refers to the dyad of craving and views. He does not approach means he does not draw near to or cling to the course of craving and views such as "this is mine.
He does not grasp means he does not take a firm hold. He does not resolve means he does not resolve by means of the grasping of craving and views.
It proceeds. It is said that the grasping for "mine" occurs when there is grasping for a self; thus it says, "my self.

This grasping for suffering has the five aggregates of clinging as its basis, because there is no suffering apart from them; thus it says, "only suffering," meaning "only the mere five aggregates of clinging.
For it is said: "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. "He does not harbor doubt" means he does not entertain uncertainty.
It does not arise because doubt has been completely eradicated.
"Not by another's influence" means not through another's lack of faith.

He speaks of "mixed right view" because right view is described starting from the discernment of name-and-form; thus, he refers to right view that is mixed, comprising both the mundane and the supramundane. "Without crookedness" means...
“Nihīnanto. For this word *nikūṭa* is a synonym for “inferior” (*nihīna*). Therefore he said, “from what is base” (*lāmakanto*).

And in the phrase “the first end,” the syllable *ka* is used in the sense of censure. “All does not exist”: according to the conditioned, because of the arising of destruction, it simply does not exist;
the intention is that “all does not exist” means it is cut off and perishes. And “all exists” [refers] to the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*).
"It exists" (*atthi*) means "it is found"; the intention is that it is apprehended at all times.

Here, "all" (*sabba*) should be understood as the "all" of personal existence (*sakkāya*), as in such passages as "the discourse on the root of all phenomena" (*sabbadhammamūlapariyāya*). For that [personal existence] is the condition for the knowledges of full understanding.
The word "iti" is used in the sense of indication. What does it indicate? That which was stated by the word "exists"—namely, "existence," meaning permanence.
For here, the first extreme is intended as the grasp of eternalism (*sassataggāha*).

The second is the grasp of annihilationism (*ucchedaggāha*), while the middle way is this very conditionality (*idappaccayatā*) which is free from both. And herein, by avoiding eternalism through the teaching on the cessation of what has arisen, and avoiding annihilationism through the teaching that those things ceasing do not simply vanish into non-existence but recur according to conditions upon attaining Nibbāna, one proceeds by the middle way.
The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma by way of the principle of specific conditionality (*idappaccayatā*). Therefore it is said: “These... [and so on]...
at the end,” etc. The commentary to the Kaccānagotta Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary to the Dhammakathika Sutta.
16. “For the purpose of dispassion” means for the attainment of the contemplation of dispassion (*nibbidānupassanā*).

For that [contemplation] proceeds by way of dispassion toward conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) described under the heading of aging and death. “For the purpose of fading away” means for the attainment of the contemplation of fading away (*virāgānupassanā*).
“Starting from virtue” means starting from the undertaking of virtue based on turning away (*vivaṭṭa*). He is endowed with the factors of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-aṅga*).
Even a lay follower established in virtue based on turning away from the world, let alone a monk established in the fourfold purification of virtue, is said to be "one who practices rightly.
Therefore it was said: "He should be understood as one who has practiced up to the path of Arahantship.
"Of the dhamma of Nibbāna" means of the Noble Path that brings about Nibbāna. "Consisting of a corresponding nature" means having a nature that is suitable for the attainment of Nibbāna.

By the term "disenchantment" (*nibbidā*), he refers to insight (*vipassanā*) leading to emergence. By the two phrases "fading away" (*virāgā*) and "cessation" (*nirodhā*), he refers to the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*);
by the other [phrase], the Fruit (*phala*). "In this" means in this discourse. "By one method" means by the first method;
for therein, the Blessed One, having been asked by that bhikkhu about the characteristics of one who expounds the Dhamma, brought that matter to its ultimate conclusion.
He answered. For he who is able to explain after having attained insight, the path, and liberation through non-clinging is an absolute preacher of the Dhamma.
Therefore it was said: "The question of the preacher of the Dhamma has been answered. "By two" means by the second and third methods. "That" refers to the question.
"Having distinguished" means having made it specific; that is, not merely answering exactly what was asked, but also [answering] what was not asked.
Demonstrating the meaning by attaining the distinction known as liberation through practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhammapaṭipatti*),
the Blessed One— like a noble person who gives much when asked for little— when questioned regarding the characteristic of one who speaks on the Dhamma,
taught that very thing by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), and further, both the practice in accordance with the Dhamma and liberation without clinging (*anupādāvimutti*).
He answered. Therein, by the phrase "he teaches the Dhamma for disenchantment...," he showed the teaching of the Dhamma as pertaining to the stage of spiritual cultivation (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
By the phrase "he is practicing for cessation," he showed [the teaching] as pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*);

and by the phrase "he is liberated through non-clinging," he showed the teaching as pertaining to the stage of one beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*). Therefore, he said: "The stages of those in training and those beyond training have been demonstrated."
The commentary on the *Dhammakathikasutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Acelakassapasutta* 17.

"By his outward mark he is an ascetic" (*acelaka*) means that by the outward mark of one who has gone forth, he is an ascetic; because of that practice of asceticism, he is an ascetic, not merely by the state of being naked.
He shows [this]. "By name" means by the clan-name, "Kassapa. It is called a *desa* because one teaches (*deseti*), proclaims, and thereby effects the removal of doubt;
thus he says, "some particular *desa*," and so forth. For that [instruction] brings about the removal of doubt, it is therefore the cause.
"Occasion" (*okāsa*) refers to a place for connecting [the discourse]; hence he says, "a moment, a time. "Within the house" (*antaragharaṃ*) means inside the dwelling.
“Among the houses” means within the houses; thus, *antaragharaṃ* refers to the interior of a village. “Whenever you wish” means whatever you desire.
In this way, the Blessed One invites [a question] by means of the invitation of the Omniscient One. Therefore he said, “Whatever you wish.
“Whenever you wish” means, Kassapa, even though you have refused three times, you still ask; the meaning is: ask precisely that which you desire.
Because it is stated, “He refused up to the third time,” there ought to have been a reading beginning with “And for a third time, however...

That [reading] has, however, been abbreviated according to the method (naya); this should be understood. To show the reason why the Blessed One had the naked ascetic (acelaka) make his request three times and then answered his question, he said, “But why...,” and so forth. It was for the purpose of generating reverence.
He refused up to three times because of his desire to hear the Dhamma; for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, hold the Dhamma in high esteem.

Having analyzed the grammatical case-ending and joined the phrase in a general sense as "waiting for the ripening of the knowledge of beings, he made him request up to three times," it should then be applied specifically to Kassapa by way of the time limit: "after such a period of time."
*Mā* is a particle used for prohibition. *Bhaṇī* is a verb in the sense of speaking again; it means "do not speak thus," that is, "do not say so.
The phrase "Thus the Blessed One spoke" (*iti bhagavā avoca*), however, is the statement of the compilers of the canon. Regarding "suffering is self-made":
this refers to the suffering arising in a person, which is said to be "made by him" because it was previously produced by his own karma.
The method [of explaining] "because it has been accumulated" is blameless.

However, one who holds a wrong view, having imagined a self that is permanent, distinct from the five aggregates, and characterized as an agent and an experiencer, asks "Is suffering self-made? on account of that [imagined self].
Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Do not say so," and thus he stated: "It is not permissible to say that suffering is self-made," and so forth.
And here, if there were some such thing as a "self" postulated by outsiders, and if that self were eternal— because it is devoid of change,
because it does not relinquish its prior form, and because it is impossible for anyone to produce any distinction in it—
then instruction for the purpose of turning away from the harmful and engaging in the beneficial would be useless for the proponent of the self-theory. Or how could such instruction [be possible]?

How does it proceed? Because there is an absence of modification (*vikāra*). And thus, for one who maintains the doctrine of a self (*attavādin*), neither acts such as giving and so forth nor acts such as violence and so forth are possible—just as they are impossible for the unclouded sky.
Likewise, the connection with the experience of pleasure and pain is not tenable for the proponent of a self, because of the absence of a connection with karma (*kamma-bandha*).
Furthermore, since birth and the rest are impossible, how could there be liberation? Now, [if you say] "it is merely a phenomenon (*dhammamattaṃ*)..."
"It arises and perishes; it is on account of this that one might speak of 'activity' (kiriyā).
Even in this way, it is impossible to establish that there is a mere phenomenon (dhammamatta) called "self" which remains stable without abandoning its prior form.
Furthermore, those phenomena would either be its states or they would be other than it or non-other than it. If they were other, then [the self] would not [be identical] with them...
There would be no distinction between that [self] and those states even when they have arisen. For it is desired that [the self] is the one who acts, experiences, passes away, and is reborn;
therefore, the aforementioned fault applies precisely to that purpose. Furthermore, the conceptualization of phenomena (*dhamma-kappanā*) would also be rendered useless.

Moreover, if [the self] were not other than [the states], then since the self is non-different from the states that possess arising and passing away, the occurrence of arising and passing away would belong to the self just as they do to those states.
How could there be any room for permanence? Or else, if those [aggregates] were to attain permanence just like the self, then bondage and liberation would be impossible;
thus, this doctrine of a self is indeed untenable. Therefore he said: "It demonstrates that there is no such thing as a 'self' who is the maker of suffering.
"From another" refers to the threefold method regarding another, beginning with "suffering is made by another. "Arising by chance" (adhiccasamuppanna).
"Arising by chance" means arising through mere whim, or arising for someone without any prior cause. Therefore he said: "Arising without cause, by mere whim.
The question "Why did he say this? intends to refer to what is about to be explained. "His" refers to the naked ascetic (Acela).
"He" speaks with reference to the Blessed One. "Purifying" means having himself made it pure, [he asks] regarding the matter to be inquired about.
Thus, demonstrating the purity of his own position, he says this for the purpose of refuting the false grasp of the doctrine that "suffering is self-made.
"He acts" means he performs the deed. "He experiences" is intended to show the non-difference between the agent and the experiencer;
it does not, however, intend to show the simultaneity of the performance of the action and the experience of its fruit. "Thus" (iti).
The particle [eva] is used in the sense of illustration. "Kho" is used for emphasis; it shows that "it is precisely that. For these particles have indefinite scope.
Regarding "from the beginning," he says "precisely at the beginning," as this is an ablative form used in the sense of a locative.

For one who holds the view that "suffering is self-made," there will arise, all the more so, the perversions of perception and mind in the form of the notions: "He acts, he experiences. From the perversion of perception...
For there is perversion of mind, and from perversion of mind comes perversion of view; therefore he said:
"When this is so, the following adherence arises: 'Suffering is self-made.

When this is so, there is a false insistence fostered by the perversions of perception and mind, namely, the adherence that "suffering is self-made. Therefore, one should relinquish this evil course of view.
He shows this. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Self-made... [etc]... this pursues one.
Because it is stated without distinction that the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) exists, it illuminates and makes known to others the eternalist view;
and being thus disposed, one grasps the firm grasp of eternalism. “Of him” means of the one who holds such views. That [view]: “Suffering is self-made.”

Such is the distorted view that has thus arisen. This is the grasping at eternalism (*sassataggahaṇa*). It approaches [the object] as "another" (*pareti*). Therefore he said: "The agent... [and so on] ...the meaning.
"Grasping it as one and the same" means grasping it as if it were one and the same, despite the difference in the basis (*vatthu*), due to its arising through improper attention (*ayoniso*).

Here, in the phrase "right from the beginning," it is according to the method stated here by such expressions as "long before" in regard to the tenet that "suffering is created by another" (*parakataṃ dukkhaṃ*).

The meaning should be understood. Herein, this is the construction: according to the view that "suffering is created by another," even more so [is it true] that one person acts while another experiences [the result];

thus, the perversions of perception and mind arise—all of which should be applied in the same manner as explained above. "When this is so" means: when these mild perversions of annihilationism have first arisen, subsequently, "created by another..."
The connection is: "this is the [wrong] view that 'it is suffering'. "An agent" means the doer of the action. "Done by him" means done by the agent of the action.
For the designation "fruit" is applied to the action because of the metaphorical treatment of them as non-different.

"Thus" means that feeling accompanied by views has a pleasant nature, yet is fraught with danger and distress due to the fever of the defilements; thus it is. "All the more so the others" refers to the aforementioned feeling.
"Of one who is struck and pierced. Having stated, "It should be applied according to the method already explained," he spoke the passage beginning with "In this regard, here...
to demonstrate that application. "Annihilation" (uccheda) means the cutting off or destruction of an existing being; the meaning is "non-existence" (vibhava).

For since destruction is impossible for that which does not exist, annihilation is necessarily tied to the state of existence. Just as in the case of intrinsic phenomena (sabhāvadhamma) proceeding by way of cause and effect...
Even though there is a distinction between those factors included within a single continuum and those fallen into separate continua— due to the ultimate inseparability of cause and fruit—
the grasping at diversity through a conclusion of absolute difference, as if they were fallen into separate continua,
is a cause for the dogmatic adherence to annihilationism (*ucchedābhinivesa*). Thus, even while the phenomena existing as causes and fruits [are present]...

In order to show that even the apprehension of absolute non-difference is indeed a cause [of the view of self], because of the inclusion within a single continuum despite the difference in intrinsic nature, the phrase "of a being" (sattassa) is stated in the Pāḷi.
For, regarding the aggregates that proceed by way of a continuum, the apprehension of a "being" is based on the apprehension of unity due to the absence of a clear discernment of the mass;
and the apprehension of annihilation is based on the apprehension of the existence of a "being."
Because one grasps that "as long as this self is not annihilated, so long does it exist," here "annihilation" (uccheda) is intended in the sense of cessation without rising;

thus it is called "annihilation. Specifically, "destruction" (vināsa) means non-existence. Furthermore, since that [non-existence] occurs precisely when something passes beyond the range of vision of both the fleshly eye and the eye of wisdom, it is called "invisibility" (adassana).
For in common worldly usage, the word "destruction" (nāsa) is conventionally established in the sense of invisibility.

The departure from intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), the passing away of intrinsic nature, is non-existence (*vibhava*). For that which is cut off by way of non-arising and destruction does not persist by its own intrinsic nature.
"These two" refers to those two extremes—namely, eternalism and annihilationism—which were rejected by me when you asked, "Is suffering self-made?
and I replied with such statements as "He who acts is he who experiences [the result]" and "One acts, another experiences [the result]."
The construction is: "those two extremes. Alternatively, the construction is:

"not approaching those two extremes," where "those" refers to those many followers of other sects who, because they have not accumulated the equipment of knowledge, do not understand the supreme, profound, subtle, and delicate emptiness, and being submerged in eternalism and annihilationism, are unable to lift their heads. "Teaches" is the first [term].
Thus, by the power of his knowledge, he stands upon the Middle Way in the Dhamma of practice that is not shared with others;
and by the power of his compassion, he stands upon the Middle Way in the Dhamma of teaching and teaches the Dhamma. Here, the word *hi* has the sense of a reason.
Because it has been demonstrated for this reason... [etc. ...therefore, standing upon the Middle Way, he teaches the Dhamma.
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "The fruit is illuminated by way of its cause"—this is the construction; for gender and number conform to the referent (*abhidheyya*).

"Of it" means of the fruit. No agent or experiencer whatsoever is indicated; rather, it is merely rejected because the teaching shows only the state of cause and fruit, and because it grasps only the mass of suffering (*dukkhakkhandha*).
"To this extent" refers to: "These, Kassapa... [the mass of suffering]... and so forth.

“...there is cessation,” by this much alone [is the first question answered]. As for the remaining questions: the four remaining questions beginning with, “Is suffering both self-made and made by another?
In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, the question, “Venerable Gotama, is it that suffering does not exist?
is not cited because it was rejected in the very words of the Canon (*pāḷi*). They are refuted: this refers to the third question.
That [position] has already been refuted by the very rejection of the first and second questions; for that question was refuted both individually and collectively.

Therefore he said: "Both... is refuted. And herein, for one who intends the self to be the agent or the experiencer, a self subject to change (vipariṇāmadhamma) is admitted. This being so, regarding the successive occurrence of phenomena—
Because its mode of existence is dependent upon conditions—just like the phenomena of form and so forth, and just like the phenomena of pleasure and so forth—it follows that it possesses arising.
And since cessation is necessarily concomitant with arising, there is no room for permanence. His rejection of the first question, "Is it self-made?
implies that if its origin occurs only after it has already been established as a self, then, as before, by this [it would follow that it is not self-made].
It must be so, either as before or even afterwards. "The remaining questions" refers to the third question and those that follow.

The third question is rejected; thus the third question should be understood as rejected: by demonstrating, through such statements as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," that suffering is constantly and continuously dependent upon conditions, its accidental origination (adhiccasamuppannatā) is rejected. Therefore...
Thus, his lack of knowledge is also rejected. Therefore the Blessed One said: "In this way there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.

The construction is: "Having undertaken that probation, he undergoes it. "By way of the smoothness of the phrasing" means by way of the smoothness of the words spoken by him as he was requesting, "May I receive the going-forth and the full ordination in the presence of the Blessed One."
Regarding "entering villages and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is included not returning too late in the day, frequenting new women and the like as objects of sense,
skillfulness in the duties of one's fellow celibates, intense desire for recitation and other such practices, being pleased when disparagement of non-Buddhist teachers is spoken,

being displeased when disparagement of the Buddha and others is spoken, and being displeased when praise of non-Buddhist teachers is spoken [while being pleased when praise of the Buddha and others is spoken].

The inclusion of these [terms] is "joyful satisfaction in the recitation of praises. Regarding "the eight observances": this refers to fulfilling these eight observances of the non-Buddhist sects (*titthiya*).
And herein, not entering the village too early, having wandered for alms with purified conduct of body and speech, and returning from there before midday—this constitutes one observance.
"This is the reading here" means this is the reading in this *Kassapa-sutta*. "Elsewhere" refers to the *Sīhanāda-sutta* and others.

"Having rubbed and having ground" means that just as gold is taken as flawless after being rubbed and ground on a touchstone, so too, having been rubbed by the observance of the probationary period and ground by the testing of one's purity, he is pure.

Thus, one who was formerly a member of another sect is understood here. "Intense desire" means a stronger inclination and a more firm preference for dwelling in the holy life after having entered the Dispensation.

"He addressed a certain bhikkhu" means he commanded a certain bhikkhu whose name and clan were not well-known, because of the absence of the necessary support (*upanissaya*) for the *ehibhikkhu* ordination. "Sitting in a group" means...
The monks sat in a group near him, using their own bowls as seats.
The commentary on the Acelakassapa Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Timbaruka Sutta.
18. Since Timbaruka held the view that “feeling is the self; the self alone feels,” he asserted on the basis of that view that “pleasure and pain are self-made.
To withdraw him from that position, the Blessed One said, “That feeling...,” and so forth.
Therefore it was said: “The passage beginning ‘That feeling’ was spoken for the purpose of refuting the view that pleasure and pain are self-made.”
"In this too" means in this sutta as well. "Therein" refers to that passage which was stated: "That feeling... [and so on] ...happiness and suffering.
In the phrase "at the very beginning," the word *to* is used in the locative sense (*bhummavacana*) meaning "from the beginning," and not in the ablative sense (*nissakkavacana*).

By the particle *eva*, he shows that the word *kho* functions as a term of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). Whatever else needs to be said regarding this has already been stated in the immediately preceding sutta.
In that context, however, the doctrine of the theorist who holds the view that "the self is other than feeling" or "there is a maker of feeling" was refuted;
here, it is the doctrine of one who holds the view that "feeling is the self"—this is the only distinction. Therefore he said:
"For if this were so, feeling itself would have been made by feeling," and so forth. "Of this" refers to that feeling by which pleasure and pain are produced.
Of this [sutta]. "Even previously" means even previously from the perspective of the mode of eternalism (*sassatākāra*).
"The prior meaning" refers to the meaning stated in the immediately preceding sutta. "In the commentary" means in the ancient commentary (*porāṇaṭṭhakathā*).
"That" refers to the meaning stated in the previous sutta. "Of this" refers to this sutta. Because Timbaruka grasps that "feeling alone is the self," it is therefore said: "I am she..."
“Feeling... [and so on]... I do not say,” he said.

Regarding the statements “another feeling,” etc., what is to be said there follows the same method as stated in the immediately preceding sutta. “The feeling of an agent” means feeling that has become the agent (the doer).
“The pleasure and pain of feeling” refers to the pleasure and pain that have become the feeling itself, not the pleasure and pain of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).
“It is only the pleasure and pain that are the result [of kamma] which are subject to the round of existence,” as stated in such passages as, “Pleasure and pain are self-made.
The commentary to the *Timbaruka Sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary to the *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta*.
19. Ignorance (*avijjā*) is an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*); because it conceals and hides the danger of existence (*bhava*) and so forth, it is called "the obscuration of ignorance.
One is "obscured by ignorance" (*avijjāya nivuto*); thus he says, "of one who is obscured by ignorance.

This body refers to the present personal existence (*attabhāva*) of a fool whose defilements (*kilesa*) have not been abandoned, [described] by way of the non-perception of things as they truly are due to the concealment of its dangers by ignorance.
For one whose mind has been seized by craving, the formations that lead to various states of existence are conditioned. Through these, the manifestation of a personal identity occurs;
therefore, this body is produced by ignorance. "Of him" means of the fool.
This meaning—that "this body is called name-and-form"—should be illustrated by its inclusion within the six sense bases and the aggregates of clinging.

Of those phenomena. "In this way it is a dyad" means that because it is obstructed by ignorance and conjoined with craving, there is thus a dyad consisting of the conscious body belonging to one's own and others' continua. "Elsewhere" refers to other discourses (suttantas), such as:
"Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact," and so forth.
Having analyzed the internal and external bases, contact such as eye-contact was explained in dependence upon the dyads of eye and visible form, and so forth;
however, here, without analyzing them, contact such as eye-contact is explained in dependence upon the six internal and external bases by the formula, "In dependence upon a dyad, there is contact.
