Therefore, this is indeed called the "great dyad," because it includes the internal and external bases without exception.
Because they are included. In the phrase "internal and external bases," the sixfold bases (saḷāyatana) are indeed included here as well.
"Causes of contact" means conditions for the occurrence of contact. By saying "by which," he indicates the mere presentation of the cause, thus stating, "by which [bases] acting as causes.
Contact itself has the function of touching; it is not the sense-bases that touch. Therefore, it is said, "touched by contact."
“By way of being complete” means by way of being without deficiency. For those whose sense bases are incomplete, the causes for contact are inferior;
it is in reference to them that it is said, “or by one or another of these. “In the production of the body, etc.”:
the production of the body endowed with consciousness is “the production of the body”; or, that by which the body is produced is “the production of the body.”

The defilements and volitional formations. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of contact, the six sense bases, and so forth. That by which one applies oneself excessively is "excessive application" (adhippayāsa);
thus he says "excessive exertion" (adhikapayoga) to mean a specific cause.
The Blessed One is "rooted in the Blessed One" (bhagavaṃmūlaka) because of his state as our progenitor and his state as the root. "These phenomena" (ime dhammā) refers to these causal phenomena.

"By this we shall know the distinction between fools and the wise, even though they are equal in the production of a body and so forth"—for this reason he said, "Previously established by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa," and so on. "We understand" (*ājānāma*) means we know directly and face-to-face.
"We penetrate" (*paṭivijjhāma*) is a synonym for that same term; its meaning is "we attain. "They lead" (*netā*) means those who cause [the truth] to reach our mental continuum.

“Vinetā” means one who leads specifically so that there may be a distinction in noble knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*), or one who disciplines by means of discipline through the abandonment of specific factors (*tadaṅgavinaya*) and so forth.
“Anunetā” means one who leads in a manner that is appropriate.

He said, “one who shows according to their true nature,” etc., because there is a showing of the things established according to the Dhamma from time to time in accordance with their suitability. [The word] *āpāthaṃ*.
The Blessed One is the refuge and the meeting place for those who approach; thus, phenomena have the Blessed One as their refuge (*bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā dhammā*).
Therefore, he said, “phenomena of the four planes,” and so forth. It is called a “refuge” (*paṭisaraṇa*) because one turns back toward it and penetrates it;
therefore, since they have the Blessed One as their refuge by way of such penetration, they are “those having the Blessed One as their refuge. Thus he said, “Moreover,” and so forth. Contact comes.
Through the mode of penetration, contact comes within the range of knowledge;
as it enters that range, it is as if asking for its name in substance, "What is my name?", and the Blessed One is as if bestowing a name upon it.
Thus it is said, "I am, Blessed One," and so forth. "Let it stand" means let it be present to knowledge. "Let the Blessed One himself appear" means...
The meaning is: "Let it be the portion of the Blessed One alone; let the Blessed One himself, having made it his own portion, distribute it.
The intention here is this: "The portion of the Blessed One is the proclamation of the Dhamma, whereas our portion is the hearing of it.
For it is thus that it accords with the characteristics of the words. Some, however, state the meaning as "let it occur to [him]," [meaning] let it be seen by means of knowledge.
Or, the meaning is "let it be taught. Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'you yourselves must tell us and give [the answer]'";
ignorance and craving are the conditions for the production of the bodies of both the fool and the wise. Therefore he said: "Kamma... [etc. ...ceased.
"Having caused to impel" means having performed the impulsion (javana); [it is so called] because it draws forth rebirth-linking.
It is capable when acted upon in this way. If [the defilements] have ceased, how is it said that they are "not abandoned"?
To this he says, "But just as... and so forth. For there is indeed a figurative designation of a thing for something similar to it, as in the expressions:

"That very same partridge," "Those very same medicinal herbs," and "By the remaining result of that very same karma. He says [this] because "for the destruction of suffering" is intended as a qualification of its purpose.
“For the sake of exhaustion”: “the body with rebirth-linking” means the body preceded by the act of taking rebirth-linking.

In the text, the instrumental case “by the fool” (*bālena*) is explained as being used in the sense of the ablative, hence he says “from the fool” (*bālato*). “With rebirth-linking” means together with the rebirth-linking that is yet to come.
However, one who is capable of attaining Arahantship in that very same existence through that future rebirth-linking—[he is said to be] with rebirth-linking by way of that future rebirth-linking.
Regarding the term "without rebirth-linking" (*appaṭisandhika*), the phrase "with rebirth-linking" (*sappaṭisandhika*) is stated for the purpose of providing a distinction from it.

Although this has been said, since one remains a possessor of the qualities of a fool (*bāla-dhamma-samaṅgin*) as long as one has not yet entered the plane of the Noble Ones (*ariya-bhūmi*), it is stated that "every worldling (*puthujjana*) is a fool.

For likewise, in the passage "the one without rebirth-linking who has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) is wise," the word "one who has destroyed the taints" refers to the one without rebirth-linking.
I shall specify this. If that is so, one might ask how those in training (sekha) are described; thus he says, "stream-enterers" (*sotāpanna*), and so forth.
For they cannot be called "wise" (*paṇḍita*) like those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), because they lack the characteristic of having reached the pinnacle of wisdom;

yet they cannot be called "fools" (*bāla*) like worldlings (*puthujjana*), because they have abandoned the stronger states of folly. However, when categorized according to their penetration of the Four Noble Truths:
They associate with the side of the wise, not with the side of the foolish, for the reasons stated above.
The commentary on the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Paccaya Sutta.

20. There is nothing whatsoever among conditioned phenomena that has arisen without depending [on conditions]. Thus, a conditioning phenomenon (paccaya-dhamma) is "dependently arisen" (paccayuppanna) by way of its own conditioning phenomenon;
likewise, a dependently arisen phenomenon is a "conditioning phenomenon" by way of its own dependently arisen phenomenon.

Such is the relationship of condition and dependently arisen between phenomena as appropriate. For those disciples for whom the teaching of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) alone [is sufficient],...
Because it appears clearly to those [of duller faculties], dependent origination was taught by making a thorough distinction according to their needs.

However, for those disciples who attain the breakthrough to the Dhamma through the Suttas themselves by means of distinguishing between those two, the Blessed One, intending for them, showed both of those by distinguishing them, saying: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you dependent origination..."
Explaining the meaning of the statement, "He began this teaching, 'And [the] phenomena that have arisen dependently,'" he said, "In this sutta, the Teacher...

and so forth. The state of being a condition is "conditionality" (*paccayatā*), which is the state of being produced by conditions. Because it is not found in phenomena that lack intrinsic nature (*asabhāva-dhamma*), it is stated as "phenomena possessing intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva-dhamma*).
But is it not the case that birth, aging, and death are also phenomena possessing intrinsic nature?
It is not that [the aggregates] do not exist; rather, those very aggregates which possess birth, aging, and death are themselves phenomena with intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*).

Why, then, are they included in the teaching? This is not a fault. For birth, aging, and death are merely the modifications of phenomena with intrinsic nature produced by conditions, and not of anything else;
therefore, they are included. Alternatively, the phrase "or from the arising of Tathāgatas" does not refer to individual persons who are to be trained (*vineyya-puggala*).
Just as the arising of the paths and fruits depends upon the appearance of a Tathāgata, so too does the arising of aging and death conditioned by birth;

yet, that [arising] occurs whether Tathāgatas appear or do not appear. Therefore, although that [arising] is not permanent—just as the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) is—it is nevertheless called "occurring at all times" (*sabbakālika*), which demonstrates that the arising of aging and death occurs from the condition of birth.
Therefore he said: "Birth itself is the condition for aging-and-death. And "conditioned by birth" means conditioned by that which is designated as birth.

The word is used in the ablative case (nissakkavacana) to denote the cause. That element remains constant—namely, this specific conditionality (*idappaccayatā*), which is the state of birth being a condition for aging-and-death—because there is no deviation from it.
Now, there is never a time when birth is not a condition for aging-and-death.

“‘It is, it is indeed’” determines the state of being a condition for aging and death. By both [phrases], he shows that wherever the aforementioned state of being a condition exists, there its existence is necessarily established.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “That element remains indeed.

By these two phrases, he shows that “they remain” means that by virtue of which the stability of phenomena occurs—that is, this specific conditionality (idappaccayatā), the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitatā).

“Dhamma” refers to phenomena that have arisen through conditions. “Niyameti” means to specify or distinguish. For the conjunction of specific qualities residing in the cause is precisely this fixed nature (*dhammatā-niyāma*) of the cause-and-effect relationship.
Another method: “That element remains established” refers to this specific conditionality for aging and death, namely, “with birth as condition, aging and death come to be.”
This is the element (dhātu), this is the intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

It was not produced by the Tathāgatas—being unpenetrated before their arising and after their passing away, yet being penetrated in the interim—but rather, it is simply that this element remains established as the perpetual arising of aging-and-death from the condition of birth;
it is merely [revealed] by means of the knowledge of the Self-Existent One (sayambhuñāṇa).

Because he has fully awakened to it and because he proclaims, "This Dhamma has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata," the Tathāgata is called the "Lord of the Dhamma," not because he produced something previously non-existent.
Therefore it is said: "That element remains just as it is.
Precisely because there is no distortion here in the statement, "With birth as condition, aging-and-death [comes to be]," for one who understands it in this way—of that person...
“Dhamma-sthitatā” (the stability of phenomena) means the persistence of an intrinsic nature or a cause in its very same state.

Alternatively, it refers to birth as the arising, persistence, occurrence, accumulation, conjunction, obstruction, origination, and causal condition for aging-and-death; thus, its persistence by way of such arising and so forth is “dhamma-sthitatā.
This term refers specifically to the cause with respect to the fruit, by virtue of its functional capacity. It is so called because it is "sustained" (dhārīyati) by conditions.

Or, *dhamma* is that which persists; it is "stability" (*ṭhiti*) because the fruit exists there, depending upon it for its subsistence. Thus, the stability of the *dhamma* is "dhamma-stability" (*dhammaṭṭhiti*).
Alternatively, *dhamma* refers to the cause, so called because it sustains (*dhāraṇato*) the fruit by way of being a condition. Its stability is its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

Since there is no intrinsic nature other than the *dhamma*, it is "dhamma-stability," meaning the condition. Therefore he said: "Wisdom in the discernment of conditions is knowledge of the stability of *dhammas*."
The stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhiti*) is itself the fixedness of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*).

That very element (*dhātu*) is the fixedness of phenomena (*dhammaniyāmatā*), because there is no otherness in this nature or cause—namely, that "with birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be"—and because there is an absence of that state when it is understood that "aging-and-death does not come to be with birth as condition. Or, it is the fixedness of the result, aging-and-death.

When there is birth, there is occurrence; when there is a cause, there is stability—this is the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*). When there is no [birth], there is no occurrence; this is the fixed order of phenomena (*dhammaniyāmatā*).
Thus, one discerns the cause by means of the fruit; this is what is expressed by the passage beginning, "That element remains ever stable.

One fully awakens to, that is, directly realizes face-to-face, this specific conditionality (*idappaccayatā*) which consists in the state of being a condition for these factors such as aging and death.
One penetrates it as it truly is; from that very penetration, one realizes it—that is, one encounters it face-to-face.
To "declare" means to state it at the outset; the sense is that one recites it. To "teach" means to bring that very recitation to its conclusion.
To "make known" means to cause it to be understood through various modes by way of demonstrating exactly what was recited. To "establish" means to firmly settle it through those very same modes.
He explains and analyzes what has been stated according to its restatement (*paṭiniddesa*).
Having explained and analyzed the meaning, he makes it clear by showing reasons and examples; making it clear, he renders it as something directly manifest and says, "Behold! by way of conclusion.
"In such cases as ‘with birth as condition, aging-and-death’ and so forth" means: regarding the state of birth and the other factors being conditions for aging-and-death.

"By those respective conditions" means: by whatever number of conditions a particular fruit is fit to arise, its arising occurs through those very conditions when they are complete, not when they are deficient or excessive.
Therefore he said: "by those that are neither deficient nor excessive. Just as [consciousness arises] through the eye, visible forms, light, and attention...
"Arising of eye-consciousness. By this, he shows that the "suchness" (tathatā) is said to be the specific character of that collection of conditions in the production of each respective fruit.
"Sāmaggī" means combination; its meaning is "assemblage" (samavāya).
"From the absence of non-arising" means from the absence of non-occurrence. For even when there is a collection of conditions of such a kind, if the fruit does not arise—
Its non-falsity would [then] exist. "By conditions for another dhamma" means by conditions for another resultant dhamma.

"Due to the non-arising of another dhamma" means because no other resultant dhamma arises from those [conditions]. For there is never the occurrence of ear-consciousness through the eye, visible object, light, and attention;
if it were to occur, there would indeed be what is called the "alteration" of that causal complex, but not [otherwise].
Because this exists, it is called "unalterability" (*anaññathatā*). "From conditionality" means from the state of being a condition.
The same method applies here as well for "from the collection of conditions. "Conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*) is simply "this-condition" (*idappaccaya*);

the word is extended by the suffix *-tā*, just as "the deity itself is divinity" (*devoyeva devatā*). Alternatively, the suffix *-tā* has the sense of a collection, meaning "a collection of these conditions," just as...
With reference to the meaning "a multitude of people is a *janatā*," he said: "In this context, however, the etymology should be understood from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).

"Not permanent, not eternal" means impermanent (*anicca*). Aging and death are not impermanent because they are unconditioned (*anipphanna*) due to being the state of transformation of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*);
nevertheless, they are called "impermanent" by way of figurative usage (*pariyāyena*). This same method applies to the terms "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) and so forth. [It is] made by coming together.

It is called "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) because it is produced by conditions that have come together and met according to their respective natures; thus it is made by conditions through their conjunction.

It is called "dependently arisen" (*paṭiccasamuppanna*) because, being worthy of conditions, it arises in dependence upon a condition—not without it—but precisely as something conjoined and met with it.
Therefore he said: "arisen by depending on a condition. "The nature of destruction" means the nature of breaking up.
"Having the nature of vanishing" means having the nature of departing from its own state. "Having the nature of fading away" means having the nature of decaying.
"Having the nature of ceasing" means having the nature of being fragile by way of momentary dissolution. "In the manner stated" refers to the manner stated regarding aging.
Regarding "the productive conditions such as karma": here, "functional power" (*kiccānubhāvo*) refers to how—
When the condition is present, its fruit arises; such is its occurrence at the moment of its functioning.

This is what is meant: at whatever moment a condition is said to be engaged in producing its own fruit, at that very moment those phenomena—such as material form—which are perceived, yet were unperceived prior to it and will be unperceived afterwards, [arise].
Their arising from that [source] is extracted; in the same way, the arising of birth must also be extracted as "that which is apprehended at that very moment.
If this is so, and the arising of birth from something is established even in a non-figurative sense, then why was it said, "in one figurative sense"?
Because the phenomena in the process of being born are to be apprehended as having the nature of a transformation (*vikāra*). If [they were not], they would be like phenomena already produced.
If birth were perceived [as a primary entity], its arising from some source would have to exist in an absolute sense;

however, it is not perceived in that way. Rather, because it is unproduced, it is perceived as a state of transformation. Therefore, it is said: "In this context, [the terms] 'impermanent' and so forth are applicable in one sense.
But this does not apply to aging-and-death, at the moment when the productive conditions exercise their functional efficacy.
Because it is unobtainable. For this very reason it was said: "And herein, 'it is impermanent'... [etc] ... that which is called 'impermanent' has arisen.

Regarding the phrase "together with insight" (*sativipassanāya*), here the word *sa-* indicates a subordinate status, as in expressions such as "with flies" (*samakkhikaṃ*) or "with chaff" (*samakasa*).
For insight is subordinate; it is the path-wisdom, which is the seeing of things as they truly are, that understands. "The former..."
When "the end" (*anta*) is mentioned, there might be the apprehension of the present state as well; therefore, it is said: "The prior end is the past.
Based on the suspicion of eternalism (*sassatavāda*), one considers the existence of oneself in the past, thinking, "Did I exist in the past time?
And based on the suspicion of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppatti*), [one considers] from what point onward I [have existed].
He doubts the non-existence of himself in the past, wondering, "Did I not exist previously? Why? Because doubt clings to two modes of apprehension.
Furthermore, because it grasps the past as its object, it is shown to be dependent on the modes of eternalism (*sassata*) and fortuitous origination (*adhicca-samuppatti*).
Doubt is a state that flows back and forth, a cause for never turning away from anything whatsoever.
Showing that one should not investigate why it arises, he said, "The reason why should not be stated.

Alternatively, the cause of doubt should be understood as unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), the state of being an ignorant worldling (*puthujjana*), and the failure to see the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
"Birth, gender, and destination" refers to birth as a kshatriya, brahmin, and so forth; and gender as a householder, a renunciant, and so forth.

And [rebirth] among gods, humans, and so forth. "Depending on" (*nissāya*) means "having taken as a basis. At that time, that continuum which possesses a medium size is "of medium measure" (*pamāṇika*);
because of the absence of such [medium] size, or because of being excessive, it should be understood as "immeasurable" (*appamāṇika*).
"Some" refers to the teachers of the *Sārasamāsa*. For they [ask]: "How indeed could this be?"—whether by an *Īśvara*, or by Brahmā, or by past deeds...
They say that one thinks, "It has arisen without a cause. For even doubt regarding arising without a cause is merely a perversion of the cause (*hetuparāmasana*).

"Succession" (*parampara*) refers to the continuous flow of preceding and succeeding moments. "Duration" (*addhāna*) is a designation for time; it should be understood as being used in the accusative case with the sense of the locative.
"Both existence and non-existence" refers to the suspicion of eternalism (*sassata*), based on which one wonders: "Shall I exist..."
The phrase "I [shall exist] in the future time" refers to the existence of oneself in the future;

however, based on the suspicion of annihilationism, one doubts the non-existence of oneself in the future, thinking, "In whatever state of being there is a suspicion of annihilation, will I then exist beyond that?
This should be construed according to the method explained below.
Regarding the phrase "the present period": since it is the present period of time that is intended here, the words "beginning with rebirth-linking," and so forth, are stated.
"Doubt" (*kaṅkhā*) means vacillation; because it proceeds by thinking, "How is this? How is this?", it is called *kaṅkha*. One who possesses this is a "doubter" (*kaṅkhī*).
Therefore he said, "one who is doubtful. What reflection can there be in this case? [None at all]; such a person is like a madman, a foolish worldling.
The intended meaning is that it was said "only after [the fact]. That refers to the son of the chief queen. "They shaved him" (*muṇḍesuṃ*):
they shaved him while he was unwilling, as he was unable [to comply] during the time of waking;

this was done according to the family custom, just as some ascetics of noble lineage do, or so they say out of fear of the king. "Became cool" (*sītibhūtaṃ*): this is a statement of the cause for his attainment of a state of sweetness.
“*Setabhūtan*” is also a reading; the meaning is that they have attained a white state by remaining in the water for a long time.

He doubts his own status as a kshatriya, perceiving himself as the son of a *sūta*, just like Kanna. “Perceiving himself as the son of a *sūta*” means perceiving himself as the son of the deity Suriya.
Referring to his grasping at himself as “I” when his birth was being made clear, he said: “In this way also...”
“There might be doubt. And “humans, like kings” means that some humans are like certain kings;
this is the intended meaning. It is according to the method already stated, beginning with “by way of the mode of configuration,” and so forth. “In this” refers to the phrase “how indeed am I?
“A living being within” refers to the inner self (antarattāna) imagined by others. By the word “etcetera” in “the sixteen essences, etc.,” [other factors are included].
It includes the measurement of the body, such as the size of a thumb, a barleycorn, or an atom.

The notion that "the sevenfold designation has the living being (jīva) as its object" is merely the opinion of those who hold to wrong views; in the ultimate sense, however, it has the personal existence (attabhāva) as its object.
Thus he says, "the place of the coming and going of the personal existence. The meaning is: the place from which this [being] has come and where it will go. A stream-enterer (sotāpanna)...
This is intended because it is seen as the abandoning of doubt. The other three—the once-returner and so forth—are likewise not excluded.
And the statement, “And this... is well-seen,” is because it illuminates the penetration of the truths without exception.
The commentary on the *Paccaya-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Āhāravagga is finished.
3. Dasabalavagga 1. Dasabalasuttavaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Discourse on the Ten Powers)
21. First, the summary [of the second] is for the sake of the first; for the second sutta was taught by way of an expansion upon the meaning already stated in brief in the first sutta.
Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that first sutta in brief and the second in detail from that.
Alternatively, he taught the first in brief out of consideration for those persons who take delight in what is concise.
The second [discourse], however, is more extensive than that because it is according to his own preference. For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have a conduct equal to that of lions;
when they speak according to their own preference, they speak while demonstrating their own power.
Therefore, we shall provide a commentary on the meaning here by way of the second sutta, with the intention that once that has been commented upon, the first is effectively commented upon as well.
The commentary on the Dasabalasutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Dasabalasutta.
22. “Therein” means in the second sutta. “By the ten powers” means by the ten powers of knowledge that are not shared with others; these are...
"Belonging to the Tathāgata alone" means they are called "the powers of the Tathāgata.

While it is true that some of these may arise even in certain disciples, the kinds of powers such as the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇa*) that arise in Buddhas do not arise in anyone else at any time.
"According to the breeds of elephants" means according to the elephant breeds that will be explained later. "Black-necked" (*kāḷāvakam*).
This is a neuter designation in consideration of the word *kula* (family/species). This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

"A natural elephant-species" (*pakati-hatthi-kula*) refers to the entire species of elephants that are naturally strong, including all those known as *gocariya* and *kāḷāvaka*, which are divided into those that roam the mountains, those that roam the rivers, those that roam the forests, and so forth.
"Of ten men" (*dasannaṃ purisānaṃ*) means of ten men of middle strength. The connection is made by supplying the words "the bodily strength of one Tathāgata. And [the word] "of one" (*ekassa*)...

Thus, it is stated according to the flow of the teaching because it appeared in the preceding discussion. Regarding the phrase "the strength of the Nārāyaṇa-composition": here, *nārā* refers to reins;
since many various kinds of these arise from this [body], it is called *nārāyana*. It is the diamond (*vajira*).
Therefore, the meaning of "the strength of the Nārāyaṇa-composition" is "the strength of the diamond-composition. "The bodily strength of the Tathāgata" refers to the Tathāgata’s...
Ordinary bodily strength does not enter into the [classification of] inclusion because it lacks its own power;
for that very reason, it has both an external nature and an inferior quality. To show the cause for both of these, it was said: "For depending on this," and so forth.
"Other" means other than bodily strength, distinct from it. "In ten places" means in ten points to be known. Because of penetration according to reality...
Because it itself is unshakable and makes that person who possesses it preeminent among those to be guided, it is said:
"in the sense of being unshakable and in the sense of providing support.

"From the standpoint of the possible and from the standpoint of the cause" means from the standpoint of the reason and from the standpoint of the cause; for it is because the fruit abides [therein] through its dependence on that [cause] that it is called a cause.
Because it arises and proceeds, it is called a "ground" (*ṭhāna*). By contrast, "non-ground" (*aṭṭhāna*) should be understood as that which is not a cause.

The Blessed One, by means of that knowledge, knows which specific phenomena are the causes and conditions for the arising of which specific phenomena—that is a "ground"—and which specific phenomena are not the causes and conditions for those specific phenomena.
He understands that specific basis for the arising of each [result]. With reference to this, it is said: "The knowledge of the possible... is one.
Regarding "of undertakings of action" (*kamma-samādānānaṃ*): it refers to wholesome and unwholesome actions performed after having undertaken them;

or, the action itself is the "undertaking of action. "By way of basis and cause" means by way of condition and by way of cause. In that context, there are destination, foundation, time, and application.
The fruit of maturation is the locus; karma is the cause.

"Knowledge of the path leading everywhere" means the knowing of the path that leads to all destinations, both those leading to wrong paths and those leading to right paths. For example, among many people who kill a single living being, [one knows] by this method:
"The volition of this one will lead to hell; the volition of this one will lead to the animal womb."
Even regarding a single object, it is the unerring knowledge of the intrinsic nature of the practices comprised by wholesome and unwholesome volitions.
"Knowledge of the world as having many elements and various elements" means the knowledge of the world of aggregates,

bases, and elements— which possesses many elements such as the eye-element and so forth, or the sense-sphere element and so forth— and which possesses various kinds of elements due to the diversity of those very same elements.
"Of other beings" means of other sentient beings. "Knowledge of their various inclinations" means the knowledge of the state of having various inclinations through low and other such inclinations.

"Of those very ones" means of those very other beings. "Knowledge of the high and low development of the faculties" means the knowledge of the superior and inferior states, as well as the increase and decrease, of the faculties such as faith and so forth. "Of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments..."
The knowledge of defilement, purification, and emergence regarding the four jhānas beginning with the first; the eight liberations beginning with "possessing form, one sees forms";
the three concentrations beginning with that accompanied by applied and sustained thought;
and the nine successive attainments beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna. [This pertains to] the knowledge of what pertains to decline and what pertains to distinction.

"Emergence is also purification; emergence from this or that concentration is also emergence"—thus it is the knowing of both the familiar jhāna and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the attainment of fruition.
For each lower familiar jhāna serves as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for each higher one; therefore, even purification is called "emergence. But by means of the life-continuum...

Emergence occurs from all jhānas. It is specifically with reference to emergence from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—and not merely from the fruition attainment—that it is said, "emergence from this or that concentration.
"Knowledge of past lives" is the knowing of the aggregates belonging to previous existences by means of the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*).
"Knowledge of passing away and rebirth" is the knowing of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to reality.
"Knowing. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Knowledge of the destruction of the taints" (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*) means knowledge of the destruction of the taints, that is to say, path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*).
To show where these [knowledges] are presented in detail and commented upon, he says, "In the Abhidhamma, however," and so forth.
Confidence (*sārada*) is the seeking of refuge and the state of being terrified due to the fear of delusion; it is the fear of delusion.
One who is free from such confidence is *visārado*. The state of being so is *vesārajja* (self-confidence).

This, moreover, is the fourfold knowledge of reviewing that proceeds based on the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of specific teaching, and security. Therefore he said, "In the four instances," and so forth.
"In the four" means in the matters imagined by others; or rather, in the mere grounds for accusation imagined by others.
"By you who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One" means by you who claim thus: "I am a Perfectly Enlightened One.
"These phenomena" refers to: "This is the fifth Noble Truth," "this is the sixth aggregate of clinging," "this is the thirteenth..."
These phenomena are to be understood as "bases" (*āyatana*). "Not fully awakened to" and "not penetrated":
herein, "therein" refers to that basis for censure consisting of phenomena not yet fully awakened to. "Anyone" means anyone other than a recluse (*samaṇa*) and so forth.
"In accordance with the Dhamma" means together with the cause; it is a figurative expression for "cause," as in the case of the term "analytical knowledge of the Dhamma" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).
Here, the word *dhamma* [is used]. And "cause" (*hetu*) should be understood as a cause for origination or accomplishment, not as an agent or a bringer-about.

"Sign" (*nimitta*) means a reason; however, in this context, it refers specifically to the basis for censure. "I do not see [any ground]" means from the standpoint of being a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*).

"One who has attained security" (*khemappatta*) means one who has reached a state free from calamity and has reached a state of immovability, in contrast to the basis for censure which consists of that which is not secure. "One who has attained fearlessness" (*vesārajjappatta*)...
He has attained a state of confidence. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. However, this is the distinction:

regarding the phrase "these taints," among the taints of sensuality and so forth, the statement "these taints are not yet exhausted" refers here to the abandoning of all defilements by means of the expression "the destruction of the taints.
For there is no defilement that would not be abandoned when the taints have been entirely exhausted. The term *antarāyikā* means "obstructive."
The meaning is that they create obstacles to the attainment of liberation for the heavenly realms. For a teaching (*dhamma*) that leads away from defilement is called "leading out" (*niyyānika*).

Since it is conventional usage to say that a person who possesses such a teaching is "one who leads out" when that teaching leads them forth, [the opponent] says "it does not lead out" in order to reject that notion. But how is it said that the teaching of the discourse leads out?
Because it is concentrated for the purpose of leading out, it is called "leading out" by way of figurative designation through its non-differentiation.
Alternatively, since the term "Dhamma taught" intends the Noble Dhamma, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
"Āsabhaṃ" means "belonging to a bull" (usabha); it is "bull-like" in the sense of being fearless, and thus it is the preeminent state.
Omniscience (*sabbaññuta*). Because they stand in the place of the bull (*āsabhaṭṭhāna*), the previous Buddhas are called "bulls" (*āsabha*).
They go forward toward omniscience by virtue of their claim to it, or the four assemblies approach them;
thus they are "bulls. For even the four assemblies stand facing the Buddha in this way, and do not stand with their backs turned. "This too" refers to the term "the bull" (*usabho*).

The word *pada*. "Of him" means of Nisabha. It should be understood that while the "bull-like state" (*āsabhaṭṭhāna*) of a bull is intended by way of those factors through which strength arises, the [Buddha's] bull-like state exists by way of those very factors in their most preeminent form.
Whatever is called a "simile" in the world, being stated as an illustration of the Buddha’s qualities, all of it is indeed inferior.
"And even while standing" means that even though he is not actually standing, he is said to "claim" that he is standing. "He approaches" means he consents.
"These eight indeed" is the demonstration of the power of the knowledge of fearlessness (*vesārajja-ñāṇa*).
For just as the skill of a preacher of the Dhamma is made manifest when, having plunged into an assembly of experts, he is capable of delivering a discourse that satisfies the minds of the wise.
Thus, when these eight assemblies have been reached, the power of the Teacher’s knowledge of self-confidence (*vesārajja-ñāṇa*) becomes manifest. Therefore it is said: "In the assemblies.
"A kṣatriya assembly" (*khattiya-parisā*) is a gathering, a collection, of kṣatriyas who have assembled. This same method applies everywhere.
"A Māra assembly" (*māra-parisā*) is a gathering, a collection, of those belonging to the host of Māra who have assembled. It is the assembly of Māras who resemble Māra.
The assembly of Māra. All these assemblies are included by way of their appearance as formidable.
For when it is said, "The king is sitting here," ordinary people are unable even to utter the words; sweat breaks out from their armpits.
Thus formidable is the assembly of Khattiyas. The Brāhmaṇas are skilled in the three Vedas, and the householders in various trades.
They are skilled in the analysis of syllables, and these recluses are experts in their own doctrines as well as those of others;
for them, to deliver a discourse on the Dhamma in the midst of such people is exceedingly difficult. There is no need even to mention the formidable power of the devas.
For when it is merely said, "A non-human being," the entire bodies of humans tremble; and upon seeing their forms or hearing their voices, beings even lose consciousness.
Thus the assembly of non-human beings is fierce. In this way, these assemblies have been described by way of showing their fierce nature.
But why are the assemblies of the Yāma devas and others not included here? Because of their intense greed for sensual pleasures and their lack of proper attention (yonisomanasikāra).
For the Yāma devas and others, while enjoying exceedingly magnificent sensual pleasures, are by nature incapable of listening to the Dhamma due to their obsession with them.

They do not even give rise to the thought [of going there], yet by the power of the Great Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas, being drawn along, they occasionally perform services such as paying homage during such great occasions.
For this very reason, the description of the *Vimānavatthu* was not frequently based on that [reason].
"The supreme cry" (*seṭṭhanāda*) means the highest cry because it is unopposed by anyone. "The fearless cry" (*abhītanāda*)...
“From the state of possessing intrepidity” means from being fearless toward anything. “By the *Sīhanāda-sutta*” refers to the *Sīhanāda-sutta* found in the Khandhaka section.
“From enduring” means from forbearing. “From striking” means from dispelling or destroying. The passage beginning with “Just as...
and so forth is an explanation of the meaning stated in brief as “he roars a roar similar to the lion’s roar.”
“*Etanti brahmacakkhan*”: this is the phrase. “Developed by wisdom” (*paññāpabhāvita*) means produced by the perfection-wisdom and insight-wisdom that have been cultivated over a long period of time.
“Developed by compassion” (*karuṇāpabhāvita*) means produced by the great compassion that proceeds in such a manner as, “Alas, this world has fallen into hardship,” and so forth.
Just as, from the time of their Great Renunciation onwards, for the Great Bodhisattvas, [that which] opposes the attainment of the Noble Path...
There is no practice [of the path], starting from the attainment of the state of certainty in the Tusita heaven; thus, the second and third methods are included.

"At the moment of the fruit" means at the moment of the supreme fruit (aggaphala). Because it is the culmination of penetration, the knowledge of the path to Arahatship is a penetration preeminent by virtue of its adamantine nature;
therefore, it is said to be "arisen at the moment of the fruit. By this, even though the knowledge of teaching has been acquired...
"It is said that the attainment of the fruit for Aññā Koṇḍañña occurs at the very moment of his awakening; this refers to its occurrence at the moment of the fruition (phala-khaṇa) of stream-entry.

Thereafter, until his final Nibbāna, the continued operation of the knowledge of teaching should be understood as the "standing" of that very Wheel of Dhamma which had been set in motion, just as the Wheel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch continues to function after it has been set in motion.

Like a place. By the word *pi* (also) in the phrase "both," he groups together the similarity between mundane teaching-knowledge and the other [supramundane knowledge] by way of its being not shared with others.
Because it is born in the breast (*urasi*), it is "born of the breast" (*orasa*)—that is, knowledge.
In the expression "thus is form" (*iti rūpaṃ*), the word *iti* has the sense of indicating the specific nature of form without remainder; therefore, of that [form], [he says] "this..."

By the phrase "matter" (*rūpa*), he states the definition of matter in its general sense. By the phrase "only this much is matter," he indicates the absence of any other sign beyond this, meaning that there is no matter whatsoever exceeding this extent. Now, in order to demonstrate this meaning in detail, it is said:
"having the nature of being affected (*ruppana-sabhāva*)," and so forth. Therein, "being affected" refers to [the state] when there is a concurrence of opposing conditions such as cold and so on.
"Arising with diversity. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the internal, external, and other such divisions are included.

"By way of characteristic... etc. means by way of the characteristics such as hardness, by way of the functions such as supporting, by way of the manifestations such as receiving, and by way of the proximate causes such as the triad of primary elements. "Of that which has been thus discerned" means thus, both in terms of commonality and in terms of characteristic and so forth.
And of that which is grasped. "From the origination of ignorance" means from the arising of ignorance;
the meaning is "from its existence. For existence is the opposite of cessation; therefore, when there is no cessation, there is existence.

Thus, when ignorance established in the previous existence exists, there is the origination—that is, the arising—of form in this present existence. This is the meaning. "From the origination of craving..."

The same principle applies here to "from the origination of kamma. Furthermore, it should be understood that because ignorance and the other two [craving and clinging] belong to the past, clinging—which serves as their cooperative cause—is already included therein.
Among the conditions for the process of existence (*pavatti*), edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) is specifically mentioned because of its strength;
however, by mentioning "from the origination of nutriment," temperature and consciousness are also included by virtue of being mere conditions for the process of existence.
It should be understood that since they are indeed already grasped, the demonstration of the conditionality of material form—arising from twelve origins—must also necessarily take place.
By the passage beginning with "the characteristic of production," he speaks of the vision of arising (*udaya*) in terms of time.

Therein, having stood after seeing the arising on the path by way of the elements (*bhūta*), one here sees it successively by way of the continuity (*santati*) and by way of the moment (*khaṇa*). From the cessation of ignorance...

"Ceasing of form": through the non-arising cessation of ignorance by means of the knowledge of the supreme path (aggamagga-ñāṇa), there occurs the non-arising cessation of that which has not yet come into being, because in the absence of conditions, there is an absence [of the effect]. "By the cessation of conditions": by way of the cessation of the condition known as ignorance.
The same method applies here to "cessation of craving. "Cessation of nutriment": [refers to] the physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra) which is a condition for the process of existence.
"Absence": "The cessation of form" means the absence of the materiality originated by that [consciousness].
The rest should be understood according to the method explained below. "The characteristic of change" is shown by way of two causes based on the period of existence (*bhava-kāla*).
Therefore, having first seen it while standing by way of its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), one sees it here by way of continuity (*santati*) and subsequently by way of moments (*khaṇa*).

The meaning in the case of "feeling" (*vedanā*) and so forth should be understood according to the method already stated. "The division of pleasure and so forth" means the classification into pleasure, pain, neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and so on.
"The division of form-perception and so forth" means the classification into perception of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dhamma*).

"The division of contact and so forth" means the classification into contact, volition, attention, and so on. "By way of characteristic," etc., refers to the characteristic of experiencing what is desirable, and so forth.

[It is established] by way of the taste of enjoying desirable forms, the taste of flavors, and so forth; by way of the manifestation of bodily gratification and so forth; and by way of the footing of desirable objects and so forth.
Because of the statement, "Touched, one feels; touched, one perceives; touched, one wills," it should be said that contact is the origin for the three aggregates beginning with feeling.
Because of the statement, "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises]," [it is the origin] for the consciousness aggregate.

"It should be said that name-and-form arises": by means of those very factors, one should apply it according to the sequence beginning with "the cessation of ignorance is the cessation of feeling," and so forth.

Although this is not within the domain of the sectarians, it is a "lion's roar" that is partial [in scope], being made by way of the arising and passing away of the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
It has been demonstrated. Now, the entire range of the modes of conditionality—both in forward and reverse order, both in brief and in detail, and unique to this [teaching] alone—is to be shown;

thus he says, "This too is another lion’s roar. "Of that" refers to the discourse on dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) stated in brief as "When this exists, this comes to be," and so forth. And here, "when this exists, this comes to be... [the text continues].

By stating that "with the cessation of this, that ceases"—that is, by explaining that when ignorance and the rest exist, formations and the rest exist, and when ignorance and the rest cease, formations and the rest cease—the restriction regarding the characteristic of conditionality in the previous case is shown: "only when this exists, not when it does not;
only with the arising of this, not without its arising; only with the cessation of this, not without its cessation. Therefore, this...
It should be understood that the definition stated here for dependent origination includes an implicit restriction.
"Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the non-arising and non-occurrence in the future through the fading away and disappearance of ignorance and the other factors; for it has been said:

"But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance," and so forth. Furthermore, arising is the opposite of cessation, by which [dependent origination] is distinguished as arising and cessation.
It was said: "With the cessation of this, that ceases. By this, he shows: "In the absence of cessation, there is what is called 'arising,' and that here is spoken of as 'existence' (atthibhāva).
For this alone is the characteristic: "When this exists, that comes to be.
By the other who says, "With the arising of this, that arises," the former [characteristic] is specified by way of a different formulation.
Therefore, it is not with reference to what is merely present that it was said, "When this exists," but rather it is understood as meaning "that which has the nature of not being ceased by the Path.

And because the Blessed One, in stating the exposition of the characteristic already indicated in both ways—namely, "When this does not exist, this does not come to be; with the cessation of this, this ceases"—[he shows that it refers to the future].
By such statements as, “With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations,” only cessation is mentioned;
therefore, even the state of non-existence is indeed cessation. Thus, it is shown that the state of existence, which is the opposite of non-existence, is non-cessation.
By means of that state of existence termed “non-cessation,” he distinguishes [the nature of] arising. Consequently, what is meant here is not merely the state of existence alone.
The meaning intended is "arising," yet the meaning that is clarified here is also the state of existence characterized by non-cessation.
Thus, this statement of the two characteristics should be understood as purposeful through their mutual relationship as qualifier and qualified.
But what is this so-called "non-cessation" which is described as both "the state of existence" and "arising"? It is the state of being unabandoned.
And its fitness for producing fruit by virtue of not yet having produced that fruit—this is the summary here.
The detailed exposition, however, is to be understood according to the method stated in the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā* within the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
[The phrase] "by way of the analysis of the five aggregates, etc. refers to the five aggregates of clinging and the twelvefold formula of dependent origination (*paccayākāra*).
By way of analysis. For in this *Dasabala Sutta*, the manner in which the Dhamma is taught consists merely of the five aggregates and the mode of their conditions.
Therefore, it says: "the Dhamma of the mode of conditions of the five aggregates. Because it was not treated as a teacher’s closed fist (*ācariyamuṭṭhi*), it is manifest;
yet, in its meaning and its expression, it is not concealed or turned downward. Thus, it says: "not inverted" (*anikujjito*).
“Opened” means made manifest. Therefore he said, “having opened, it was set down. “Revealed” means illuminated by the light of knowledge;
thus he said, “illuminated, made radiant. “In those various places where it was cut or torn”:

sewn together means having taken thread, it was stitched; and knotted means having been knotted with thread in places where it could not be sewn. By virtue of being rags that have been cut [and mended].
The Dhamma is free from shreds; showing that for one whose shreds are cut there is a state of being "cut and broken" by way of its contrary nature, he said, "There is not here," and so forth.
"Wearing" refers to the lower garment and the upper robe. Having fashioned it according to their own ingenuity, they expand their own tenets.
"The refuse of recluses" refers to the semblance of a recluse by virtue of wearing the dress of a recluse.

It is like refuse among ascetics. It is called *kāraṇḍava* because it blows about—meaning it carries along—that which is wretched, fraudulent, and rotten within its own vessel for the manifestation of form;
thus, it refers to one who is immoral. "Expel that *kāraṇḍava*" means drive him out. "Refuse" (*kasambu*) refers to a sham ascetic. "Cast out" means drag away.
"Chaff" (*palāpa*) refers to those similar to chaff; for they are devoid of the essence of grain, just as chaff lacks the core of rice.
That which is merely husk, resembling grain but empty, is called "chaff. Likewise, one who resembles a recluse but lacks the essence of virtue and so forth is like chaff;
thus, he is "chaff," meaning one who is immoral. "Those chaff"—"drive them away," meaning remove them. "Be mindful"—be possessed of firm mindfulness.

"By one who has gone forth out of faith"—by one who, unafflicted by royal calamities and the like, [reflects]: "For thus is that fear of the saṃsāra of birth and so forth into which I have entered..."

"By one who has gone forth through the power of faith that has come for the sake of escaping the round of existence, thinking ‘I shall conquer’—a son of good family by conduct (*ācārakulaputta*) means one who is noble by virtue of his conduct.
Therefore he said, ‘From whatever [source],’ and so forth. A son of good family by birth (*jātikulaputta*) means one who is noble by virtue of the excellence of his birth.
The factors praised by the wise are [praised] because they constitute the factors of right exertion and because of their lack of regard for body and life."
For one who exerts energy, it is said that “the skin is one factor” by virtue of the energy proceeding in such a manner.

This same method applies to the remaining factors as well. Regarding the instruction to “concentrate the energy in nine instances,” this means that energy should be concentrated and maintained in nine instances: in five instances by way of time, and in four instances by way of the postures.

Thus, he dwells in suffering: the indolent person, by failing to exert energy within the liberating teaching, dwells in suffering because of the non-attainment of the goal of asceticism (*sāmaññattha*).
Alternatively, having changed the letter *ka* to *da*, one may read it as *sakam attham* (one’s own goal) or *sadattham* (the true goal).
To demonstrate from the very root how the indolent person falls away from his goal, the passage beginning with “six doors” was stated. By way of sitting...

He is called *pīṭhamaddana* because he crushes the seat; the meaning is that his speech is devoid of substance, for he does not retain any purpose whatsoever, but serves merely as a burden upon the seat.
Elsewhere, however, he is called *makhamaddana*; there the meaning is:
one who looks upon the sacrifice (*makha*) of others with a desire for gifts. He is called *laṇḍapūraka*: having eaten until his belly is full, he fills the latrine.
In passages such as "one who has aroused energy" (*āraddhavīriyo*), the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated regarding the "lazy person" (*kusīta-puggala*);

he is praised by virtue of his aspiration. "One who has aroused energy" means one whose energy is exerted. "One who has sent forth the self" (*pahitatta*) means one whose mind is directed toward Nibbāna.
By this, he demonstrated both the right practice of the disciples and the benefit of venerating the Teacher.

“By the inferior” means by a teaching dependent on the round of existence (*saṃsāra*). Therefore he said, “by inferior faith,” and so forth. “By the superior” means by the supreme teaching dependent on the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*);
even though it is clear, liquor and the like should not be drunk, because it has even slightly removed the turbidity [of defilements] and because of its meaning as the “essence” (*maṇḍa*).
“The Dispensation” (*sāsana*) refers to the Dispensation characterized by the study (*pariyatti*), the practice (*paṭipatti*), and the penetration (*paṭivedha*). It is clear.

It is "serene" because it is free from the stains of hatred and because it inspires confidence. It is "to be drunk" because it is to be enjoyed with ease, like water in a bowl, and because it is free from the stains and mire of the defilements and the dregs of misconduct.
The teaching of the factors conducive to enlightenment is also the "essence of the teaching" (*desanāmaṇḍa*). And of that single essence of the teaching...
The four assemblies who are recipients, well-practiced, and free from fault, constitute the excellence of the recipient.

Because it leads to that same goal, the entire collection of factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), which constitutes the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the path, is the excellence of the holy life. Therefore he said: "What is the excellence of the teaching? and so forth.
In this context, "those who understand" refers to those who have realized the truths. For it was said at the beginning: "Of the four noble truths..."

“Explaining,” and so forth, was said. In the preliminary stage, the very resolve (*adhimokkha*) that proceeds through the removal of confusion regarding this world and the world beyond—by means of such statements as “this world exists”—is the essence of resolve (*adhimokkhamaṇḍa*).
Having discarded it, that is, having abandoned it by way of complete eradication.

Resolve is that which has become the essence through the essence of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) belonging to the four planes. By the word “etcetera,” [the following is included]: “the essence of exertion (*paggahamaṇḍo*)…”

The phrase "the faculty of energy [is the antidote] to laziness and deceit," and so forth, includes the remainder of the canonical texts. "In this" means in this teaching, or in the expression "in the cream.
This is a statement of reason; by it, he shows that the application of being in the presence of the Teacher brings about the fruit of freedom from fear.
Therefore, he says "not in his presence," and so forth. "Measure" refers to what is appropriate for the medicine.

The measure. "Urging" refers to the inducing of vomiting or purging by means of medicine, or the inducing of vomiting or purging of the humors (*doṣa*) and elements (*dhātu*) by means of that [medicine].

"In the very same way" means: just as those who drink the medicinal elixir (*maṇḍa*) in the presence of the physician do so without hesitation, even so, thinking "the Teacher is present before us," you should exert energy and drink the teaching, which is like a medicinal elixir (*maṇḍapeyya*).

The construction [of the compound] is as follows: it is "with its benefits" (*sānisamsā*) by virtue of the attainment of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*); it is "with its increase" (*savaḍḍhi*) by virtue of the realization of the paths and fruits (*maggaphala*).

Regarding the phrase "for the welfare of others" (*parattha*), the meaning here should be understood as follows: it is for the welfare of others who, having followed one's own example, practice correctly.
The commentary on the second Discourse on the Powers (*Dutiyadasabalasutta-vaṇṇanā*) is concluded.
3. Commentary on the *Upanisā-sutta* 23.
Regarding the phrase "of one who knows and sees": here, "seeing" is intended as seeing by means of the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*) alone, not by the physical eye (*maṃsa-cakkhu*).

Therefore, it is said, "both terms have the same meaning. Even so—that is, even though the two terms have the same meaning—[it refers to] the object of knowledge characterized by knowledge and the power of knowledge.

The meaning is: because there is no contradiction with the state of seeing. Therefore he said, “For knowledge has the characteristic of knowing,” and so forth. “By the power of knowledge” means by the majesty of knowledge;
the meaning is that the objects of the function of knowledge appear. Therefore he said, “One sees phenomena as they unfold through knowledge.

And regarding the phrases “of one who knows” and “of one who sees,” he said this because the teaching proceeds by way of a reference to a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) through the medium of knowing and seeing.

“By taking the characteristic of knowledge,” and so forth. “Of one who knows” means either knowing by means of preliminary knowledge (*pubbabhāga-ñāṇa*) and seeing by means of subsequent knowledge (*aparabhāga-ñāṇa*);

or, having said “of one who knows,” what is intended here is not mere knowing in the sense of hearsay or conceptual reflection, but rather [knowing] by making the arising and so forth of those [aggregates] directly manifest, just as the eye-consciousness makes visible forms and so forth manifest.
In order to clarify the meaning of "seeing," it is said "of one who sees"; this is the sense intended here.
"The destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khaya) means the absolute abandonment of the taints.

Furthermore, since that is their non-arising, cessation, and total absence in every respect, he says: "Non-arising, the state of being exhausted, the state of non-existence. [This refers to] the term *āsavakkhaya*.
In order to show the places where [the terms] such as "the state of being exhausted" (khīṇākāra) occur, it is said: "With the destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khayā), and so forth.

"Following the straight path" refers to one who recollects the lower path-factors together with insight, which have become straight through the abandoning of the crookedness of defilements, the crookedness of body, and so on.

For whatever has been completely destroyed for him—in the destruction, the first knowledge arises—and immediately after that, the subsequent knowledge [arises]; thus, in what is termed "destruction" (khaya)...
In the path of the summit (aggamagga), it is precisely the knowledge included therein that arises first; immediately after that, however, there is "final knowledge" (aññā) which is Arahantship.
Although in the verse only the word "in destruction" (khayasmiṃ) is stated, because it is by way of total eradication that the path is called "the destruction of the taints" (āsavakkhaya), he said:
"The path is called the destruction of the taints. By "recluse" (samaṇa), one who has stilled evil (samitapāpa) is intended.

"And he is one whose taints are destroyed. Here, "through the destruction of the taints" refers to the fruit; however, by way of figurative usage, the destruction of the taints is the path, because the fruit is that which is to be attained by means of it. By this very fact, it should be understood that Nibbāna also has the nature of the destruction of the taints.

The restriction "only for one who knows and only for one who sees" is intended here; it is not otherwise, because there would be no distinction [otherwise] and it would lead to an undesirable conclusion.
To show the fruit of that discipline, it was said, "not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see";

thus he said, "But as for one who does not know and does not see, I do not speak to him—this is the meaning. By this, he shows that the full understanding of the aggregates (*khandhā*) is the single, decisive cause for the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).
"By this" refers to the statement, "not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see. Those...

"Those who reject [this view]—who are they? They are those who hold such doctrines as: "Fools and the wise alike, having run on and wandered through the cycle of existence, will make an end of suffering;

beings are purified without cause and without condition. Among them, some maintain that purification from the cycle of existence occurs merely by transmigrating through different births, while others do so by means of a Supreme Lord (Īśvara), Pajāpati, or other such causes.
All of this is included under the category of "those who [hold views regarding] the cycle of existence," and so forth.

It should be understood that this is included right here. By the first two phrases—namely, by the phrase "of one who knows and sees"—the means (*upāya*) has been stated, because the context concerns the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*).
By this [latter] pair of phrases—"not of one who does not know, not of one who does not see"—this becomes the non-means for the destruction of the taints; namely, regarding the five aggregates.
Regarding "not fully understood": by this very indefinite expression, "for one who knows and sees," the prohibition of what is not the means (*anupāya*) is also understood by implication.

It should be seen that this commentary was composed precisely to clarify that state of being understood by implication. "Of a substantial nature" (*dabbajātika*) means having a substantial form (*dabbarūpa*).
For that is called "substantial" (*drabya*) in such passages as, "The substantial perishes, not the non-substantial."
“Of a *dabba* nature” means having the character of a *sāra* (essence), that is, possessing conduct and virtue appropriate to such a state. As it was said:
“Indeed, Dabba, those who are not *dabbas* do not unravel [matters] in this way. “Standing at the head of the duties” means making the duty one’s supreme responsibility.

For one who lives a pure livelihood might provide things such as an umbrella for fellow celibates who do not know how to perform their duties, or for the purpose of warding off the rain, wind, and so forth upon oneself.
He performs [the duties]; it is said that he performs them while standing at the head of the observance (*vatta*).

It should not be said that there is no "proximate cause" (*padaṭṭhāna*), because by virtue of being a quality that acts as a protector (*nāthakaraṇadhamma*), it serves as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the attainment of the Path and its Fruits. For it is said: "He is skillful in those various high and low duties and tasks of his fellow celibates," and so forth.
"Knowing thus" means: by reason of knowing [the requirements of] medical practice and so forth in this manner.
Due to wrong livelihood, the taints such as the taint of sensual desire increase and are certainly not abandoned. Regarding the passage, “In this way...

there comes to be the destruction of the taints,” it is appropriate to understand this as referring specifically to Arahantship, because when the fruit is mentioned, the cause is established even if not explicitly stated.
Therefore, he said: “Because of being born at the time of the destruction of the taints.”

*Āgama* means arrival; that which brings about this [arrival] is *āgamanīya*, referring to the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*). In the phrase "in destruction" (*khaye*), the locative case is used to indicate a characteristic by way of its state (*bhāvena bhāva-lakkhaṇe*);
however, in the word "destruction" (*khaye*) itself, it is used in the sense of a sphere (*visaye*). Therefore he said: "designated as the destruction of the taints" (*āsava-kkhaya-saṅkhāte*).

That wherein the fruit sits down is the cause, the basis (*upanisā*). The liberation of the fruit of Arahantship is mentioned here because it is the highest description. "That" refers to liberation. "His" refers to...

Regarding the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*): however, when the mind is based on turning away (*vivaṭṭanissita*), even proximate decisive support conditions (*anantarūpanissaya*) can arise;
thus it is said, "the state of being a condition should be understood according to what is actually obtainable.

It is called *virāga* (dispassion) because by means of it one becomes dispassionate toward all formations without exception; it is the Path (*magga*). It is called *nibbidā* (disenchantment) because by means of it one becomes disenchanted; it is powerful insight (*balavavipassanā*).

Therefore he said, “By this,” and so forth. With the intention that even the contemplation of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*) belongs to the side of the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*), it is stated as “a designation for the four knowledges.

For, according to the statement, “As long as there is not yet the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, so long is it ‘tender insight’ (*taruṇavipassanā*),” insight subsequent to the knowledge of rise and fall free from imperfections (*upakkilesavimutta-udayabbayañāṇa*) is “powerful insight” (*balavavipassanā*).

The knowledge of whatever individual or general nature exists among material and immaterial phenomena according to their respective natures is "knowledge of things as they are" (*yathāsabhāvajānana*).

That itself is vision (*dassana*). In the sense of making [the object] directly present, both full understanding through knowing (*ñātapariññā*) and full understanding through investigating (*tīraṇapariññā*) are included.

Therefore he said, "nascent insight," and so forth. "Knowledge of the delimitation of formations" (*saṅkhāraparicchedañāṇa*) is the knowledge of the discernment of mind-and-body (*nāmarūpapariggahañāṇa*).
It says: The overcoming of doubt, the discernment of conditions, and the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) are also so called.

The knowledge of contemplation beginning with the method of insight (*nayavipassanā*) is "comprehension" (*sammasana*). The "knowledge of what is and what is not the path" (*maggāmaggañāṇa*) is the knowledge established after having determined what is the path and what is not the path.
For that foundational concentration of jhāna (*pādakajjhānasamādhi*) is the condition for nascent insight (*taruṇavipassanā*). "One who is concentrated understands things as they really are."
For it is said: "He sees.

"Initial happiness" (pubbabhāgasukha) is the happiness accompanied by access concentration (upacārajjhāna). "The subsiding of distress" (darathapaṭippassaddhi) is the calming of the distress of the defilements, such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and so forth.
This is the happiness intended in the passage: "Bhikkhus, I say that happiness has a proximate cause."

To show this, it is said: "of the happiness prior to absorption" (*appanāpubbabhāga-sukha*). There is no need to state that calmness (*passaddhi*) is a condition for the absorption-happiness mentioned in the passage, "With a tranquil body, he feels pleasure.

The same principle applies here to the term "pleasure" (*sukha*) as well. "Strong rapture" (*balavapīti*) refers to rapture that has reached the characteristic of pervasion (*pharaṇa-lakkhaṇa*); for such [rapture] is [accompanied] by applied thought, sustained thought, pleasure, and concentration.
Having obtained the requisite conditions, they suppress the hindrances and pacify the distress and fever caused by them.
Therefore it was said: "For that is the condition for the subsiding of distress. "Weak rapture" means tender rapture. Therefore it was said:
"For that is the condition for powerful rapture. "Faith" [refers to] the qualities of the Triple Gem and the fruit of kamma.
Adhimokkha is the act of resolve that proceeds by way of conviction. Since it arises repeatedly toward its own object rather than only once, he says:
"conviction arising again and again. Because one who has conviction is gladdened regarding the object of faith, he says:
"for it is a condition for weak joy. [This refers to] the suffering of suffering and the other divisions of suffering...

Since all suffering is included within the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*), and that is what is intended here, it is said: "Suffering means the suffering of the round. Some say "the suffering of aging and death," while others say "sorrow and so forth.
Because it encompasses both of these, the first meaning alone is appropriate. For one who has experienced suffering believes in the fruits of karma and in the Triple Gem.
And one arouses confidence; therefore it is said: "For that is a condition for successive faith.
Because when one hears the Dhamma from the presence of teachers and reflects upon the suffering of the round of existence (*pavattidukkha*), the thought arises:
"This Dhamma leads exclusively to the transcendence of this suffering," and thus faith (*saddhā*) is born. Therefore he said: "Having heard the Dhamma from the Tathāgata..."
“He acquires faith,” and so forth. “Accompanied by change” means that the category of aggregates (khandha-jāti) is accompanied by change through the change of arising, in the sense of being born.
Since there is no occurrence of suffering in this or that state of existence when birth is absent, he said: “For that is the condition for the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha).
“Kamma-existence” refers to the threefold kamma-existence, beginning with kamma-existence itself; for that [is the cause] of rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava).
"Condition. It is with reference to such passages that he says, "by this method. "The remaining terms" refers to the terms beginning with "clinging" (*upādāna*).
Knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) is included under the mention of Nibbāna because it belongs to the side of equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*);

knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu-ñāṇa*) is the adverting consciousness for the first path. For that [change-of-lineage] performs some specific function for insight; therefore, having not touched upon it [here], [he proceeds].
“Dispassion (virāga) has disenchantment (nibbidā) as its proximate cause”—thus it is called “dispassion.
Because it is a place reached after being split open by water, it is called a *kandara* (cleft). *Nitamba* (slope) is also [a term for a place] of water.
Just as water flows downward, so too, by way of its turning back [from the heights], it is called a *nadīkuñja* (river-glen). By way of the winter and summer seasons...
The term *padara* refers to a fissure in the earth that has opened over eight months.
The term *sākhā* refers to small water-channels, as they are like branches; and *kusobbhā* refers to small pools, where the vowel *o* has been changed to *u*.

The passage beginning with "Even so" (*evameva kho*) and so forth links the subject of comparison (*upameyya*) with the simile (*upamā*) introduced by the words "Just as, monks" (*seyyathāpi, bhikkhave*) and so on; this is shown by applying that connection.

“It should be seen as a mountain of ignorance,” and so forth, was said. In that context, ignorance is called a “mountain” because it has persisted for a very long time in its continuity and because it is difficult for ordinary people to abandon.

Volitional formations are like clouds because they pervade the three worlds and because they pour down [rain]. The connection is made by supplying the words, “Volitional formations should be seen as clouds. Likewise...

The same applies to the remaining two lines. Because it continues to revolve as the cycle of consciousness and so forth, and because it serves as a condition in a continuous succession, it is like a mountain cave and the like.
Because it has a single flavor and is devoid of decrease or increase, liberation is like the ocean; such is the correlation of the similes.

In this regard, since volitional formations (*abhisankhāra*) exist when ignorance (*avijjā*), which was established previously, exists, and do not exist when it does not, they are like the upper slopes of the mountain.

It is said, "Ignorance... should be understood as raining," because they act like rain-clouds. The passage beginning with "For the uninstructed person" is an elaboration of the meaning already stated.
By the phrase "having formed a longing through craving," he illustrates that this applies to all volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) arisen from the mind.
For craving is called "affection" (*sneha*). The volitional formation that produces the final existence for one in their last birth—

Because he has not yet attained Nibbāna, but stands as if having reached the very limit of that portion [of existence] which precedes it, the simile "as if standing having reached the great ocean" is given.
For even though the round of consciousness and so forth has been fulfilled, by this too the occurrence of consciousness for one in their final existence alone is shown;
for that [occurrence] may be said to have been fulfilled, and beyond that—
Because of the very absence of the cycle of consciousness and so forth. For a person who is born, listening to the Dhamma must be desired as a condition for the suffering of the cycle of birth;
although that is not mentioned in this sutta, it is indeed mentioned in other suttas.
Showing that it should be stated by bringing it from those [other sources], he said, "But the word of the Buddha... and so forth. This [is] for the disciples and bodhisattvas.

This was stated by way of taking this as the primary teaching. However, since there would be no purpose in speaking by way of the others for the sake of including other suttas, he said, "For that which...
and so forth. "Taken precisely according to the Pāḷi" is a detailed exposition of the meaning stated in brief.

He said, "with their modifications," because the aggregates (*khandhas*) currently arising are taken [as the subject], owing to the illumination of the characteristic of impermanence (*aniccatā-lakkhaṇa*) and the rest.

"Bringing forth the characteristics" (*lakkhaṇāhaṭaṃ*). "The determination of what is action and what is not action" (*kammākamma-vinicchayaṃ*). "Free from thorns" (*nijjaṭaṃ*) means free from tangles; the meaning is "pure.

It is stated [in the commentary] because, having taken into account that in the Pāḷi—starting with "one undertakes action upon the earth-kasiṇa, etc."—insight preceded by serenity (*samatha-pubbaṅgamā vipassanā*) is shown, for it is in this way that the manifestation of joy (*pāmojja*) and so forth becomes possible. "Of the god" (*devassa*) means of the cloud. But why is this [stated] here?

It has been stated: “The time of one whose taints are destroyed... should be understood as the time of stability. Is it not the case that previously, volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*) was said to be the state of a deity, whereas one whose taints are destroyed is not volitional formation?
This is not a fault, because the fruit is expressed by way of a metaphorical designation for its cause.

For the continuity of the aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) is rooted in volitional formation, and when the fetters are severed within that continuity, the conventional designation “one whose taints are destroyed” (*khīṇāsava*) is applied.
The commentary on the Upanisā-sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Aññatitthiya-sutta:
