24. "He" refers to the Elder Sāriputta. If he had not yet entered, why was it said, "He entered"? To this he replied with the words, "I shall enter," and so forth.

This shows that there is a figurative usage (upacāra) as if the thing were actually occurring, even though it is necessarily [only] a future event. Now, illustrating this meaning by means of a simile, he says:

"Just as... and so forth. "On a day when he had gone out too early" means on a portion of the day when he had departed from the monastery far too early, at a time before the usual hour for wandering for alms. "It occurred to him" refers to this thought beginning with "It is indeed too early."
There was reflection. "Of the southern gate" means it was between the southern gate of the city of Rājagaha and the Veḷuvana;
therefore, the intention was that there was the thought, "I shall approach him from there.
"What do you profess?"—which among the four doctrines do you teach? "What do you declare? is a synonym for the same. Furthermore, "what do you say" refers to the four...
Having taken the word *vāda* in its general sense, he speaks using the neuter gender, as in: "What is your birth-gender? For this neuter gender is a pronoun (*sabbanāman*).
It is called *vāda* because one speaks by means of it; thus, it is "seeing" (*dassana*). With reference to that, he says: "What is the seeing here...? asking [the question].
In phrases such as "the analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the word *dhamma* has the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

He said: "It is the 'counter-reason' for that which was stated as a reason. The non-arising of the discourse—that is, the speech—is the "non-occurrence of the discourse" (*vādappavatti*). This "speech" refers to the statement beginning with "I say this one," and so forth.
That [discourse] is the talk occurring in such a manner as: "Some recluses and brahmins are proponents of action" (*kammavādā*).

It is called "marvelous" (*acchariya*) because it deserves a clap of hands or a snap of the fingers. It is "extraordinary" (*abbhuta*) according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*).
The establishment of the terms should be understood as follows. "Of all doctrines" means of all fourfold doctrines.

Herein, the first is the doctrine of eternalism, the second is the doctrine of annihilationism, the third is the doctrine of partial eternalism, and the fourth is the doctrine of fortuitous origination;
the reason for the refutation of all these has been stated by way of their negation. Or, it is the proclamation of dependent origination that [serves] for the understanding of ordinary people.
It is profound because it provides no foothold for grasping, and it makes itself appear profound because it manifests thus in the mind.
Taking the very first term—namely, the term "contact" (*phassa*)—he [states this].
The commentary on the *Aññatitthiya-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Bhūmija Sutta 25.
Regarding the phrase "in the previous sutta," this refers to the immediately preceding sutta.

The phrase "should be understood in the same manner" means that without specifying any meaning distinct from that [previous] word-meaning, he says "this, however, is the distinction" and so forth, in order to clarify the other [meaning] through its sense. It is not only...
It arises with contact as its condition; however, it also arises through other conditions that serve as the cooperative causes for contact.

"By means of the body" refers to the mobile body (*copana-kāya*); the meaning is "by means of bodily intimation. Although this [intimation] may indeed not function as a condition for volition (*cetanā*) by way of any of the twenty-four conditions enumerated in the *Paṭṭhāna*, nevertheless, it is only when the body exists that bodily action occurs.
It exists, it does not cease; therefore, it is to be desired by way of its state of concordance.
Thus it is said: "Even when performed by body, it is performed. For this reason the Blessed One said:

"Ānanda, when there is a body, pleasure and pain arise internally conditioned by bodily volition. The same method applies here for speech as well. By "mind" (manasā), [it means] that which has become manifest.
"By mind, not by mere mind": [this means] by oneself, without being incited by others. "By another" means by the incitement of another.
"With full awareness" means by way of a consciousness associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa*), [thus] understanding. "Without full awareness" means not understanding in that manner.
"Of that" refers to pleasure and pain. "Caused by bodily volition" means the sign of bodily action; [it is] of bodily karma.
The meaning is: "because of having been done" and "because of having been accumulated. This same method applies to the remaining types of volition as well.

It is stated that "twenty volitions are obtained" because volition accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*) certainly gives its result during the course of existence (*pavatti*). Likewise, regarding the phrase "in the door of speech," the expression "twenty volitions are obtained by way of wholesome and unwholesome [volitions] of the sense-sphere" is concluded by means of the word "likewise" (*tathā*).
"By means of form-sphere and formless-sphere volitions" refers to the wholesome volitions of the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere.
The intention is that [this applies] to each respective condition. "Those volitions" refers to the nineteen types of volition mentioned above;
they have ignorance as their condition because such volitions arise only when ignorance—which has been previously determined—is present, and do not arise otherwise.
"The aforementioned classification of volitions" refers to the division into bodily volition and so forth. Without being urged by others, [one acts] by one's own impetus.
"Occurring": being caused to be done by others means being performed after having been urged by others.
"Even though knowing": even though knowing by way of hearsay and so forth. "Knowing only the action": at that time, knowing only the very action being performed by oneself.
"In the four": in the four instances stated thus: "either by oneself or by another, either with full awareness or without full awareness."

Having multiplied the nineteen mental factors already mentioned by four—by way of being unprompted and prompted, and by way of being done with full awareness and done without full awareness—it is said:
“one hundred and seventy-six mental factors consisting of volition.

Even for those [factors] that possess the limit of co-nascence (*sahajātakoṭi*), the limit of decisive support (*upanissayakoṭi*) is certainly found; thus they are described as “falling within the limit of decisive support. These...
All phenomena (dhammas) as previously described. Regarding the phrase "that body does not exist," here the "body of sensitivity" (pasādakāya) should also be included.
Therefore, he said: "In which body being present," and so forth. "That body does not exist" means that body does not exist due to the cessation of its conditions.
"Speech" refers to vocal sound. "Mind" refers to whatever consciousness there may be. Now, in order to apply this specifically by way of kamma, he said: "Furthermore," and so forth.
The same method applies to the statement: "Speech is also a door; mind is also a door. How is it that for one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) the body does not exist?
The intended meaning is that bodily action is no longer a basis for him. "Because it is without fruition" means because it is of a nature that does not produce karmic results.
It is said that "the body does not exist" because there is no performance of kamma.
That is the action (*kamma*). It is not a field because it is not a place for that suffering to grow. The terms "place for growth" and so forth are stated by way of contrast (*byatireka*).
Therefore he said, "it is not. "In the sense of a cause" means by way of being a supporting cause.
"Rooted in volition" means having volition as its source. "Of the meanings of growing and so forth" refers to [the phrase] "in the sense of growing," and so on.
Of the meanings already stated. By this state of growing and so forth, feeling is called "pleasant and painful feeling" (*sukhadukkha-vedanā*);
however, here "pleasure and pain" do not refer to the primary characteristics [of pleasure and pain], because what is intended is pleasure and pain that are devoid of purposeful activity.
Furthermore, equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*) here is simply feeling that has become a result characterized by a subtle nature of pleasure.
The commentary on the Bhūmija Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Upavāṇa Sutta: 26.
Only the suffering of the round of existence (saṃsāra) has been discussed here, because it includes the ripening of all other forms of suffering as well.
The commentary on the Upavāṇa Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Paccaya Sutta. 27.
"In sequence" means by way of arranging them in their proper order. The end... [omission] ...the beginning is stated in order to show the application of the Four Noble Truths.

It has been said. "By way of the truth of suffering" means by way of its state as something to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*). For, under the designation of aging and death, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) have been stated;
and these are not conditions for their own fruit. With reference to this, it was said: "He knows the condition.
Here, the teaching proceeds according to the inclination of those to be trained (*vineyyajjhāsaya*). "Endowed" (*sampanna*) means possessed. "Come" (*āgata*) means arrived.
The meaning is "attained. "He sees" means he sees directly through the knowledge of review;
he sees by way of the penetration of non-delusion through the wisdom of the path (*maggapaññā*). It is by the knowledge of the path itself, not by the knowledge of the fruit (*phalañāṇa*).

"Has entered the stream of Dhamma" means he has correctly entered and reached the stream of the noble Dhamma. Because of proceeding toward what is not a wrong course (*anaya*) and proceeding toward what is a right course (*aya*).
Because he does not fail to take refuge even from the world with its devas, he belongs to the side of the Noble Ones and has transcended the plane of the worldlings.
"With penetrative wisdom" means with the wisdom that pierces through the four noble truths. It "stands having reached" [its object] at the moment of the Path;
however, at the moment of the Fruit, it is said to be "standing as having reached" [the goal].
The commentary on the *Paccayasutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Bhikkhusutta*. 28.

This discourse is entirely clear in every respect, as it follows the method already established in the seventh [discourse]; for this sutta was spoken with the intention of training those who are to be disciplined (*vineyyajjhāsayavasena*).
The Teacher’s teaching is handed down as having been taught by the Teacher on another occasion and as being purposeful due to the specific context of the assembly;
thus, it is dependent upon those who receive it, and so they indeed include it in the collection out of reverence for the Dhamma.
The commentary on the Bhikkhu-sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta. 29.
"Of those who recite syllables" means those who delight in syllables (*akkhara-rucīnaṃ*). Even with a prefix, the word *ruci* can mean "to delight. Therefore he said, "For they," and so forth.
The commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins (Dutiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasutta).
30. "In two discourses" refers to the ninth and tenth discourses.
The commentary on the Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins is concluded.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Ten Powers is finished.
4. The Chapter on the Kaḷāra Khattiya. 1.
Commentary on the Bhūta Sutta.
31. By the young brahmin Ajita: by the young brahmin named "Ajita" among the sixteen attendants of the brahmin Bāvari.

"Saṅkhāta" means wisdom; those by whom phenomena (*dhammā*) have been reckoned—that is, fully understood—are "those who have reckoned the phenomena," meaning those who have penetrated the truths and whose taints are exhausted.
However, those in training (*sekkhā*) are not called "those who have reckoned the phenomena" because they have not yet fully understood the result [of their practice].
They are not so called [as "ordinary persons"]. They are "trainees" (sekkhā) by virtue of being endowed with the qualities of a trainee.

While these individuals may indeed number in the thousands according to their specific personal attainments, they are not more than seven types when defined by the commonality of possessing the four paths and the three lower fruits.
Thus, having restricted the number by saying "seven types," he distinguishes them. [This refers to] defilement and the objects of censure; from that...
Or, one who protects the world by training it as if it were oneself is called *nipaka*; the state of being such is *nepakka*.
He said, "Knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is what is meant by *nepakka*; because he is endowed with that, he is *nipaka*.
Thinking, "What indeed is the meaning of this question? one wavers regarding the question; thus, one is said to "doubt" (*kaṅkhati*) concerning the question. "How, in answering..."
Thinking, "Am I not now contradicting the Teacher's intention? he is said to be "doubting" (kaṅkhati) regarding that intention.
Here, "doubt" (kaṅkhā) is intended as the act of reflecting after having determined the meaning of what is easily understood; it is not "perplexity" (vicikicchā).

For the Great Elder, having abandoned perplexity, was right there in the presence of the Venerable Assaji the Great Elder; rather, this is a mere investigation consisting of a form of scrutiny similar to remorse (kukkucca).
It should be understood thus: "carrying the bowl" (*pattaṃ ādāya caranto*) is a characteristic mark of the state of one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*).
Alternatively, the meaning here should be seen as: "carrying the burden of my teaching of the Dhamma, by virtue of being the General of the Dhamma.
"Born" (*jātaṃ*) means arisen from appropriate conditions; the sense is "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*). "The answering of the question presented itself" (*pañhabyākaraṇaṃ upaṭṭhāsī*): [text continues].
The manner of answering the question occurred to him. The reading is “sammappaññāya passatī” (he sees with right wisdom);
however, in the Aṭṭhakathā, having cited the phrase “sammappaññāya passato,” the meaning “of one who sees” was stated.
That does not accord with this text, “‘It is real’ … pe … he is one who has entered upon the way”; therefore, the reading as it has been shown is indeed appropriate. Up to... [end of fragment]

They say the term refers to the factors associated with the path to arahantship for the sake of disenchantment (*nibbidā*) and so forth, by virtue of the qualities that are to be pacified. "Arising from nutriment" means having conditions as its cause.
The "way of practice for those in training" (*sekkha-paṭipadā*) is stated because of the expression: "he is practicing for the sake of disenchantment, for dispassion, and for cessation.
This same method applies to the section on cessation as well. "Disenchantment" is used here in the instrumental sense as a nominative case; [the sequence is] "for dispassion, for cessation."
Because the word is used in the sense of an ablative (nissakkavacana), he says, "All [the terms] are words expressing a cause.
He states, "This has come to be" (*bhūtamidam*), and so forth, while treating the entire sutta as the very word of the Victor (*jinavacana*) spoken directly.
The commentary on the *Bhūta-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Kaḷāra Sutta 32.

The name of that elder was derived from his birth. He was called "Nivatta" (Turned Back) because he had previously begun to go against the stream of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭasota*), but being unable to endure that, he was going with the stream; having turned back from that, he is one who has dispelled all afflictions (*pariklesa*).

He is unassociated and detached. Here, "volition" (cetanā) is a term for reassurance (*assāsa*). By showing that "returning to the inferior" means having expectations regarding sense pleasures, while "not having such expectations" results from the attainment of the third path, he said, "the three paths," and so forth.

The disciple’s knowledge of perfection (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*) was accomplished by the Elder through his attainment of Arahatship; therefore, for him, that [knowledge] is stated as the reassurance at the highest limit.

“Opened up” (*ugghāṭitā*) means uncovered; the meaning is that they have been stilled. “Therein” (*tattha*) refers to the attainment of Arahatship. “The state of being free from doubt” (*vicikicchābhāvaṃ*) means the condition of having no more perplexity.

“Not declared in such a way” means it was not declared in such a plain manner as “birth is exhausted,” and so forth; however, it was declared by way of a figurative method (*pariyāyena*). “By anyone” (*kenaci*) means by any cause whatsoever. “He will declare it in such a plain manner.
“Of that condition” (*tassa paccayassa*) refers to the exhaustion of that condition known as kamma-existence, together with its co-operative factor, ignorance (*avijjā*).
"Through the destruction, non-arising, and cessation of that which has been grasped. "In what is destroyed" means in that which has been exhausted.
When the conditions for birth, as previously described, have ceased through non-arising and cessation, the fruit designated as "birth" is destroyed and brought to a state of non-occurrence.
It is "known" (vidita) and "understood" (ñāta). One "fully understands" (ājānāti) the Four Truths by penetrating them without overstepping what has already been known through the lower paths.
"Full knowledge" (*aññā*) is the supreme path (*aggamagga*). Here, the fruit of the supreme path (*aggaphala*) is called "full knowledge" by way of metaphorical designation.
"Condition" (*paccaya*) refers to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), which is the condition for the arising of existence.

"By me" (*me*) means by myself. "He understood" (*aññāsi*) means he knew the movement of the mind by grasping its mode. "By him" (*tena*) means by the Blessed One. The "explanation" (*byākaraṇa*) was expressed as a blessing (*anumodita*), because it was made the subject of the answer to the question.
"This is his domain" means that this feeling is within the domain of the Elder Sāriputta, because it occurs there as an object of his range.
"Even though" means: even though pleasant feeling is happy in its persistence, painful feeling is happy in its change, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is happy through knowledge.
"By way of the limit of change" means by way of their impermanent nature—all feelings indeed [are subject to change].
It is called "suffering" (dukkha). For it is suffering by way of being the opposite of pleasure; by way of the intensity of the pervasion of the rapture of pleasure;
by way of changeability, because it lacks permanence; and by way of the moment of the cessation of pleasure, through the attainment of its non-existence.
Thus it is said in the *Papañcasūdanī*: "The state of existence of a pleasant feeling is 'pleasure'. One who desires pleasure [finds] suffering...
He endures it. For those who have not fully understood the basis [of feeling], the cessation of pleasant feeling appears as suffering;
therefore, this meaning should be illustrated by way of separation. The same method applies here to the statement, "Pleasant [feeling] is suffering because of its change.
Thus it is said in the *Papañcasūdanī*: "The absence of painful feeling is 'pleasure'. For the cessation of painful feeling is what is meant by "pleasure" in the cases already mentioned.
They say that it indeed arises. Through the subsiding of that exertion, the state of knowing through neutral feeling—“Oh, happiness has arisen!”—is happiness as understood according to reality.
Even the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is happiness for one who discerns it, because of its subtle nature and its state of being cognizable.
Just as with material and immaterial phenomena, [it is known] by way of their specific characteristics and general characteristics.
And right awakening is the supreme happiness. Therefore it was said:
"From whatever [aspect] one comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one gains rapture and gladness; that is the deathless for one who understands."
"Ignorance as suffering" means that the state of non-knowing is the suffering of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. The nature of knowledge is the arising of correct discernment.
For neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling associated with knowledge and supported by knowledge has a praiseworthy aspect, since it is both desirable and has desirable results.
The phrase "the state of non-knowing" should be understood here according to the opposite of what was stated above.
It is to be understood. Regarding the phrase “known as suffering,” while this is the reading in the *pāḷi*, the word *vidita* has been extracted in the *Aṭṭhakathā*;
however, that should be regarded as merely an illustration of the meaning.
“In the knowing of the delimitation of feelings” means in the knowing by way of delimitation thus: “These three are feelings. “He knew” means...
When did he know this? They say it was at the time of the teaching, but it is more appropriate to say it was at the time of penetration;

for it is the feeling as it was penetrated that was taught here by the Elder. "For this reason" means by the reason consisting in the knowledge of the state of suffering due to the impermanence of feelings—namely, that "whatever is impermanent is suffering.
For it is on account of that [knowledge] that his craving for feelings [ceased].
It does not arise. "Excessive prolixity" means excessive elaboration. It is included within suffering because it is comprised within suffering.

"Suffering": all that is felt is suffering by virtue of its nature as the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*). "Merely upon knowing" means merely upon understanding according to reality.
"Craving does not remain" means it does not persist; it does not proceed.
"How liberated" means they are liberated from the distinctions between the internal and the external. In this context, the word "from" (*nissakka-vacana*) expresses the sense of cause;
thus, by using the instrumental case in the sense of cause, it states the meaning as "by which liberation.

Alternatively, this word "from" is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), and so it is stated in that way. "Adherence" (*abhiniveso*) refers to the commencement of insight (*vipassanā*). External phenomena (*bahiddhādhammā*) are also indeed to be seen.
Because everything that is to be fully understood must be fully understood. Having set forth knowledge. "Those" refers to internal formations.
"Having defined" means having delimited them by way of their specific characteristics. "He extends it outward" means he extends knowledge into external formations.
"He extends it inward" means he contemplates internal formations. "Therein" means in that tetrad.
"At the time of their defining" means at the time of insight (*vipassanā*) regarding those internal formations.
"Through the destruction of all clinging" means through the total destruction of all forms of clinging.

While it is true that the clinging to views, to rules and observances, and to a doctrine of self are destroyed by the first path alone, the clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) is destroyed by the final path; therefore, it is said "through the destruction of all clinging" with reference to that.
Speaking thus, the Elder declares his own attainment of Arahatship. Therefore he said: "The taints do not flow. By the word "mindful" (sato), he demonstrates the perfection of his mindfulness.

"They flow from the eye toward forms" means that the taints having form as their object arise within the cognitive process of eye-consciousness and the subsequent cognitive process of mind-consciousness.
Although there is also the occurrence of wholesome states and so forth therein, [the taints referred to are] the taints of sensual desire and the rest.
Just as pus flows from a wound, they flow with a nature of oozing impurity; so it is in the remaining cases. Therefore he said, "Thus," and so forth;
for that reason, these alone are called "āsava" (taints). For in this context, the word *āsava* is conventionally established in the sense of oozing impurity.
Because it was stated, "I do not despise myself," he said, "the abandoning of self-depreciation is taught. By that [statement], regarding the taints...
It should be understood that this is stated as an illustration of the group as a whole. For one does not abandon inferior conceit alone without abandoning superior conceit and the rest.
"Full understanding" means he is endowed with the full understanding expressed as, "There is no more of this state of being.

"Also by way of specific distinction" means also by way of defining the number, such as "four. The connection is: "The Blessed One spoke this, demonstrating [this]. And the word "this" refers to the statement beginning with, "This too... and so forth.
"Asambhinnāya eva" means exactly as she was sitting; "avutṭhitāya eva" is the meaning.

"Puggalathomanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of praising and exalting individuals such as the Elder Ānanda and others who are skilled in teaching. "Dhammathomanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of praising the Dhamma of practice.
"Tepi" refers to those monks, such as the Elder Ānanda and others, who were recipients of the Dhamma.
"Bhikkhus" refers to the monks. "Attha" means the meaning of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.

"Dhamma" refers to the *pāḷi* (the canonical text). "Assa" refers to the Blessed One. He will demonstrate his power through the passage beginning with, "Even if the Blessed One were to [teach] for a day," and so on. "Naṃ" refers to the Elder Sāriputta.
I too shall praise him in the same way through the passage beginning with, "For he, O bhikkhus," and so on. "Thus he thought" means as follows, according to what is about to be said.
He reflected in the manner he had previously contemplated regarding the teaching on the heirs of the Dhamma. Therefore, he said, "Just as," and so forth.

"Of one intention" means of a common purpose. "With wisdom" means with *paññā*. This was said because the Blessed One, considering that this teaching is supreme, thus extols the General of the Dhamma (*Dhammasenāpati*) by way of his qualities.
“Having made manifest” means having made it evident and well-known by way of its qualities, desiring to establish him in the state of being the foremost among all disciples.

By the turning of the body according to the movement of the mind—that is, through the mental power of the intention (*adhiṭṭhāna*) that “may this body become like this mind”—because the body comes to share the same course as the mind.
But how can the body, which functions slowly, [be made to follow] the rapid transformation [of the mind]?
“Does it go to the same destination as the mind? It does not go to the same destination in every respect.

For while the mind goes to the same destination as the body in every respect when the mind undergoes transformation according to the body, at that time the mind cannot persist for the duration of a moment of material phenomena—which proceed slowly—without ceasing within its own naturally established moment. [This is because... “This... ”

Furthermore, by means of the resolution, "Let this mind be like this body," because the slow-moving body follows the mind, the mind—proceeding in a continuous stream in accordance with the movement of the body until it reaches the desired location—is said to have been transformed by the movement of the body.
Likewise, [one resolves]: "Let this body be like this mind."

Because it was accomplished through resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*)—and even more so through the perception of ease and lightness—it does not proceed slowly like those who have not developed the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).
Rather, it is understood that the nature of the form as it occurs is such that it reaches the desired location in just a few light moments of consciousness.
This is because the praise of the Blessed One was performed in accordance with his very intention; for this particular matter, the Blessed One...
"He will ask" means that he did not previously know or see it. "For the purpose of knowing the Teacher’s intention" means:
"By answering in this way, the Teacher’s intention is grasped"—thus, for the purpose of knowing the Teacher’s intention.
When the Blessed One asked the second question, he approved of the first question; for by the very act of asking the second question, [the answer to] the first question was provided.
Because it has the nature of being received.
"This was" means this reflection occurred. "Of him" refers to the bhikkhu Kaḷāra-Khattiya.

"It burns regarding phenomena" means the element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), which is the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections; it burns regarding phenomena within the domain of the disciple, grasping them as they truly are.
The meaning is "having made [it], he establishes it. Therefore he said, "the dharma-element," and so forth. It has as its object only that which falls within the range of omniscient knowledge.
Regarding "gocara-dhamma": it refers to the knowable phenomena (ñeyya-dhamma) that constitute the field of activity.
The commentary on the Kaḷāra Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Ñāṇavatthusutta* 33.
Knowledge itself is the "basis of knowledge" (*ñāṇavatthu*) because it is the cause for the attainment [of the fruits].

"In the four" refers to the four types of knowledge described by way of awakening to the Four Noble Truths. "The first" refers to the knowledge stated thus, "knowledge regarding aging-and-death," by means of which—through the processes of retention, familiarization, and attention—...
He grasped all that had arisen. This should be understood as the knowledge consisting of accumulation, which is called "knowledge consisting of hearing.
The knowledge of encompassing these [phenomena] by way of their intrinsic nature and their conditions should be understood as "comprehension-knowledge" (*sammasana-ñāṇa*).

And here, under the heading of aging-and-death, only those phenomena possessing aging-and-death are grasped. "Penetration-knowledge" (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) is the knowledge of penetrating [them] through non-delusion.

“By means of this Dhamma”: here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). For it is by means of the attainment of this Dhamma as the cause that this Noble One fully awakens to the Dhamma of the Four Truths according to the method of the past and the future.
However, in order to show that path-knowledge itself is like a guide for the past and the future, the second alternative, “or by means of the Dhamma of path-knowledge,” was stated. For in this way—
“It is timeless” is established.
“Seen with the eye of knowledge” means seen directly through the eye of knowledge that has become the Dhamma-eye, by way of penetration free from delusion.
“Known by wisdom” means known in that very same way by the wisdom of the Path. Because it is thus...
When it is seen, known, and fully attained, it becomes a great means; therefore, it is said, "by one who has fathomed it.
Alternatively, "by what is seen" means by vision—that is, by one who stands having seen the Dhamma. "By what is known" means by one who stands having known and made manifest the Four Truths.
"By what is timeless" means not by that which yields its fruit after an interval of time. "By what is attained" refers to the Four Truths.
"By one who has attained" means by one who stands having attained the Dhamma. "By one who has plunged into" means by one who stands having plunged into the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
"He leads the method regarding the past and the future" means he leads, carries, and directs the method concerning both the past and the future.
This, however, is the function of the knowledge of review; the Teacher, moreover, made the knowledge of the path similar to leading [the way] for the past and the future.
Because it is rooted in that. For there is indeed a reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa) of the past path;
therefore, path-knowledge (maggañāṇa) is said to be like the leader, while reviewing-knowledge leads the way. Hence he said, "And here," and so forth.
To show the manner in which it leads the way by means of that [reviewing], he stated, "Whosoever... and so forth. And herein, the production of the leading is—
It is simply a specific mode of the activity of the knowledge of guidance (*naya-ñāṇa*). Therefore it is said: "the function of the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*).

Although it is stated, "by means of this [dhamma]—that is, by means of the dhamma of path-knowledge," nevertheless, the two-fold knowledge of the path and fruit is the primary cause for the reviewing of the knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*), but not for the knowledge of guidance.
Thus, it is not incorrect to say "by means of the two-fold dhamma of knowledge. Likewise, regarding the dhamma of the Four Truths...

Because it has known [the truth], or because it has attained association with the penetration of the truths (sacca-paṭivedha) consisting of the path and its fruit, the meaning “let there be guidance” is not untenable;
for by that phrase “by this Dhamma,” there is the state of being an object for knowledge, and through association with knowledge, it is also understood as “by what was previously unknown.
In the term *anvaya*, it refers to the knowledge of awakening (*buñjana-ñāṇa*) regarding the goal (*aya*) in accordance with the knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhamma-ñāṇa*). Of those [knowledges] seen...

It is so called because it brings about the seeing of what was previously unseen, and because it makes known the state of having seen that which was not yet seen. Therefore he said: "Knowledge in the following of the knowledge of the Dhamma.
The stage of the trainee (*sekkhabhūmi*) for one whose taints are destroyed refers to the moment of the supreme path (*aggamagga*). But why is this stated in such a way?
Because the teaching proceeds by way of the present tense, as in: "In this way one understands aging-and-death," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Ñāṇavatthusutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the Second *Ñāṇavatthusutta*. 34. *Sattarī*:
this is stated with the substitution of the letter *ra* for the letter *ta*. Alternatively, the word *sattari* has the same meaning as the word *sattati*.

They are called "reciters of the phrasing" (*byañjanabhāṇaka*) because they recite the phrasing according to their preference for the phrasing. Therefore, he said, "having made it with much phrasing," and so forth.

It is a "station" (*ṭhiti*) because the fruit stands there, owing to its dependence upon that [cause]. The "station of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhiti*) is the station of a phenomenon characterized by the present.
Alternatively, "phenomenon" (*dhamma*) means cause; the meaning is "condition. That which is the inherent nature of the station of a phenomenon—

Since there is nothing other than the Dhamma [for its own persistence], it is the "establishment of the Dhamma" (dhammaṭṭhiti), which is to say, the condition. Knowledge regarding that is "knowledge of the establishment of the Dhamma" (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa).
Thus the Venerable Dhammasenāpati said: "Wisdom in the discernment of conditions is knowledge of the establishment of the Dhamma.

Likewise he said: "Knowledge of the mode of conditions," and so forth. In this context, "of phenomena" (dhammānaṃ) means of those phenomena arisen through conditions. "As the cause for the persistence of their occurrence" means...

Because it is the cause for the persistence known as the process of existence (*pavatti*). By means of the three periods of time—through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—there is the sixfold knowledge regarding the statement, "With birth as condition, aging-and-death [comes to be]," and so forth.
"Destruction" (*khaya*) means dissolution; that itself is "breakup" (*bheda*).
"Fading away" (*virajjana*) means crumbling away. "Cessation" (*nirujjhana*) means disappearance. "In each one" refers to each individual factor among aging-and-death and the rest.

Previously, by the term "knowledge of things as they really are" (*yathābhūtañāṇa*), nascent insight (*taruṇavipassanā*) was meant. Therefore, here too, taking the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) as insight, it is said that "insight and counter-insight" have been explained.
The commentary on the Second Knowledge Basis Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Condition of Ignorance (Avijjāpaccayasutta) "35.
He brought the teaching to a conclusion" means he set aside the discourse as it had been commenced.

This was because he intended to speak further in order to shatter the views held by the proponent of false views who was seated there. For [the Buddha] would not allow the opportunity for the Buddhas' teaching to be interrupted.

There is no one capable of questioning him. Therefore he said, "for the purpose of granting an opportunity to the holder of a wrong view. This is a difficult question because it is asked on the basis of the apprehension of a being (*sattūpaladdhi*).

By the phrase "the doctrine of the apprehension of a being" (*sattūpaladdhivādapadena*), it refers to the words that manifest the view occurring in the form, "A being, a soul (*jīva*), is apprehended.
It is called a "doctrine" (*vāda*) because they speak by means of it. Furthermore, the word "view" (*diṭṭhi*) includes two types.
But since living the holy life (*brahmacariyavāsa*) is, in the ultimate sense, the cultivation of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), he says "dwelling in the Noble Path.
"This view" refers to the view that the body and the soul are non-different; they call the soul simply "life-force" (*jīva*).
"The cycle" (*vaṭṭa*) is twofold. "Bringing to cessation" means causing it to reach the state of non-arising. "Cutting off" means by bringing about its non-occurrence.
"Cutting off": this is to be construed as "the round of existence (vaṭṭa), which must be ceased by the Path, is being ceased.

When there exists—that is, when there is the actual reality of—the mode apprehended by the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*), namely, "this sentient being, having reached destruction and non-existence, is utterly annihilated," [the statement] "it does not exist" is not meaningful.
"It goes" means that having emerged from the body, it departs. "Turning away" (*vivaṭṭento*) means bringing about non-occurrence;

it cannot turn away because it is impossible to bring about the non-occurrence of something permanent. False view pierces right view by way of associating with persons who are not concentrated and by way of failing to provide the conditions for such [right view] to arise, thus through the non-abandoning of what ought to be abandoned.
It pierces right view. "Like a thorn" means like a splinter. It is not merely non-conformable;
it is also contradictory, because it makes known the nature of things as they proceed by way of [wrong views] such as "permanent. "Virūpa" means deformed, loathsome, quivering, or writhing.
The palmyra tree itself, being the basis for the leaves, flowers, fruits, and shoots, is called "tālāvatthu."

It is like the conventional expression, “the auspicious in the inauspicious. Some, however, read it as “tālavatthukatāni,” meaning they have been made like a palm tree because they have become like a stump (avatthu).
Therefore he said, “like a palm tree cut at the top. *Anubhāva* means destruction.
The commentary on the sutta concerning the condition of ignorance (*avijjāpaccaya*) is finished.
6. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Condition of Ignorance (Dutiya-avijjā-paccaya-sutta).

36. *Iti vā* means "in this way. This refers to whoever might speak of aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) and the owner of aging-and-death according to the momentary perspective. Being of a nature lacking confidence, he became abashed due to his inability to answer the question; therefore, it is said: "He is not able to ask.
The commentary on the Second Discourse on the Condition of Ignorance is concluded.
7. Commentary on the *Natumhasutta* 37.
As for the phrase "Not yours," this is precisely the demonstration of the body's lack of self-ownership (*anattaniyatā*).
To show that lack of self-ownership, it is said: "In the self... and so forth. [An objection: "If it is not one's own, then it must belong to another. To that, [it is replied]: "That too..."
Showing that it does not exist [independently], he said, "nor of others. This body is not merely past karma;
thus, the physical frame referred to as "this body" is not simply past karma, for the body is not of the same nature as feeling (*vedanā*).

"By way of a metaphorical designation for the cause" means by way of a figurative expression for the condition. "Conditioned," etc., is expressed in the neuter gender. "Because of its similarity in nature to the previous gender" refers to the phrase "this karma is old."
This is because it shares the same grammatical gender as the preceding [terms] stated thus.
It is called "conditioned" (*abhisaṅkhata*) because it is produced by conditions that come together and face one another; therefore he says, "it should be understood as 'made by conditions'.

"Volitionally intended" (*abhisañcetayita*) means that which has been intended and fashioned by way of the state of facing [the object], which is designated as being thus conditioned; the meaning is that it has been set in motion.
“Having volition as its basis” means having volition as its cause. “To be felt” means beneficial to feeling by way of being its basis and object, because it serves as a condition for feeling.
Therefore he said, “bases to be felt.
The commentary to the *Natumha Sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the Cetanā Sutta 38.
Regarding the phrase *yañca*, the particle *ca* here is used out of its usual place.

By this, it illuminates the fact that, just as with volition (*cetanā*), the objects of intention (*pakappa*) and underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are likewise to be understood as the undifferentiated objective bases for the persistence of consciousness, which will be explained later. Granted, in all three locations, the verb "makes proceed" (*pavatteti*) alone [is used].
The general meaning has been stated; however, the specific meaning of "turning" (*vattanattha*) should be understood as the distinct functions of volition and so forth, namely:

intending, planning, and underlying tendency, respectively. This is intended to specify the conditions for kamma-consciousness (*kammaviññāṇa*), wherein wholesome and unwholesome volitions of the three planes are included.
The intention is that craving and views are included according to their respective roles. For indeed, in all eight types of greed-accompanied consciousness...
The "conception through craving" (taṇhākappa) refers to that [craving], while among those four, the "conception through views" (diṭṭhikappa) is intended.

Granted, latent tendencies (anusaya) do indeed underlie even mundane wholesome volitions (cetanā), but because their active manifestation (pavatti) is evident in unwholesome states, it is said: "of twelve volitions. Regarding the phrase "by way of co-nascence" (sahajātakoṭiyā):
this is stated because even present lust for sense-pleasures (kāmarāga) and so forth are called "latent tendencies" due to their similarity to them. For it is not...

There is a distinction of characteristics based on the difference in time. For it is only future states such as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and the rest that, in the primary sense, deserve to be called "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*).
Since what arises from conditions is appropriate [to be so designated], he says: "The object is the condition.

"For the persistence of karmic consciousness" means for the very occurrence of karmic consciousness itself. "When that condition exists" refers to that which is designated as the latent tendency consisting in the mental formation of volition (*cetanā*).
When a condition exists, there is a foundation for consciousness. It is precisely because of its capacity to yield fruit within the continuum that it is said, "there is a foundation;
when it is founded. By way of the decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*), it is "grown. For by the term "founded," the state of having been performed by the karma is expressed;
by the term "grown," the state of having been accumulated is expressed. Therefore he said: "Kamma..."

"Having caused [it] to reach [its fruit]," and so forth. In this context, because it has obtained conditions through the volitions of karma that arose previously, the kamma-consciousness—by means of the decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*) which has attained strength—becomes firmly established and possesses grown roots; thus it is said:
"when the root has been produced. For in that way, the decisive volition, by way of an immediately succeeding birth, gives rise to the result (*vipāka*).
"It gives karma to be experienced upon rebirth.

"Of the volition belonging to the three planes" means: of the wholesome and unwholesome volition belonging to the three planes. "The moment of non-occurrence" here refers to the moment of occurrence, the moment of arising.

It is not only the moment of dissolution that is the moment of non-occurrence for one whose underlying tendencies have not been abandoned; rather, the moment of arising is also a moment of non-occurrence [of the result].
Because it is intended [in this sense]. "By way of the limit of not having been abandoned" means by way of its state of being uncut.

This refers to the fact that when wholesome and unwholesome volitions of the three planes are not occurring, there is no occurrence of the underlying tendencies (anusaya) by way of co-nascence (sahajāta) and so forth;

rather, they occur by way of the limit of not having been abandoned in the case of resultant states and so on, because for one who is performing [a kamma], they are absent. It is said with reference to this meaning. "Because of not being obstructed" means in the presence of an opposite [state].
Because it is not to be prevented, it becomes a condition for the persistence of consciousness.
Having shown the round (*vaṭṭa*) by means of the first and second sections, the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*) is shown in the third section by the words "If not," and so forth;
thus it was said: "In the first phrase, wholesome and unwholesome volitions of the three planes are excluded," and so on. In that context, "excluded" means because they are not performed.

They have departed from non-occurrence; the construction is that craving and views have ceased. "In the aforementioned types" means in the types mentioned by the phrase "in the kamma-results of the three planes," and so forth.
"Here" means in this sutta. Here, the delimitation of phenomena is shown by way of the occurrence of volition and mental application;
thus, it is demonstrated right here that the method beginning with "one intends" includes the wholesome and unwholesome volitions of the three planes.

"Fourfold" refers to the four unwholesome volitions (akusalacetanā) associated with the two roots of aversion and delusion. "In the four unwholesome volitions" means precisely in those four unwholesome volitions as already stated;
however, the others are excluded by the negation in the phrase "does not intend.
This is said having excluded what is mentioned in the Sutta, namely, by way of negation in the Sutta: "And he does not intend."

Having excluded what has already arrived. For by the phrase “he does not form a resolve,” the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) that occurs simultaneously with the eight greed-associated consciousnesses is excluded, because those consciousnesses do not arise [at that moment]. Therefore, the meaning is: having set aside that state.
It should be understood as being similar to the preceding [cases], according to the method stated in the previous sections, because it is a classification of phenomena (*dhammapariccheda*).

In the term *tadappatiṭṭhite*, the case ending is elided due to its being a compound (*samāsa*). The letter *da* is inserted by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*). "Not established in that" is *tadappatiṭṭhitaṃ*;
[the locative form] *tasmiṃ tadappatiṭṭhite* means "in that which is not established in that. Thus, the formation of the compound word here should be understood in this manner.
"Therein" (*ettha*) means in this third stage; the function of the path of arahantship has been explained, because it completely breaks the arising of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
It is appropriate to say that for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), there is "the performance of duties," because of the total rejection of feeling and the other aggregates.

It is also appropriate to say that there are "nine supramundane states," because of the eradication of the underlying tendencies (anusaya) through the sequence of the paths, as well as the fruits immediately following the paths, and Nibbāna, which has both of those as its object.
"Of consciousness" means of kamma-consciousness, under the heading of renewed existence.
Since "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is included within the intermediate existence, or rather, it is understood as the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa) itself, he says:
"And there is one link in the interval of renewed existence. Regarding the phrase "of the types of existence," this should be understood through a successive sequence, such as:
"from birth in a second existence to birth in a third existence. However, by the mention of the production of renewed existence in the future, it does not follow immediately [without an interval].
It should be understood that *kammabhava* (kamma-existence) is included here, and it is stated that the establishment of the cause and fruit of birth is intended in this context.

Furthermore, regarding this, the Blessed One—in the second method, at the preliminary stage—spoke thus: "If, monks, one does not intend and does not resolve, yet there is still a latent tendency (*anuseti*).

In this way, even for one who has seen the danger in the various states of existence, there is the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome kamma that produces existence, as well as the act of resolving (*pakappana*).

It is stated for the purpose of showing that even the volition of insight (vipassanā-cetanā) of a yogi can produce rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) due to the condition of underlying tendencies (anusaya-paccaya);

and also for the purpose of showing that even when there is no occurrence of wholesome or unwholesome [kamma], at that time, because of the condition of defilements (kilesa) that lie dormant (anusayita) to the extent they have not been abandoned among the existing resultant and other phenomena of the three planes, there is the establishment of kamma-consciousness (kamma-viññāṇa) excluding existence (bhava). "He does not intend... [is said].
“...he intends and he underlies [it]”—this method is not accepted because there can be no intending without volition (*cetanā*).
The commentary on the *Cetanā-sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the Second *Cetanā-sutta*.

39. Between consciousness (*viññāṇa*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there is one connection (*sandhi*): the connection between cause and fruit. This is because, by the mention of "consciousness," karmic consciousness is included. Furthermore, it is self-evident that "name-and-form" refers specifically to resultant name-and-form.
The rest is easily understood. The commentary on the Second Cetanā Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Third Cetanā Sutta.
40. Regarding the six objects, beginning with visible form (*rūpa*). By this, the three realms of existence (*bhava*) are here subsumed, because they are included within the six objects.

The inclination (*nati*) toward those very three realms occurs by way of aspiration (*paṇidhāna*), longing, and so forth. It is called "coming" (*āgati*) because it is a movement or occurrence directed toward [the object] by way of its manifestation;
thus, "coming" refers to the sign of karma and so on, wherein the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) arises.

There is the movement, the proceeding, and the arising. Therefore he said, “When it has come,” and so forth. “Death and rebirth”: death (*cuti*) is passing away, dying; rebirth (*upapāta*) is the process of being born, arising.
Rebirth from death is re-arising. Therefore he said, “Thus of consciousness,” and so forth. “From here” means from the state that has arisen.
“Therein” means in the future existence designated as renewed becoming (*punabbhava*). “Only one link (*sandhi*)” means one—
Only the connection between cause and fruit has been explained.
The commentary on the Third Cetanā Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Kaḷārakhattiya Vagga is finished.
5. Gahapativagga 1.
Pañcaverabhayasuttavaṇṇanā 41.
*Yato* means at which time. For this word *to* here has the sense of time, just like the word *dā*. Therefore he said: "when."
"Bhayaveracetanāyo" refers to volitions (cetanā) that have received the name "fear" (bhaya) in the sense of being something to be feared, and "enmity" (vera) in the sense of producing enmity.

For those for whom acts such as the destruction of life (pāṇātipāta) proceed, and those directed toward whom they proceed—both are "with fear and terror" because they themselves generate the fear and enmity that are to be feared. From the beginning of that noble path (ariyamagga)...

The attainment of the practice starting from that point is stream-entry (*sotāpatti*); the factors for one established therein for the sake of that [attainment] are the factors of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-aṅgāni*).
Referring to both of these, it is said: "The factor of stream-entry is twofold," meaning a factor for the purpose of stream-entry.
"That which is in the prior stage" means that which leads to that purpose in the stage prior to the actual acquisition of the path and fruit of stream-entry.

But what is that? He says: "Association with good persons," and so forth. Association with good persons—such as the Buddhas and others—is the act of attending upon them who possess the mark of noble knowledge.

Hearing the true Dhamma is hearing the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. Systematic attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) is the mental engagement with [the truths] from the perspective of impermanence and so forth by means of the proper method (*upāya*).
Striving is the practice in accordance with the Dhamma of Nibbāna by one who exerts himself.
"Practice in accordance with the Dhamma" (dhammānudhammapaṭipatti) refers to these factors of stream-entry.
However, in the commentary, it is stated that "it has come down thus" in view of the term "factor of stream-entry. It is a factor for a person who stands [in that state].

It is also called a "factor of one who has entered the stream" (sotāpannassa aṅgaṃ) because by means of this, the stream-enterer is defined or known. This is the factor mentioned last. "Far from faults" (ārakā dosehi).
He said, "The Noble One," meaning "faultless" (*niddosa*). How so? Because he cannot be refuted by anyone through such arguments as "how can ignorance be a condition for volitional formations?

thus he is "beyond reproach" (*nirupārambha*). Some say that "faultless" is stated with reference to knowledge (*ñāṇa*), while "beyond reproach" is stated with reference to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
Others, however, maintain that both terms are stated with reference to both. But here, dependent origination is intended.
For it has been said: “by means of the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā) that arises again and again. For the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa) is not itself the wisdom of insight.

Because it is the correct means (sammā-upāya), it is called *ñāya*—that by which dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is known as it truly is regarding things arisen dependently; thus it is dependent origination.
But *ñāṇa* is called *ñāya* because one knows by means of it.
*Therein* means in hell. *Stream of the path* means the stream of the path. *Attained* means reached.

One whose nature is to fall into the states of loss (*apāya*), which is defined as arising in those states, is one "whose nature is to fall" (*vinipātadhamma*). One who does not have that nature is "one whose nature is not to fall" (*avinipātadhamma*).
*It goes beyond* means it must be traversed and understood exceedingly well within its own domain. For those verbal roots whose meaning is "going," they also possess the sense of "understanding."
This is their meaning. Therefore he said, "one who will certainly awaken.
"Because of committing the deed of taking life" means because of performing the evil deed known as *pāṇātipāta*. "Enmity" (*vera*) is called opposition;
since that very thing is to be feared, it is "fear," thus he said, "in meaning, 'fear' and 'enmity' are one. This is the external [danger].
“Vera” (enmity) is so called because it exists externally to the person who constitutes the source of that enmity, which is its root.
For this very reason, with reference to the enmity arisen toward that person who acts as the source of enmity, it is said: “This is what is called internal enmity.
Thus, the volition of the person acting as the source of enmity—which is the root of the enmity dependent upon that [external object]—arises even in one who is unable to strike back.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). For those in hell are not able to strike back at the hell-wardens.
By the statement "an intention arises in the hell-warden," it is shown that "there are hell-wardens in hell.

As for this "external enmity" (*bāhiravera*), it refers to whatever external enmity exists both pertaining to the present life and the future life. "Personal enmity" (*puggalavera*) refers to what has been described as one's own duty (*attakicca*).
Being unable to accomplish it, one regards it merely as enmity that has arisen toward another person.

In terms of meaning, it is stated as a single term, distinguished as “mental factor” (*cetasika*). Regarding the remaining phrases: in the other sections that appear in the sequence beginning with “due to taking what is not given,” the meaning is “broken”;
thus, the meaning is exhausted. By “attained” means attained by the path; it may also be read as “fully attained” (*abhigatena*).
The meaning is "by what has been admitted"; thus he said, "with unshakable confidence.
The commentary on the *Pañcaverabhayasutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second *Pañcaverabhayasutta*.

42. By the phrase "the distinction consists merely in the fact that it was spoken to the bhikkhus," it is shown that whatever teaching was taught by the Teacher to some individuals, and was later taught at another time to others who were to be trained by him—being skilled in training those to be converted—the compilers of the Dhamma recorded separately, thinking:
"Lest the Teacher’s teaching be lost without being received [in its entirety]."
The commentary on the Second Discourse on the Fear of the Five Enmities is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discourse on Suffering. 43.
"Arising" (*samudaya*) means that which arises; it is called "arising" because suffering arises from this. Thus, the meaning of both these terms [of arising] is the same.
The distinction should be understood. The conditions themselves are the origin of conditions.

One who has begun insight meditation, seeing that "these phenomena arise moment by moment in dependence upon this and that convergence of conditions," is said to be "a bhikkhu who, while seeing the origin of conditions, also sees the momentary origin. This is stated by way of showing the conditions for the moment of their production.
...from the perspective of seeing. Furthermore, having begun to see the arising of formations moment by moment, he sees:
"By means of these very conditions, they arise. They say: "Seeing the momentary origination, he sees the condition.
For, while seeing the arising of formations from the perspective of their conditions, his seeing of their arising from the perspective of moments—

For one who sees their arising from moment to moment, the vision of them by way of conditions succeeds with ease, all the more so because the conditions have been correctly grasped; therefore it is said, "even while seeing the arising of conditions," and so forth.

The same method applies to the vision of their passing away (*atthaṅgama*). "Absolute passing away" (*accantatthaṅgama*) is non-occurrence, cessation, Nibbāna. "Dissolution passing away" (*bhedatthaṅgama*) is momentary cessation.
When one perceives both of these during the preliminary stage through means such as learning and inquiry, the perception of one necessarily establishes the perception of the other.

Furthermore, when perceiving the dissolution and passing away of formations by way of their objects during the preliminary stage—at times such as the contemplation of destruction and vanishing—one perceives their absolute passing away by way of inference and so forth. However, at the moment of the Path, by way of the object...
One sees the ultimate disappearance, and through non-delusion, one also sees the other. With reference to this, he said: "Even while seeing the ultimate disappearance," and so forth.
"The arising and disappearance of the origin" means both the production known as the origin and the dissolution known as the disappearance.
"By way of dependence" means by way of the eye's support as a condition.
"Having made [it] the object": by making form the object. Whatever else needs to be said here should be understood according to the method explained in the *Madhupiṇḍika-sutta-ṭīkā*.

Regarding "the meeting of the three is contact": it is stated that contact arises from the meeting and coming together of these three—eye, forms, and consciousness; thus he says, "contact through the meeting of the three."
The phrase "crossed over" (*tiṇṇa*) is stated by way of the obvious condition; however, others such as attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth are indeed also conditions for contact (*phassa*).

"In this way" means by way of the sequence of the fading away and cessation of craving (*taṇhā*) and the rest without remainder. "Is broken" means it is ceased through non-arising cessation (*anuppāda-nirodha*).
Therefore he said: "without rebirth-connection" (*appaṭisandhiyaṃ*).
The commentary on the *Dukkha-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Loka-sutta*. 44.

"This is the distinction here" means that the phrase "this of the world" demonstrates the distinction between the arising and the passing away [of suffering]. Herein, this is the distinction of the fourth sutta from the third sutta.
The commentary on the Lokasutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Ñātika Sutta: 45.
Since it is said that a village belonging to two relatives is called a "relative's village," he says, "in the village of two relatives."

“Giñjakā” means bricks; a dwelling made of bricks is a “giñjakāvasatha. It is said that this residence was built by piling up and covering it with bricks alone, such that there was no need for plastering work.
Indeed, it was with reference to such a roofing that the Blessed One permitted a roof of bricks. Therefore it is said: “by bricks...”
“...when the great palace was finished. In this context, the door-frames, door-panels, and so forth were made entirely of wood.
It is called a *pariyāya* because it proceeds by encompassing its own fruit; thus he says, “a discourse on the Dhamma (*dhammapariyāya*) means a cause for the Dhamma (*dhammakāraṇa*).
The meaning is that the Dhamma as the formal teaching (*pariyatti*) is the cause for the attainment of distinction. It is called *upassuti* because one listens there after having approached.
It is said: “*Upassuti* means the place of eavesdropping. “One’s own business” refers to the task for which one went there—namely, the act of sweeping the courtyard.
“Having abandoned” means not doing it. For indeed, for one who stands at the head of the *Vimuttāyatana* (the Place of Liberation) and listens in this way, it leads to great benefit.
“It became a single open space” means that everything was uncovered. In the three...

Indeed, as he brought to mind the conditioned states within the realms of existence by way of their arising through conditions, all of that—without exception—came into the range of the Blessed One’s knowledge.
Therefore it was said: “As far as the peak of existence, it became a single plane.
Reciting that meaning with his voice according to the sequence [of the text], he is described as “reciting the text aloud. By way of the condition and the conditionally arisen...
And because the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) was established through the cessation of those [defilements] by bringing forth the meaning, it is said: "according to the sequence" (*yathānusandhinā*).
He saw with the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*).
Reciting mentally, he is described as "making it proficient while remaining silent. "Word by word" (*padānupadaṃ*) means both the word and...
"And word by word": for the preceding is called a "word" (*pada*), and that which follows immediately after it is "word by word" (*anupada*).
Having joined them together, having established a connection, and without interruption—this is what is meant by "mastering," that is, reciting. "Reached the basis" (*ādhārappatta*):

because it has reached the basis, namely the continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*), and because it has been gone over so as not to be forgotten, it is called "reached the basis. "Dependent on the cause": dependent on the cause of supramundane phenomena (*lokuttaradhamma*).
The "limit of the first holy life" (ādibrahmacariyakoti) is the first holy life itself; that very thing is "pertaining to the first holy life" (ādibrahmacariyaka).
The masculine designation is used in view of the discourse on the Dhamma. "In these three" refers to the three suttas—the third, fourth, and fifth.
The commentary on the Ñātika Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Aññatarabrāhmaṇa Sutta. 46.
"By way of name" means he is not well-known either by way of his clan-name or by way of his reputation; therefore, it is said, "a brahmin by way of birth.
The commentary on the Aññatarabrāhmaṇa Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Sutta 47.
"One who has thus obtained a name" means one who has obtained the name "Jāṇussoṇi" from the presence of the king.
The commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Lokāyatika Sutta 48.
It is called *lokāyata* because people do not strive (*yatati*) or exert themselves (*īhati*) for their welfare in the future by means of it.

For, relying upon that doctrine, beings do not even arouse the thought of performing meritorious deeds; how much less the actual application? That [doctrine] belongs to this [person], or else, in that [doctrine]...
“Niyutta” means a Lokāyatika (proponent of worldly philosophy). Because the word “first” (paṭhama) denotes the sense of “beginning,” it is a synonym for “eldest”; thus he said, “the first Lokāyata.
Although the word “world” (loka) is a common term, it is intended here in its specific sense; thus he said, “of the world of foolish worldlings (bāla-puthujjana).
Demonstrating that this [philosophy] is merely an appearance to fools—due to its transience, its hunchback-like nature, and its lack of vastness and so forth—he says:
He said, “long, great,” and so forth. “Limited” means small. “Of a single nature” means having one and the same nature.
He said, “of an unchanging nature,” because he asks, “is it indeed of a permanent nature? “Of a different nature from its previous nature” means having a nature distinct from its previous nature.
“It does not exist later” means that nothing exists at all later on, due to its total cessation. Therefore he said:
“[The Buddha said: ‘He asks with reference to annihilation. *Ekattaṃ* means the continuous existence of a self at all times.

By grasping [the self] in that way, both doctrines constitute the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). “There is not; it does not exist. *Puthuttaṃ* means a manifold nature, or grasping it as not being of a single form;
by grasping [the self] in this way, both doctrines constitute the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).
The commentary on the Lokāyatika Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Ariyasāvaka Sutta: 49.
The arising of doubt and the demonstration of the mode [of reasoning] refers to the question, "When what exists, what comes to be," regarding both cause and fruit.
This is a demonstration of the manner in which doubt arises through mere conditionality (*idappaccayatā*) alone, without recourse to personal experience.
He says "it arises" (*uppajjati*), meaning that it originates (*samudayati*) or emerges (*samudeti*).
The commentary on the *Ariyasāvaka-sutta* is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Second Discourse to the Noble Disciple (Dutiya-ariyasāvaka-sutta) 50.

"Both methods are stated together" means that because the method stated in the ninth discourse—beginning with "When consciousness exists, name-and-form comes to be"—is included within the method stated in the tenth discourse—beginning with "When ignorance exists, volitional formations come to be. "Diversity" (nānatta) refers to...
The distinction between the ninth and the tenth [discourses] from the beginning is thus.
The commentary on the Second Discourse to a Noble Disciple is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Householders is finished.
6. The Chapter on Suffering (Dukkhavagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Investigation (Parivīmaṃsanasutta) 51.
"Investigating" means weighing and scrutinizing the cause for proceeding in saṃsāra and the cause for turning away from it. From what [source]?
"Why is it said 'this'?"—because of the statement, "for the complete destruction of suffering. For the complete destruction of suffering is not possible without an investigation into all suffering.
With the words "Why? and so forth, he asks for the reason why only aging-and-death is mentioned.
The intention is that the occurrence of birth and the other factors is also of the nature of suffering. Since when aging-and-death is grasped, birth is also thereby grasped.
Because in the absence of that [birth], there is likewise the absence of aging-and-death. This same method applies to existence (*bhava*) and the other links as well.

Thus, when aging-and-death is included, everything subject to birth is already included; by means of the term "aging-and-death," all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) belonging to the three realms that possess those characteristics are included.
In this way, by the inclusion of aging-and-death, the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is indeed included.
Therefore he said: "Because when that is grasped, all suffering is grasped. "Of many kinds" (*anekavidha*) means manifold, consisting of many parts.
Alternatively, the reading is "aneka"; "aneka" is a plural expression. "Vidha" refers to a distorted part by way of being broken, split, and so forth.
"Of various modes" (*nānappakāraka*) means for that very reason it is of diverse types. "Like a man standing after bathing" refers to the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of fools.
He spoke with reference to its manifestation in the form of beauty (*subhākāra*).

When it was said, "by way of its suitability" (*sāruppabhāvena*), one might ask: "In what sense is it suitable? To this he replied, "by way of being free from defilement and by way of being utterly pure.

For this [manifestation] is not similar to it [the unconditioned] by way of such states as being unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) and so forth. "One who has entered upon" (*paṭipanno*) means facing toward [the goal], facing toward the volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
"Having sacrificed, he has attained. "Anugataṃ" means gone by way of being appropriate; and it means gone by way of being conformable to that, just as the attainment of Nibbāna occurs.

And here, in the text, "he understands" is stated with reference to the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*), while "and he practices accordingly" is stated with reference to the fixed [stage]. Others say it is "with reference to the subsequent stage" (*aparabhāga*).
Some, however, say: "One who practices in such a way that aging and death cease is one who has practiced accordingly.

This investigation of the words should be understood by way of the preliminary stage (*pubbhāga*), not by way of the moment of the path (*maggakkhaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "for the cessation of formations" (*saṅkhāranirodhāya*):
here, this is not a reference to formations conditioned by ignorance (*avijjāpaccaya-saṅkhāra*), but rather a reference to conditioned formations (*saṅkhata-saṅkhāra*).
He said: "For the sake of the cessation of the suffering of formations. Therefore he said: "Up to this point, the teaching has been explained as far as Arahantship.

Having shown the reviewing of the fruit of Arahantship by means of the passage beginning with "He attains final Nibbāna within himself," and having shown the constant dwelling by means of the passage beginning with "He experiences pleasant feeling," the teaching must be brought to a conclusion in every respect by turning away from the teaching on the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
It may be so. Regarding the term *avijjāgato*, the word *iti* here has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*);
by this, it further includes this exposition of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) starting with that.

Since the word *puggala* (person) is a designator for the other two natures as well, [the author], in order to distinguish it from those, shows only the first nature in the phrase "a person who is a man" (*purisapuggalo*), and thus says: "The person is simply a man."

"By both" means by the inclusion of the person as a male being (*puruṣapudgala*). A discourse or teaching concerning that which does not exist conventionally is a conventional discourse (*sammutikathā*).

A discourse or teaching concerning the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is an ultimate discourse (*paramatthakathā*). "Therein" refers to the discourses on the conventional and the ultimate, not to the conventional and the ultimate themselves.
Therefore he said: "Thus occurring is what is called conventional discourse," and so forth. Herein, this is [the distinction] between the conventional and the ultimate:
The characteristic [of conventional reality] is this: when an object is broken or its constituent parts are analytically separated by the intellect, the designation for it no longer applies;

such conventional designations as "pot," "cloth," and so forth, are *sammuti* (conventional reality). By contrast, that which is the opposite is *paramattha* (ultimate reality). This method does not apply to the intrinsic nature of hardness, touch, and so on.
In this context, the conventional expression "sentient being" (*satta*) and so forth is employed in dependence upon the occurrence of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) as a collection and a continuum.

He said: “A being, a person... [etc. ...is called ‘conventional discourse’ (sammutikathā). Since ultimate phenomena such as form and so forth are spoken of as “aggregates,” “elements,” and so on—not merely as a linguistic convention—therefore it is said: “The aggregates... [etc. ...are called ‘ultimate discourse’ (paramatthakathā).

Is it not the case that even the discourse on the aggregates is indeed conventional discourse? For a convention (sammuti) is a designation, and the meaning of “aggregate” (khandha) is the meaning of a “heap” (rāsa).

Or does it mean "the meaning of a constituent part"? This is true. However, this designation "aggregate" (khandha-samaññā), like the designation based on specific conditions applied to contact and so forth, is closely related to the ultimate reality (paramattha) because it depends upon it;
it is not distant like the designations "person" (puggala) and so on. Therefore, it is said to be included within the ultimate reality.

Or rather, by the term "aggregate," only those phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma) which are the basis for that [designation] are intended. But are not all phenomena possessing intrinsic nature...
If it were the case that they ascend to the teaching only by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*) and not directly, would it follow that all teaching is merely a teaching of convention?
This is not so, because the distinction between teachings is intended here based on the distinction between the phenomena (*dhamma*) to be taught;
furthermore, a word does not manifest its meaning without some basis for its application (*pavatti-nimitta*). Therefore he said: "Even when speaking of the ultimate truth (*paramattha*)..."
“They speak without abandoning conventional designation (sammuti). They speak what is true and indeed non-erroneous. “Conventional designation” means common usage (samaññā).
“Ultimate reality” (paramattha) means the supreme, highest meaning; it is the actual intrinsic nature of phenomena as they truly are.
That is the ultimate reality, whereas conventional designation is established merely by worldly convention. If this is so, how [is there] discourse on conventional designation?
He said, "It is true," because it proceeds by relying on worldly convention (*loka-samaññā*).
For, without adhering to worldly convention, the designation [of things] is like the teaching of a certain portion of the Sutta; it is not false, because that convention is not to be transgressed.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "One should not adhere to local dialects, nor should one override common usage."

“Of phenomena” (dhammānaṃ) means of those phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (sabhāva). It is said “they illuminate the characteristic of being” (bhūtalakkhaṇaṃ) because they reveal the characteristic of existence (bhāva).
“The division into thirteen volitions” (terasacetanābhedaṃ) refers to the division into eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions and five wholesome fine-material-sphere volitions.
It is called “meritorious formation” (puññābhisaṅkhāra) because it causes one’s own continuum to increase and because it conditions the fruit of a praiseworthy existence.
“By merit consisting of action” means by that which has become action. “By merit consisting of result” means by that which is designated as result.
For even the fruit of merit is called “merit” through the elision of the latter member of the compound, as in such passages as “thus this merit increases.
The phrase “consciousness goes to demerit” follows the same method as that stated for “consciousness goes to merit,” and thus it is not recorded separately. [This refers to] the fruit of demerit.
By the elision of the latter member of the compound, it is called "non-meritorious" (*apuñña*).
