Because "formations" (*saṅkhāra*) are included, by the phrase "one who is immersed in ignorance" (*avijjāgato*), the condition for formations is grasped; and by the phrase "consciousness proceeds toward merit," etc., consciousness as the result of conditions is grasped.
When that is grasped, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and all the rest are necessarily grasped as well. Therefore he said: "consisting of twelve factors."
“The mode of conditionality is indeed grasped.
“True knowledge” (*vijjā*) refers, in its highest sense, to the knowledge of the path of Arahantship; for with its arising, ignorance (*avijjā*) is abandoned in its entirety.
“At the very first” is a demonstration of the simultaneity of the abandoning of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge. Therefore he said: “Just as...”
“...and so forth. “With the lighting of the lamp” means together with the cause of lighting the lamp. “The arising of light” means the cause of the arising of light;
the intention is that even though they are simultaneous, this is the case. “Does not grasp” means he does not grasp it by way of [the notions] “this is mine,” and so forth.
“He does not crave” and “he does not fear” because of the absence of one who is driven by craving, and for that very reason, because of the absence of the basis for fear.
"Having swallowed and brought to completion" means having brought it to completion by making it, as it were, swallowed and beyond the scope of anything else.
Because carnal pleasure is followed by manifold suffering, and because the delighting in pleasure is itself a cause of suffering,
one who delights in pleasure is said to be delighting in suffering— just as one who desires the pleasure of the heat of fire is subject to the suffering of the smoke.
"Having encountered suffering, one yearns for happiness": in this context, those with weak digestion and the like should be understood as examples.
For they, even if they have not eaten until the evening time, undergo hunger and the like while preparing their evening meal and so forth.
One who delights in happiness because it is subject to the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha) actually delights in suffering.

The construction is: "It is called [suffering]. However, some say that because suffering is absent [in that state] and because it is a pleasure of transformation (*vipariṇāma-sukha*), one who delights in that pleasure is delighting in suffering. That is not so; for no one has ever been seen delighting in suffering as a cause for such a kind of pleasure.
Rather, one is seen delighting in sensual pleasure (*sāmisa-sukha*), which is a cause of suffering. Sensual pleasure...
The meaning of this has already been stated: one who delights in pleasure, in effect, delights in suffering. "The body" refers to the five-door body;
because that is its limit and its end, it is called "ending with the body. Therefore he said: "As long as the five-door body continues, so long does it continue.
The same method applies here to the phrase "ending with life."

"Arising later, it ceases first": having arisen after the mind-door feeling within a single personal existence (*attabhāva*), it ceases before that [mind-door feeling]. Precisely for the sake of showing this established meaning in its own form, it was said:
"The mind-door feeling, having arisen first, ceases later. Now, in order to explain what was stated there in brief:
He said, beginning with “She indeed,” and so forth. “As long as she is even thirty years old” means up to the first stage of life.
“At the time of fifty years” means from the first stage of life until the time of fifty years; during that interval, she remains without undergoing increase or decrease, remaining in her very form.
“Dull” means soft and not sharp. “Then” means at the time of eighty or ninety years. The same applies even when she has reflected for a long time.

"Broken, devoid of energy, shattered and fragmented, weak"—this refers to the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) alone, which has become the ultimate limit (*koṭi*) because those [other bases] have ceased without functioning as the eye-base and so forth.
"As long as this feeling persists" means until that point. "Like a great lake" refers to a large reservoir.
"Endowed with five water-channels" means it is provided with five channels for the entry and exit of water; because it is completely full, it overflows from every side.

"First, when the devas are raining," etc., is the correlation of the similes. "With reference to this feeling" means with reference to this aforementioned feeling pertaining to the mind-door that has reached its conclusion.
"Upon the breaking up of the body" means from the destruction of the personal existence (*attabhāva*). The Pāli reads "after the exhaustion of life" (*uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā*);
however, in the Commentary, the phrase "from the exhaustion of life" (*jīvitapariyādānā*) has been transposed to follow "after" (*uddhaṃ*). "Without going to the other world. Of feelings...

"Coolness" (*sītibhāvo*) refers to the state of being free from the feverish distress of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*). However, this [coolness] occurs by way of non-occurrence; thus he said: "The occurrence... will not be.
"Relics of the elements" (*dhātusarīrāni*) refers to the bodily relics consisting of the skeletal framework. For the designation "body" (*sarīra*) is applied even to a single part of the body.
"Kumbhakārapākā" means from the kiln of a potter. Here, "pāka" is that in which something is cooked; it is a place of cooking. That very thing, by way of the act of cooking—
It is called an *āvāsa* because they dwell (*āvasanti*) there; therefore, [the phrase is] "from the potter's dwelling.
Having removed the jar that was fashioned while its subsidence was not yet complete, he sets it down; since ashes are present, he sets it down by way of covering it.

It is with reference to setting it down in such a manner that it is said, "he would replace it. Because they are constituent parts forming a portion of the jar, the attached fragments are called "jar-shards" (*kumbhakapālāni*).
These are intended [as such], not as broken or shattered. For the whole is expressed by way of its parts. In this context, a jar is indeed a collection of shards.
Therefore he said: "joined together at the rim. "Should remain" means they would remain as the very constituents of the jar, having lost their specific colors and heat.
The three realms of existence (*bhava*) are to be seen as burning with eleven fires because of their state of being ablaze.

Just as a potter reviews his kiln when it is ablaze, so too does this practitioner who has initiated insight review the three realms of existence as ablaze with lust and the other defilements; thus it is said, "The meditator is like the potter.
The knowledge of the path of arahantship is like a removal-stick because it removes [the defilements] from the ripened fruit of the three realms. The level ground is like the surface of Nibbāna.
Because all irregularities are turned back.

One who contemplates by means of these seven aspects— “from taking up and laying down, from the decline of youth and the arrival of old age, from that consisting of nutriment, from that consisting of temperature,
from that originated by mind, from that born of kamma, and from natural materiality”— insights into the sevenfold materiality.

“By way of groups, by way of pairs, by way of moments, by way of sequence, by way of uprooting views, by way of uprooting conceit, and by way of exhausting craving”—contemplating in these seven ways is what is called “insight into the sevenfold immaterial.
Therefore, for one who extracts and contemplates this aforementioned sevenfold materiality and the sevenfold immateriality: even if...

The personal existence (*attabhāva*) of an Arahant has been extracted from all states of becoming; however, until he reaches final Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-parinibbāna*), he may still be said to remain within that state of a happy destination (*sugati*).
Therefore, it is said: "having extracted his personal existence from the four states of misery.
For this reason, he says: "But one whose taints are destroyed... and so forth. And thus he will say: "without residue..."
“The cessation of the round (vaṭṭa) is to be understood as the parinibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu).

The intention is that one does not parinibbāna in the element of Nibbāna with residue (saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu); rather, parinibbāna in the element of Nibbāna with residue is simply the attainment of Arahantship.

For here, because the subsiding of the fever [of defilements] is intended by way of its state of subsiding (upasama-bhāva) due to the cause of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), there is also the illustration of the extinguishing of a hot pot.
It is not contradictory. "Bodies not clung-to" refers to material groups (rūpakalāpa) produced by temperature (utusamuṭṭhānika).
Here, in the phrase "O bhikkhus," the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning. This statement, however, is for the purpose of posing a question:

"When a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed experiences a feeling that ends with the body, would he still perform kamma such as the formative action of merit? Thus it is for the purpose of raising an inquiry.
Alternatively, it is stated for the purpose of posing a question: "Could a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted still perform a volitional formation of merit? and so forth;
the meaning is that this was said in order to raise a query, not yet to bring the teaching as it had begun to its conclusion.
Once rebirth-linking consciousness is established, there may be the possibility of the arising of those types of consciousness that are destined to arise in that existence.
It was said, “‘Nāsatī’ means ‘consciousness would not be discerned’; that is, rebirth-linking consciousness would not be discerned.
If all formations were entirely absent, would rebirth-linking consciousness be discerned?
For if that were not discerned, no consciousness at all would be discerned. “Of the elders” refers to the elders addressed with the words “O bhikkhus. This is the answer to the question.
It gladdens because it accords with his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). "Non-cognition" (*appaññāṇa*) means the absence of cognition. By the word "etcetera," it includes such passages as:
"In the absence of consciousness, there is no manifestation of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth.

"Designated as a resolution" (*sanniṭṭhāna-saṅkhāta*) means that which is designated as a resolution occurring in the mode of conviction. "Resolve" (*adhimokkha*) means liberation in the mode of certainty.
And there is liberation through faith (*saddhā-vimokkha*). Therefore, it is said in the text: “Believe this, monks.

For he says, “resolution characterized as conviction (*adhimokkha*) known as certainty,” referring to liberation in the form of a decisive determination accompanied by faith. “End” (*anta*) means limit.
“Delimitation” (*pariccheda*) is that wherein one is cut off from all sides.
The commentary on the Parivīmaṃsana Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Upādāna Sutta: 52.
Because they lead to the states of being objects and so forth, they are "conducive to clinging" (*upādāniya*); [the text refers to] those things conducive to clinging (*upādāniyesu*).
Therefore he said: "In the conditions for the four kinds of clinging. "Contemplating gratification" means contemplating that which is to be enjoyed by means of wrong knowledge.
"That is its nutriment" (*tadāhāra*): it has sixteen, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty nutriments—conditions—as its food;
thus it is "that-nutriment. Because the three realms of existence are ablaze with eleven fires like a mass of fire, this very [realm] is...
The three states of existence (*bhava*). "Fire" ... [etc] ... because the worldling is obstructed by the three states of existence, which resemble a mass of fire.

"Of the meditation subject" means of the meditation subject of insight (*vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna*). Therefore he said: "In the phenomena of the three planes. "The palace of the Dhamma" means the palace of the supramundane Dhamma;
for it is called a "palace" in the sense of being loftily elevated. On the great street of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
"Arising at the moment of the fruit.
The commentary on the *Upādāna-sutta* is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the two *Saṃyojana-suttas*.
53–54. Because the oil lamp was brought [as an illustration] by way of the simile of the great wick and its continuity, it is said: “Having taken a large wick-holder.
“In the same manner as before” means in the very same manner as stated in the previous *Upādāniya-sutta*.
Indeed, these suttas are spoken and taught in this way according to the inclinations of the persons to be guided.
This same method applies to the following [suttas] as well.
The commentary on the two Saṃyojana-suttas is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the two Mahārukkha-suttas.
55–56. "They bring forth nutritive essence (*oja*)" means that, like sap-conducting vessels, they cause the roots of a tree to transport the nourishment from the earth and water upward into the tree.
That their transporting [of it] in such a manner is clarified by the passage beginning with "by means of nutritive essence.

"A hundred cubits high" means one whose height is a hundred cubits; it refers even to one that has risen to a hundred cubits. "In this" means in this discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*). "The ascent of karma" means the condition of karma.

"Again, here" means in this discourse on turning away (*vivaṭṭakathā*). With reference to the strong, arisen knowledge of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in one who wishes to destroy the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*), he said, "like a spade.

The knowledge of the commencement of insight (*vipassanārambha*) that is to be practiced by relying on the knowledge produced from that [urgency], which stands supported by the mat of concentration (*samādhi*), is "like an axe for felling a tree. Such is insight.
"It leads exclusively to the cutting off of the round [of existence]," he said, "the wisdom of one who brings the body to mind...
and so forth. Therein, "meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna*) refers to the meditation subject of insight (*vipassanā*). That consists of forty-two parts:
twenty parts of earth, twelve parts of water, four parts of fire, and six parts of air, according to the fourfold determination.

In the phrase "and of consciousness," the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" and the sense of "manner. By this, it includes both primary material phenomena (*bhūtarūpa*) and the mental states associated with consciousness (*viññāṇasampayuttadhamma*).

Regarding the expression "one suitable condition," he says this with reference to one for whom the meditation subject does not become clear and manifest when seven suitable conditions are lacking. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the two *Mahārukkha* suttas is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Taruṇarukkha* sutta (57–59).
"One should polish" means one should bind the text around [the tree] by means of making it moist. For one acting in that way, since—
And there, by grasping the continuity of the roots of grass, shrubs, and so forth, one is said to "cleanse" that place; therefore it is said, "one should cleanse.
"Dust" (paṃsu) means that which causes its increase, i.e., adventitious dust; the meaning is "adventitious dust. "One should give" means one should throw in.
Thus he said, "hard," and so forth. "In the manner already stated" refers to [the passage beginning] "like a man wishing to destroy a tree," and so on.
According to the method stated in the fifth sutta. The eighth and ninth [suttas] have their meanings already explained because they follow the same method.
The commentary on the *Taruṇarukkha-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Nidāna-sutta*.
60. "By way of the plural" means: there were royal princes of the country named Kurus;
their single inhabited district, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), was likewise called "the Kurus" by way of the plural.

In a place where there is no monastery that served as a dwelling-place for the Blessed One, it is the custom in the introductory narrative (*nidānakathā*) to mention only the village of his alms-round, as in: "among the Sakyans."

“He dwells at the Sakyan town named Devadaha. As for the phrase “Venerable One” (*āyasmā*) or “Beloved of the Gods” (*devānaṃ piyo*), since these are terms of endearment used for him, he said, “‘Venerable One’ is a term of affection.
Since this term of affection is spoken out of a sense of reverence, he said, “It is a term of respect.
[He avoids standing] too far away, too close, directly in front, behind, or with the wind blowing from above.
"High places"—these are the six faults regarding sitting. "By way of the six colors" refers to blue, yellow, red, white, madder, and bright.
"For the sake of gathering families" means for the purpose of supporting families out of compassion for them.
By receiving alms and by accepting their salutations and so forth, he is like one depositing a thousandfold storehouse of merit for them.
"By generating. "Having swept," means having swept again with due care the place already swept by the pupils.
"From both ends toward the middle" refers to the act of comprehension (*sammasana*) by bringing the feeling from the beginning toward the end, and from old age and death back toward the beginning.
"Three times" refers to that which is endowed with the four modes mentioned as "from the beginning to the end," and so forth.
Three times. By that, he speaks of the contemplation occurring twelve times.

Because it was spoken by our Blessed One precisely because of its profound nature, it is said—standing on the basis of the sequence of the Dhamma—that "it was spoken by all Buddhas...," implying that it was spoken by other Buddhas in exactly the same way.

In the phrase "exceeding measure" (*pamāṇātikkame*), it has the sense of being immeasurable, as in such passages as "to this extent indeed [was it done] by that Blessed One. It is an expression intended to indicate a state of excess.
Indeed, this is the meaning of the word *yāva*. Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'extremely profound'. It shines forth, appears, and presents itself to knowledge.
For it is with reference to its presenting itself in such a way that it is said to "be seen. But is not this dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) absolutely profound?
Then why is its appearance as profound emphasized? This is true; [the emphasis] is solely for the purpose of demonstrating its absolute profundity.

Because there is for it the apprehension of a deep appearance, therefore, having demonstrated elsewhere by way of contrast the fourfold permutation (cātukoṭika) that is found in other cases, the words beginning with "One indeed" were spoken in order to clarify its absolute depth.
"This does not exist" means that this dyad—being shallow and having a shallow appearance—does not exist. By that, regarding the fourfold permutation as it has been shown:
This shows that the latter single point is obtained. Therefore he said, "For this," and so forth.
Indicating by means of four similes those depths on account of which dependent origination is called "profound," he said, "For the sake of grasping the peak of existence," and so forth.
Just as, having stretched out one's hand for the purpose of grasping the peak of existence, one would attempt to grasp it...

It is not possible because of its distance; likewise, the meaning of the origination and accomplishment of formations and so forth, which have arisen from conditions such as ignorance, cannot be grasped by ordinary knowledge (*pakatiñāṇa*).

Just as it is impossible for an ordinary person to split Mount Sineru and extract the marrow, the essence of the mountain, so too it is impossible to split apart and analyze the factors and meanings contained within dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) by means of ordinary knowledge.

It cannot be known by way of penetration. Just as it is impossible for an ordinary person to cross to the far shore of the great ocean by means of their two arms alone, so too it is impossible to maintain, through the medium of teaching, dependent origination—which resembles the great ocean in its vastness—by means of ordinary knowledge.
Just as [it is impossible] for an ordinary person to turn over the earth...

Just as it is impossible to grasp the potency of the earth, so too it is impossible for one with ordinary knowledge (*pākatika-ñāṇa*) to extract and grasp the nature of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-sabhāva*)—namely, that ignorance and the other factors serve as conditions for volitional formations and the rest.
Thus, the four similes should be applied according to the fourfold profundity. And this application of the meaning has been made by way of ordinary knowledge for those who have seen the Truths.

In this regard, because there is penetration [of the truth], nevertheless, since the knowledge of disciples and paccekabuddhas concerning that matter is only partial, whereas for Buddhas alone it is complete, it is therefore said: "a question within the domain of the Buddhas.
*Mā* is a particle used in prohibition. This was stated with reference to the expression: "it appears as if it were something quite obvious."
He said: "The meaning is 'do not speak. "Exalting" means elevating by way of wisdom.
"Disparaging" means scolding; the meaning is restraining. "By that" means by virtue of his great wisdom.
"Therein" means despite the Elder’s clarity [of understanding] and the profundity of dependent origination for others. "Of one who has been nourished by the essence of fine food."
"For one nourished by excellent food and flavors. "One who has practiced yoga" means one who has gained proficiency through the practice of wrestling.
"The wrestler’s stone" refers to a stone that must be thrown by wrestlers of great strength.
"Where is the heavy part of this?"—by asking this, he speaks while demonstrating the lightness of that stone, meaning: "On which side is the heavier portion of this stone?"
They shine like a lamp that is smoky-tawny because of its great radiance. Therefore he said, “It is said of that,” and so forth.
*Pakkuthati* means it turns over and rolls about as if boiling; for this is a description of its characteristic. *Piṭṭhipattaṃ* refers to the flat bones of the back, the ribs.
*Kāyūpapannassa* means possessed of a large body; the meaning is “of one with a massive body. *Piñcha*...
*Vaṭṭī* means a bundle of feathers. *Supaṇṇavāta* refers to the wind arising from the flapping of wings during the seizing of nāgas and other such acts.
The passage beginning with "By the excellence of prior supporting conditions" was stated in order to explain in detail the causes that were briefly mentioned;
therein, "from here" (*ito*) means from this auspicious eon (*bhaddakappa*). "A hundred thousand" (*satasahassime*) means one hundred thousand. *Haṃsavatī*.
The city named [Nādikā] was his birthplace. "Outer petals" refers to the outer petals, which are the longest.
"Younger brother" refers to a half-brother who is younger, such as our Blessed One’s Elder Nanda.
For Buddhas have no brothers born of the same womb; among them, first, elder brothers do not arise, but as for younger brothers—
It is simply impossible. "Bhogāni" means loss. "Upasanto" refers to a country that has become peaceful through the subsiding of disturbances caused by thieves.
"Having put on two robes" means having made only those two robes one's own body-covering, and having relinquished all other belongings for oneself.
"For the purpose of taking the bowl" refers to the fact that because of the hot food placed inside the bowl, one’s hand must turn back and forth over it.
"For the sake of easily receiving [the bowl]. "An upper garment" (*uttarisāṭaka*) means one's own upper cloth.

"These are public places" means that these aforementioned locations for the Elder’s performance of merit were dedicated to the Blessed One’s teaching, to the Buddha, and to the disciples of the Buddha;
however, there are indeed many other locations for the Elder’s performance of merit dedicated to the Paccekabuddhas and the Bodhisattva.
"Having taken rebirth" means having taken rebirth on the very day our Bodhisatta took rebirth.
"Uggahanaṃ" (learning) is the grasping of the text; "savanaṃ" (hearing) is hearing the meaning; "paripucchanaṃ" (questioning) is questioning about the meaning in difficult passages;
"dhāraṇaṃ" (retention) is fixing both the text and the meaning of the text in the mind. And all this here is by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
It should be understood that this is also appropriate by way of the entire word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*). And for stream-enterers...

[as before] ...it appears there through the removal of delusion, because it appears by way of personal direct experience (*attapaccakkha*) as: "Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.
"Delimitation of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpapariccheda*) is the distinct comprehension of name-and-form together with its conditions.
“By four” means that all forms of profundity are included within the four types of profundity, beginning with the profundity of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, even a teaching delivered by disciples is the Teacher’s own teaching; thus he said, “standing on the method given by me.
As for the statement, “Nibbāna has not been fully penetrated in every aspect by one who is still in training (sekha),” this does not refer to its profundity.
The profundity of that profound clinging is indeed clearly seen. Therefore he said:
"This very nibbāna is profound, whereas the mode of conditions has become shallow. For all those beyond training (asekha) penetrate nibbāna in its entirety due to its being without limitation;
however, only the Perfectly Enlightened One (sammāsambuddha) [penetrates] the mode of conditions without remainder.
They penetrate [the truth], but others do not. Therefore, by way of conditions, it was said by one who was disparaging the Elder, "This has failed.
Indeed, in order to clarify that very absence of penetration in its entirety, the passage beginning with "Then why... was stated.

Even though there is no difference in terms of the Dhamma itself, however, having taken into account the difference found among them by way of the meaning of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the meaning of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), [it is so described].
“It is said, ‘these four defilements. For their meaning as fetters is one thing, and their meaning as becoming firmly established is another.

This same method applies to the remaining [defilements] as well. Thus, because these defilements have not been abandoned, for one who does not cultivate such a perfection of decisive support (upanissaya-sampadā), it is intended that the Dhamma which is truly profound cannot at all be called ‘shallow. [The four...]

"Eight or sixteen incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*)" refers to the demonstration of the specific durations required to achieve the sharp, medium, or dull degrees of the qualities that ripen for enlightenment within the mental continuum of Great Bodhisattvas;

and they say this is reckoned from the time of the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*). "By these" means by the specific attainments of the aforementioned Buddha, Chief Disciples, Individual Buddhas (*paccekabuddha*), and Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas (*sammāsambuddha*).

“Adverse” (paccanīka) means repulsive and contrary. It is said, “striving only to penetrate the mode of conditions,” because the penetration of the mode of conditions in every way is indeed the attainment of perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).
“By nine modes” refers to the nine modes of conditions, beginning with arising (uppāda), etc. For this has been stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
“With regard to the arising, the persistence, the occurrence, the accumulation, the bondage, the impediment,
the origination, the cause, and the condition of ignorance and volitional formations—
in these nine ways ignorance is the condition and volitional formations are conditionally arisen,” and so forth.
In that context, "in nine ways" means by way of the nine modes of functioning as conditions. "Arising" (*uppāda*) is so called because the fruit arises from it;
it is the state of being the cause for the arising of the fruit. When ignorance exists, volitional formations arise, and not when it is absent;
therefore, ignorance is the arising of volitional formations. Likewise, when ignorance exists, volitional formations proceed.
And they are fixed. Just as they are cast into the various states of existence (bhava), so too ignorance (avijjā) becomes their condition;
likewise, they exert themselves, strive for the arising of the fruit, and become conjoined with their own result. In whatever continuum (santāna) they themselves have arisen, they bind it;
when other conditions assemble, they emerge and arise, and they impel the formative forces (saṅkhāra).

It enters into the state of being a cause. Because dependent on ignorance, formations go—that is, they proceed—it should be understood that arising and so forth are the specific ways in which ignorance enters into the state of being the cause of formations.
Regarding "arising and stability" (*uppādaṭṭhiti*): it is called "stability" (*ṭhiti*) because by means of it something stands;

thus, it is a cause. Arising itself is the stability; hence, "arising-stability. This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. And this is a demonstration of the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*).

Showing that just as it was set in motion by previous Buddhas at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree, so too was it set in motion by our Blessed One, the ten-thousandfold world system—struck by the force of its wondrousness—trembled and shook violently; thus he said, "At the mere sight," and so forth.
"Of this Dhamma" means of this Dhamma known as dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). Furthermore, as for its meaning:
It is the cause of those things that arise from a cause. Therefore he said, "of this conditioned phenomenon. The meaning is:

by way of being the condition for birth and so forth, [namely] aging-and-death. The discernment of name-and-form and the discernment of its conditions do not occur merely through the first application of attention;
rather, they occur through a successive awakening characterized by the arising of knowledge again and again. The state of both these [discernments]—
However, showing this, he said: "non-comprehension by way of full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*).

When insight (*vipassanā*) proceeds by way of abandoning the perception of permanence and so forth, it is indeed called "penetrating" the phenomena because it attains a state of sharpness and clarity through the suppression of their opposites;

and both the full understanding by way of investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*), which serves as its basis, and the Noble Path proceed by way of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of full understanding and abandoning.
And by saying, "due to the non-penetration by way of the full understanding of investigation and abandonment," he shows the absence of penetration into both of those.
It is called *taṇḍa* because it is stretched out for the purpose of weaving;
it is so called because, having been drawn out and spread, it is woven from a roll of thread, and yet, due to its state of being a tangled skein (*taṇḍākulatā*), it is indeed confused.
He said, "It is seized," meaning "it has become as tangled as a thread. To show the meaning stated in brief in detail, he spoke the words beginning with "Just as if.
"To make even" means to bring the preceding and the following into equality; the sense is to make it straight and not uneven.
Or else, *tantākula* means a tangled thread; one who has become or been produced like a tangled thread is "one who has become like a tangled thread" (*tantākulakajāta*).
Failing to enter upon the Middle Way and leaping toward the two extremes, they stumble over the mode of conditions and become utterly confused.

Because of that very leap toward the two extremes, wandering about by grasping at various views, they do not know how to penetrate the straight thread of the established nature of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhititanta*).
Therefore he said: "They are unable to make the mode of conditions straight. "The two Bodhisattas" refers to...
Regarding "paccekabodhisatta-mahābodhisatta": "By his own nature" means by his own intrinsic character (*sabhāva*), that is to say, without the instruction of another;
this is the meaning. "A ball formed here and there" means a ball or a lump of thread produced in various places;
for that very reason, it is said to be "knotted together. "Having stumbled over the conditions" refers to [stumbling] over the essential natures such as impermanence, suffering, and non-self.

"Having stumbled by way of grasping at the conditioned phenomena as permanent and so forth"—meaning, being unable to make the conditions straight because one does not relinquish that very same grasping at permanence and so on;

thus, being unable to make straight their own vision regarding the sign of the conditioned phenomena, they become like knots through the bodily tie of the dogmatic adherence to the view "this is the truth. Therefore he said: "Sixty-two... [etc. ...bound by knots."
For whatever ascetics or brahmins are dependent upon and attached to views such as eternalism and so forth—
just as a weaver’s knot (gaṇṭhika), which receives its name from the feminine gender of the word *kulā* (family),

is a tangled skein of thread whose constituent parts are difficult to discern from either the top or the bottom due to its state of confusion— thus he said: "The 'knot of families' is called the confused thread of the weaver."
“Sakuṇikā” means a bird that builds a round nest. For she makes her nest by hanging it from the branches of trees;

she brings grass, fibers, and so forth from here and there and weaves them together in such a way that, like a weaver’s dyed thread, it is impossible to join tip to tip or root to root, nor to separate them. Therefore he said, “Just as,” and so forth.
"Both of these" refers to what was called the "family-knot," namely the *kañjiya*-sutta and the bird's nest.
"In the same manner as before" means by the very method previously stated, beginning with "In this very way, beings...
Granted, even though the *muñja* and *pabbaja* grasses grow according to their kind, they fall down due to their length and [become] intermingled with one another in forest areas.
Having become entangled and disordered, they remain; however, to show that they are so difficult to disentangle as to be like ropes, the passage beginning with "Just as" (yathā hi) was stated.
The rest here follows the same method as explained below.

"Apāya" means devoid of *aya*, which is happiness or the cause of happiness. [It is called such] because it is a destination (*gati*) for suffering. Regarding the one who belongs to the states of loss (*apāyika*):

Because it is the locus for the occurrence of suffering. Regarding "from the ruin of happiness": it means "because of falling away from prosperity," that is, because one has fallen into a state of deformity;
it is so called because one has fallen into such a state that, by virtue of that individual existence (*attabhāva*), there is no longer any basis for happiness.

As for "the other," namely *saṃsāra*—is it not true that *saṃsāra* itself was already mentioned in the passage beginning with "the states of loss" (*apāya*)? This is indeed true; however, [the distinction is made] regarding hell and the other realms...
However, the mention of the "states of misery" (apāya) and so forth is for the purpose of showing the state of extreme suffering;

this meaning should be understood according to the analogy of the "cow and the calf. "And the succession of the aggregates" refers to the arising of the five aggregates one after another in the manner of cause and fruit.
"Proceeding uninterruptedly" means occurring without cessation.

"All that" refers to all the suffering of the states of deprivation (*apāya*) and the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), as described by the passage beginning with "the states of deprivation.

The phrase "like a ship tossed by the wind in the great ocean" should be understood both to show the vastness of the place of wandering and to show that the wandering is without end. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the Nidāna Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Dukkha Vagga is finished.
7. The Mahāvagga.
1. Commentary on the *Assutavā Sutta* 61.
"Unlearned" (*assutavā*): That which has been apprehended by means of the ear-door, or the act of apprehending itself, is "heard" (*suta*). One who possesses such hearing is "learned" (*sutavā*).
By way of its opposite, one who does not possess it is "unlearned" (*assutavā*). This particle *vā* is used here in the sense of praise, indicating excellence.
Or [it refers to] one who awakens others; therefore, he for whom there is praise or who has heard [the Dhamma] with exceptional thoroughness is "one who has heard" (*sutavā*).

One who is capable of destroying defilements through familiarity with the Dhamma of the scriptures is indicated by this phrase: "having heard that, practicing for its sake, and being one who has heard.
Alternatively, one is "one who has heard" because they have heard what is worthy of being heard and have heard of the accomplishment of what must be done. By way of contrast with that—
"Not learned" means one who has not heard. Regarding this, the ancients said: "One should be known as 'unlearned' due to the absence of both scriptural tradition (āgama) and realization (adhigama).
Likewise, it is said: "Devoid of the discernment of the aggregates, elements... [and so forth]. In that context, "learning" (uggaha) is the act of committing to memory;
"interrogation" (paripucchā) is the questioning therein; and "discernment" (vinicchaya) is the cause for resolving through the process of challenging and answering with those who are skilled.

The analysis (*vinicchaya*): "Of many" (*puthūnaṃ*) means of many. The details regarding the defilements and so forth—the defilements and volitional formations—should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-niddesa*.
The "blind worldling" (*andhaputhujjana*) is included because of such statements as, "he is not capable of becoming disenchanted," and so on.
Since the word "this" (*idaṃ*) expresses that which is near and perceptible, he said, "In 'in this,' he shows the present, perceptible body. Regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*):
“Engaged” means composed of the four great elements (*cātumahābhūtiko*). Just as an object made of clay is produced from great clay, so too this [body] is produced from the four great elements;
thus it is said to be “composed of the four great elements. “One should become disenchanted” means one should arrive at disenchantment.
Disenchantment is defined as weariness and a state of lack of delight; thus it is said, “one should grow weary.”
"Virajjeyya" means he would become free from lust; therefore he said, "he would not be attached. "Vimucceyya" refers here to absolute liberation;
thus he said, "he would desire to be liberated. "Ācaya" is accumulation, meaning growth, which comes about through the four conditions that produce form.
"Apacaya" is the departing from accumulation, meaning decline. "Ādāna" means grasping.
There is the arising of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "Dissolution" (*bheda*) means the dissolution of the aggregates (*khandhā*);
for it is said that this is the casting off of the physical body, thus he says:

"Casting off is dissolution. "Are discerned" (*paññāyanti*) means they are known in their various modes. To comprehend form (*rūpa*) means both by way of grasping it and by taking it as an object (*ālambana*).
Having made it unsuitable for grasping by means of craving and so forth, he makes it suitable for grasping the formless (arūpa), because it is conducive to those bhikkhus.
Therefore he said, “Why? and so on. “Expelling” means driving it out from that grasping.

It is a name specifically for the mind-base (manāyatana), and not for the designations of concentration or wisdom, as in such passages as: “Developing the mind and wisdom, Cittagahapati... and so forth.
That which has a basis to be made beautiful is "beautiful-basis" (*cittavatthu*); the state of being that is "beautiful-basis-ness" (*cittavatthutā*).
By that reason, he speaks of its nature as beauty. "By way of being the domain of the beautiful" means by way of being the object of the various beauties of the mind.

"By way of having a nature of mind associated with mental states" means because it has the intrinsic nature of mind through association with mental states such as lust or faith; by that, he speaks of its "mind-ness" (*cittatta*) through its state of being mind.
"In the sense of cognizing" means in the sense of awakening. "Clinged to" means grasped by craving that has become a state of clinging. Therefore he said, "by craving," and so forth.
"Having misapprehended" means having overstepped the true nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva), such as impermanence and so on, and having grasped them from the outside as permanent and so forth.
"One hundred and eight" means one hundred plus eight. "Nine types of conceit" refers to [the conceit] of one who is superior, thinking "I am superior," and so forth.
The ninefold conceit has been included. The sixty-two views, beginning with the eternalist views, have been included in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.

In the manner thus described, because the worldling has grasped a firm hold by way of the seizing of craving, conceit, and views, he is therefore incapable of becoming disenchanted with that and generating the knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidā-ñāṇa*).
In the phrase "Bhikkhave," the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*); by this, it includes [the words] such as "vara.
This introductory statement asks for the reason why [the Blessed One] spoke thus, out of a desire to explain. Therefore, he says "firstly," and so forth.
By the "unlearned worldling" (*puthujjana*). By "him" means by the Blessed One. An inappropriate thing was done [by saying] "one might become disenchanted," and so on.
Because the danger [of form] has been made manifest. However, because the danger of the formless has not been made manifest in that way, it is said:
"It is appropriate to comprehend the formless. The intended meaning is that it is made as if it were appropriate. "Grasping" (gāha) refers to grasping by means of craving, conceit, and views.
By saying, "Having emerged, he went to the formless," the Blessed One, having shown the danger, rejected grasping at form.

It is not in the formless realm; therefore, for those who grasp it incorrectly, thinking, "Should that [aging] be produced there as well?", it is said that as if it had emerged from that form and gone to the formless, it has departed. "Remaining" means persisting.

The phrase "as if having entered" indicates that while the nature [of matter] is proceeding, one demonstrates the differentiation of matter through its stages such as youth by analyzing it according to "the first stage of life" and so forth.
"Uplifting the foot" means lifting up the foot as it has been placed down. "Drawing back" means drawing it back beyond the place where it was lifted and where it had been standing.
"Shifting forward" means shifting the lifted foot slightly toward the side so that it does not touch the foot already standing there, and then moving it forward.
"Releasing" refers to [placing] the other foot in that same manner.

"Spreading out" (*vītisāretvā*) means not letting go for the purpose of placing [the body] on the ground. "Setting down" (*sannikkhepana*) means having let go, placing it evenly and setting it upon the ground.
"Pressing down" (*sannirujjhana*) means the complete cessation and pressing together of that which has been placed there.

"Right there and then" (*tattha tattheva*) refers to each respective stage, such as the first period of life; by this restriction, he indicates the absence of transition to any other part of the process.
*Odhī* means state; *pabbanti* means joints. Here, only the first stage of life and so forth are intended by the terms *odhī* and *pabbanti*.
"Paṭapaṭāyanta" means as if making the sound "paṭapaṭā"; by this, he shows the brevity of their moment of occurrence.
"Etam" refers to this very breaking up of material phenomena, as previously described, occurring right there and then in the manner just stated.
"Vaṭṭippadesaṃ" means a portion or section of the wick; for that lamp-flame breaks off without even reaching the end of that portion of the wick.
"By way of connection in succession" means by way of a continuous series.
"Rattiṃ" means during the night; this is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative. However, the meaning should not be taken in that way.
Because there is no cessation of that which has not yet arisen. "From the previous sequence" means from the sequence described in the case of material form (*rūpa*).
To illustrate by way of the Theravāda the point already stated—that many hundreds of thousands of millions of consciousnesses arise—the passage beginning with "And this too has been said" was stated.
"Half of seven" (*aḍḍhacūḷa*) means half less a little; however, because of the context, that half is understood to be of one hundred thousand. "Thirteen and a half" (*aḍḍhacuddasa*).

Some say "three and a half," while others say "more than one hundred and fifty spans. One should investigate whether they are speaking with such firmness [as to mean] "more than one hundred and fifty spans.
A *tumba* measures four *nāḷikas*. Because it has grown in a great forest, he says "in the woods" (*pavane*) means "in a great forest" (*mahāvane*).
"That" refers to the branch first grasped. "This is the meaning" refers to the branch that remains without having descended to the ground.
Such is the meaning designated as "grasping. For it is precisely for this purpose that the Blessed One, having said "in the forest" (*araññe*), further said "in the woods" (*pavane*).
"Like a great forest in the wilderness" means like a vast forest in a wilderness location. "Grasping of the object" (*ārammaṇālambana*) means the supporting of the object.

It should not be said [that it does not exist], because it does not arise without the condition of the object (*ārammaṇapaccaya*). "Of a single nature" (*ekajātika*) means having a single intrinsic nature, such as visible form (*rūpa*) or blue (*nīla*), etc.

By saying, "Bhikkhus, both the accumulation and the disintegration of this body composed of the four great elements are seen," one is said to have extracted [the self] from form and established it in the formless.
By saying, "Bhikkhus, better than that is the uninstructed worldling," and so forth, one is said to have extracted [the self] from the formless and established it in form.
"Later" means subsequently. "From both" means from both the material (rūpa) and the immaterial (arūpa). "I will take away" means I will remove. "Having turned over" means having recited the mantra.
"Having blown into the ear" means having fanned [the poison] into the ear. "Of it" refers to the poison. "Having crushed" means having rubbed out;
the intended meaning is "having extracted."
“Maggā” means the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*). By the word “nibbinda,” powerful insight (*balavavipassanā*) is expressed.
The commentary on the *Assutavāsutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second *Assutavāsutta*.
62. That which is beneficial to pleasant feeling by way of being a condition is "to-be-experienced-as-pleasant" (*sukhavedaniya*). Therefore he said: "a condition for pleasant feeling.
And this state of being a condition is by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), not by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*). Therefore he said: "Is it not the case that... and so forth.

"For the feeling of the impulsion" means for the feeling associated with the impulsion-consciousness. "With reference to that" means with reference to that state of being a decisive-support condition.

Thus has this statement, “a condition for pleasant feeling,” been spoken. By the phrase “the same method applies,” he extends [this principle] to such [objections] as, “But is not ear-contact a condition for pleasant feeling? and so forth.

That contact is “congenial” (*tajjātika*) because its birth—that is, its place of arising—is appropriate to it; it is what is felt (*vedayita*). And that, moreover, is precisely what is suitable to that contact.
Therefore, the meaning stated is that its "appropriateness" (*āruppa*) is in accordance with that contact.

"In the manner stated" means according to the method explained in the passage beginning with "the condition for pleasant feeling. Just as there is a friction by way of rubbing the lower fire-stick against the upper fire-stick, so too is "contact" a joining together;
and because of the uninterrupted occurrence of that friction—

“Being massed together” (*piṇḍitabhāva*) here means a coming together (*samodhāna*), not the simultaneous presence of two or three things; thus it is said, “the meaning is ‘by collision and aggregation’.
“A spark of fire” (*aggicuṇṇa*) refers to a flying ember. “Basis” (*vatthu*) refers to the bases such as the eye, because of their collision with objects.
Since even a phenomenon that is being apprehended is grasped as if it were a collision, it is said, “collision...”
“Contact is like the flame. Feeling is like the heat element because its intrinsic nature is suffering.
The commentary on the second Discourse to the Unlearned is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discourse of the Simile of the Son’s Flesh.
63. "In the same manner as stated above" means in the very same manner as stated in the first sutta of the preceding *Āhāra-vagga*.

Some say it is by way of the occasion for the teaching (*aṭṭhuppatti*) consisting of gain and honor (*lābha-sakkāra*). Others say it is by way of the occasion for the teaching regarding gain and honor.
For when, on account of gain and honor, there arose among the bhikkhus an unreflective enjoyment of the requisites due to greed; [it was for that reason].
Taking that as the occasion for the teaching, the Blessed One delivered this discourse.
"The twin great cloud" refers to a pair of great clouds consisting of a hundred layers and a thousand layers, hanging below and rising above.
They remain with the Blessed One, following him whether he dwells in a fixed residence or travels on his wanderings.
And because for the most part the monks had also accumulated a store of the perfection of giving fulfilled for more than a hundred thousand aeons, great gain and honor arose at that time;
thus it is said, "In this way, for the Saṅgha of monks as well. "Honored" means having attained honor.
"Venerated" means having attained veneration. "Revered" means highly esteemed and beloved in the mind. "Worshiped" means by means of worship with garlands and so forth.
And he is honored by the offering of the four requisites. "Honored" (apacita) means having attained honor (apacāyana).
For one to whom they respectfully bring the four requisites—well-prepared and most excellent—he is "respected" (sakkata).
One toward whom they give while establishing a sense of reverence is "revered" (garukata). One whom they love in their minds and hold in high esteem is "highly regarded" (bahumata).

He for whom all these things are done by way of worship is "worshipped" (*pūjita*). He for whom they perform the highest forms of reverential service—such as prostration, rising from one's seat, and joining the palms in salutation—is "honored" (*apacita*).
The world behaves in this manner toward the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Therefore it was said: "At that time... [down to] ...requisites. Having attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame.
He had attained the pinnacle and the highest excellence of gain and fame.
Regarding the first description of nutriment:
"Assa" refers to the Blessed One. Spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*) is the knowledge of self-reproach that arises by way of reflecting upon the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).

For this is the place where beings constantly indulge: namely, the consumption of nutriment. Therefore, the intention is that it is not possible to prescribe a *pārājika* offense for that [act] merely by failing to reflect upon it.

Regarding the word "nutriments" (*āhārā*), he says "nutriments" and so forth with reference to the method previously stated regarding nutriments in the passage beginning with "conditions" (*paccayā*).
Now, with reference to the explanation of the meaning to be made therein, [he says] "below..."
It is said, "The meaning is exactly as stated.
*Ādīnava* means fault (*dosa*). *Jāyā* means wife; *pati* means husband.
These two words, *jāyā* and *pati*, are like the words *pitā* and *putta*; however, in the Pāḷi text, the vowel *ā* has been shortened and nasalized, thus it is written as "*jāyampatikā*."

It is called *sambala* because it carries forth the fruit rightly; the meaning is that it brings about happiness. For it is said: "That which is beneficial on the path is *pātheyya* (provisions for the journey).
Because the road is included within the wilderness (*kantāra*), it is stated: "the road that has become a wilderness. Because water is difficult to find there, one crosses through it;
thus, a wilderness is a great forest devoid of water. By way of conventional usage, the other [type of] great forest is also [called a wilderness].

Thus it is said; therefore he says, “a robber wilderness,” and so forth. Even a forest that is dangerous due to hostile kings, enemies, and the like is included within this very category; hence it is stated as being “fivefold.
“From a place where [the flesh] is thick and dense” means from a place where the flesh exists in a state of being very thick, very bulky, and very large. For such...
Meat that has been taken and dried is *vallūra*. Meat roasted on a spit after being impaled upon it is *sūlamaṃsa*.

They sat in the sparse shade because they were unable to walk further. By means of such things as the cow-vow, the dog-vow, and supplications to deities—that is, by practicing vows such as the cow-vow and the dog-vow, as well as through acts of aspiration consisting of supplications to deities—they experienced great suffering.

However, because the Blessed One has introduced here the consumption of the flesh of those husband and wife as a simile for the enjoyment of food by a bhikkhu who is practicing rightly in the Dispensation, he began the passage starting with "That food of theirs,
the flesh of their son," in order to clarify its status as a simile through various aspects. In that context, the phrase "because it is the flesh of one's own kin" means:
"By way of being flesh of a similar kind" means by way of being human flesh;

for the flesh of humans born of noble families is unpleasant [to eat] because it is unfamiliar and because it is contemptible. For that very reason, it is said, "by way of being the flesh of kinsmen," and so forth.
Furthermore, the phrase "by way of being tender flesh," and so on, is stated considering that it is unpleasant both by its very nature and when not prepared.
It has been said. "By way of being undisturbed" means by way of the state of being undisturbed. They remain precisely in a state of equanimity.
For that very reason, it is said they remain in the enjoyment of food free from desire and lust, due to their inclination toward crossing over the desert. Now, as for those [qualities]:
not having removed [the previous meal], not eating until full, the absence of the stain of stinginess, the absence of delusion, and the absence of longing for that [food] in the future—
The specific modes found in the simile— namely, the absence of hoarding, the absence of non-renunciation, the absence of selfishness, the lack of contempt,

and enjoyment without dispute— are stated as "not dependent on the bones, marrow, skin, or places" and so forth, in order to extract them from the simile and apply them to the subject of comparison (*upameyya*).
"That reason" refers to the reason consisting of the consumption of the son's flesh for the sake of crossing the wilderness by that husband and wife.
Even while reflecting on the repulsiveness of the outflow [of excrement], one investigates physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*).
The application of the similes, such as "just as those husband and wife," and so forth, should be connected by supplying the phrase "nutriment that is to be consumed.
This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. "Without rejecting" means without removing. "Like a snail and like a cock" is a comparison of dissimilar things.
"Without showing a limit" means without establishing a limit by way of grasping at a large quantity. "Like a lion" is an illustrative example based on similarity;
it is said that he eats only in regular succession (sapadāna).
Because it should be consumed without being attached, infatuated, and so forth, the words "without being miserly," etc., are stated. Internally...
The view that "there is such a thing as a self" is the acquisition of a self; through the delusion associated with that, one thinks, "the self is consuming food.

"By way of mindfulness and clear comprehension" means by way of the mindfulness and clear comprehension stated here in the passage: "He acts with clear comprehension while eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting.
The construction is: "without making either the aspiration, 'Oh, may we... obtain [it],' or the lamentation, 'As yesterday... was not obtained.'"

The construction is by bringing in the negative particle *na*: “They did not store it up, or they buried it in the ground, or they consumed it by fire. This applies in all instances. The construction is:
“It should be consumed without disparaging the alms-food, or without disparaging the donor. “He with bowl in hand” means he who has the bowl in his hand.
“Should not despise” means one should not look down upon. “He thinks too highly” means he thinks beyond [his station]; the meaning is that he treats it with contempt (*avajānāti*).

Having stated, "When fully understood by means of the three kinds of full understanding," he spoke the passage beginning with "How" in order to show the method of fully understanding edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) by means of those [three].

Therein, "by way of its basis" (*savatthuka-vasena*) means by way of its constituent parts; for as to its intrinsic nature (*sabhāvato*), the bringing of material form (*rūpa*) is merely nutritive essence (*ojamatta*).
For this is the characteristic of edible food. Granted that it has taste as its object in the tongue-sensitivity (*jivhāpasāda*), [it is still so called].

It is struck; however, because it is inseparable from that [tongue-sensitivity] and because it apprehends the object presented to it, it is said regarding the tongue-sensitivity: "Where does the material form consisting of the eight factors beginning with nutritive essence (ojā) strike? "Of that" means of the tongue-sensitivity.
"These phenomena" refers to these phenomena consisting of the primary elements and the derived matter as previously described.
"That" refers to the aggregate of material form. "Of one who comprehends" means of one who is comprehending. "The phenomena having contact as the fifth that have arisen" means...
All these [factors] indeed proceed together with all those that have been defined as they are.

"By way of their own characteristic" means by way of their own function and by way of their defining mark. Consciousness is the condition for the five aggregates when they have been determined as name-and-form.
Thus, in the manner of ascending upwards, it is the condition: "For that, volitional formations; for those, ignorance."
Furthermore, by way of descending (adhoorohana), while seeking the six sense bases and so forth, he perceives dependent origination in forward and reverse order.
For the six sense bases and the rest must also be defined as the appropriate conditions for material and immaterial phenomena. "Because they have been seen as they truly are" means:
"This is material form; this is the extent of material form, and not more than this; this is name; this is the extent of..."
Because he has seen it as it really is, thinking: “This is its name, and there is nothing more than this.

By means of these seven contemplations—contemplation of impermanence, contemplation of suffering, contemplation of non-self, contemplation of disenchantment, contemplation of dispassion, contemplation of cessation, and contemplation of relinquishment—he [understands] that nutriment, which is physical food, through the three characteristics... [as previously described] ...as being reckoned.

By means of the knowledge termed "comprehension" (saṅkhātā), which occurs through the penetration of the three characteristics beginning with impermanence and through the comprehension of that which possesses those characteristics;
and by means of full understanding (pariññāta) through the thorough knowing of name-and-form and because nutriment is included therein.
Therefore he said, "In that very [nutriment]," and so forth. "By the drawing out of desire and lust" means by the abandoning of desire and lust.

One who possesses the five strands of sensual pleasure as their cause is called "one characterized by the five strands of sensual pleasure. Therefore, it is said: "arising from the five strands of sensual pleasure.

The full understanding of a single craving is "single full understanding" (*ekapariññā*). The full understanding of all lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is "all-full understanding" (*sabbapariññā*).
The full understanding of the nutriment that serves as the root of both of these is "root-full understanding" (*mūlapariññā*). Now, regarding these three types of full understanding...
In order to show this by way of analysis, the passage beginning with “The monk who... is commenced.
“He fully understands craving for a single taste at the door of the tongue” means that having tasted a flavor with the tongue, he reflects thus:

“Whatever taste there is here, in terms of the objects of sensual desire (*vathukāma*), it consists of the eightfold material form of nutritive essence (*ojā*) and the tongue-base (*jivhāyatana*) along with its sensitivity (*pasāda*). What does that depend upon? It depends upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).”
The color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, and life-faculty born together with that [taste]—these phenomena are called the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).

Whatever gratification there is in that taste, this is craving for taste (*rasataṇhā*). The phenomena associated with it, such as contact and so forth, are the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*).

All of this should be understood according to what has been set forth in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary). Therefore he said: "By that, lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is indeed fully understood."
"...occurs. In that context, "by him" means by that bhikkhu who thoroughly understands craving for tastes at the door of the tongue.
But how is it that for one who thoroughly understands craving at a single door, lust is fully understood across all five doors? To this he says, "Why? and so forth.

"Of that very [craving]" is said because of the unity of craving through the principle of identity (*ekattanaya*), based on its commonality as craving. In that regard, "in the five... [refers to the five doors].
"At the doors. "By way of arising" means by way of arising as lust for forms (*rūparāga*) and so forth.
For greed itself is called "craving" (*taṇhā*) in the sense of yearning, and it is also called "lust" (*rāga*) in the sense of coloring. Therefore he said, "That very same [greed]," and so on.
Now, he summarizes the very meaning just stated with the simile beginning with "Just as," etc. "In the five paths" refers to sexual misconduct (*sañcaritta*) in the five courses of action.
One who kills while walking on a path is described as "one killing on the path.
Within the agreeable collection of food known as alms-food—which includes visible forms and possesses other factors such as sound and so forth—the five strands of sensual pleasure arise;
it is to demonstrate the origin of lust for these five strands that the passage beginning with "How" was stated. "Having encompassed [it] with mindfulness and clear comprehension... means:
Having been embraced by that which pertains to all [realms] and which protects the meditation subject. “By enjoyment free from desire and lust” means:
enjoyed by the enjoyment free from desire and lust established through the attainment of the Path. “That” refers to the lust pertaining to the five strands of sensual pleasure.
“When that exists” means: when edible food exists. “Of that” refers to the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. “From its arising” means: from its originating.
For indeed, when one is overcome by hunger and weakness due to the lack of food, the desire for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures does not arise.
"A mind that broods" refers to a mind that gazes at one another out of lust.
"There is no such fetter" is said with reference to all five kinds of higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*). Therefore he said:
“By that lust... [as before] ... there is none. “By that” means by sensual lust. “To this extent” means by the teaching as it has been stated.
“It is fitting to speak” means by the preacher of the Dhamma who is speaking this first discourse on nutriment.
The commentary on the first nutriment is finished.
The Second Explanation of Food: "In the second" means in the second type of food. "With the skin torn off" means with the skin flayed; the meaning is that the skin has been entirely removed.
"It is not able [to move]" because of its weakness; for it is in this sense that a woman is called "weak. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "stones, hammers, etc.,"...
This is a collective term for brick-paving, clay-paving, and so forth. *Uṇṇanābhi* refers to a spider. *Sarabū* refers to a house-lizard. *Uccāliṅgapāṇaka* refers to hairy insects.
*Ākāsanissitā* means those that move through the air. *Luñcitvā* means having torn out.

*Tisso pariññā* refers to the three kinds of full understanding previously mentioned, namely, full understanding by knowledge (*ñātapariññā*) and the others. *Tammūlakattā* means because they are rooted in contact (*phassa*). The teaching is expounded up to the stage of Arahantship because, when all feelings are fully understood, there is not even a trace of the defilements remaining.
The second commentary on nutriment is finished.
The third commentary on nutriment:
"A heap of embers" means a pile of charcoal. "Scattering" means they are pouring [it] over themselves of their own accord; thus he said.
“Men weeping, their limbs consumed by fire. *Narā* means males (*purisa*), not humans (*manussa*).
For one who acts under the influence of fear, saying “fear finds me,” is said to “experience fear. “Trembling” means being in a state of extreme haste.
*Porisaṃ* refers to the measure of a man; therefore, those who are *atirekaporisā* are those exceeding that human measure.
Therefore he said, "measuring five ratanas. *Assā* means of the pit (*kāsuyā*). *Tadabhāve* means in the absence of those nets and smoke.
*Ārakāvassa* means it must be far away from it.
The cycle of existence in the three realms (*tebhūmakavaṭṭa*) is like a pit of glowing coals because of its great feverish heat due to the eleven fires. *Jivi...* [etc.]
The worldling is to be burned by those fires. The two powers... [and so on] ...because they cast him down into the suffering of the round (saṃsāra) even against his will.
One need not consider a difference in time between the exertion and the dragging along, because the fruit that is absolutely certain has already been produced;
thus he said, "Kamma, indeed," and so forth.

“By the same method as stated for contact”: there it was said, “Contact is the aggregate of volitional formations (saṅkhārakkhandha),” whereas here it should be said, “Mental volition is the aggregate of volitional formations.
The rest is exactly according to the method already stated. Because of the statement, “With craving as condition, clinging;
with clinging as condition, existence,” craving is the root cause of mental volition; thus he says, “Because mental volition has craving as its root.”
Therefore he said, “Indeed not,” and so forth. Some, however, say that it was stated thus because craving arises dependent upon feeling, which is the fruit of mental volition (*manosañcetanā*).
The commentary on the third nutriment is concluded.
The fourth explanation of nutriment:

It is called *āgu* because it comes upon (*āgacchati*) the person who possesses it by way of bringing about what is undesirable; it is evil (*pāpa*). One whose nature is to practice that is an *āgucārī*. Therefore he said, "one who practices evil.
Action is like a king because of its state of supreme sovereignty. The worldling is like a man who practices evil... [and so on] ...because of being the basis for suffering.

The three wounds from the inflicted blows are like three hundred spears; they establish the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa) of the worldling (puthujjana) in great suffering, which is like a sick man’s pride. Therefore he said: “The spear... [etc]... suffering.
Because it is rooted in that means because the name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that proceeds from this point onward is rooted in the rebirth-linking consciousness.
The commentary on the fourth discourse on nutriment is finished.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Simile of the Son’s Flesh is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Existence of Lust.
64. In the fourth [case], "it" (so) refers to greed (*lobha*). "By way of coloring" means by way of coloring that consciousness, like a dye.
"By way of delighting" means by way of taking pleasure in the object through being accompanied by joy (*sappītika*). "By way of craving" means by way of the desire to possess the sense-object.
For greed is indeed one and the same, though it is described in such ways according to its modes of manifestation. "Established" (*patiṭṭhita*) means having acquired its own nature.

“Therein” means in the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). Some say it refers to nutriment (*āhāra*). “Consciousness” (*viññāṇa*) refers to the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*). “Grown” (*viruḷha*) means having reached growth through the production of its fruit.
Therefore he said, “having made the kamma impel,” and so forth. Therein, “having made impel” means having caused the fruit to be grasped.
For the formative consciousness, by means of its co-nascent and other conditions as well as the condition of nutriment, [causes the result to arise].
And because it has become a condition, it possesses the capacity for the production of its own fruit, thus it has reached growth. Therefore he said:
"Kamma has attained the state of being acquired within the continuum and has reached growth. Considering that this is a discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), it is stated:
"'Where' refers to the locative case in the threefold cycle of existence. "'In all places' means in all [beings]. This is the locative case for the preceding word.
“*Yattha tatthā*” (wherever) is a locative expression that has come down [in the text] with respect to each preceding word serving as its object;
for it is with reference to those that this locative expression “*yattha tatthā*” was stated. “In this round of kamma-result (*vipākavaṭṭa*)” means in the present round of kamma-result.
It is said, “where there is,” with reference to the formations (*saṅkhāra*) that have the round of existence as their cause in the future.
This is because of the statement: "the production of renewed existence in the future. And by "production of renewed existence," rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is intended;
thus it is said: "Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is birth, aging, and death in the future.
Furthermore, "birth" here is intended as the emergence from the mother's womb. "In which place" means when which cause exists.

And here, the volitional formations (saṅkhāra) should be understood as the cause. For these are the causes for the production of renewed existence in the future—namely, craving and ignorance—while death, destiny, and so forth, are the requisites for karma.

Some, however, say that "death, destiny, and so forth, are the requisites for karma" with the intention that they include the cycle of defilements (kilesa-vatta), the cycle of karma (kamma-vatta), and the cycle of time (kāla-vatta).
[This occurs] through the aspiration for this or that state of existence in such and such a way.
Existence (*bhava*) is threefold; it is the round (*vaṭṭa*) of the three planes. Therefore he said: “Where? In the round of the three planes. Likewise he said:
“Materiality, together with its equipment, produces form within the existences. “Form” here means the personal organism (*attabhāva*).
“Having condensed” means having made a single summary by means of consciousness, rather than treating them as three. “One link” means one...
The junction of cause and fruit (*hetuphalasandhi*). "The process of ripening" (*vipākavidhi*) refers to the process of ripening beginning with the six sense bases and ending with feeling.

This is connected by bringing forward the phrase "together with name-and-form" (*nāmarūpena saddhiṃ*). Alternatively, "by name-and-form" (*nāmarūpena*) is used in the instrumental case to express accompaniment (*sahayoga*).
Here, "one junction" means one junction of cause and fruit. "Of future existence" (*āyatibhavassa*) means of the existence at rebirth (*upapattibhava*). And by that, here—
The single connection is to be understood as the connection between cause and fruit.
It is non-existent because, for one whose taints are destroyed, once the supreme path has been attained, the karma that was being set in motion lacks its companion in the path.
It is "equal to the rays of the sun" precisely for that reason; it is equal to the rays of the sun in the manner already described, being without a fixed foundation.

*Sāti* means ray. *Kāyādayo* refers to the body-door and so forth. *Katakammaṃ* is said with reference to the state of being produced by conditions, not because it has attained the characteristic of kamma.

Therefore he said: "It is not called wholesome or unwholesome. *Kiriya-matte* means that, because it is a non-resultant phenomenon, it remains merely as a physical or other type of functional activity.
It is non-resultant because those [phenomena] are of a non-resultant nature.
The commentary on the *Atthirāgasutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Nagarasutta*. 65.
In the fifth sutta, the passage beginning with “Bhikkhus, before my full enlightenment... has already been commented upon below; therefore, it is not repeated here.
He began [the exposition] with the words, "When name-and-form exist," in order to provide a detailed commentary.
Regarding that, in the twelve-membered dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), there are two members not included in this sutta;

wishing to ask for and then answer the reason for their non-inclusion, he first shows the reason why they ought to be included by saying, "In this [context]," and so forth. [This refers to] the present, which is directly perceived.
Having first taken up the present existence (*bhava*), when one subsequently takes up the future [existence] as "the second," the past becomes the third;
thus he said, "For ignorance and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are the third existence.
But is it not the case here that taking up a future existence is impossible, since the adherence is manifested by way of the present existence? This is true; however, regarding the cause—
It should be understood that when the fruit is grasped, it is indeed grasped; thus it was said.

Furthermore, in this context, the future period is already included by way of its actual meaning, since the teaching proceeds by including the future period in such passages as "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases," and so forth.

There is a distinction, however, in that according to the fourfold plane (catuvokāra), there is the specific statement: "With consciousness as condition, name. Therefore, [the text specifies] "by way of the fivefold plane" (pañcavokāra).
It has been said. "By those" means by ignorance and formations which have become the object.

"This insight" refers to the insight that occurs for one who sees rise and fall by way of the present momentary duration (addhā-paccuppanna). "It does not fit" means it does not succeed. [The passage] "Mahā... pe...
adhered to" states the reason why it does not fit: the intention is that because they were already grasped previously, they do not need to be comprehended separately.
“In those not yet seen” means in those not yet understood. Because one must not fail to awaken to the Four Noble Truths, he said, “it is not possible to be a Buddha.
“By this” refers to the Great Being (Mahāsatta). “Those” refers to ignorance (avijjā) and volitional formations (saṅkhārā).

“By way of existence, clinging, and craving” means by way of the vision of existence, clinging, and craving. They are indeed “associated with that” because they share the same functional capacity (yogakkhema). Not...

One might dig up the other side because what one desires has already been taken by oneself, and because there is nothing else remaining on that other side. Therefore he said, "due to the non-existence of anything [else] for anyone.
"He turned back" means he withdrew. To show the reason for turning back, he said, "This very...
and so forth. "An unbroken place" means a spot that has not been dug up.
“By way of condition” means by way of cause; that is, by way of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
When the succession of fruits is being described through the succession of causes, starting with the inquiry, “When what exists does aging-and-death come to be?

and so forth, and when there is the investigation, “When what exists does consciousness (*viññāṇa*) come to be?”, the specific volitional formation that serves as the particular cause for consciousness is not grasped [as such] when it is simply stated, “When volitional formations exist.”
Then consciousness is said to "turn back," but not from every condition. Therefore it was said: "When name-and-form exists, consciousness comes to be.

What is intended here as the condition for name-and-form is only by way of co-nascence and so forth, and not by way of kamma or decisive support, because the adherence is manifested in the present. "From an object" means from the object consisting of ignorance and volitional formations.
[This means] from the object designated as past existence. For ignorance and volitional formations are included within the past half [of the life-continuum].
