Consequently, when consciousness turns back from that, it is said that consciousness also turns back from past existence. "Both" refers to both the rebirth-linking consciousness and the insight-consciousness.
"It does not transcend name-and-form" means it does not transcend name-and-form as a condition and as an object.
Because it does not proceed without that. Therefore he said: "It does not go beyond name-and-form.
"When consciousness is a condition for name-and-form" means when rebirth-linking consciousness is a condition for name-and-form.
"When name-and-form is a condition for consciousness" means when name-and-form is a condition for rebirth-linking consciousness. This is by way of fourfold and fivefold existence (*bhava*).

The application [of the terms] should be understood according to what is appropriate. "When both are present as mutual conditions" refers, however, to existence in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokārabhava*).
"By this much" means by way of the occurrence of consciousness and name-and-form through their mutual support.

"One would be born or would reappear"—this is the conventional designation (*samaññā*) for a "being" (*satta*) who is born or reappears, [referring to one] distinct from consciousness and name-and-form.
Because there is no phenomenon that serves as the basis for the designation of a "being. Therefore he said, "For from this," and so forth.
"This very same" refers to these two alone: "consciousness and name-and-form.
"By successive deaths and rebirths" means by those [terms] indicating successive deaths and rebirths, namely, "one deceases" and "one is reborn."
By two phrases. "Five phrases" refers to the five phrases beginning with "one might be born.
Is it not the case that, in that context, the fourth and fifth phrases are identical in meaning to the first and third? True;

however, this was stated for the purpose of showing the successive arising of consciousness and name-and-form. Therefore he said: "by successive deaths and rebirths. "To this extent" means the very meaning already stated.
By the phrase “to this extent,” he restates that very same matter previously mentioned, presenting it again with the words “namely” (*yadidaṃ*) and so forth.

“By way of the mode of conditions in direct order” means by way of first showing the conditioning states and then showing the states arisen from those conditions. For the state of being a condition for its own effect—that is, the fact of being a specific condition (*idappaccayatā*)—is the mode of condition (*paccayākāra*).

And that [conditioning], stated as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" and so forth, is the "method of conditions in forward order" (anulomapaccayākāra) because it follows the sequence of the arising of volitional formations; it is by way of this.

"From the water in the moat" means from the water that has entered the moat. It is said that the city is delightful because of the facility for entering and exiting for those dwelling there due to the excellence of its gates, and because of the physical and mental happiness resulting from the excellence of the objects of enjoyment and utility.
“...on all sides ... pe ... delightful. Having previously been like a wilderness due to its emptiness, it becomes endowed with the characteristics of a city when people settle there;
thus it is said, “At a later time, that place shall become prosperous and flourishing.
Furthermore, because of the statement, “But his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood were already perfectly pure,” [it is established] by means of these three.
It is said, "of the eightfold path of insight," because even the preliminary path, together with the abstinences, is worthy of receiving the designation "eightfold.
"Practicing insight" means that by way of the movement of insight, one has investigated and sought here and there through that very insight.
"Seeing the supramundane path" refers to the supramundane path by way of inference and so forth.
"Seeing. For indeed, the seeing of the city of Nibbāna is what is to be seen. "The time of having seen" refers to the time of having seen by way of attainment (*adhigama*).
The more than fifty blameless states that have arisen by way of the paths and fruits are what is established; however, the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) is their determiner.
"Having maintained" means having caused to proceed.

"In the sense of not turning back" means that because [the path] does not occur in the mental continuum of anyone while the world is empty of a Buddha, it is described by way of its "turning" through its arising and so forth.
For this reason, the Blessed One was praised with such words as: "He is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced.
Indeed, the Noble Path practiced by the Great Seers of the past has not been defiled by any others in the interval.
It is said: “The ancient path in the sense of being a long-worn track. By the relish of jhāna means by the bliss of jhāna and the rapture of jhāna.
It is well-supplied with food because it brings satisfaction through the nectar of the sublime Dhamma. It is in full bloom and beautifully adorned.
The phrase “as far as the ten-thousandfold world system” is used because the Buddha-field is delimited; for its very existence implies such a boundary.
It exists. "In this interval" means in this occasion.
The commentary on the *Nagarasutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Sammasasutta*.

66. "Sixth": this refers to the Blessed One. It is "subtle" because it elucidates the subtle and refined Dhamma. It is "struck by the three characteristics" because it is marked by the three characteristics;
the meaning is that it elucidates the characteristics of impermanence and so forth.

It is "caused" by the cause that serves as the proximate support for the attainment of the noble Dhamma. [It is endowed with] the wisdom of the threefold root-linking rebirth and the wisdom of the miracle.

To show that those possessed of wisdom do not merely possess the perfection of internal factors (*ajjhattika-aṅga*), but also possess the perfection of external factors (*bāhira-aṅga*), the passage beginning with "siniddhāni" was stated.
"Internal" (*abbhantara*) means within oneself (*ajjhatta*). "Comprehension of conditions" (*paccaya-sammasana*) is the investigation of the conditions for things arisen from conditions.

"Connection according to the undertaking" (*ārambhānurūpā anusandhi*) means connection as it follows [the subject]. "Not gone" (*na gatā*) means not attained. "Unmixed phrase" (*asambhinna-pada*) means a phrase that is not intermingled.
The meaning is that elsewhere such a statement is not made to come [as it does here]. Therefore he said: "For nowhere else is it stated thus.

The meaning is that there is no instance where the singular form "tenahānandā" has been used while employing the plural forms "suṇātha" and "manasi karotha. However, some read even here as "tenahānandā," making it plural.
As in the passage beginning with “Well said, Anuruddhā,” [the term] *upadhi* is so called because suffering is accumulated (*upadhīyati*) therein. It arises;

it acquires the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) and the phase of increase (*udaya*). The state of being manifest is the phase of presence (*ṭhitika*), while the acquisition of selfhood is the phase of increase (*udaya*).
It settles; it acquires a station (*nivesa*) or a locus. For a phenomenon that has arisen for only a single moment is weak.
There is no such thing as finding a footing as if in empty space; rather, when it occurs repeatedly toward an object, it is said to be "settled" and "established.
Therefore he said: "It settles means it establishes itself by way of repeated occurrence.
"Of a pleasant nature" means of a kind that is to be loved. "Of a sweet nature" means of a kind that is desirable. "Adhered to" means...
They are immersed by the adherence of craving. "In prosperity" means in the prosperity of existence (*bhava*).

"By following the grasping of signs" means by following the grasping of reflected images. The opening of the ear is like a silver tube, while the earring-string attached to the ear is like a *pāmaṅga* thread.
A nose that is high, elevated, and long is a "prominent nose" (*tuṅganāsā*). [He perceives] himself as having such a designation.

The nose. Alternatively, there is the reading *laddhavohārā*. If that is the case, the construction is: those beings who have obtained the designation “tuṅganāsā” (high-nosed) because their noses are high (*tuṅga*) are called “those with high noses.
Thus, the connection is that beings obtain the designation for their own nose. In terms of color and shape, it is like a piece of red woolen cloth;
in terms of touch, it is soft and glossy; in terms of function, it provides a smooth and sweet-scented flavor. *Sālalaṭṭhi* means a sal tree trunk.
*Addasaṃsu*: they saw. *Evaṃ vuttaṃ*: it was said thus, namely “in the bronze bowl,” by way of conventional designation (*adhiṭṭhāna-vohāra*).
*Sampattiṃ*: excellence, such as beauty and other qualities. *Ādīnavaṃ*: the danger, from the perspective of being subject to death.
*Sattupānīyena*: with water into which flour has been thrown and stirred. The four paths are like the four drinks, because they allay the thirst of craving (*taṇhā-pipāsā*).
The commentary on the *Sammasa Sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Naḷakalāpī Sutta*: 67.
Regarding the seventh [question], why did he ask? The Elder Mahākoṭṭhita, being himself free from doubt in that matter, asked: "Why..."

The intention is that he asks. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of knowing his disposition": this too might be considered not a definitive proof (*appaṭihīra*) for that great disciple’s knowledge of the minds of others;
therefore, being dissatisfied with that [explanation], he said, "Moreover," and so forth.

In that context, "the two chief disciples" means the supreme disciples by virtue of qualities such as moral discipline (*sīla*); for the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika had not attained the characteristics of a chief disciple.

Now, having first presented the teaching by showing how the conditions and the conditionally arisen phenomena are not confused—starting with "Just now we [have attained the characteristics of a Great Disciple]" and so forth—the Elder here has explained it by mixing them together and reversing the order according to his specific intention;
wishing to clarify that very intention of his, he says: "But now... and so on.
The Elder Mahākoṭṭhika said, “Just now indeed we...,” and so forth. Therefore he said, “This the Elder...,” and so forth.
“In this much of a place” means from the first beginning with “What, friend...? down to the phrase “there is cessation”;
it refers to this extent of the teaching that does not include ignorance and volitional formations, starting instead with “With name-and-form as condition, consciousness.”
Because it is occurring, it is said: "The teaching is explained by way of the five-aggregate existence that has arisen through conditions.

Just as when the fruit is grasped, the cause is necessarily grasped, so too when consciousness is grasped, the volitional formations are grasped, and their cause—ignorance—is necessarily grasped as well;
thus it is said: "In the twelve items answered below. In each one: in every single one.

Regarding the phrase "in each instance": it is by way of each set of three [occurrences] as they have come down in the text: "He taught the Dhamma for the sake of cessation, he was practicing for the sake of cessation, and through cessation he became liberated through non-clinging.
In expressions such as "by eighteen grounds," the word *vatthu* here is used in the sense of a cause; thus he says, "by thirty-six causes."

The first method of rejoicing (*anumodanā-vidhi*). The "quality of the preacher" (*dhammakathika-guṇa*) is stated here by way of a non-differentiated metaphorical designation for the object of insight (*vipassanā-visaya*).

The same principle applies to the other two as well. Regarding the second and third [methods], they should be designated as "the second rejoicing" and "the third rejoicing," respectively, in accordance with their literal meaning.

The perfection of the teaching (*desanā-sampatti*) has been explained because it was said: "He teaches the Dhamma for the sake of disenchantment... [and so forth]. This is the stage of those in training (*sekkha-bhūmi*).

The stage of the trainee (*sekha-bhūmi*) is described because it is stated: “He practices for disenchantment... [and so on]... for the sake of liberation. The stage of the adept (*asekha-bhūmi*) is described because it is stated:
“Through disenchantment... [and so on]... he is liberated by non-clinging.
The commentary on the Naḷakalāpī Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Kosambī Sutta 68.
In the eighth [verse], "having trusted another" means having trusted the words of another. Therefore it is said: "He accepts what this person says as being true.
For such a person relies on others; his intellect is led by others. "Whatever reason" means whatever...

A matter considered by oneself (*attanā cintitavatthu*). "It is pleasing" (*ruccati*) means that it is pleasing to one who considers according to their own judgment, thinking, "This shall be so, and not otherwise.
"One accepts through liking" (*ruciyā gaṇhāti*) means that one accepts it oneself, finding it agreeable in that way, rather than merely following the assertions of others.
"Tradition" (*anussava*) means "heard again and again"; thus, it refers to what is obtained from a long-standing oral tradition, [thinking], "How is this?"
"It might be; why? Because this is real"—thus one grasps it through hearsay. "While reflecting" means while imagining, "this might be so.
"One reason presents itself" means that the object as it was imagined presents itself to the mind.
"By way of reflection on the mode" means one grasps it by means of the mode one has oneself imagined. "A single view arises" means [the thought] "something is as it was imagined..."
For one who adheres with the thought, "The meaning is thus, it is not otherwise," a single form of adherence arises.
"Yāyassa" means by whichever view that person possesses. "Nijjhāyantassa" means reflecting as if it were directly before the eyes.
"Khamati" means it is capable of being grasped in that way. Therefore he said, "He... pe... grasps. "Etāni" refers to faith and the other [faculties].
For these are called "causes" because they serve as the grounds for grasping things that are to be believed.
"Cessation of existence is Nibbāna": the cessation of the ninefold existence occurs here, in this attainment; thus it is the cessation of existence, which is Nibbāna.
Since this existence consists of the five aggregates and exists nowhere apart from them, he says: "the cessation of the five aggregates."

“Nibbāna. Nibbāna is the cessation of existence (*bhavanirodho*). Thus, the question “Nibbāna is the cessation of existence” is something that must be understood even by those in training (*sekkha*), not only by those who have completed their task (*asekha*).
“This point”: this true state of affairs. “Well seen”: “The cessation of existence is Nibbāna”—this has been well seen by me according to reality; of existence...

Because he has seen with right wisdom, as it truly is, the state of oppression, formation, torment, and changeability, as well as the state of escape, seclusion, unconditionedness, and the deathless which is the cessation of existence.
For one established in the fruit of non-returning is indeed said to be "established on the path of non-returning" because the higher path has not yet been attained;
thus it is said, "because of being established on the path of non-returning. With reference to Nibbāna—
Although this knowledge of the Elder is active, it is not like the knowledge described as "reviewing Nibbāna";
therefore, it is called "the reviewing-knowledge of nineteen [factors]," and so forth.

By this, he shows that this [knowledge] is not like the reviewing of Nibbāna because it possesses a limited scope (*sappadesabhāva*). And by taking it thus, the illustration of the well given here is also made consistent.
It should be seen. "By the knowledge of review" means by the knowledge that reviews the remaining defilements or indeed Nibbāna itself.
"The subsequent occasion of the fruit of Arahantship" means that because it is accomplished subsequently, there is likewise the attainment of Arahantship;
one knows: "By this [knowledge], while seeking it, I shall realize Nibbāna."
The commentary on the Kosambī Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Upayaṅgī Sutta: 69.
Regarding the ninth [verse], "at the time of the increase of the waters": within the great ocean on all days, there are great mountains of moonstone (*candrakanta-maṇi*).
At the time when water increases by means of the pouring of water, due to being struck by the contact of heat;
"going upwards" means going above the natural standing place of the water. "Causes it to persist upwards" means he causes the water to increase further and further there.
And being thus, while making it grow, he is said to "fill it"; therefore, he says, "he makes it increase."

The meaning is "it fulfills. Because the conditioning states, when acting as the presence-condition for their own fruit, stand as if above it and bring it under their own control, it is therefore said that "ignorance goes above.
For it is spoken of in that way by virtue of its status as a condition. Hence he said: "being able to become a condition for the volitional formations."
“Going away” means departing. Therefore he said, “descending,” which means not increasing, but rather declining.
The commentary on the *Upayantīsutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Susimasutta*.
70. "Venerated" (*garukato*) means venerated with a unique reverence because he has reached the pinnacle of the supreme qualities that are the causes for being held in high esteem.
"Honored" (*mānito*) means honored through right practice; for it is by this that he is pleasing to the wise, as it says: "beloved by the mind.
And "worshipped" (*pūjito*) by the worship of the four requisites—this is a synonym for the same meaning. For the purpose of which...
The compilers of the collection established the introduction to this sutta with the words, "Now at that time the Blessed One was honored," and so forth;
it should be understood that this was stated by way of indicating its subject matter. This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
From the right shoulder-peak means: having stood while covering both shoulder-peaks with the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), [he spoke] from the right shoulder-peak.
Or they remove [the texts] from both sides. By virtue of his well-mastered books, he became a wise wanderer (*paribbājaka*) who subsequently attained distinction.
Because he delivered discourses on the Dhamma through diverse methods, they called him "the best of poets" (*kaviseṭṭha*).

"Abounding in brilliance" (*tejussada*) means possessing great splendor. "Devoted to the observance of rules" (*niyamamanuyutta*) refers to his fixed practice of duties such as those before the morning meal. "In the characteristic of insight" (*vipassanālakkhaṇamhi*)...
Knowledge is what was spoken there. "The Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma taught by the Elder in various assemblies in his absence;
he speaks by bringing it forth because it had been granted to him as a boon.
Although Susīma did not claim to be a teacher like Pūraṇa and the others, he was nevertheless regarded by the sectarians as one who had gone forth as a brahmin.
Being wise and skilled in the Vedangas, he was appointed to the position of teacher of the community and was thus honored by them.
Therefore it is said, "claiming 'I am the Teacher,'" not because he held the view of eternalism (*sassataditthi*). For indeed, he was unable to approach the Blessed One in person.

"Aññā" is a name for *arahatta* (Arhatship), because it occurs when the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) has been practiced. That which occurs is the "declaration of final knowledge" (*aññabyākaraṇa*).
It was said; having heard that. Of him, Susīma, "the supreme measure" means the highest limit. "The teacher’s fist" means a doctrine kept secret by the teacher.
"Due to the tranquility of the factors" means due to the subsiding of the jhāna-factors through their remoteness from opposing states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
For it is because all distress and fever have been extinguished that those jhānas possess a more sublime nature. "Due to the tranquility of the object" means...
This is due to the peaceful nature of the object, which has attained a state of subtlety and refinement through the departure from its coarse appearance.

For to the extent that those objects—characterized by modes of extreme subtlety and refinement developed through the excellence of meditation—are peaceful, to that same extent the peace of the jhāna factors should be understood. Or rather, the peace of the mental states that take that object is due to the peace of the object itself.

It should be illustrated by means of the reviewing knowledges that have supramundane states as their object. "Formless liberations" refers to the liberations consisting of the perceptions of the formless jhānas.

They are liberated by wisdom alone, not liberated in both ways. "The stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhiti) is the persistence of phenomena and their intrinsic nature—namely, impermanence, suffering, and non-self;
the knowledge regarding that is "knowledge of the stability of phenomena. Thus he said, "insight-knowledge. So it was said.
“First, Susīma, there is knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa), and afterwards, knowledge of Nibbāna,” and so forth.
“Even without concentration” means even without the concentration that has reached the characteristic of serenity (samatha) and was previously established;

this is said with reference to one who takes insight (vipassanā) as their vehicle. “In this manner” refers to the way already stated. It is not the outflow (nissanda) of concentration, unlike the successive dwellings (anupubbavihāra); nor is it the benefit (ānisaṃsa) of concentration.
It is like the mundane higher knowledges (*lokiyābhiññā*). The accomplishment of concentration is not like the peak of all existence (*sabbabhavagga*).
The accomplishment of insight (*vipassanā*) is either the path or the fruit; this is the construction [of the meaning].
Regarding form and so forth, the teaching by way of the rotation of the three characteristics is the "threefold-turning teaching" (*teparivaṭṭadesanā*). [Regarding] the inquiry...

"Is it not said, Susīma, 'they are applying themselves'? Now, having penetrated the mode of conditions in every way through the attainment of Arahantship, you are applying yourself there, being free from delusion. For the purpose of making it clear:
just as you, Susīma, having been both a meditator and a dry-insight practitioner, were well-established in the contemplation of the destruction of the taints, so too these [others]..."
Therefore, monks, you should not question them with such words as "But, venerable sirs... and so forth.
The commentary on the Susīma Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
8. The Chapter on Ascetics and Brahmins.
1. Commentary on the Discourses on Aging and Death, etc., 71–72.
Eleven discourses are stated by treating each as a single sutta, because the teaching has not yet arrived at the point concerning ignorance (*avijjā*).
Likewise, there is no mention of its non-arrival because each term has been extracted according to the Four Noble Truths.

Although there is indeed another sutta passage elsewhere stating, "With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance," it should be understood that it was not stated in this way here due to the inclinations of those to be trained.
The commentary on the Jarāmaraṇasutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇavagga is finished.
9. Antarapeyyālavagga.
1. Commentary on the *Satthusutta*, etc. 73.
"This one is called the Teacher (*satthā*)": he is called the Teacher because he instructs for the sake of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) and teaches the Dhamma of liberation.

The training (*sikkhā*) is threefold, consisting of higher virtue (*adhisīla*) and so forth. "Yoga" means application to cultivation (*bhāvanānuyoga*). "Chanda" means the leader toward deliverance (*niyyānetā*).

The desire for skillfulness is the wish to act. It is "all-enduring" (*sabbasaha*) because it endures all perils encountered in meditation, or because it endures and carries away everything that brings benefit.
It is "unyielding" (*appaṭivānī*) because it does not turn back. It is "ardor" (*ātappa*) because it heats up (*ātappati*) delusion;
it is the energy that destroys delusion. It is so called because it must be impelled and set in motion according to the proper method.
Energy (*vīriya*). "Constant application" (*sātacca*) refers to the work of the practice of development that proceeds continuously; thus he says, "constant activity" (*satatakiriya*).
"Just such" means that knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is exactly as mindfulness (*sati*) was described—that is, knowledge that comprehends the Four Truths by way of aging-and-death and so forth.
The commentary on the Intermediate Peyyāla Chapter is finished.
The Elucidation of the Obscure Points in the Commentary on the *Nidāna-saṃyutta* of the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the Commentary on the *Saṃyutta-nikāya*, is completed. 2.
The *Abhisamaya-saṃyutta*.
1. Commentary on the *Nakhasikhāsutta* (74).
"Subtle" (*sukhuma*) means tender and minute, because they are the size of a hair-tip.
Just as the hairs [of the head] are at all times only two finger-breadths in length and do not exceed that measure, so too the tips of the nails are only the size of a hair-tip and do not exceed it.
Their cutting off is due to non-increase. "From the beyond" means in the passage where it is said, "a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold.
"Having fully understood" means having penetrated; therefore, the meaning is "one who has fully understood," that is, one who has penetrated the Truths.
Granted, it is also appropriate to state the first phrase by way of the pastness of the mass of suffering (*dukkhakkhandha*). Even earlier...
In order to show that it was spoken by way of its having been previously stated, the words “the former mass of suffering,” etc., were said.
“The former” is said in relation to the latter; for the status of being former or latter is expressed in dependence upon this or that.
Having thus extracted the “former” intended here, the words “But which one? and so forth were said. [And] “the past, too, is exhausted.”
In order to clarify that what is intended here is indeed [the suffering] completely exhausted, it was said: “But what is completely exhausted? and so forth.

Since the destruction of suffering for a stream-enterer is what is being questioned here, in order to demonstrate that, it was first stated: “It might arise because the first path has not been cultivated.
Now, in order to show its specific nature, it was further stated: “What is it? and so forth. Regarding the seven personal existences (attabhāva):

Whatever suffering might arise in the states of misery—beginning from the eighth rebirth-linking and including any other place within those miserable realms—all that is to be understood as completely exhausted. "Of him" (assā) means of the stream-enterer;
the intention is that beyond whatever measure [of births] there may be, there is no further rebirth. "Great purpose" (mahattho) means a great benefit or quality.
Because he possesses this, he is "one who has great benefit" (*mahatthiko*); the letter *k* is changed to *y*. Therefore it was said: "the producer of great benefit.
The commentary on the *Nakhasikha-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Pokkharaṇī-sutta*
75. "In depth" means by way of penetration (*avavedha*), due to its downward direction. Therefore he said, "by way of profundity.
The commentary on the *Pokkharaṇīsutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Saṃbhejjaudakasutta*, etc.
76–77. *Sambhijjaṭṭhāne* means at the place where there is a meeting or a coming together. They meet; they have come together. Therefore he said, "they come together.
Since this is a designation in the text by the elision of a case ending (*vibhattilopa*), he said "three or [four]" in order to show that meaning.
*Sambhejjaṃ* is that wherein things meet—that is, become mixed—hence it is a place of mixture. Therein...
“Water at a confluence” means water where [two streams] have met. Therefore he said: “water at the place of confluence.
The commentary on the *Saṃbhejjaudaka-sutta* and others is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Pathavī-sutta* and others.
78–84. "Within the world-system" (*cakkavāḷabbhantarāya*) means within the confines of the World-Sphere Mountains (*cakkavāḷapabbata*).

"In the same manner as stated in the sixth [sutta] and so forth" means that here, in the sixth sutta and the others, the meaning should be understood as being exactly in the manner stated in the first sutta and the others, because there is no difference.
"At the conclusion" (*pariyosāne*) means at the final place of this *Abhisamayasaṃyutta*. "Of the ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of other sects" (*aññatitthiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇaparibbājakānaṃ*)...
"Of those belonging to other sects. "Attainment of qualities" refers to the attainment of qualities accompanied by the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
It does not approach even a hundredth part... [etc] ...of the penetration of truth, because of its great power. Therefore the Blessed One, who has directly realized all phenomena, said:
"Monks, a person perfected in view possesses such a great attainment; he possesses such great direct knowledge."
The commentary on the *Pathavīsutta* and the following discourses is concluded.
The *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Points) for the commentary on the *Abhisamayasaṃyutta* within the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the sub-commentary on the *Saṃyuttanikāya*, is completed.
3. Connected Discourses on Elements (Dhātusaṃyutta) 1.
The Chapter on Diversity (Nānattavagga) 1.
The Exposition of the Discourse on the Diversity of Elements (Dhātunānattasuttavaṇṇanā)
85. "First" means that it is the first among the Saṃyuttas to be recited in this Nidāna-vagga.

"By way of the sense of being devoid of a living being and the sense of emptiness" means by way of what is reckoned as the state of being devoid of a living being due to the mere nature of phenomena (dhammamattatā), and by way of what is reckoned as the sense of emptiness regarding permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self.

"By way of the sense of intrinsic nature" means by way of the intrinsic nature as it actually is. For that very reason, they are called *dhātu* (elements) in the sense of "bearing their own intrinsic nature."
The diversity of elements (*dhātunānatta*) is the state of having various intrinsic natures and mutual dissimilarity. The sensitivity termed "eye" is the eye-sensitivity (*cakkhupasāda*).
That very thing is the "eye" in the sense of seeing, and it is an "element" (*dhātu*) in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being; thus, it is the "eye-element" (*cakkhudhātu*).

Taking the basis of eye-sensitivity as its support, that which proceeds is "based on eye-sensitivity. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. There are two [types of] mind-elements that receive [the sensory object].
The single functional [consciousness] is the mind-element (*manodhātu*); thus there are three mind-elements, because the mind-element is defined as "the element that is merely the act of cognizing.
Feeling and the rest... [and so on] ...up to Nibbāna are the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*), because they function under a general designation by setting aside specific designations.

For these phenomena are taught in the teaching on the bases (*āyatana*) simply as the "mental-object base" (*dhammāyatana*). Indeed, they do not possess the same [specificity] as the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) and the others.
Among consciousnesses, there is a mode of being graspable by a consciousness other than itself. "All" refers to the seventy-six kinds of mind-consciousness.

Those belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are so called because they are included within the sense element (*kāmadhātu*). "The last two" refers to the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*) and the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
This is the summary here; for the detailed exposition, one should consult the *Visuddhimagga* and its commentaries.
The commentary on the *Dhātunānatta Sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Phassanānatta Sutta* 86.

Contact (*phassa*) is a state of diversity (*nānābhāva*) due to distinctions such as birth, lineage, object, and so forth. For, according to the distinction of the conditions for its arising, [the diversity] of that which has arisen through conditions...

There is indeed a distinction. In the teaching on the elements by way of the classification of phenomena (*dhamma*), the three elements that are mere cognizing are themselves the mind-element (*manodhātu*).

However, in the teaching on the elements by way of the analysis of the arising of consciousness—which consists of functional states—as things arisen through conditions, it is stated that mind-door adverting (*manodvārāvajjana*) is intended as the "mind-element" in its general sense, because it possesses the nature of an element in the sense of cognizing.

“Mind-contact associated with the first impulsion at the mind-door,” and so forth. Therefore—because although the contact associated with the investigating consciousness-element that arises immediately after the receiving mind-element is indeed called ‘mind-contact,’ it is not included in its entirety here;
for, being weak and because it does not occur in all states of existence, its inclusion would not be exhaustive—at the mind-door...
There is impulsion-contact; therefore, this is the meaning here—this is the meaning following the intended purpose (*adhippāya*) in this context.
The commentary on the *Phassanānattasutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Nophassanānattasutta*.
87. "Dependent on mind-contact" means: mind-contact is the contact associated with the first impulsion (javana) at the mind-door;

dependent on that mind-contact. "Mind-element" refers to the functional mind-element of adverting (āvajjana). The statement "mind-consciousness-element is the mind-element" is said according to the inclinations of those to be trained (veneyya).
Therefore he said: "At the mind-door... thus the meaning is to be understood."
For he will say: "And all these volitions," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Nophassanānattasutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Vedanānānattasutta*.
88. All feelings at that door would proceed as feeling born of eye-contact, conditioned by the state of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
"For the sake of the suitability of production" means for the sake of the pleasure of seeing, which occurs through the state of being a decisive support for production.
It is appropriate to take only the receiving-feeling (*sampaṭicchana-vedanā*); when that is taken, the inclusion of the others follows as a matter of course.
This was stated in the Ancient Commentary (*Porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*). "Adverting-contact" means contact of the mind through adverting.

The construction is: "It arises by way of the first impulsion (*javana*), depending on that which has become its immediate and decisive support (*upanissaya*). This is the intended meaning, because the decisive support is what is intended here.
The commentary on the *Vedanānānatta-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Diversity of Feelings (Dutiyavedanānānattasutta) 89.

"The method stated in the third and fourth [discourses] is as follows": the method stated thus, "Eye-consciousness does not arise in dependence upon eye-contact," and in the fourth, "Bhikkhus, eye-contact arises in dependence upon the eye-element," and so forth.
And the method [of exposition] has been stated. "Combined together" means taught collectively. But why does the teaching proceed in this way regarding those suttas?

He says: "And all these," and so forth. However, there is a negation because those various feelings and so on have the various types of contact and so on as their conditions, and thus their arising in that manner is impossible.
Regarding "in the following ones": "not depending on the variety of search..."
"...the diversity of fevers arises," and so forth.
The commentary on the second Discourse on the Diversity of Feelings is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Diversity of External Elements.
90. Five elements belong to the sense-sphere because they have the nature of form.
The commentary on the Sutta on the Diversity of External Elements is finished.
7. Commentary on the Sutta on the Diversity of Perceptions.
91. "Falls within the range" means it has come into the range of the eye; that is, the collection of elements known as the cloak, turban, and so forth, which is properly supported [by the body].

Because perception associated with the reception and other [mental processes] at the eye-door has the nature of conceptualization (*saṅkappa*), or because it should be understood by the very inclusion of the perception associated with eye-consciousness, it is called "perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*)—that is, the perception associated with eye-consciousness.

It is said, “perception,” because it is perception alone that is obtained there. By this very fact, it should be understood that the statement, “the intention associated with that [perception],” has also been explained.
Therefore he said: “Perception, intention, and desire are found both in a single impulsion-moment and in various impulsion-moments.
Because thought-conception (vitakka) associated with the impulsion follows the course of desire, it was said: “by three types of consciousness...”

“...the intention associated [with it]. In the sense of making desire (*chandikataṭṭhena*) means in the sense of producing desire; the meaning is “in the sense of longing. In the sense of burning up (*anuḍahanaṭṭhena*) means in the sense of consuming.
For the fires of lust and so forth have the function of providing a basis (*sannissaya-ḍāharasā*); however, the statement “in form” is merely a demonstration of its object (*ārammaṇa*).
“Fever” (*pariḷāho*) refers to expectation by way of the head-term “fever. Therefore he said: “In fever...”
"Arising," and so forth. Regarding "fever" (*pariḷāha*), it is said that this refers to a state of intense attachment that has reached a powerful manifestation;
thus he says, "But the fever of seeking is found only within the various classes of javanas. This shows that these [seekings] have obtained their supporting conditions (*upanissaya*).

The meaning should be understood according to the method stated here: "The diversity of perceptions arises," by the same method as that taught in that passage. "The diverse nature of the perception of form, etc."...
"It should be understood by way of such a method as: 'In dependence on perception, a diversity of intentions arises, such as the intention for sensual pleasures,' and so forth.
The commentary on the *Saññānānatta Sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Nopariyesanānānatta Sutta*.
92. The intention is that the diversity [of the search] consists merely in its negation; the remainder is exactly as explained below.
The commentary on the *Nopariyesanānānatta-sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Bāhiraphassanānatta-sutta*, etc.
93. Regarding the "object of the aforementioned kind": this refers to the visible-form object (rūpārammaṇa) described below in the passage beginning with "fallen within the range of sight.

"Perception" (saññā) here refers specifically to perception of form. Although it is a non-material phenomenon (arūpadhamma), because it occurs in relation to an object, it is said to be "as if touching that object";
thus it is stated, "touching the object. It is precisely the visible-form object that serves as the basis for craving.
Having established that [the term] "obtained" (labbhati) is intended here as "acquisition of form" (rūpalābha), he said: "The acquisition of form is the object together with craving.
The "all-inclusive method" (sabbasaṅgāhikanaya) is the method shown by way of including all phenomena—perception and the rest—within a single object.
Therefore, he said: "In one and the same," and so forth. This is the all-inclusive method.

Alternatively, the "all-inclusive method" (*sabbasaṅgāhikanaya*) is that which does not make a distinction between an object fixed by habitual enjoyment (*dhuvaparibhoga*) and a casual object (*āgantukārammaṇa*).
Another method: "Mixed" (*missaka*) means mixed with a fixed object in terms of its domain, whether that object be casual or fixed.
For beings, defilement (*kilesa*) is weak toward a fixed object; for it is precisely perception (*saññā*), intention (*saṅkappa*), contact (*phassa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) [that operate there].
It was shown. "Like anything whatsoever" means like one thing to another. "Having agitated" means having agitated the mind by way of arousing curiosity.
"The female lay devotee" refers to the wife of that minister’s son. "In that" refers to the newly arrived object. "Gain" is so called because it is "obtained.
"A resident of Uruvalliya" means a resident of the Uruvalliya cave; some say it means a resident of the Uruvalliya monastery. "In the text": "The diversity of elements..."
"Monks, [contact] arises dependent on this," and so forth—by means of this Sutta passage proceeding in such a manner.

"Having turned it over" means having turned the Pāḷi over by taking contact and feeling from the middle and placing them at the end. "In the manner stated," etc., is a demonstration of the way in which it should be turned over.
Therein, "in the manner stated" refers to when a visible form as an object has come into the range of the senses. "The section on the non-manifest" (avibhūtavāra).
The section on non-manifested objects (*avibhūtārammaṇa*). Or rather, this very reading is correct. They grasp [the object] and speak of it.

These [states] are obtained even in a single impulsion-moment (*ekajavana-vāra*), because there is no long-term settling [of the object]. It is only in various impulsion-moments (*nānājavana-vāra*) that there is a more firm settling.
94. The tenth [section] is self-evident, as it follows the method already stated in the ninth; here, the difference consists merely in the negation.
The commentary on the *Bāhiraphassanānattasutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the *Nānattavagga* is concluded.
2. The Second Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Sattadhātusutta 95.
It shines, thus it is *ābhā* (light); it is produced as luminosity, or its meaning is that it appears.

That very thing, in the sense of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*), is an element (*dhātu*), thus it is the light-element (*ābhādhātu*). "Of light" means of the light-kasina (*ālokakasiṇa*). It shines well or beautifully, thus it is *subha* (the beautiful).
Jhāna is beautiful because it accompanies the kasiṇa. The rest is exactly as stated in the method already explained. The kasiṇa is a color that is perfectly pure.
Some say that even the base of infinite space and the others have beauty as their object. "He brought the teaching to a conclusion" means he left the teaching at the mere enumeration [of the topics].
In the Pāḷi, in the passage "it is discerned in dependence on darkness," the object itself is what is taken.

Likewise, in the passage, “This element is discerned dependent on the foul,” it is also thus. For just as here “gold-kasiṇa” is intended as beautiful (*subha*), so too “the ugly” is intended as foul (*asubha*).
“Dependent on darkness” means dependent on the condition that conceals the darkness. “Is discerned” means it becomes manifest.
It exists. Therefore he said, “For it is darkness,” and so forth. The construction is: even light is delimited by darkness.
Let it be granted, then, that darkness is delimited by light, in the sense that “where there is no light, there is darkness”;
but how is light delimited by darkness? To this he says: “For it is made manifest by darkness.”
For mental form is perceived as being delimited on all sides by darkness, just as sunlight is [perceived] by means of its shadow;

such is the method. Having thus extended [the principle] to the mutual delimitation of the foul and the beautiful, he said, "When the foul exists, the beautiful is perceived," pointing out precisely what was intended therein. Thus he spoke: "The foul..."

“Dependent upon the beautiful, it is manifested,” he said. He stated, “dependent upon form,” meaning “dependent upon the attainment of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-samāpatti),” because this is an expression using the elision of the latter member of a compound, as in the case of “one possessing form sees forms.

For when that [attainment] has been achieved, there is the surmounting of form; that is, the attainment of the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-samāpatti) occurs through the surmounting of the fine-material jhānas which have intrinsic nature as their object.

The meaning is that it "comes to be so named. By the phrase "In the same way," he extends by analogy two further modes, beginning with: "With the surmounting of the base of infinite space, the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness comes to be so named," and so forth. "By means of reflection" means by means of the knowledge of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā-ñāṇa*).
"Non-occurrence" means non-occurrence for the duration as delimited; by this, he rejects [the notions of] momentary cessation and the like.
"How is attainment to be reached?"—among these seven elements, which kind of perception-attainment (saññā-samāpatti) is to be entered after having become diverse?
Therefore he said, "What kind of attainments," and so forth. "By the presence of perception" means by the presence of perception whose function is active.
"Because of the remaining of subtle formations" refers to their persistence within that attainment. "Cessation" (nirodho).
It is simply the cessation of volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*).
The commentary on the *Sattadhātusutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Sanidānasutta*.
96. This is a neuter gerundive (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*), as in such expressions as “the moon and sun revolve unevenly.
*Sanidāna* means that which gives its own fruit; thus it is called a "source" (*nidāna*), meaning a cause. Therefore he says: "with a source, with a condition" (*sanidāno sappaccayo*).
*Kāmapaṭisaṃyutto* means either conjoined with desire, which is defined as sensual lust, or bound by sensual desire. *Takketi* means it conjectures; it is a fabrication of what is unreal.

It is called *saṅkappa* because it applies and prepares [the mind]. It is called *appanā* because the mind fixes itself upon the object. It is called *byappanā* because it fixes itself specifically [upon the object].
It is called *cetaso abhiniropanā* because the mind proceeds as if directing itself toward the object.
It is called *micchā-saṅkappa* because it is wrong, perverted, and evil intention. And while other [states] associated with sensual desire (*kāma*) exist...

It should be understood that *vitakka* (applied thought) alone is conventionally established by the term "the sense-sphere element" (*kāmadhātu*), because *vitakka* possesses a preponderance of association with sensual desire.

This same method applies to the "element of ill-will" (*byāpādadhātu*) and the others as well. All unwholesome states (*akusaladhammā*) constitute the sense-sphere element, because they are elements to be desired by those with inferior inclinations.
Since they serve as the objective basis for the defilement of sensual desire, the other two elements are included within the sense-sphere element, which encompasses all unwholesome states.
The exposition is all-inclusive. The discussion of the three elements is "unmixed" because they are not confused with one another.
"This" refers to the sense-sphere element, known as the sense-sphere and characterized by sensual thought. "Dependent upon" means having obtained that which serves as a condition.
"By way of three reasons" means by way of three essential reasons.

“Ill will-thought” (*byāpādavitakka*) is “ill will” (*byāpāda*) through the elision of the latter member [of the compound]. That very same [state], in the sense of being devoid of life and in the sense of maintaining its own nature, is a “constituent” (*dhātu*);
thus it is the “ill-will constituent” (*byāpādadhātu*). It is called “ill will” (*byāpāda*) because the mind is corrupted (*byāpajjati*) by it;

it is hatred (*dosa*). The construction is: “Ill will, too, is a constituent. “By way of the co-nascent condition, etc. means by way of the conditions of co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance.

Specifically, *vihiṃsā* is the causing of suffering to oneself and others; it is that very element (*dhātu*). In terms of meaning, it is resentment and the harming of others, or the arising of a state of consciousness accompanied by hatred (*dosa*) that functions in such a way.

"In a forest thicket of grass" means in a forest that has become dense with grass. "Calamity and ruin" refers to the calamity of the states of misery (*apāya*), being devoid of the means for protection.
Or, "misfortune" (vipatti) is the meaning. Regarding "decline and destruction" (avaḍḍhi-vināsa), they say it means both decline and destruction—that is, being entirely devoid of growth.
The object [of the mind] is like a dry grass thicket in the sense that it increases the fire of the defilements.
Unwholesome perceptions are like a grass torch in the sense that they burn [the mind]. Grass and wood... [omission] ...beings fall into ruin and calamity. "These..."
For it is those who practice unreasonably (*ayoniso*) who are intended by the term "beings" (*sattā*). Therefore he said, "Just as in a forest of dry grass," and so forth.

Because they are uneven due to their lack of evenness, their opposition to evenness, and because they are causes of unevenness, lust and the other defilements are "uneven" (*visama*); thus he said, "followed by the unevenness of lust," and so on. They are "to be desired" (*icchitabba*) in the sense that they are bound to occur.

It is "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) in the sense of emerging from defilement; that very thing is the "element" (*dhātu*) in the sense of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*), hence "the element of renunciation" (*nekkhammadhātu*).
Since this term *nekkhamma* (renunciation) is conventionally established in the sense of going forth (*pabbajjā*) and so on, as well as in wholesome thoughts (*kusalavitakka*), he says:

"The thought of renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*) is also the element of renunciation (*nekkhammadhātu*). He refers to the other two elements—the non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*) and non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*) elements—as "the other two elements.

They are to be explained separately because they have come down [in the texts] in their own specific forms. "Thoughts and so forth" refers to the intention of renunciation (*nekkhammasaṅkappa*), zeal (*chanda*), feverish passion (*pariḷāha*), and seeking (*pariyesanā*). [These are to be understood] according to what is appropriate.
Each according to its own respective condition. But how is it that "fever" (pariḷāha) is mentioned here in relation to wholesome states (kusaladhamma)?

This was said with reference merely to the fever of formations (saṅkhāra-pariḷāha); it is mentioned as one of the sixteen aspects within the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca), specifically the aspect of "torment" (santāpa), by the disappearance of which the attainment of coolness (sītibhāva) by an Arahant is declared.
It is non-ill will (*abyāpāda*) because one does not become ill-willed oneself, or because the person possessing it does not cause anyone to be ill-willed;
it should be understood as the opposite of what was said regarding cruelty (*vihiṃsā*). One is "friendly" (*mitta*) because one is moistened and softened by the state of wishing well;

that which belongs to a friend (*mittassa esa*) is "friendliness" (*metti*), which is non-ill will. "By means of friendliness" (*mettāyanā*) means the cause of friendliness, or the proceeding and occurrence of friendliness. "The state of having been friendly" (*mettāyitattaṃ*)...

The state of one who has practiced loving-kindness and who is engaged in loving-kindness. "Liberation of mind through loving-kindness" refers to the concentration of mind that proceeds by way of practicing loving-kindness.
The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the *Sanidāna-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Giñjakāvasatha Sutta 97.
"From here onwards" means starting from this third sutta, "The relic, monks. An *āsaya* is that wherein one lies, having led [the mind] and approached [it], until the end of the Kamma Chapter.
An *ajjhāsaya* is an inclination (*āsayo*) that is dependent upon states such as the inferior and so forth; that [is what is meant].

The meaning is "inclination" (*ajjhāsaya*) or "resolve" (*adhimutti*). In such passages as "perception arises," it means that depending upon an inclination classified as inferior and so forth, there arise perceptions classified as inferior and so forth, as well as views based upon them and applied thought (*vitakka*), by way of co-nascence and decisive support (*upanissaya*).
The phrase "among teachers" is stated because they claim to be teachers, not because they possess the actual characteristics of a teacher.

Regarding the phrase "among those who are not perfectly enlightened" (*asammāsambuddhesu*), this is stated by combining the locative case used for the substratum (*ādhāra*) and the object (*visaya*) into one.
First, showing this, he says, "We are perfectly enlightened ones," and so forth; then, showing the other [view], he says, "Among them, these are the perfectly enlightened ones," and so forth.
Here, the view arisen among them—"We are perfectly enlightened ones"—is questioned as being the root, while the other is mentioned as a secondary consequence (*anusaṅga*).
“He asks indeed” means he speaks with apprehension.
Here, in the word “great” (*mahatī*), the term *maha-* should be understood as signifying multiplicity, as in expressions such as “the great multitude” (*mahājana*).

Ignorance (*avijjā*) is likewise of many kinds, distinguished by categories such as inferior, more inferior, and most inferior. “Of that” refers to that view. But why is it said here: “namely that...”?
By extracting "ignorance as an element" (*avijjā dhātu*) and then stating "dependent on a lowly element," is the "element of disposition" (*ajjhāsayadhātu*) being indicated?
This should not be viewed in that way, as if "one thing were extracted and another indicated. Rather, it is the very element of disposition that is grasped under the heading of ignorance.
For a person who is possessed by ignorance has a disposition toward views, such as the classification into the lowly and so forth.
Depending on the element of ignorance, one then forms intentions such as perceptions and views. Aspiration (*paṇidhi*) is longing;
however, because it occurs by way of fixing the mind in various ways, it is called "fixing of the mind" (*cittaṭṭhapana*). Therefore he said, "But this...
and so forth. These inferior conditions—perception, view, thought, volition, longing, and aspiration—are the inferior states known as *paṇidhi*.

"Inferior" (*hīna*) means by way of association with inferior qualities (*dhamma*). Regarding the phrase "all terms," the terms beginning with "describes" (*paññapeti*) are to be connected with the word "inferior," because there is no possibility of an intermediate or superior state between [the categories]. He says that "rebirth" (*upapatti*) means "arising" (*upapajjana*), stating:

"There are two kinds of rebirth: acquisition and manifestation. In that context, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "inferior family and so forth," [he includes] inferior physical form, enjoyments, retinue, and so on.
"Compendium. "By way of the inferior triad" means by way of the three categories stated in the *Hīnattika* (Inferior Triad); this is the intended meaning.
"At the moment of the arising of consciousness" is stated because [this compendium] is found here and there in relation to the types of consciousness included within the inferior triad.
"In the five low-born families" refers to the families of the Caṇḍālas, Veṇas, Nesādas, Rathakāras, and Pukkusas. Of the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness...
But the construction is: "whatever acquisition there may be, that is inferior. The same method applies to the other two [cases] as well.
"In this place" means in this context where it has been stated: "Venerable sir, as for this view... and so forth. Because it has been stated:
"Monks, it arises dependent on an element," etc., only origination (*nibbatti*) is intended here, not acquisition (*paṭilābha*).
The commentary on the Giñjakāvasatha Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Hīnādhimuttika Sutta. 98.
"They are on one side" means they are on one side by virtue of having a common desire and intention. "They are contiguous" means by that...
Thus, through having identical inclinations, they become indistinguishable in mind. Here, "resoluteness" (*adhimutti*) is said to be the "element of disposition" (*ajjhāsayadhātu*);
as it is said: "Those of inferior resoluteness are those of inferior disposition.
The commentary on the *Hīnādhimuttika-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Caṅkama Sutta 99.
“Among those of great wisdom” means among those of vast wisdom. “He” refers to the Elder Sāriputta. “The analysis of the aggregates” (khandhantara) means the differentiation of the aggregates;
or, because there is a distinction or difference between the aggregates, it is called *khandhantara*. This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. “Preparatory work” (*parikamma*)...

The preliminary preparation and the subsequent preparation for the attainment of the various kinds of supernormal power (iddhividha). The benefit refers both to the benefit of supernormal power and to other benefits.
Resolution and transformation refer both to the method of resolution and the method of transformation.
"In the manner already stated" means by way of the passage beginning with "as if stretching out upon the earth," and so forth.

“Practice of the ascetic practices” (dhutaṅgaparihāra) means the method of undertaking the ascetic practices. Since the act of undertaking is already established by the mention of "practice," it is not explicitly mentioned here.
“Blessing” (ānisaṃsa) refers specifically to the benefit to be seen in the practice of each respective ascetic practice.
“Combination” (samodhāna) refers to the classification according to the requisites, such as: “this many are connected with almsfood, and this many are connected with lodgings.”

And they are mutually included because they are contained within one another. "Foundation" (adhiṭṭhāna) refers to the method of establishing a foundation. "Division" (bheda) refers both to the divisions such as the superior (*ukkaṭṭha*) and so forth, and to the various modes of manifestation.
"Preliminary work" (*parikamma*) refers to the instruction on the preliminary practice, such as: "The divine eye is to be produced in this way; it is to be purified in this way," and so on.

"Benefit" (*ānisaṃsa*) refers to the classification of benefits such as the spheres of perception that accord with the inclinations of others. "Defilement" (*upakkilesa*) refers to that which is common [to all].
The uncommon [hindrance] is twofold: the defilements of insight-cultivation are to be understood as the defilements of the divine eye.

Regarding the phrase "in concise, detailed, profound, superficial, and varied discourses, etc.": this refers to those various modes of explaining the Dhamma, such as conciseness, detail, profundity, superficiality, variety, implicit meaning (*neyyattha*), and explicit meaning (*nītattha*). In these, that...
That is the manner in which it should be explained. The word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*) or the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*). By this [it is meant]:
"At the beginning, one should teach virtue..."
One should designate the mind as being in the middle;
wisdom is to be explained at the end—
this is the method for delivering a discourse on the Dhamma.
Thus it encompasses the modes of expression:
"The loose and the firm, the long and the short, the heavy and the light, the nasalized (niggahīta),
the connected, the distinct, and the released— this is the tenfold classification according to the cognition of phonemes."

Thus has been explained the tenfold intelligence regarding phrasing (*byañjanabuddhi*). "The origin of the subject" (*aṭṭhuppatti*) means the occasion for the arising of this or that discourse (*sutta*) and birth story (*jātaka*).
"The connection" (*anusandhi*) means the subsequent connection and so forth. "The sequence" (*pubbāpara*) means the relationship;
namely, "this word should be spoken thus," and "this preceding and following sequence should be understood thus."

"Avoiding the practice of associating with families" means avoiding the method of cultivating relationships with families for the sake of acquiring gain; it refers to the exclusive and absolute avoidance of the practice of such association.
The commentary on the *Caṅkama-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Sagāthā-sutta*.

100. Regarding the phrase “they blend according to their elements” (*dhātuso saṃsandanti*), this demonstrates a similarity based on underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*), not a physical intermingling of bodies.

Thus he says, “in the midst of the ocean,” and so forth. “Without interval” (*nirantara*) means without distinction. “Through association” (*saṃsaggā*) refers to the cause of the fivefold association.
By the mention of “association” here, craving—which has association as its object—is included. Therefore he says, “through seeing... through affection,” and so forth.

It is called *vana* because one desires (*vanati*), clings to (*bhajati*), and adheres (*sajjati*) to it; thus, *vanatha* is said to be defilement (*kilesa*). Therefore he said: “The ‘thicket of craving has arisen’ means the forest of defilements has arisen.
The other two are rooted in social contact; rejecting that very point, he said: “by not being seen.
“One who lives well” means one who lives rightly and thoroughly, whose nature is that way of living. Therefore he said: “living a completely pure life.”
The commentary on the Sagāthāvagga is finished.
7. Commentary on the Assaddhasaṃsandana Sutta 101.
"Lacking vigor" (niroja) means being without the moisture of faith; for that very reason, they are "lacking flavor" (nirasa) due to their lack of essence. "Uniformly alike" (ekasadisa).

They are equal and without distinction. Therefore he said, "without interval. Because they lack a sense of shame (*alajjitā*), they have broken the boundaries by being established within a single jurisdiction.
They are "possessing faith" (*saddhā*) because they have faith. "Guardians of the lineage" (*tantipālakā*) means guardians of the lineage of the True Dharma (*saddhamma*).

"Protectors of the tradition" (*vaṃsānurakkhakā*) means protectors of the noble lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*). "Aroused in energy" (*āraddhavīriyā*) means those who have exerted energy; for such as these, energy [is characterized as follows].
It is called "complete" because of the accomplishment of what is to be done; therefore it is said, "with complete exertion.
"Grasping all duties" means grasping the duty of cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness.
The commentary on the *Assaddhasaṃsandana Sutta* is finished.
8–12. Commentary on the Discourses Rooted in Lack of Faith, etc.
(102–106). Regarding the phrase "the eighth and so forth": some say these are five discourses—the eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth.
Others, however, maintain that there are nine discourses. This matter has indeed been stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary).
And it is written in some manuscripts in the Pāḷi itself.
The commentary on the suttas beginning with those rooted in lack of faith is finished.
The commentary on the second chapter is finished.
3. *Kammapathavagga* 1–2.
Commentary on the *Asamāhitasutta*, etc. (107–108).

"In those following this" means in the suttas subsequent to this second chapter. "The first" means the first [sutta] in the first chapter. But why does the teaching proceed in this way here? He says: "When it is spoken thus," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Asamāhita-sutta* and others is concluded.
3–5. Commentary on the *Pañcasikkhāpada-sutta* and others (109–111).

"That which is reckoned as fermented liquor and spirits" refers to what is reckoned as fermented liquor such as flour-wine (*piṭṭhasurā*), etc., and what is reckoned as spirits such as flower-distillate (*pupphāsava*), etc.

“Intoxicant” (*majja*) is so called in the sense of intoxicating. It is termed “intoxicant liquor, fermented liquor, and the intoxicant that causes negligence” (*surā-meraya-majja-pamādaṭṭhāna*) because one becomes intoxicated by it.
“They stand in that” means they stand in that negligence by way of being intoxicated. The remainder is easy to understand in the third and fourth [sections].
In the fifth, the phrase beginning with “In the fifth” is commenced in order to comment upon those terms. Therein, “a living being” (*pāṇa*) is, according to common usage—
A "being" (*satta*) is, in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). They "take the life of that breath" (*pāṇaṃ atipātenti*):
they cause it to fall away prematurely, or having surpassed [it], they overcome it with weapons and the like; the meaning is that they cause it to fall quickly, not allowing it to fall slowly.
"By body or by speech" refers to what is not given, belonging to another. "They take" (*ādiyantīti*) means they seize. "Wrongly" (*micchā*) means not rightly, in a censurable manner.
"Musā" means a non-factual matter. "Vadanti" means they speak by way of deceiving. It is "pisuṇā" because it makes [what is] dear empty;
or, it pierces (pisati) other beings—this is the meaning of "it harms.

By the term "mammacchedikā," he shows that harsh speech is a volition that is exclusively cruel by way of cutting the vital parts (mamma) of another. The word "abhijjhā" is established in the sense of coveting.
He said: "The meaning is 'those whose nature is to covet another's goods. "Corrupt" (*byāpanna*) means ruined by way of hatred; it has become putrid through the loss of its natural state.

That which has reached a state where it ought to be censured by the virtuous—namely, the views of nihilism, causelessness, and non-action that proceed in the manner of "there is no gift," and so forth—is called "included within the paths of action" (*kammapatha-pariyāpanna*).
All views included within wrongness (*micchatta*) are contrary to the supramundane path and constitute perverted view (*viparīta-diṭṭhi*).
"Those" refers to the courses of kamma. "By way of conventional usage" means by way of a mere designation based on the possession of sense faculties.
"Among animals and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," there is the inclusion of hungry ghosts (petas).

Their great reprehensibility arises from the greatness of the application, the basis, and other such factors, because the volition arising through those conditions is of a powerful nature. Even when the conditions are the opposite of those previously mentioned, [the same applies] to those respective conditions.

The degree of slight or great offense should be understood by way of the strength of the volition (*cetanā*). "Consisting of psychic power" means consisting of the power of the maturation of kamma (*kamma-vipāka-iddhi*), such as in the case of [the Buddha] biting the fangs and so forth.
"In sexual misconducts" refers to the two kinds of sexual misconduct: approaching one's own wife and approaching the wives of others. These too...
Sensual pleasures are so called because they are to be performed by those of inferior inclination. "Misconduct" (*micchācāra*) means censurable conduct;

and its censurability is due to its being exclusively base, hence he said, "a thoroughly reprehensible and base practice," with the intention of referring to what is not the true Dhamma—that is, with the intention of practicing what is not the true Dhamma.
"Protected by family" means protected by those of the same clan. "Protected by the Dhamma" means protected by those who share the same Dhamma. "One who has a husband."
One who has a name [assigned] is *nāmasārakkhā*. One for whose going forth a penalty has been established is *saparidaṇḍā*.
One purchased with wealth for the sake of becoming a wife is *dhanakkītā*. One who lives according to her own will is *chandavāsinī*.
One who lives for the sake of enjoyments is *bhogavāsinī*. One who lives for the sake of clothing is *paṭavāsinī*. One who was taken after touching a water-vessel is *odapattakinī*. A *cumbaṭa*...

"Taken away" refers to those taken by force after removing their head-covers. "Brought as captives" means those brought back with a banner of victory. "Taken for the moment" refers to those taken for a brief duration.
Sexual misconduct committed by overcoming another's will is a great offense; it is not so [grave] when two people act out of mutual desire.

Even though there is an act of transgression by overcoming another's will, because there is an absence of the prior intention and application to engage in the practice, it is classified as "practice on the wrong path" (maggenamaggapaṭipatti).

They say that for one who is being overcome, there is no sexual misconduct. However, the absence of the actual act (*payoga*) when the mind of pursuit (*sevanā-citta*) is present is not a sufficient criterion, because for the most part, the act of pursuing a woman does not actually occur [in such cases].

If that were the case, then even if the mind of pursuit had arisen earlier, there would be no sexual misconduct for her; likewise, there would be none for the man as well, provided the act of pursuit is absent. Therefore...
There are three types by way of what proceeds according to one’s own preference, and three by way of what proceeds through force;
thus, including all of them together, they are called "the four requisites.
Regarding "due to the weakness of repetition": the volition by which one prattles nonsense is weak because that volition lacks repetition due to its occurrence over only a short period of time.
Since verbal roots (*dhātu*) express specific meanings by means of prefixes (*upasagga*), the meaning of the word "abhijjhāyati" is stated as "directed toward another's property," and so forth.
"Tanninnatāya" means by way of being inclined toward that other person's property through the act of coveting it.

It should be understood that the root *jhe*, preceded by the prefix *abhi*, is conventionally established in the sense of coveting. That [covetousness] is of slight offense due to the inferiority of the person whose property one covets.

The distinction between what is slightly blameworthy and what is greatly blameworthy therein should be understood through the method beginning with "due to its great quality" and "due to its great blameworthiness.
Therefore he said, "like taking what is not given," and so forth. It should be understood that the dedication to oneself occurs by means of the mind alone.

One who brings about harm to welfare and happiness is one who, when there is a convergence [of conditions], brings about harm to the welfare and happiness of both the one who produces it and the one for whom it is produced.

"He destroys. By the phrase "O that," just as in the case of covetousness the absolute dedication of the object to oneself is shown, so too here, by the phrase "O that," he shows the state of being absolutely determined by the thought of another's destruction.
For it is in this way that these [unwholesome states] proceed as courses of kamma through their cruel manifestation.

"By way of the absence of apprehension according to reality" means by way of the absence of apprehension of things as they truly are, through apprehending the intrinsic nature of impermanence and so forth as permanent and so on.

"Views wrongly" means one views what is false. By the phrase "like frivolous chatter," the slight or great degree of blame for wrong view is shown according to the small or great extent of its habitual practice. "Of the object" refers to the object that has been grasped.
"Contrariety to the mode grasped" means the contrariety to the mode grasped by wrong view.
"By way of its being thus" means the manifestation of that view, or of the object grasped by it, in the very mode grasped by itself, [thinking]: "It is exactly so; it is not otherwise than this.

"By way of nature" means by way of intrinsic essence (*sabhāvato*). "By way of constituent part" means by way of the constituent parts of the factors of consciousness; that is, from whichever constituent part they arise. "From that" [means] from that [constituent part].

Meaning: “Of the nature of volition” means having volition as their very essence. Regarding the phrase “seven in succession,” one might object: “Is it not the case that volition is not mentioned among the courses of action (*kamma-patha*) in the Abhidhamma?
Therefore, it is not logical for volition to constitute the state of being a course of action in the sequence of seven. This is not so, because the omission is due to another cause.
For the reason it is not mentioned there in the collection of courses of action is not because volition itself is not a course of action; rather, it is because [the specific context] sometimes...
However, because the status of being a course of action (*kamma-patha*) is not fixed—since it does not exist at all times—it is not mentioned [in the definition].
But when its status as a course of action does occur, its inclusion within the category of courses of action is not precluded. Here it is asked:
if the status of being a course of action is indeterminate because volition (*cetanā*) does not always possess that status, then why is it included in the category of courses of action?
[Objection: Is it not the case that covetousness and the rest, since they have not attained the status of a path of action (kamma-patha), are of indeterminate status as paths of action;

and thus, their non-inclusion in the category of paths of action would follow? [Reply: It does not so follow, because they are mentioned there by virtue of their being paths of action and their sharing in the same nature as them.
If this is so, should volition (cetanā) also be mentioned there? [Reply: That is true. However, that...
Regarding the phrase "killing living beings and so forth," it need not be explicitly stated that these constitute the paths of action (*kammappatha*), as this is already evident.
For the nature of volition (*cetanā*) as action is well known from such statements as: "O monks, I say that volition is action; O monks, the threefold bodily volition is unwholesome bodily action.
Furthermore, it is action itself that leads to happy and miserable destinies, as well as to the pleasure and pain arising therein.
It is well known that when something proceeds as a path, it is called a "course of action" (*kamma-patha*); such is the nature of that [path] as a course of action.

However, covetousness and the rest possess the nature of good and bad conduct by virtue of being the exertion of volition (*cetanā*), and they possess the nature of a path for happy and miserable rebirths, as well as for the pleasure and pain arising therein, by virtue of being the "backing" produced by volition; thus, their status as courses of action is not so well known.
It should be understood that those very [factors] are presented in the Abhidhamma as the "kamma-path aggregate" (kammapatha-rāsi) in order to show them by way of their intrinsic nature;

or else, volition (cetanā) is not mentioned along with them because it does not possess the same essential character (atathājātiyaka). "Having reached the root" means having reached the teaching on the roots;
the sense is: when the phenomena whose intrinsic nature is that of roots are being taught.
The statement that “taking what is not given has sentient beings as its object” contradicts this scriptural passage: “The five training precepts have only limited objects.
For whatever is the object of unwholesome conduct such as killing living beings is precisely the same as the object of the abstention from it;

for abstinence consists simply in the desisting from the very thing that was to be transgressed. Alternatively, the phrase “having sentient beings as its object” means that it has as its object the formations known as “sentient beings.”
Because it is stated by way of dependence (*upādāya*), there is no contradiction whatsoever. For it is said in the *Sammohavinodanī*:

“As for those training rules (*sikkhāpada*) here that are described as ‘having beings as their object’ (*sattārammaṇa*), they take as their object only those formations (*saṅkhāra*) that have come to be designated by the term ‘being’ (*satta*).
This same method applies to what follows as well. Regarding the discordant basis, [the terms] “woman” and “man”...

Some say that because it is to be grasped, its object is beings (*sattārammaṇa*). [This is so] because, in the case of idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*), one speaks by way of what has been seen, heard, sensed, and known, as in the phrase, "One thing was seen, two were heard," and so forth.
Likewise, in the phrase "covetousness for such things" (*tathā abhijjhā*), the word "such" (*tathā*) here also includes the phrase "by way of what has been seen, heard, sensed, and known";

it does not indicate that the object is exclusively beings or formations (*saṅkhārārammaṇa*), because covetousness occurs by way of seeing and so forth. [For example: "There are no spontaneously born beings" (*natthi sattā opapātikā*).

Even though wrong view is occurring, it is stated that its object is *saṅkhāras* (conditioned phenomena) with the intention that its objects are indeed the phenomena belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmakadhammā*).
But how can lofty (*mahaggata*) states be the object of wrong view? It is by way of commonality.
For when it occurs in the form "there is no fruit or result of well-done or ill-done deeds," in its actual meaning, the phenomena of the fine-material and immaterial spheres are also included.
Because of their abundance of pleasure, kings may say, "Kill the thief," even while laughing; however, since their laughter pertains to another object, it is said:
"But their decisive volition (sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā) is associated only with suffering. There is no neutral feeling (majjhattavedanā), but only pleasant feeling (sukhavedanā).
