In this regard, the classification of feelings should be understood through such passages as "from the arising of sensual pleasures" and so forth. [It is] originated by greed (lobhasamuṭṭhāna).
False speech may be accompanied by pleasant feeling, neutral feeling, or—when originated by hatred—it may be accompanied by painful feeling;

thus, false speech may be associated with all three types of feeling. Following this method, the classification of the remaining [unwholesome courses of action] should be understood accordingly, according to the principle that "greed is the source for the origination of kamma," and so forth.
The statement that "killing living beings has two roots by way of hatred and delusion" is said with reference specifically to the associated roots.

For in that case, the state of being an assistant in the sense of being a root is a specific type of hatred; however, if the "root as cause" (nidāna-mūla) is intended, it is also appropriate to include greed and delusion.
For one who is deluded may kill a living being even out of desire for food or wealth. Therefore, it is said: "Greed is the cause for the arising of kamma," and so forth.
The same method applies to the remaining [types of abstinence] as well.
Abstinence from transgressing the objects that have appeared, by virtue of one who has not yet undertaken the precepts, is *sampattavirati* (abstinence by attainment).
Abstinence arisen through formal undertaking is *samādānavirati* (abstinence by undertaking). That which occurs by way of the total eradication of the defilements, associated with the Path, is...

Abstinence is twofold: abstinence as restraint and abstinence as eradication. Although in this context only abstinences are mentioned in the text, in the *Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga* volition is also brought forward and shown;
therefore, taking both together, he said: "Both volitions and abstinences are included.
To show how those [abstinences] which have non-unruly conduct as their object, or which have the life-faculty and so forth as their object, abandon unwholesome conduct, he says: "Just as..."

The passage beginning with “panā” has been stated. Because they proceed by way of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth, one abandons those very things precisely through their being the objects [of that abstention].
For it is not possible to abandon something by taking that very thing as its object, since [the mind] would then remain unemancipated from it.

“Of one who abstains from covetousness,” etc.—the meaning is “of one who abandons covetousness. For there is no separate abstention from mental misconduct, since the abandonment of such misconduct is accomplished by means of non-covetousness and the other [virtues] themselves.
The commentary on the *Pañcasikkhāpadasutta* and others is concluded.
7. Commentary on the *Dasaṅgasutta* 113.
Regarding the phrase "by way of wrongness and rightness": here, the state of being wrong is wrongness (*micchatta*), and likewise, the state of being right is rightness (*sammatta*).
Unwholesome aggregates that arise in such and such a manner are themselves wrong mindfulness; in this same way, wrong knowledge (*micchā-ñāṇa*) is also to be understood.
For there is no such thing as a "wrongness" of knowledge itself. Therefore, "those with wrong knowledge" means those with wrong perception (*micchā-saññā*);
the intended meaning is: those whose mental states arise through improper attention (*ayoniso*). "By wrong reviewing" refers to wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) and so forth.

By way of wrong and improper reflection. "Liberation from the wholesome" refers to the recognition of one's own internal nature as an ordinary person, or the persistence in one's own selfhood devoid of noble qualities;

those who stand taking such unwholesome occurrences as "liberation from the wholesome" are those with wrong liberation. "Proper reflection" is reflection that proceeds rightly and non-erroneously regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, and so forth.
The commentary on the *Dasaṅgasutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
4. The Fourth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the *Catudhātusutta* 114.
"The element of support" (*patiṭṭhādhātu*) means the element that serves as the support for co-nascent phenomena.
"The element of cohesion" (*ābandhanadhātu*) means the element that acts as the binder of co-nascent phenomena, like water for bath-powder. "The element of maturation" (*paripācanadhātu*)...
The heat element is that which brings to maturity co-nascent phenomena, like the sun [ripens] fruits and so forth.
The distending element is the element that acts as a distender of co-nascent phenomena, like the second wind [the air element]. The twenty parts beginning with head-hairs;
by the word "etcetera," bile and so forth, the warming [element] and so forth, and the upward-moving winds and so forth are included. These are the elements.
The commentary on the *Catudhātusutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Pubbesambodhasutta*. 115.
This is the gratification that arises depending upon and directed toward this earth element. Of those that have arisen thus... [and so forth].
[This refers to] those [phenomena] that occur by way of manifesting radiance within the body.

"Having been, they become non-existent" means that, having previously been non-existent, they arise through the completeness of conditions, and then, after passing away, they exist in the mode of non-existence beyond that point of dissolution.

"Not permanent" means impermanent because of their lack of stability; "stable" (dhuva) means permanent (nicca). "By way of oppression" means by way of constant oppression through the process of arising and passing away.
In the sense of suffering (*dukkha*). "By way of the mode of the disappearance of intrinsic nature" means by way of the manner in which one's own intrinsic nature vanishes.

For phenomena possessing intrinsic nature cease after reaching a moment of no measure; therefore, they undergo transformation in two ways, namely, "by aging and by death. Hence he said, "subject to change" (*vipariṇāmadhammā*).
"It brings about the beginning, etc."—thus it is a disadvantage (*ādīnava*), meaning extreme wretchedness. It is "disciplined" (*vinīyati*).
It is stilled. It is the "escape" because by means of it one escapes through absolute abandonment.
Having lain down thus, she spent the entire night and rose at dawn; our bodies were like full jars of water due to the absence of any discharge.
Even at the mere touch of water—even when there is only a slight touch of water.
They let the time pass. Persons proceeding in the manner thus described "relish" these elements, such as the earth element and so forth, because they generate a desire for them through attachment.
"By means of distinguished knowledge" refers to the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamagga-ñāṇa*). A tree is called *bodhi* (enlightenment) in the sense that "one awakens here.
The path is called *bodhi* in the sense that "one awakens by means of this. Omniscient knowledge is *bodhi* because it is perfectly and directly [known] regarding all phenomena.

Because it is awakened to (*bujjhanato*). Nibbāna is awakening (*bodhi*) because it is to be awakened to (*bujjhitabbato*). "Of these" (*tesaṃ*) is the genitive case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*).
"Disciple’s knowledge of the perfections" (*sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ*) refers to the basis for seeing things as they truly are through the disciple’s knowledge of the perfections.

"Unshakable" (*akuppā*) means it cannot be disturbed by opposing factors. "From the cause" (*kāraṇato*) means from the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*); for its unshakability arises from that. Therefore he said, "For that [path]... and so forth. "From the object" (*ārammaṇato*) means from having Nibbāna as its object; for there is an absence of mundane attainments (*lokīyasamāpatti*) that have Nibbāna as their object.
"By way of detail" means, they say, by way of each individual element (*dhātu*); however, it refers to the demonstration of the analysis of the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) of each single element.

"Yaṃ" is a particle used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is "that which is the sign" (*nimitta*). "Assāda" (gratification) is so called because one relishes by means of it; it is craving (*taṇhā*).

In the phrase "this is the gratification of the earth element," the word "this" (*ayaṃ*) should also be brought over and connected here with the words "penetration as abandoning" (*pahāna-paṭivedho*).
“This penetration of abandoning is the truth of the origin in the sense of what is to be penetrated. This same method applies to the remaining truths as well. As for the phrase “that which”:
whatever view... up to ... whatever concentration occurs in these three points—namely, gratification, disadvantage, and escape—this is the penetration of development;
it should be applied in exactly the manner already stated as being the truth of the path.
The commentary on the Pubbe-sambodha Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Acariṃsu Sutta 116.
Just as there is a search for the danger in every instance where there is a search for escape, so too [is there a search for the escape] in every instance where there is a search for the danger.

Regarding the phrase "for one who has entered upon the right practice in the search for gratification," it is said: "I have wandered by way of the range of knowledge; I have wandered by way of the range of experience.
The commentary on the *Acariṃ* Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the *No cetaṃ* Sutta.
117. The words beginning with *nissaṭā* (escaped) refer to the negation (*na*) expressed by the word *neva* in the initial prohibition.

Therefore he said, "not escaped," and so forth. Furthermore, in the phrase "by the making of the boundary-less" (*vimariyādikatena*), the instrumental case is used because it refers to the act of dwelling.

In the second method, as stated in the passage beginning "But from whence, monks," [it is shown that] by means of the complete removal of the boundary of the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa-mariyādāya*)...
By means of a mind that is without existence and without boundaries. Therefore he said, “Therein,” and so forth. “In three” means in the three beginning with the second.
The commentary on this sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Ekantadukkha Sutta (The Sutta on Being Exclusively Suffering).
118. "Exclusively painful" means that, like the great Avīci hell, they are exclusively painful and unmixed with pleasure.
"Assailed by pain" means they are entirely overtaken by pain. "Plunged into pain" means they have descended into and entered pain both internally and externally.
These elements are pleasant because they serve as the condition for pleasant feeling.
The state of being a condition for painful feeling should be understood in the same way; however, the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*) is indeed present everywhere.

"Everywhere" means in all elements (*dhātu*) or in all locations. Although pleasure was shown first, because suffering was subsequently discussed, it is said that "the characteristic of suffering has been explained."
The commentary on the *Ekantadukkha-sutta* is finished.
6–10. Commentary on the *Abhinanda-sutta* and following, suttas 119–123.
In the sixth and seventh [suttas], the process of saṃsāra (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are discussed. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "The cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) is discussed."
It has been stated. Regarding the three suttas: "The Four Truths alone" means that the four truths taken together constitute the "Four Truths," which is their grasping as a single unit;
the restriction [to these alone] is due to the non-existence of any ultimate reality apart from them.
The commentary on the *Abhinandana-sutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is finished.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,
titled *Sāratthappakāsinī*, within the commentary on the *Dhātusaṃyutta*, is completed.
4. Saṃyutta Nikāya: The Book of Without-End (Anamatagga-saṃyutta) 1. First Chapter 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Grass and Wood (Tiṇakaṭṭha-sutta)
124. Since a prefix indicates an action along with its instrument within the scope of a compound, it is said: “even having followed by means of knowledge.
The phrase “a hundred years, a thousand years” is merely an illustration; even following for more than that, saṃsāra is indeed beginningless (anamatagga).
Here, the word *agga* signifies a limit; and since this expression is indefinite, he says: “its prior and posterior limits are undetermined.”

Otherwise, it would be impossible to speak of the limits of the beginning and end being undetermined, given such factors as the qualities that ripen liberation for those in their final existence who have already completed their task.
"Saṃsāra" means wandering. The intention is that even the subsequent limit is not discerned for the sake of the blind and foolish.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Long is the saṃsāra of fools. Yet, beings wander only within the middle.
Because the prior and posterior limits [of the beginning and end] cannot be found, the meaning is limited due to the absence of realization of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*).
"In the Buddha's system" means "in the Dispensation" (*sāsana*). Because realization of things as they truly are arises, the meaning is great;

since there is no simile similar to it because of the vastness of that meaning, the intention [of the author] is that they bring forward only a limited simile. Now, regarding this very meaning stated [above], in the *Pāḷi*...

He establishes this with the words beginning "Hī" and so forth. "Mother's mother" means the grandmothers of one's mother. "Of that very same" means of suffering itself. "Intense" is a synonym for suffering.
The commentary on the *Tiṇakaṭṭhasutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Pathavīsutta*.

125. [The Blessed One] said, "as far as the limits of the world-system (cakkavāḷapariyanta)," meaning that he intends to encompass the great earth without distinction and without remainder. This is a hypothetical expression.
The commentary on the *Pathavīsutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Assusutta*.
126. "Wailing" (*kandana*) means crying out with sound, whereas "weeping" (*rodana*) is simply that; thus he says, "of those wailing" (*kandantānaṃ*), meaning of those crying out with sound.
"Flowing" (*pavatta*) means occurring by way of flowing. Expanding upon the meaning stated briefly as "delimited by the rays of Sineru," he says "of Sineru," and so forth.
"Made of jewels" (*maṇimaya*) means made of sapphire (*indanīlamaṇi*). This refers to the region on the southeastern corner of Sineru.
“Pubba-dakkhiṇa-passā” refers to the intended [directions]. The silver rays and the indanīla (sapphire-blue) rays emerging from them become one.
“In the intervals between those rays” means in the four intervals between the rays emerging from the four corners.
“Four” refers to the four great oceans, distinguished as the southern and so forth. “Viasanam” means specifically.
The throwing away. But what is it? He says: "The meaning is 'destruction'.
The commentary on the Assu-sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Khīra-sutta.
127. "Mother’s milk" should be understood as the greater amount of milk produced from the mother’s breast that has been drunk.
The commentary on the Milk Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Mountain Sutta.
128. Regarding the phrase “it is not easy, nor is it easy, to know the length of this beginningless saṃsāra,” this is the reading in the Aṭṭhakathā.
How does one not cut it? How does one not bring it to an end? The intention is: by grasping even a single body.
“Three cotton fibers” means three single cotton fibers. Even finer than those by which it was touched is [the space] the size of a mustard seed.
It would wear away a mountain on all sides after an extremely long time by rubbing it.
The commentary on the Mountain Discourse is finished.
6. Commentary on the Mustard Seed Discourse.

129. "Nagara" is stated with reference to the fact that a city is surrounded by a rampart as its defining characteristic. However, the interior is entirely filled with mustard seeds; thus it is bound together like a mass of powder. Therefore he said: "But... [should not be seen]," and so forth.
The commentary on the Mustard Seed Sutta is finished. 7. Commentary on the Disciples Sutta (Sāvakasutta).
130. "From the place where he stood" means from the place where the bhikkhu stood after having recollected;
the meaning is: starting from the kalpa immediately preceding the hundred thousand kalpas that he had recollected. "In this way" means in the manner described.
All four bhikkhus were attainers of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). They say [this] by way of supposition: "They would recollect four hundred thousand kalpas day after day."
The commentary on the *Sāvakasutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Gaṅgāsutta*: 131.
"In this interval" means in that place, delimited by the region of the source ocean, measuring five hundred yojanas in length, or perhaps slightly more than five hundred yojanas.
The commentary on the Gaṅgā Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Daṇḍa Sutta: 132.
Regarding the ninth [verse], "thrown" (*khitta*) means thrown again and again. For if it were thrown only once, it would fall upon one [of the targets] such as the roots and so forth.
If that were the case, the intended lack of restriction regarding "morning" would not have been demonstrated.

Furthermore, the monks hearing the Dhamma there [in the world of devas] are in the human world; with reference to them, he said "from this world," and with reference to others, he said "the other world.
Or else, for each individual person, this world is as intended, and anything other than that is the other world.
The commentary on the Daṇḍa Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Puggala Sutta. 133.
*Samaṭṭhikāla* means the time when bones are obtainable in an even manner. *Giriparikkhepa* refers to Rājagaha, which is named "Giriparikkhepa" because it is surrounded by five mountains.
The commentary on the Puggala Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. The Second Chapter.
1. Commentary on the *Duggatasutta* 134.
"Duggata" (miserable) means having gone to or arrived at suffering in every respect due to a difficult livelihood.
One who has become thus is called "poor" and "wretched"; hence it is said, "poor and miserable. "With hands and feet" is merely an illustration.
He is ill-favored because he is possessed of other bodily parts that are misshapen.
The commentary on the *Duggata-sutta* is concluded.
2. Commentary on the *Sukhita-sutta*.
135. *Sukhitaṃ* means one in whom happiness has arisen. Therefore he said, "endowed with happiness," and so forth. *Susajjitaṃ* means thoroughly adorned with delicate requisites.
The commentary on the *Sukhita-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Tiṃsamatta-sutta*.

136. By way of undertaking the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and not merely by dwelling in the forest and so forth. "Possessing fetters" is because the fetters have not been entirely abandoned, and not because of being an ordinary worldling (puthujjana).
By the phrase "only one color at a time should be taken," he shows that one should take only one [color] from among the short, long, tawny, and so forth, of buffaloes and other animals.
The commentary on the *Tiṃsamatta-sutta* is finished.
4–9. Commentary on the *Mātusutta*, etc., 137–142.
By way of the restriction of gender and the restriction of world-systems: "For it is the time for women when men [are born], and for men when women [are born]."

Regarding the phrase "the time of men": just as there is no fixed gender within the continuum of a being, so too there is no fixed world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), for they are sometimes born in this world-system and sometimes in another.

Such being the case, one should understand that within these world-systems, during the period of women, there is no fixed gender or world-system, such as the rule that "there has been no one previously who was not his mother," and so forth. Therefore he said, "Among them," and so on.
The commentary on the Mātusutta and others is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Vepulla-pabbata Sutta: 143.
He brings forward a single apadāna to demonstrate: “Having thus generated a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), I shall cause the bhikkhus to attain distinction.”
They ascend in four days because they are four *yojanas* in height. "Of two Buddhas" refers to these two Buddhas: Kakusandha and Koṇāgamana.

It should be understood that the names of the people there at those respective times—“Tivaras,” “Rohitassas,” and “Suppiyas”—arose as designations for the teaching in those places, just as [the name] “Māgadhas” is used now.
Regarding "again, a hundred years": there is no human being known as one who lives beyond the first hundred years plus another hundred.
This was stated in the teaching as if it were a decline. "Having increased" means having increased from the state of a ten-year lifespan up to the state of an incalculable lifespan.
Having said "declined," he spoke the passage beginning with "how" in order to demonstrate that state of decline. That which...
"In terms of the measure of lifespan" means "as much as the measure of lifespan.
The commentary on the Vepulla Mountain Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the *Anamatagga Saṃyutta* of the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the Commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, is completed. 5.
The *Kassapa Saṃyutta*.
1. Commentary on the *Santuṭṭhasutta* 144.
"Contented" (*santuṭṭho*) means one who is satisfied with whatever requisites he has, whether superior or inferior. Therefore, he said: "with this or that," and so forth.
In this context, "this or that" (*itarītara*) is of two kinds: ordinary and that produced by knowledge. Of these, having rejected the ordinary—
Showing that it is produced by knowledge itself, he said, "coarse or fine," and so forth. The one is called "inferior" because it is different from the superior;
likewise, the superior is also "the other" because it is different from the inferior. For the terms "one" and "the other" depend on mutual relation.
Thus, non-greed is that which functions as such when one is content with any requisite, whether inferior or superior, such as robes and so on.
Contentment with whatever is mutually provided is being satisfied by possessing that.

Contentment with what is obtained is contentment according to one’s own gains, in accordance with the gains one receives. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. Alternatively, "gain" (*lābha*) means that which is obtained;

whatever gain there is is "what is obtained" (*yathālābha*), and contentment with that is "contentment with what is obtained" (*yathālābhasantosa*). "Strength" (*bala*) refers to physical strength. "Suitability" (*sāruppa*) refers to being appropriate for a monk.
"Non-longing for anything other than what has been obtained" is indeed a mode of conduct arising from fewness of wishes;
thus, showing the true nature of contentment as being precisely the turning away from that [longing], he said: "Even when obtaining [something], one does not take it.

"Having exchanged that" means: for those who are naturally weak and so forth, a heavy robe does not bring comfort but rather brings bodily affliction—therefore, it is for this purpose, and not out of a lack of desire or similar motives.
Having exchanged them. He said, "Even while subsisting with light robes, one is indeed content," because the use of light robes does not conflict with contentment.

He said, "Even while wearing those... [and so forth], because receiving expensive robes or many robes, and then discarding them to take others, does not conflict with contentment, as it stands within the method of appropriateness (*yathāsāruppa*).

“He is indeed contented. In this way, the intended meaning of the inclusion of the word “api” (even/also) should be understood in the descriptions of the remaining requisites according to their strength and suitability.
“Natural disposition” (*pakati*) refers to the natural tendency of speech and so forth. Because one is overcome by the remaining sleepiness, evil thoughts suddenly manifest upon waking.

“Muttaharītakaṃ” means either that which has been infused with cow’s urine, or “urine-harītakī” because it was discarded due to its state of putrefaction. “Praised by the Buddha and others” means commended by the Perfectly Enlightened One and the rest, as in the passage: “The going forth that relies upon the medicine of putrid urine,” and so forth.
One person is contented but does not speak in praise of contentment, such as the Venerable Elder Bākula.
Another is not contented but speaks in praise of contentment, such as the Elder Upananda the Sakyaputta.
He is not contented, nor does he speak in praise of contentment, just like the Elder Lāḷudāyī.
"This one" refers to the Venerable Mahākassapa. "Wrong search" means the seeking of requisites by way of improper and wrong livelihood.
"Is terrified" means he is terrified by the fear born of the thought, "How indeed might I obtain [them]? Likewise, he is agitated. "This one" refers to the Elder Mahākassapa.
Thus, like the aforementioned certain bhikkhu, he does not become agitated; he does not fall into agitation through the distress caused by the fear of non-acquisition.
Greed itself, in the sense of binding together with its object and in the sense of clinging, is "greed for greed" (*lobhagedha*).

They are "deluded" (*mucchanti*) by means of that greed, which is the state of delusion (*momūhatta*). "Disadvantage" (*ādīnava*) refers to fault (*dosa*). "The very escape" (*nissaraṇameva*)—means...
Regarding the robe, he understands precisely the deliverance characterized by non-attachment, preceded by the demonstration of its purpose. "Of whatever has been obtained, etc.
refers to alms-food and so forth that have been obtained as they may be; this is the genitive case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*).

He speaks according to the manner in which he himself would express it—as in the phrase "just as the Elder Mahākassapa"—whereas [the Blessed One] speaks according to the manner in which the Blessed One would express it.
It should be understood as: “Just as Kassapa [instructed] the bhikkhus. By means of Kassapa acting as the exemplar.

The act of speaking is a burden because it conforms to the promise: “Having been liberated myself, may I liberate others. The fulfillment of practice is a burden because it must be received upon the head in accordance with the Teacher’s command.
The commentary on the *Santuṭṭha-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Anottappī-sutta*: 145.
“Devoid of that” means devoid of that right effort. “Fearless” means free from fear. Even the non-arising of wholesome states [is due to this].
For that [perception] is indeed blameworthy because it is caused by ignorance and laziness. "For the sake of awakening" means for the sake of awakening by means of the Noble Paths.
"Secure through yogas" means because of being unharmed by them.
"A pleasant object" means something delightful that is a cause for the arising of greed. "In whatever way or other" means by way of [perceiving it as] beautiful, pleasant, and so forth.
“Greed and so forth”: they should be understood as “not yet arisen” because they have not previously arisen with respect to such a basis and object.

“Otherwise”: when they are apprehended without being conjoined with the basis and object in the manner already described. “In the basis”: in the basis of robes and so forth belonging to a supporter and the like.

“In the object”: in an object distinguished as pleasant and so forth. “By such a condition”: by conditions such as improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), negligence of mindfulness (*sati-ossagga*), and so on.
It should be understood that these [defilements], arising subsequently through the acquisition of conditions in the manner already described, are stated as such in the Canon.
Because they arise in this way, they are said not to be abandoned. For it is non-arising that is declared to be abandonment in the ultimate sense;
therefore, the intention is that they should be understood according to the method explained therein.
“Not yet attained” means not yet reached. “Those” refers to the blameless states such as virtue (sīla) and so forth, as previously mentioned. “Attained” means realized.
Regarding the phrase “virtue and other states,” if the paths and fruits are also included here, then why is it said “by way of falling away”?
To this he says, “And here,” and so forth. “Of this right effort” refers to the fourth right effort.
By way of this teaching: "This teaching was given thus: 'If my arisen wholesome states were to cease, it would lead to my harm.
Or, regarding the second path... "it would lead [to harm]"—this is said with reference to the arising of the harm known as suffering that would occur in seven future existences.
This is because of such statements as: "One who is ardent and possessed of moral dread is capable of awakening."
“It has been said: ‘These four right endeavors are explained by way of preliminary insight.
The commentary on the Anottappī Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Candūpama Sutta.

146. They are called "moon-like" (*candūpamā*) because the moon is their simile by virtue of qualities such as being dear, pleasing, constant, and new. The words beginning with *santhava* (familiarity) are mutual synonyms.
*Pariyuṭṭhāna* is the further manifestation of defilements in the mind. By all these terms, he expresses the absence of both attraction and repulsion toward sentient beings in certain instances.
However, by his own gentle nature, he is dear and pleasing to the great multitude. As for the purpose of this [passage]:
The simile of the moon has been brought forward; showing that, he said "In this way," and so forth. Not only is there this much virtue by way of the moon's likeness, but there are others as well;
thus, to show those, he said "Furthermore," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*evamādīhi*), [it is implied] "just as":
just as the moon proceeds along various paths such as the path of the sun for the benefit of the world, so too does the bhikkhu [proceed] through that.

He approaches that direction out of compassion for families. Just as the moon, moving from the dark fortnight toward the bright fortnight, becomes ever-new by increasing in its digits, so too the bhikkhu, having abandoned the dark side and approached the bright side, increases in virtues;
with a mind like the moon, he is ever-new for the sake of the world’s gladness and praise.
And he moves about always as if newly ordained, ever fresh.

"Having drawn away" means having separated [the mind] from the defilements and the objects of sensual desire. Since this involves drawing the body and mind toward renunciation and withdrawing them from the body, it is said:
"The meaning is 'having drawn in and having led away'. And herein, there is a tetrad.
In order to demonstrate that this is possible, the passage beginning with “yo hi bhikkhu” was spoken.
Regarding the term *niccanavayā*, it means exactly “niccanavakā”; for the word has been expanded by the addition of the sound *ka*, and the letter *ka* has been substituted by the letter *ya*.
“They wandered thus” means that they wandered in such a manner, due to the absence of any grasping (*pariggaha*) by way of the filaments (*kiñjakkha*).
“They wandered about out of compassion for others” means they moved about with a compassionate heart.
“The story of the two brothers” refers to the narrative concerning the Elder Dvebhātika. “Improper conduct” means conduct that is unsuitable for monks.
“Having set down” means having placed it as a formal charge. “In such a manner” means just as [it was done] in the midst of the Saṅgha or in the midst of a group.
And likewise, acting inappropriately toward a person of senior standing.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes entering a private house and other unsuitable actions different from those already mentioned.
"In that very place" means in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or in the presence of a senior person.

In those aforementioned places and others as well. By the phrase "even evil desire is mental immodesty" (*manopāgabbhiya*), it is shown that the active manifestation of anger, resentment, and so forth constitutes mental immodesty.
"Heavy on one side" means tilted toward the back. "Supported by wind" means supported by the mind-originated wind.

The connection is made by bringing in the word "mind" (*citta*) from the phrase "having stirred the mind" (*anubbejetvā citta*); for the stirring of the mind from that [side] is its inclination toward that.
Therefore he said, “He gazes with affection. “Having had him take hold of the wind-support” means having caused his body to be supported in such a way.

The correlation with the simile is indeed easy to understand. Because of his greed for sensual pleasures, he was one whose inclinations were base; because of his lack of purity in virtue and conduct, he was one who practiced wrongly.
He said, “The twin lightning flashes, their radiance emerging from his fingers, having doubled through the movement of the sky, coursed through the air.”
"Moving about," [it is said]. Because the phrase "he moved his hand in the air" does not appear elsewhere, it is called an "unmixed phrase" (*asambhinna-pada*).

"With a glad mind" (*attamano*) means a mind seized by rapture and joy (*pīti-somanassa*). For whatever consciousness is blameless and accompanied by rapture and joy, that is one's own (*sasantaka*), because it brings about welfare and happiness.
Therefore he said, "with one's own mind" (*sakamano*), and so forth. Not with dejection... [the mind] is seized.
Because it is contrary to one’s own mind. "In the same manner as before" means by the very method previously stated, beginning with: "Now, he who is of inferior inclination...
"The manner of showing confidence" refers to the action that should be performed by those who are confident. He shows its specific form by saying: "They should give the requisites such as robes.
"For the sake of such a state" means for the purpose for which the Dhamma was taught by the Blessed One, and for the purpose for which [it exists] in the Dispensation...
"Going forth" means for that purpose. "The state of protection" refers to the intention to protect [beings] from the fear of the states of misery (apāya).

By the phrase "by way of the simile of the moon, etc.," the word "etc. includes such qualities as being unstained by anything—like a hand moving through space—and a pure disposition characterized by compassion toward sentient beings.
The commentary on the Candūpama-sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Kulūpaka-sutta: 147.
One who approaches families is a *kulūpaka*. "Is given away" (*sandīyati*) means it is completely given away; the meaning is that it is utterly destroyed.
Furthermore, that tearing apart, causing pain, and distressing is what is meant by "he is distressed. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"On that account, he experiences suffering and mental grief. This is according to the method stated above—that is, by following the method already explained.
The commentary on the *Kulūpaka-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Sutta on the Worn-out (Jiṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā) 148.
Because the hole at the place where [the cloth] was torn and split was not wide, it was merely sewn together with thread without applying a patch;

however, when the hole became wide, patches were applied. "Worn out by use" (*nivvasanāni*) means those whose function as clothing has been exhausted through long service; "worn out by use" (*paribhogajiṇṇāni*) means [those worn out] through being used.
This is the meaning. Therefore he said: “Formerly... [omitted] ...obtained their names. A grammatical operation preceded by a designation is considered *anicca* (irregular);
thus it is stated as “gahapatānī,” just as in the case of the word “vīriyaṃ.
“Senāpatiṃ” means one who possesses the status of a general; the sense is “one worthy of being a commander-in-chief. “By one’s own work” means by the work to be performed by oneself.

"He" refers to the Teacher. "In him" refers to the Elder Mahākassapa; this is the grammatical connection. To explain the meaning already stated—that [the Teacher] did not [grant the request]—he said, "Why?
and so forth. To address the question, "If the Teacher was not wishing to have the dhutaṅgas relinquished, then why did he say, 'You are now old,' and so on? he said, "But just as... and so forth.
“Dwelling in happiness in this very life” means a comfortable dwelling within this very selfhood (*attabhāva*).

“Non-human delight in hearing” means that because of the arising of forest sounds that transcend those of humans, there arises a delight in the Dhamma conditioned by hearing sounds dependent upon the support for living in seclusion, thinking, “I am dwelling in the forest.
“Another” means someone else; “a second,” is the meaning. “Right there” means in that very same place as the first.
In the dwelling place and at the time of dwelling, there is comfort because of the arising of mental seclusion. Therefore he said, "For one who delights alone in the forest.
"Likewise" means that just as there is delight for the forest-dweller, so too is a pleasant dwelling in this very life obtained by the alms-food eater.
This same method applies to the remaining [terms]. Since the other [qualities] depend on being an alms-food eater, they indicate a distinction; therefore, in order to show that very distinction:
“Wandering at the wrong time,” and so forth, has been stated.

Because it was granted by the owners that one who does not come to their house for a meal after taking our voting-ticket (salāka) need not be expelled for seven days, he does not receive the ticket for seven days;
this is not by way of a formal agreement (katika). Regarding the conduct of one who goes for alms (piṇḍacārika-vatta):
Because it is a duty (*vatta*), the passage beginning with “For whomsoever this...
has been stated. That which is to be done first is the *vatta*; the other is the *paṭivatta*. Alternatively, the *vatta* is the major duty, while the *paṭivatta* is the minor one.

Some read it as “the performance of duties” (*vattapaṭipatti*); the meaning is the carrying out of the *vatta*. [This refers to] the lifting up, bringing forward, moving away, releasing, setting down, and restraining.
By way of the six divisions. "By way of heaviness" means by way of stability.

He does not wander seeking the *vassāvāsa* (rainy-season residence) with the thought, "Those staying at such-and-such a lodging receive much *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season gift)," because he does not actually take hold of the *vassāvāsika*. Therefore, he thinks only of the comfort of the lodging itself.
Because of that state of having many requisites, there is no dwelling in comfort, owing to the abundance of suffering involved in guarding, maintaining, and so forth, those requisites.
The dwelling in happiness pertaining to this very life is obtained only by those who possess fewness of wishes, contentment, and the like.
The commentary on the *Jiṇṇa-sutta* is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Ovāda Sutta 149.
“In his own place” means for the purpose of establishing him in the position of a great disciple by way of being an instructor and admonisher of his fellow celibates.
Alternatively, it is because [the Buddha thought]: “Now I shall not remain much longer, nor will Sāriputta and Moggallāna.”

But the Blessed One began this teaching with the intention: "This one, having a lifespan of twenty years, will perform for the monks after my passing the duties that must be performed by me while instructing and exhorting them.
Therefore, "in his own place" means in the position of one who delivers the exhortation to be given by the Teacher.
Hence he said: "But it shall be thus," and so forth, just as the Blessed One said: "Exhort, Kassapa... and so on.

“Or you,” he said. They should be addressed as suffering because they do not grasp instructions respectfully. By the means that produce a state of being difficult to speak with—namely, anger, resentment, and so forth.
Following the Dhamma is what is called grasping instructions respectfully; having cut off the practice of the path is what is called grasping them disrespectfully (to the left).
Thus he said, “Instruction,” and so on. “Speaking by overstepping” means speaking while overstepping and disregarding one another.
They say: "He will speak much"—meaning, while preaching the Dhamma, who would speak by making it extensive?
"Incoherent" means that what precedes and follows does not cohere, being devoid of logical cause and illustration. "Not sweet" means it is not sweet, not pleasant to the ear, and not endearing.
His discourse rises up and ceases very quickly, like a bank of sand, because it lacks continuity.
The commentary on the Ovādasutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Second Ovādasutta. 150.

*Okappanasaddhā* (conviction through settling) is the faith that, having entered into the object worthy of faith, settles upon it with the thought, "It is exactly so. *Kusaladhammajānanapaññā* (wisdom that knows wholesome states) is...
The wisdom that knows blameless states in their entirety. "Decline" means decline from all forms of excellence;
for there is no such thing as excellence for one who is devoid of virtuous friends.
The commentary on the Second Ovāda Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Third Discourse of Advice (Tatiya-ovāda-sutta) 151.
"In the past" refers to the time of the first enlightenment. "Now" refers to the period subsequent to that. "In the undertaking of a task" means at the commencement of a cause.
"Among those elders endowed with the aforementioned qualities. "In him" means in that person endowed with the qualities as previously described. Thus...
“While honor is being paid”: when honor is being paid by monks who have conceived a sense of reverence, thinking, “How excellent indeed is this monk!
“These fellow-celibates”: they say to that monk, “Come, monk,” turning him toward their own faces.
For as for the word *taṃ* here, it is a mere particle; it is called a “calamity” because it produces harm. He yearns.

It is called *patthanā* because it "frequents" (*bhajati*) and "binds" (*bajjhati*). It is an "intense attachment" (*abhisaṅga*); thus he said, "aspiration" (*abhipatthanā*) means "excessive aspiration" (*adhimatta-patthanā*).
The commentary on the Third Discourse of Advice is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on Meditative Absorptions and Direct Knowledges (*Jhānābhiñña-sutta*).
152. Regarding the phrase "yāvadeva," he says that this term has the same meaning as "yāvat":

"'As far as I desire' means 'as much as I wish. This was undertaken for the purpose of demonstrating mastery over the attainments of jhāna according to one's wish. It has already been explained in detail;
therefore, the intention is that it should be understood exactly as it was explained there. "The destruction of the taints (āsavānaṃ khayo)": [this refers to the attainment of Arahantship].

Because of the total exhaustion of the taints (*āsava*) by means of the Noble Path, due to the destruction of all taints. "Becoming non-conditioned" means becoming non-conditioned by way of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
The commentary on the *Jhānābhiññā-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Upassaya-sutta*.
153. Some bhikkhus go to the bhikkhunīs’ dwelling and exhort the bhikkhunīs for the sake of gain and honor;
however, this elder does not request to go to the bhikkhunīs’ dwelling for the sake of gain and honor.
To explain why, he says, “Those who desire a meditation subject,” and so forth. For this Venerable Ānanda, having exerted himself, [spoke] regarding the quality of his practice.

Since those bhikkhunīs were practitioners of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, he demonstrated the perfection of the practice of insight by means of a Dhamma talk that elucidated the arising and passing away, etc., of the five aggregates of clinging.

He correctly demonstrated both the characteristics of impermanence and so forth, as well as the arising and passing away, etc.; he demonstrated them as if they were directly perceived with his own hand.

"Caused him to apply himself" means he caused him to apply himself there to insight (vipassanā) having the characteristics as its object; he had him grasp it in such a way that it proceeds by entering the path of practice.

"Encouraged him" means that when insight had been undertaken and the arising, passing away, and so forth of formations appeared, he encouraged him by means of exertion and equanimity at the appropriate times through the non-cessation of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga).

Having brought it to the middle path of development, he properly encouraged the mind of insight by making the faculties clear, so that insight-knowledge might flow with great serenity; or else, he incited it toward Nibbāna. "He gladdened" means:
by way of the development proceeding evenly through the insight thus occurring, [he gladdened it] for the sake of what follows.
He gladdened his mind by means of the meditation he had attained; he thoroughly delighted it by means of the satisfaction he had found. In this way, the meaning here should be understood.

He is a *muni* because he understands (*manute*) the truths by way of full comprehension and so forth. "That" (*te*) refers to that [understanding]. This genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
"Higher" (*uttarī*) means above; the meaning is "beyond your [current] true nature. "Falling into a faction" is going on a wrong path.

There was an excessive opportunity. "He examined" means he was one who did not restrain [the nun] after having investigated her; thus he was not held in high esteem. The Elder was a mere semblance of a Buddha.
By saying, "Venerable sir, please forgive her," instead of saying, "The foolish nun spoke ill," it was as if he were speaking with partiality;
therefore he said, "One nun was not restrained," and so forth.

They have disappeared from their own marks; they have not gone out of sight by departing for another region. "Like thorny branches" means like the branches of the *kuraṇṭaka*, the *apāmārga*, the *kaṇṭaka*, and the *lasikā* plants.
The commentary on the *Upassaya-sutta* is finished.
11. Commentary on the *Cīvara-sutta*.
154. To the south of Rājagaha is the mountain Dakkhiṇāgiri; by lengthening the vowel *a* to *ā* in the word *giri*, it becomes *Dakkhiṇāgiri*.
Because it is situated to the south of that mountain, the region to its south is also called "Dakkhiṇāgirī.
They were expelled in a single day because they had not attained the faith through which they had gone forth.
Where four or more monks, having accepted an improper invitation, partake together after receiving any one of the five kinds of cooked food,
that is called "eating in a group" (*gaṇabhojana*). Since eating by three monks is permitted, the rule "the eating of three is prescribed" implies that eating in a group is prohibited.
This has been stated. Because it was permitted for three reasons, they call it "eating in a group of three.
"The restraint of the ill-behaved is itself the comfortable dwelling of the well-behaved"—this is one factor.

For this very reason, he said, "By means of the restraint of the ill-behaved," and so forth. It was on account of this—that Devadatta... [and others] might cause a schism in the Saṅgha—that eating in a group of three was prescribed.
"Atha kiñcarahi" means "Now, for what reason?"—the intention being: "Why do you wander about having formed an incomplete group?
Wandering on tour with an incomplete assembly is not out of compassion for families; rather, it is because of the destruction of those families.
With this intention, the Elder said, "I think you wander about like a crop-destroyer," and so forth.
"Searching" means by way of seeing its extreme state of purity. "I do not know how to recite [it]" because the mind itself has never arisen in that manner before.
"Kiñcana" refers to the basis of defilement. "Palibodha" is the field that should be gathered; "ālaya" is attachment or concern.
"Because of the absence of opportunity" means because there is no opportunity for wholesome activity due to having many duties and tasks to perform. "Because of the place of assembly" means...
Because the dust of the defilements settles and subsides therein, as if a sign had been made.
"The holy life of the three trainings" refers to the supreme (*brahma*) conduct comprised of the three trainings, beginning with the training in higher virtue.

Having made it unbroken by ensuring it does not fall into a state of being fragmented and so forth—this is indeed a definition; [it applies] without leaving out any portion of the training whatsoever.
It is "absolutely fulfilled" because it must be fulfilled in an absolute sense.
It is "absolutely pure" because it must be maintained having made it utterly pure, without producing even a mere thought-moment of the stain of defilement.
For that very reason, it is "scratched like a tally" (*saṅkhalikhita*); hence he said, "like a scratched tally. The fangs also...

By the very mention of "hair," it is included; thus it is called "beard," but the meaning is not that only the beard is meant here. *Kāsāyāni* means dyed with ochre. *Vaṅgasāṭako* means a garment produced in the region of Vaṅga.
*Eso* refers to the Elder Mahākassapa. From the time of his initial resolve—that is, from the beginning of his aspiration—this [attainment] which is now being described [occurred].
Because he is the third when reckoned starting from the two Chief Disciples, he is called the "Third Disciple."
It was said: "Six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus" means one hundred thousand bhikkhus, sixty thousand, and eight thousand.
And as for "this and that quality," he spoke while praising their qualities from the virtue of morality up to the supreme fruit (arahantship), as if filling the great ocean.
"Confusion" (*kolāhala*) refers to the clamor produced by the deities.

It is of five colors, beginning with the small. Just as a man plunging into a great flood might think, "Let there be crossing or let there be death," so too, while crossing the ocean of stinginess, he later...
[omission] ...placed [his foot] at the base of the Blessed One’s feet through the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma.

Because the abandoning of stinginess has been taught, it is said, "while speaking of the Teacher’s virtues," meaning that the Teacher’s qualities have indeed been recounted. "From then on" means from the time of hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.

"Of the Tathāgata’s couch" means of the couch used by the Tathāgata. Having given a gift, he appointed him to the position of brahmin chaplain. She became the daughter of a merchant of exactly such [standing].
"Of one whose result has not been given at all" means: of that karma which was previously performed and accumulated, but whose result had not been given in any way whatsoever.
"Of that karma" refers to the karma of cutting off the alms-food intended for the bowl of that Paccekabuddha, which was sufficient to fill a lump of raw flesh.
Because of that, in that very same existence, he was turned back due to having a foul-smelling body in seven places. "A row of bricks" means a row of golden bricks.
"By the bricks joined with the first brick" means that it was deficient by the number of bricks to be joined together with the first brick placed in that row.
"In an auspicious time" means she arrived at the very moment such bricks were desired.
"By that bond" means by that connection of cement.

"Hanging ornaments" means hanging ornaments made of pearls and gems. "Merit" means there is no merit for us by which—by what sign or by what cause—the acquisition of something even more subtle than this might occur;
such is the meaning. "By the power of merit" means by the fixed order established through the majesty of merit.
And he had been granted permission to bestow the sovereignty of Bārāṇasī upon him.
"Phussaratha" means an auspicious chariot. The fivefold regalia of royalty consists of the turban, the yak-tail fan, the sword, the jewel, and the white parasol;
here, the white parasol is mentioned separately. Urged by the power of his merit to accept the celestial cloth, he said, "Is it not too thick, father? and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "five hundred walking-places" (*pañca caṅkamanasatāni*): here, by the word "etc. (*iti*), places suitable for renunciants such as fire-halls and so forth are included.
"Well-played" (*sādhukīḷita*) refers to the honors that should be performed at the place where Noble Ones have attained final nibbāna. "The noble ladies are free from illness;
do not neglect them" is an illustration of the manner in which she was questioned. "The deities have attained final nibbāna" is the queen’s reply.
He gave. "Having prepared" means having offered. "The going-forth of the recluses" (samaṇakapabbajjā) refers to the going-forth to be practiced by the Noble Ones who have stilled their evil.
For that king, having seen the appearance of the Paccekabuddhas, thought, "This alone is excellent," and thus he took on such a very same outward mark (liṅga).
"Right there" means in the Brahma-world itself. The connection is made by bringing forward the phrase, "having arrived at the twentieth year. From the Brahma-world...
Because he had come and been born [there], and because his commitment to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) had been maintained for a long time, he said, "Do not speak such words," and so forth.
They say that twenty *dharaṇas* are a "nikkha. The connection is: "If I do not receive [this], I will not stay; I shall make them understand."
"Itthākaroti" refers to the place of origin of the Woman-Jewel (itthiratana). "Ayyadhītā" means our noble master’s daughter; the sense is "Bhaddakāpilānī.
Because she was distinguished by her graceful form, he says "Mahāgīva" to express her resemblance to the statue. Therefore he said, "Of the noble master’s daughter," and so forth.
"Samānapaṇṇaṃ" means a similar leaf—the leaf recording the account of both the prince and the princess. "Itoca etocā" means from here and from there.

Those men, setting out from the place of assembly toward Mahātittha village in the kingdom of Magadha and toward the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda, were said to be "sending each other off" because they were parting from one another; thus it is said, "send them here and there.
"A flower-garland" (pupphadāma) refers to a flower-garland the size of an elephant's trunk. "Those" refers to those flower-garlands. "They" refers to both Bhaddas.
And Pippali-kumāra as well. "By worldly bait" means by affection rooted in the household; the meaning is "by the gratification of sensual desire. "Unassociated" means not associated.
They deliberated with their minds uplifted by the seed of liberation, which was blazing like a lamp burning within a jar.
"Fastened to machines" refers to [mechanisms] placed here and there for the purpose of producing crops.

"Water-jars with outlets fastened by machinery" refers to water-jars that discharge water according to the arrangement of bricks, doors, and panels. "Workplace" (*kammanta*) means a place for performing agricultural labor.
"Slave-villages" (*dāsagāma*) means villages inhabited by slaves. "Having poured out" (*osāpetvā*) means having cast in.

"By way of deportment and gestures" (*ākappakuttavasena*) means by way of physical appearance and by way of action. "Inappropriate" (*ananucchavika*) means unsuitable for the garb of one who has gone forth. "At its summit" (*tassa matthake*) means at the place where the two paths diverge.
The connection is: "He sat down because it was fitting to provide a summary of these [qualities].
To show that the Teacher’s sitting there was of such a nature, the passage beginning with "But as he was sitting" was stated.

Therein, that which has been produced by the accumulation of an inconceivable and immeasurable store of merit gathered over an infinite period of time for the Buddhas, and which is illuminated by the discerned qualities of a Buddha— (End of sentence fragment)

The glory of the physical body—resplendent with the primary marks (*lakkhaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*), adorned with a halo of fathom-wide radiance like a garland of jewels—is, by virtue of being established through its own nature, beyond description;

yet, in order to increase the faith of Mahākassapa, who had never before seen it, the Blessed One sat down without concealing that very splendor, and thus he is said to have "sat down having assumed the appearance of a Buddha...". Spreading over an area of eighty cubits,
In common usage, it is said to be "eighty cubits" [in height]. "Satasākha" means having many branches, having numerous branches.
It was golden-colored because it was completely covered on all sides by the continuous rays of the Buddha. It should be understood in the manner thus described.
Regarding the words "Rājagahaṃ" and "Nāḷandaṃ," he says "of Rājagaha" because the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive (sāmivacana) due to its connection with the word "antara."

"And as for Nālandā": indeed, it is not possible for there to be another teacher other than me, because in this world with its devas, there exists no one else capable of instructing beings according to their needs regarding the ultimate truths pertaining to both the present life and the future life.
Nor is it possible for there to be another Sugata other than me, because there exists no one else endowed with the multitude of qualities of "beautiful going. Not...

For it is not possible for there to be another Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) other than myself, because of the absence of anyone else who has fully awakened through self-dependent knowledge regarding all phenomena.
"By this" refers to the statement, "Venerable Sir, you are my Teacher.
The intention is that [the Buddha] spoke while not yet knowing [of his own omniscience]. "With all his heart" means with a mind complete in all internal faculties.

“Endowed with” (*samannāgata*) means possessed of, having properly and sequentially arrived at, or attained. “It would bear fruit” (*phaleyya*) means it would burst open. “Dissolution” (*vilaya*) means destruction.

“Thus one should train” refers to the manner that will now be described. He said “great” (*mahanta*) to signify the abundance, that is, the vastness, of moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*).
“Even earlier than that” means even before approaching [the teacher]. Likewise, he would be one who has abandoned excessive conceit (*atimāna*).
"Conscience and moral dread are established as they should. "Dependent on the wholesome" means dependent on blameless states.

"A bone" means a bone by virtue of that state. By saying, "not allowing the mind to go even slightly outward," he indicates that the mental state of listening from the beginning until the end is intended here as "the whole mind"; thus he shows their convergence.

"With all" ... [etc. ... "having applied his mind" means having applied his mind solely to the Dhamma through every intervening state of attention that occurred from the initial undertaking until the teaching was completed. "With ear pricked up" means with the ear fixed upon the Dhamma.
"Having lent" means having made it attentive. "By way of the first jhāna" refers to this very [meditation] among the foul (asubha) subjects.
In the former case, association with pleasure is stated; in the other case, as well.
For one wandering in the ocean of *saṃsāra*, the defilements stand in the place of debt because they bring about the state of being subject to the taints (*āsava*);
thus he said, "One who has a refuge is one possessed of defilement. Regarding the four kinds of enjoyment and so forth, whatever is to be said therein is found in the *Visuddhimagga*.

This should be understood according to the method already stated in the commentaries (*saṃvaṇṇanā*). Furthermore, in this context, the Blessed One gave the first exhortation for the sake of abandoning pride regarding birth, since the elder was of brahmin birth;
the second, for the sake of abandoning the conceit (*ahaṃkāra*) arising from reliance on extensive learning;
and the third, for the sake of abandoning self-affection (*attasineha*) arising from reliance on the excellence of his physical basis (*upadhi*). "On the eighth day" means:
On the eighth day from the day the Blessed One arrived.
His descent from the road occurred earlier, on the very day he arrived.
If the attainment of *arahantship* was later, then why is it stated in the Pāḷi as if it were already accomplished beforehand? To this he says: "Of the section on the teaching," and so forth.

Having said, "Friend Saraṇa, I ate the country alms-food for only seven days," he spoke the words, "On the eighth day, final knowledge arose," while announcing his attainment of Arahantship at the appropriate moment. This is the traditional account (āgama) of the section of the teaching here.
Thereafter, showing the favor bestowed upon him by the Blessed One—the exchange of robes—he said, "Then, friend," and so forth.

"By the edge" means by the edge of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) that has been laid out after being folded fourfold. "It is fitting to be one who wears [the robe] like a 'birth-cloth' refuse-rag wearer...
and so forth; it should be understood that by this, as well as by the previous mention of the "born-in-the-forest" [dweller], all thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) are included.
"To act suitably" means to undertake a practice that is appropriate. "The Elder put on [the robe]"—this is the connection.
He is "born from the breast" (*orasa*) because he was born by means of the chest, depending either on the Blessed One’s exhortation (*ovāda*) or on the Blessed One’s Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*).
Alternatively, he was born from the mouth of the Blessed One’s Dhamma-body as the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*).

For this very reason, it should be understood that his state of being "born of the Dhamma" and "fashioned by the Dhamma" has also been extolled. Because the Teacher gives the Dhamma of exhortation and the Elder receives it, he is the "heir to the Dhamma of exhortation" (*ovādadhammadāyāda*).
The meaning is "the inheritance of the Dhamma consisting of exhortation"; he is worthy of that. This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

Having stated, "And renunciation is purified," in order to show by way of contrast how it is truly purified, the words beginning with "Friend, for whom... were spoken. Therein, *evaṃ* means "just as I obtained [it], so did he from the Teacher."

The construction is: "he obtains [it] from the presence [of the Teacher]. Regarding the phrase "having roared the lion’s roar," here too the "roaring of the lion’s roar" is indeed the teaching itself.
The Elder indicates precisely the favor bestowed upon him by the Teacher in the manner stated in the immediately following sutta, and not otherwise;
for the Great Elder does not merely manifest his own power of virtue. "The rest" refers to that which has not been commented upon here.
"By the same method as before" means by the very method stated in the immediately preceding sutta.
The commentary on the Cīvara-sutta is finished.
12. Commentary on the Paraṃmaraṇa-sutta.
155. He is the Tathāgata because he has come (āgato) in the same manner as he came in past eons and past births by way of kamma and defilements;

or alternatively, he is the Tathāgata because he has come to, approached, and been reborn in this or that particular personal existence (attabhāva) exactly according to the kamma performed and accumulated.
Thus, it says: "The Tathāgata is a being. Regarding this, it says: "It is thus."
This refers to the speculative view that occurs in the form: “It exists; it remains for all eternity.
It is not based on what is beneficial (*atthasannissita*) means it is not based on what is praised as happiness in terms of the present life, the future life, or the ultimate truth (*paramattha*).

Regarding the phrase “the beginning of the holy life” (*ādibrahmacariyaka*), the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*) is intended here because of its preeminent status. And this speculative view of his—
It does not constitute even the measure of the initial path because it is unhelpful and contrary [to the goal]. For that very reason, it is likewise no support for the other holy life.
The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the *Parammaraṇa-sutta* is finished.
13. Commentary on the *Saddhammappatirūpaka-sutta* 156.

It is called *aññā* because one understands—that is, one knows and penetrates—without transgressing the boundary of what is known by the lower paths. It is the wisdom of the supreme path (*aggamaggapaññā*). It is called *aññā* because it belongs to *añña* (the final knowledge); it is the fruit of arahantship. Therefore, he said, “in arahantship. It illuminates; that is, it is the sign of illumination.
The connection is made by bringing forward the two phrases, “the mind trembles” and “it illuminates. It illuminates.
“Toward the object. The construction is: “the mind wavers due to the secondary defilements (*upakkilesa*). Therefore he said, “by which the mind trembles.
This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well.

“In the presence” means in mindfulness (*sati*). “And by equanimity” means by insight-equanimity (*vipassanupekkhā*). And here, [equanimity] is distinct from the continuity arising from the insight-consciousness.
The visible-object base that is luminous is "illumination" (*obhāsa*). Knowledge and the others are associated only with the consciousness of insight (*vipassanā*).

Resolution that functions with distinction in its own respective function is "resolution through faith" (*saddhā-adhimokkha*). "Establishment" (*upaṭṭhāna*) is mindfulness (*sati*). "Equanimity" (*upekkhā*) here refers to the equanimity of adverting;
for it is volition associated with the adverting consciousness. It is mentioned here because it functions by way of both adverting and looking on with indifference.
“Adverting equanimity” is what is said. Again, by the word “equanimity,” it is precisely insight-equanimity that is thus spoken of because of its very state of neutrality.
“Attachment” (nikanti) means the longing for or the regard for insight. Or it may be a subtler defilement, difficult to discern.
“These ten points” means these [states] beginning with illumination are the points, the bases, for the arising of the defilements.
“Whose wisdom is well-developed”: one whose wisdom is fully cultivated knows things as they truly are.

The overweening conceit that occurs, thinking, “Relying on these [qualities], I have certainly attained the path and attained the fruit,” is mental agitation regarding phenomena (*dhammuddhacca*), a basis for phenomena (*dhammūpanissaya*), and a state of distraction.
One who is skilled therein, knowing it as it truly is, does not fall into delusion regarding it.
The "counterfeit of the true Dhamma of realization" (adhigamasaddhammappatirūpaka) is so called because it brings about the state of conceit that one has realized what has not been realized.
To the extent that it is a defilement of insight-knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa), it can also be understood as a counterfeit of the true Dhamma of practice (paṭipattisaddhammappatirūpaka).
By "Discourse on Elements" (Dhātukathā), he refers to the *Mahādhātukathā*. By "Vedalla Piṭaka," he means the Vetullaka Piṭaka. That [was brought] from the abode of the Nāgas.
Some say it was brought [from elsewhere]. Others say it is a mere polemical utterance. It is not the word of the Buddha because it contradicts the word of the Buddha;

for a Perfectly Enlightened One does not speak that which is contradictory in its earlier and later parts. In this regard, they apply a "dart" [of criticism], yet no discipline of the defilements is seen therein;
on the contrary, it becomes a condition for the arising of defilements.
"Without selling" means not going to sell. "That" refers to the golden vessel.
They were unable [to do so] because of the lack of clarity in their knowledge. This same method applies to what follows as well.
Now, in order to clarify from a causal perspective the very meaning already stated in the passage beginning with "the bhikkhus had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā),"...
Furthermore, the passage beginning with “In the first enlightenment” and so forth was stated. Regarding that, the phrase “they fulfilled the practice” means:
when in the past did they fulfill the practice that brings about the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*)? It was during the time of the first enlightenment—the monks [of that era].
For such a thing does not occur without right self-application and the merit previously performed. This same method applies to those who follow as well. At that time, the true Dhamma of practice...
By the phrase "it will have disappeared," he shows that the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*) which is close to this Noble Path is the true Dhamma of practice (*paṭipatti-saddhamma*).

"In both" means even when the Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas have disappeared. For one who remains established in the training of higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), [the Dhamma] is indeed not disappeared, because it is originated from the other two trainings.
"For what reason? means by what cause; in another teaching...
The intention is that when one phenomenon has disappeared, the non-disappearance of another phenomenon is spoken of.

It serves as a condition for practice because it fully illustrates the sequence of practice. Practice is a condition for realization because of its nature as the penetration of specific characteristics.
The intention is that the scripture alone is the authority for the endurance of the Teaching.
"But is it not the case that the Dispensation has declined even while the study of the scriptures (pariyatti) continues?"—this is the intended meaning.
"Bhikkhus who do not achieve success" refers to those of immoral conduct who do not succeed even in mere virtue (sīla). "In this" means "in this Pātimokkha.
He asked [the question] thinking, "Are there those who remain without violating their virtue?"
"In these" means: in these four great elements (*mahābhūta*) which are so vast as to be capable of overwhelming the entire world.
"Therefore" means: because the True Dhamma does not disappear even through anything else that is exceedingly great, nor is there any other system to be mentioned;
therefore. "He said thus" refers to the manner in which what is now being stated is spoken.
“Grasping (ādāna) is the beginning; the beginning itself is the ‘initial’ (ādika),” thus he said, “by the initial, that is, by grasping.

“Leading downward” means leading to the lower realms; the meaning is that they produce the suffering of the states of loss (apāya) and the suffering of saṃsāra. “Devoid of reverence” means devoid of respect.
“Dependence” (patissayana) is the state of living bound [to others] through a lowly position; *patissa* and *patissaya* are one in meaning. That—
Because they have none of these, he said: "They are 'without deference,' meaning they lack respect and do not behave with humility. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Saddhammappatirūpaka-sutta* is finished.
From the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the *Kassapa-saṃyutta* is completed.
6. The *Lābhasakkāra-saṃyutta*, Chapter 1.
The First Section.
1. Commentary on the Dāruṇa Sutta 157.
"Stubborn" (*thaddho*) means harsh, because of his refusal to grant what is desired. "The acquisition of the four requisites" (*catupaccayalābho*) is the obtaining of the four requisites.
"Honor" (*sakkāro*) is the veneration by means of those very requisites when they are well-prepared; in terms of its actual meaning, however, it is simply prosperity (*sampatti*).

He said: “The gain belongs to those very [monks]... [etc. ... *Vaṇṇaghosa* means the proclamation of virtues. It is called *antarāyika* because it does not bypass an obstacle, since it brings about harm.
The commentary on the *Dāruṇa-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Baḷisasutta* 158.
One who wanders with a hook, or lives by means of it, is a fisherman (*bāḷisiko*). Therefore he said: "wandering while having taken a hook.
"Gone toward bait" (*āmisagata*) means arrived at bait, fallen into bait. Therefore he said: "smeared with bait. Even for those whose referents (*adhikaraṇa*) are different...
He said, "The compound has an external meaning," namely, "the seeing of the eye in nutriment" (*āmise cakkhudassana*). "Aya" is said to mean happiness;
because it is the opposite of that, it is "anaya," which is suffering. Thus he said, "one who has reached suffering. "Assa" means "by this.

For this genitive case is used in the sense of the agent. It was stated that as long as the defilements proceed in such a manner, the person proceeding in that way is not dissociated from the defilements.
“Just as one would act toward the Māra of the defilements, so should it be done.
The commentary on the *Baḷisa-sutta* is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the *Kumma-sutta* and others.
159–160. "Bone-tortoises" (*aṭṭhikacchapā*) are those which have a sharp bone-point on the top of their shell; a collection of them is called a "bone-tortoise family.
That which hangs from and falls upon the bodies of fish, tortoises, and so forth is called a "falling thing" (*papatā*);
it refers to the form of an iron thorn. "In an iron sheath" (*ayakosake*) means in a sheath made of iron. "Shaped like a *kaṇika* dart" means having the shape of a dart used for piercing leather.
*Ayakaṇṭako* means an iron hook with a curved point. "It emerges from there" means that as soon as it has been inserted, you can no longer say, "This is ours.
"In the sutta immediately following this" refers to the fourth sutta.
The commentary on the *Kumma-sutta* and others is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Mīḷhaka Sutta 161.
"Mīḷhakā" is said thus in the feminine gender. "Excrement-dwelling creatures" (gūthapāṇaka) means creatures that feed on excrement. "In the interior" means within the belly.
The commentary on the Mīḷhaka Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Asanisutta* (162):
“May these beings, failing to obtain gain and honor, experience the suffering of hunger and thirst”—it is not out of a desire for beings to suffer that one speaks thus;
this is the connection to be understood. One experiences endless suffering because of the great abundance of unwholesome states of consciousness arising again and again.
The commentary on the *Asanisutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Diddhasutta* 163.
Or, "smeared with hide" means smeared by what has gone [into it], that is, by the hide; therefore he said, "smeared with poison."
The commentary on the Diddha-sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Siṅgāla-sutta: 164.

He is called "Old Jackal" (*jarasiṅgāla*) because of the lack of bodily beauty. Because his body has prickly thorns, he is named "Ukkaṇṭaka" (the Prickly One). "Phuṭati" means it bursts or breaks open.
The commentary on the *Siṅgāla-sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Veramba-sutta* 165.

“He does not guard his body” means that he abandons the twenty-six types of appropriate conduct. “He does not guard his speech” means that from the vicinity of lust and the vicinity of anger, up until the point of its utterance, he fails to restrain it.
The commentary on the Verañjā Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Sagāthaka Sutta 166.
Regarding the verse, “For one who is being honored...,” the phrase *asakkārena cūbhayaṃ* means both [the states] by way of lack of honor (*asakkāra*).
The meaning is: sometimes by honor, sometimes by lack of honor, and sometimes by both. Therefore he said, "by lack of honor," and so forth.
Because of the attainment of the constant abidings, he is called "one who is constant" (*sātatika*); thus he said, "arahantship... [and] subtle vision," and so forth.
For that [vision] is indeed called "diamond-like knowledge" (*vajirūpama-ñāṇa*). "Because it has come" means because of entering into the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Because it has entered into the preliminary work [of the previous discourse].
The commentary on the *Sagāthaka-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. Second Chapter: 1–2.
Explanations of the *Suvaṇṇapāti-sutta* and others. 167–168.

He is unable to be shaken because he is firmly established upon the mountain of virtue (*sīla*). Or, he performs other duties all the more readily because he has already cast aside [attachment to] virtue. In the third [case] and those following, there is nothing new.
The commentary on the Suvaṇṇapāti-sutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
3. The Third Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discourse on Women (Mātugāmasutta) 170.

The Blessed One, demonstrating that among those things which are called "dissimilar objects" capable of obsessing a man's mind, it is specifically gain and honor (*lābhasakkāra*) that are uniquely capable of obsessing the minds of beings, said:
Showing that he spoke the passage beginning with “Not for him, monks,” he said “Not for her,” and so forth.
The commentary on the *Mātugāma-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Kalyāṇī-sutta*.
171. The second [sutta] is likewise clear; it is stated solely by way of the "Beauty of the Land" (Janapadakalyāṇī) for that same purpose.
The commentary on the Kalyāṇīsutta is finished.
3–6. Commentary on the Ekaputtakasutta and others.
172–175. The term "those with faith" (saddhā) refers to the faith that has arrived via the Noble Path; thus he says, "stream-enterers" (sotāpannā).
The commentary on the Ekaputtaka Sutta and others is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Third Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta.

176. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*evamādi*), by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of great learning, the virtue of restraint, and so on, is to be understood. [The text speaks of] the arising (*samudaya*) of gain and honor—that is, the cause of its occurrence—by way of the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*), and by way of being the cause for the arising of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
The commentary on the third *Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta* is concluded.
8. Commentary on the *Chavi Sutta*.
177. “Gain, honor, and fame cause rebirth in the hells and other realms”—this was said with reference to the mass of defilements that serve as their basis.
“Causing rebirth” means causing one to be born there. “He destroys this human existence” means by way of not permitting the further arising of a human state.
“Therefore” refers both to the fact that they cause rebirth in the miserable destinies and to the fact that they bring about the suffering of death in this very life.
The commentary on the Chavisutta is finished.
