9. Commentary on the Rajjusutta: 178.
"Harsh and rough" means capable of cutting the skin and so forth.
The commentary on the Rope Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Bhikkhu Sutta. 179.
"With reference to that" means with reference to the absence of opportunity for dwelling in happiness in this very life.
The commentary on the Bhikkhu Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
4. The Fourth Chapter.
1–4. Commentary on the Bhindisutta, etc. (180–183).
“Devadatta might be reborn in heaven,” and so forth, is a hypothetical statement.
For one whose destiny is fixed for *paccekabodhi* (individual enlightenment) is not capable of attaining the paths and fruits in the interim. “He” refers to the faultless Dhamma. “His” refers to...

Of Devadatta. He attained the eradication of the great mass of evil states he had accumulated through the power [of his path] in that very existence, because they were brought to a state of eradication;
yet it was not absolute. For this unwholesome state is weak; it does not possess great power like the wholesome.
Therefore, for such individuals, there is incurability within that very existence; otherwise, there would be the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).

...would be an absolute certainty of wrongness (*micchattaniyāma*). If this is so, how is it that there is a demonstration of the "stump of the round" (*vaṭṭakhāṇuka*)? It is by way of habitual practice (*āsevanā*);
therefore, just as it is said, "Once submerged, a fool is submerged indeed," so too is the demonstration of the stump of the round.
For whatever conditions a person relied upon to acquire that view and practiced accordingly, [even if] that [view] were not to recur again—[it remains a cause].
It should not be said that he does not lift up his head when he has fallen upon a support.
The commentary on the Bhindisutta and others is finished.
5. Commentary on the Acirapakkantasutta.

184. "When the time has arrived" means when the time for birth has arrived because the fetus has reached full maturity. "Foals" refers to the offspring of mares. "This" refers to the statement, "As a mare [bears] a fetus.
The commentary on the *Acirapakkanta-sutta* is concluded.
6. Commentary on the *Pañcarathasata-sutta*.

185. It is called *abhihāra* because it is brought forward (*abhiharīyati*). Since it is the food itself that is the *abhihāra*, he says, "food to be brought forward" (*abhiharitabbaṃ bhattaṃ*). "Fish-bile" means the bile of a predatory fish. "They would pour [it] over" means they would sprinkle it with snakes and so forth.
The commentary on the Sutta of the Five Hundred Chariots is finished.
7–13. Commentary on the Sutta of the Mother, etc.

186–187. “Also because of one’s mother”: this means also because of the cause for abandoning whatever brings harm that has arisen for one’s own mother. “In the following [passages]”: in such instances as “also because of one’s father,” and so forth.
The commentary on the *Mātusutta* and others is concluded.
From the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyuttanikāya*.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Connected Discourses on Gain and Honor is complete.
7. The Connected Discourses with Rāhula. 1. The First Chapter.
1–8. Commentary on the Discourse on the Eye, etc. (188–195).
“One who dwells alone” (*ekavihārī*) means one who dwells being solitary even in all four postures. “Withdrawn from seclusion” (*vivekaṭṭho*) means the state of being secluded;

therefore he said, “silent. “Not dwelling apart from mindfulness” (*satiyā avippavasanto*) means standing by way of not being separated from mindfulness, in the sense of never abandoning it at any time.
"Exerting" means endowed with energy; it refers to one who possesses energy that functions by way of burning away and tormenting all defilements.
"Resolute" means having a mind directed toward that specific attainment; the meaning is that it is inclined toward and leaning upon it.

"By way of non-existence after having existed" means: not existing prior to its arising, it arises through the convergence of conditions, and then, characterized by cessation following its production, [it passes away].

By way of non-existence (*abhāvākāra*). "Impermanent" (*anicca*) is so called because of the absence of permanence and stability. "Because of having arising and passing away" means because of ceasing after having arisen moment by moment.
"Because of being temporary" means because of its momentariness. "Because of the limit of change" means because of possessing the quality of transformation.
For the eye, by undergoing modification based on its dependence [on conditions], reaches a state of transformation, destruction, and oppression. "Because of the negation of permanence" means...

Because it must be rejected due to its impermanence, and because not even a trace of it is found. "In the sense of being hard to endure" means because it must be endured as a continuous state of suffering.

"In the sense of being the basis of suffering" means because it is the foundation for various kinds of suffering. "In the sense of constant oppression" means because its nature is one of frequent torment.
"By way of the negation of pleasure" means because the state of pleasure must be rejected. [This is] the grasping of craving.

The grasping at "mine" arises from the state of "mine-making" (*mamaṅkāra*). The grasping at "I" arises from the state of "I-making" (*ahaṅkāra*). The grasping at views arises from the state of the perversion that thinks "this is my self.

By the phrase "by way of dispassion," the term "dispassion" is intended as the means of apprehension. Likewise, by the phrase "by way of liberation," the term "liberation" is intended as the means of apprehension.

Only confidence (*pasāda*) is included because it is what is intended to have attained the status of a door. The intention is that the mind engaged in the process of comprehension (*sammasana*) is the mind that has become the door.
In the sixth [meditation] subject, the phenomena belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka-dhammā*) are intended for the course of comprehension (*sammasana-cāra*).

Just as in the first sutta the five sensitive organs (*pañca-pasāda*) were taken and not the eye and so forth together with their material bases (*sasambhāra*), so too in the third sutta it is not only the consciousness based on the sensitive organs that is taken, nor the states associated with it.
For in this way the restriction is purposeful; otherwise, by that [restriction], it would be meaningless.

Because there is nothing to be removed. "In all cases" means in all [the suttas] beginning with the fourth sutta. "Attained to impulsion" means associated with impulsive consciousness (*javana-citta*).
The commentary on the Sutta on the Eye, etc., is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Sutta on the Elements (*Dhātu-sutta*).

196. The space element is said to be "materiality" by way of its delimiting materiality; it is stated as "the remaining [elements] are materiality" with this intention. "Name-and-form" refers to the name and form belonging to the three planes.
The commentary on the *Dhātusutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Khandhasutta*.

"By way of the inclusive section" means by way of the method of collecting the phenomena (*dhamma*). "Here" means in this discourse. "Belonging to the three planes" is said because those belonging to the three planes are intended to be included within the range of comprehension through contemplation (*sammasana*).
The commentary on the *Khandha-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. Second Chapter. 11. Commentary on the Discourse on Latent Tendencies (Anusayasutta). 200.
In the second chapter, by the word "self," the Venerable Rāhula shows his own body possessed of consciousness. By the word "another," [he shows another's].
He shows another’s body as being without consciousness. Or, without taking immaterial phenomena in another’s continuum, he speaks while grasping only the material body.
Others say: "It was stated thus with reference to the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of non-percipient beings.
"By the former" refers to the phrase "in this conscious body"; "by the latter" refers to the word "externally."
"By way of a term": these defilements refer to the defilements known as views, craving, and conceit. "In regard to these bases" refers to internal and external bases.

"He comprehends... sees": he sees by means of the knowledge of comprehension through insight-wisdom in the preliminary stage, and by means of the knowledge of clear realization at the moment of the path, seeing well with knowledge that is directly experienced by himself.
The commentary on the *Anusaya-sutta* is finished.
12. Commentary on the *Apagata-sutta*: 201.
“I am this”: by the complete abandonment of the conceit of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, it is utterly and entirely gone away.
The commentary on the *Apagata-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
"In two" refers to the First Chapter and so forth. Because it was taught within the teaching on the stage of one beyond training (*asekkha-bhūmi*), it is called the "stage of one beyond training."
"First" refers to the first chapter, which was spoken for the Elder who made a formal request with the words, "It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One [would teach me]," and so forth;

the second was spoken for the Elder who did not make such a request, according to his own inclination. Those called the "qualities that ripen liberation" are the faculties of faith and so on, which are based upon turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭa*).
However, because they were taught in connection with insight (*vipassanā*), they are indeed explained here. According to the sequence of each respective teaching...
For indeed, the Elder brought those teachings to full maturity for him; thus, the Blessed One taught the second chapter even without being requested.
Here ends the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Points) in the commentary on the *Rāhula-saṃyutta* within the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.
8. Saṃyutta on the Marks (Lakkhaṇasaṃyutta) 1.
First Chapter (Paṭhamavagga) 1.
Explanation of the Discourse on the Bones (Aṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā)
Regarding the passage beginning with "The Venerable Lakkhaṇa," in order to clarify everything—namely, "Who was the Venerable Lakkhaṇa? Why did he receive the name 'Lakkhaṇa'?
Who was the Venerable Moggallāna? And why did he manifest a smile?"—the section beginning with "yvāyaṃ" is commenced.
"Endowed with the marks" means endowed with the marks of a great man (*purisalakkhaṇa*).
A smile that is slight is called "white" (*sita*); thus he said, "a gentle smile.
"A skeleton of bones"—this is not merely a lifeless skeleton of bones, but rather a single *peta*; thus he said, "born in the *peta*-world.
"These personal existences" refers to *peta*-existences. "They do not come into range" means they do not come into the sensory range [of sight] as do the personal existences of devas.
They come by their very nature. However, they might come within the range of perception of humans through their own inclination.
Compassion has as its proximate cause the sight of those overcome by suffering and being without a protector; thus he said, "when compassion is to be exercised.
The word *sampatti* (accomplishment) should be applied to each [term]: one's own accomplishment and the accomplishment of the Buddha-knowledge. To clarify both of these:
The passage beginning with “taṃ hi” has been stated. Therein, the phrase “having recollected his own success, he manifested a smile” should be connected by supplying the missing words.
He speaks of the *dhammadhātu* with reference to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Alternatively, *dhammadhātu* means the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.
Thus says the Elder Lakkhaṇa. "Rebirth" (upapatti) means birth (jāti); for by the term "rebirth," he refers to such a personal existence (attabhāva).
"With iron beaks" means with beaks made of iron itself. "They move about" means they travel through the air. "It is indeed a marvel" refers to a marvel of reproach.
"Becoming eyes" means having attained the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), being like eyes for the world.
The meaning here should be understood in this way.
He says, "‘Yattha’ is a particle in the sense of a cause," because elsewhere the phrase ‘yattha hi nāma’ expresses the sense of a reason.
In the immeasurable multitude of beings, they [exist] within existence (bhava) divided into categories such as the realm of desire (kāmabhava), and further divided into states such as hell (niraya).

...the various destinies, the stations of consciousness such as those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, and likewise the abodes of beings—by making all these manifest and bringing them before my eyes, [he showed] my omniscient knowledge.
"A butcher of oxen" (goghātaka) means one who habitually slaughters cattle. Therefore he said, "having slaughtered again and again. "Of him" refers to the cattle.
Of a deed that brings about slaughter. "Of a karma to be experienced in successive births" means of a karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariyavedanīyakamma*).

When the result of a powerful act such as cow-slaughter is being given, the karma to be experienced in successive births—which had not yet found an opportunity—now finds an opportunity once that [powerful] result has ripened;
it is therefore called "remaining karma. "Rebirth-linking" refers to the rebirth-linking produced by unwholesome karma. "Due to the commonality of the nature of the karma" means...
"By way of similarity to the action. "By way of similarity to the object" means by way of the state of being similar to, or identical with, the object.

For it is said, "by the remainder of the result of that very action," considering that just as that action and its result previously occurred in relation to such an object, so too does this action and its result now occur in relation to exactly such an object.

For there is indeed a figurative designation of something as being that very thing even when it is merely similar to it, as in the expressions, "That is the same partridge," or "Those are the same medicinal herbs.
"It became the sign" means that the deed previously performed and accumulated— which had created an opportunity for the production of rebirth as a peta—
now appeared in such a way as to become the sign, the objective support (*ālambana*), for its ripening result (*vipāka*).
He was that cow-slayer. He was reborn as a skeleton-ghost (aṭṭhisaṅkhalika-peta) by way of a result corresponding to his past action.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Skeleton is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Lump of Flesh (Pesisutta).
203. “Having made balls of beef” means: having slaughtered a cow repeatedly, having cut the beef, and having made them into balls.
“Having dried them” means: having dried them for the purpose of storing them for a period of time. For meat-balls that are being dried are designated as *vallūra* (dried meat).
The commentary on the Sutta on Meat Balls is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Piṇḍasutta 204.
*Nippakkhacamme*: meaning "with the skin of the wings gone.
4. Commentary on the Nicchavisutta.
205. One who kills sheep is a *orabbhika* (sheep-slaughterer). *Eḷaka* means goats. 5.
Commentary on the Asilomasutta. 206. *Nivāpapuṭṭha*:
nourished by the fodder provided by oneself; [one] who sells them after repeatedly slaughtering them with a sword.
6. Commentary on the Satti-sutta (The Arrow):
"A single deer" refers to a single dīpaka deer.
7. Commentary on the Usu-loma-sutta (The Hair of the Arrow)
208. "By means of causes" means by means of torments. "Having known" means having known the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
8. Commentary on the *Sūciloma-sutta* 209.
One who hears and fills [the ears] is a "sūta," such as a horse-trainer and so forth.
9. Commentary on the Second Sūciloma Sutta 210.

One who "indicates" (sūcati)—that is, reports what was heard here having been heard elsewhere, or what was heard elsewhere having been heard here—by means of instigating slander is a "slanderer" (sūcaka). The connection is: "He brought a man to ruin and disaster.
10. Commentary on the Kumbhaṇḍa Sutta.
211. A judge (*vinicchayāmacca*) is a chief minister of justice appointed by the king to preside over legal proceedings.
He is called a "village cheat" (*gāmakūṭaka*) because he deceives or cheats the village populace. Some say that a village headman of such a character is a "village cheat.
One must be impartial, as it is said, "one who stands firm in the Dhamma. This refers to sitting in the secret assembly (*rahasseṅga*).
The sitting was indeed uneven.
The commentary on the Kumbhaṇḍa Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. Second Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Sāsīsakasutta. 212.
"Touching" means touching with the intent to steal.
3. Commentary on the Nicchavī Sutta (214).
A woman who has a husband is not her own mistress regarding her touch. *Vaṭṭitvā* means having spoken and then gone elsewhere.
4. Commentary on the Maṅguli Sutta.

215. It is called *maṅguli* because it moves (*ulati*) by way of being inauspicious; the meaning is that it proceeds with a form that is deformed and loathsome. Therefore he said: "Deformed, unsightly, and loathsome. 5.
Commentary on the *Okilinīsutta* 216.
It is "cooked" (*uppakka*) because the body is cooked upwardly by fire; it is "moistened" (*kilinna*) because the body is drenched from below by trickling.
*Okilinī*: Because she is strewn with charcoal from this side and that, she is called *okilinī*.
Therefore he said, “She, it is said,” and so forth. *Aṅgāracitake*: on a heap of charcoal. The sweat that trickles from her body is impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome.
“Of that king” means of that King Kāliṅga. *Nāṭakinī*: a woman devoted to dancing. *Sedaṃ*: sweating; the meaning is “the act of perspiring.”
The commentary on the Okilinīsutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Asīsakasutta: 217.
He was reborn as a headless trunk because of his habituation to grasping signs in that manner at the time of accumulating kamma.
7–11. Commentary on the *Pāpabhikkhu-sutta* and others (218–222).
"A base monk" (*lāmakabhikkhu*) means he is base due to his inferior conduct; he is a monk because of his monk’s appearance and because he lives by means of alms-food (*bhikkhāhāra*).

"Playing at heart's pleasure" (*cittakeḷi*) means playing various games according to one's own fancy. "This very same [method]" refers to the method explained in the section concerning the monk (*bhikkhuvatthu*).
The commentary on the *Pāpabhikkhu-sutta* and others is finished.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning (*līnatthappakāsanā*) for the commentary on the *Lakkhaṇa-saṃyutta* within the *Sāratthappakāsinī*,
the sub-commentary on the *Saṃyutta-nikāya*, is completed.
9. Saṃyutta on Similes 1.
Commentary on the Kūṭa Sutta 223.
“They go to the peak” means they go to the peak by way of entering through the opening at the peak. And as for the rafters...
Having entered between the rafters, they too stand having struck against the peak; thus, both kinds [of rafters] converge at the peak.

By the uprooting, destruction, and breaking of the peak—by the uprooting of ignorance, that is, by the absolute non-arising of ignorance—the attainment of the Dhamma of liberation is shown, and thereby the attainment of the Dhammas corresponding to it is demonstrated. "Heedful" means...
However, by this [verse], the means for that [attainment] is shown.
The commentary on the Kūṭasutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Nakhasikhasutta.

224. "Just as the dust placed on the tip of a fingernail is small"—this is stated by way of a lowly illustration because the karma conducive to a happy rebirth is so slight that it is likewise [small] even among the devas.
For fewer beings are born among the devas, and that too only among the devas of the sense-sphere (kāmadēva). As for the others, there is no need even to mention it.
The commentary on the *Nakhasikhasutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Kulasutta* 225.
They "destroy" means they afflict. "Developed" means brought to full growth by way of the completion of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Again and again...
"Made" means brought into being through repeated practice by means of cultivation;

it is "made" in the sense of being established, just as a well-yoked chariot drawn by thoroughbreds proceeds according to the driver's will when controlled by a skilled charioteer, so too it is made to proceed according to one's wish.
"In the sense of a foundation" means in the sense of a basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*). It is "made" like a site by the complete purification of all defilements.
It is made like a well-cleansed boundary. "Established" means it is set down because it cannot be shaken due to its state of being well-developed, owing to the removal of opposing factors.
"Heaped up on all sides" means it has been brought to an accumulation of development through every aspect; therefore he said, "well-increased.
"Well undertaken" means it has been properly accomplished by reaching the pinnacle of the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
The commentary on the Kula-sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Okkhā-sutta: 226.
“Of hundred large-mouthed mortars” means of a hundred large-mouthed, large-sized jars. “Filled with choice food.”
“Of those who are filled with choice foods brought forth by ghee, honey, sugar, and so on. Regarding the reading *tassa*:
“for a mere milking-time” means for the duration of a milking. To the question of how much that is intended to be, he says: “of a cow,” and so forth.

“The pervading of welfare toward all beings” refers to the cultivation of universal loving-kindness (*mettā*); it means that one is able to develop a mind of loving-kindness that has reached absorption (*appanā*).
This is the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). That [gift] is even more fruitful than the aforementioned gift.
The commentary on the *Okkhāsutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Sattisutta*.
227. "Having struck at the tip" means having given a blow with the hand or the fist at the tip of a sharp-edged spear.
"Like a roll of cotton" means like a ball of cotton that has been struck. "Like a roll of resin" means like a ball of resin in the shape of a fruit.
"Having made them into one" means having brought the twenty or thirty balls together into a single mass by means of a cord or similar device.
*Alliyāpento* means making them adhere; *paṭileṇeti* means he draws back or bends [the threads]. *Alliyāpento* means causing those two streams to touch one another.
*Paṭikoṭṭeti* means he strikes back against it. In this context, *niyyāsa* is like the dregs.
*Kappāsavaṭṭanakaraṇīyaṃ* refers to the binding rod used for the purpose of winding together the carded cotton.
"Spinning" means spinning by way of twisting cotton.
The commentary on the *Sattisutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Dhanuggahasutta*.
228. *Daḷhadhanuno* means "of one with a firmer bow. Now, in order to show the degree of that firmness by way of its measurement, the passage beginning with "*daḷhadhanū*" was spoken.
Therein, *dvisahassathāmaṃ* means "the strength of two thousand [palas].
To make this very meaning more evident, he said the passage beginning with "*yassā*. Therein, *yassa* refers to the bow; *āropitassa* means...
“With the string fastened”: bound to the bowstring. “It is released from the ground”:
this should be understood as having the strength of two thousand [paccūsas]. “Of iron, lead, and so forth”: of black iron, copper, lead, and the like. “A load”: a man’s load;
however, that strength of his should be regarded according to the standard of an average man. “Having mastered the craft”: by way of training in archery (*dhanurveda*).

"Having attained mastery" means by way of being unerring in hitting the targets. "Those who have performed the approach" (*katūpasanā*) refers to those who, having approached royal courts and the like, have performed the act of approaching (*upasanā*)—that is, eating—therefore he says, "those who have displayed their craft in royal courts and the like.
Having stated, "The Bodhisatta brought four arrows," he then demonstrates that same matter in detail: "At that time..."
He spoke the words beginning with "Let us fly. Therein, "we shall fly" means we shall run.

"The fire arose" means that heat arose due to the heat of their rapid flight and because they were in close proximity to the heat of the sun's rays. "With the cage of wings" means within the lattice-work of the wings.
"Turning back" means turning back [thinking], "This flying is purposeless. "With a bowl covered by a leaf-plate" means with a bowl covered by a leaf-saucer.
He became like a covered bowl as he flew away; by his swift descent, he looked down upon the sky above the city.
Because he moved so rapidly, he appeared like many thousands of swans, just as when the Bodhisatta was a master archer and observed the tips of the arrows.
He said, "It is difficult," referring to the fact that [the city] could no longer be seen, not to his own falling. For the solar disk was [traversed] with extreme speed.

Even though it travels with great speed, because of its vast extent and its brilliance, it comes within the range of vision for beings over a distance of fifty yojanas; however, a swift swan traveling at the same speed as such a sun would not be perceived.
Therefore it was said: "It is not possible for you to see it. The four...
They were marksmen who could hit a moving target. Having gone to fetch a gong to hear the sound, they had it hung up;
then, sitting down facing the east, they said with reference to the arrow shot toward the eastern direction: "Flying up together with the very first arrow.
They discharged those four arrows at one and the same moment.

It is called the "life-formative force" (*āyusaṅkhāra*) because by means of it one forms life. For just as the occurrence of matter born of kamma is dependent upon the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), so too the occurrence of the personal existence (*attabhāva*) is dependent upon that [life-faculty].

The plural designation in the text is used because, at a single moment, many hundreds of life-faculties are found to exist. That is the life-faculty. From that [arises the life-span] of the aforementioned deities.
It wastes away even more swiftly than that which moves, because its duration is momentary. For this has been said:
“Life, the personal existence, and all pleasure and pain Are conjoined with a single moment of consciousness; The moment passes with extreme rapidity.”
"Bheda" means breaking up. It cannot even be defined because its duration is exceedingly brief.
The commentary on the *Dhanuggahasutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Āṇisutta*.
229. Other kings, perceiving that these [kings] were taking a tenth part as their share just like themselves, followed their example;
thus their imitation is evident. Because he brought the great multitude [of people], he is called Ānaka; thus it is said, "one who has obtained such a name.
Now, in order to show the sequence of his arrival starting from the beginning, he says, "In the Himavanta, it is said," and so forth. *Kareṇum* means a female elephant (*kareṇukā*).
"Hatthinī" means "an elephant. "Sakkariṃsu" means they honored [her] by way of avoiding harm and by way of offering praise and gifts.
"Otarī" means she entered the Kuḷīra lake. "Paṭikkamitvā ṭhapanavasena apakkamitvā pati" means she fell after having stepped back and stopped.
"Suvaṇṇarajatādimayaṃ" means that in some opening it was made of gold, in some of silver, and in some...
They fashioned and fixed a pin made of crystal. Previously, it was called "twelve-yojana-measure" because its measure was twelve yojanas when it stood pervading [the space].
Then, as many hundreds of years passed, even within the hall it could only be heard with difficulty, because it was merely the clatter of the pins.

"Profound" means bottomless and difficult to fathom. For instance, the *Salla-sutta* is profound by way of its textual phrasing—beginning with "signless and unknown"—but it is not profound in its meaning.
This is because various verses therein remain difficult to comprehend;
since that which is difficult to comprehend is difficult to grasp through knowledge, it is called "profound. Furthermore, in some cases here, there is a sequence of what precedes and follows.
Because the verses are difficult to understand, they are indeed hard to penetrate;
therefore, it is said that "by way of the text they are profound," as in the phrase, "by way of the text they are profound like the Salla Sutta.

In this same manner, the meaning should be understood here regarding the statement, "profound by way of the meaning. The profundity of the Mahāvedalla Sutta by way of its meaning is indeed evident. It transcends the world.

The supramundane consists of the ninefold immeasurable states; because they possess that which has become their object (attha), they are called "supramundane" (*lokuttara*). Therefore, it was said: "They illuminate the supramundane object.
"Merely the seven dhammas of emptiness" means that [the mind] is empty of a self (*satta*)—that is, of an *attan*—and is merely the dhamma alone.
The terms "should be taken up" (*uggahetabba*) and "should be mastered" (*pariyāpuṇitabba*) are stated with a change of gender and number.
He said: "In what should be grasped and mastered. *Kavitā* is the work of a poet (*kavī*);
for whatever is the work of someone, that is said to be "done by him. Therefore he said: "*Kavitā* means made by poets.
The other term, "*kāveyyā*," is what is called "poetry" (*kabya*). And the meaning of "*kabba*" is "that which is spoken by a poet. Thus he said:
“Synonyms for that very [term]”: *cittakkharā* means letters of various forms. “Existing outside the teaching” means not belonging to the sphere of the teaching.
“By their disciples” means by the disciples of anyone whatsoever who are not known as “disciples of the Buddhas.
“Not being grasped” means not being grasped by way of hearing, memorizing, mastering, understanding the meaning, investigating, and so forth.
They vanish; they go out of sight.
The commentary on the Āṇisutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Kaliṅgara Sutta.
230. *Kaliṅgara* refers to a small piece of wood; those for whom that serves as a support (*upadhāna*) are called *kaliṅgarūpadhānā*.
However, the Licchavis at that time lived having made a staff of acacia wood (*khadira*) their support. Therefore, it is said: "in the acacia sticks," and so forth.

Because there is no moment (*khaṇa*) for them to pierce [the target] other than what is known as natural lightning, they are "shooters of non-moments" (*akkhaṇavedhino*), meaning they are swifter than that.
“From piercing. “A flash” (akkhaṇa) refers to lightning because of its momentary duration. Those who pierce a target by means of a flash are “flash-piercers” (akkhaṇavedhino).
Or, those who pierce a hair divided in many ways are “hair-piercers” (vālavedhino). For here, a single portion of a hair is taken as “hair.”
Having bathed in order to dispel the fatigue and exhaustion arising from the practice of meditation for a great part of the day;
"referring to them" means referring to those bhikkhus engaged in such meditative practice.
This matter now being stated was spoken in the ancient commentary (*porāṇaṭṭhakathā*). "This island too" refers to Tambapaṇṇidīpa (the Island of Ceylon). At the time of engaging in meditation...
By way of being announced, it is a single sound of the gong, as if by the simultaneous striking of gongs in various places;
and by way of the monks dwelling in leaf-huts and other dwellings here and there, it is a single place of striving (*ekapadhāna*). As for "having various entrances" (*nānāmukha*):
there is one monastery in the western direction of Anurādhapura, and [another] in the eastern direction of the city of Pilicchikoḷa.
The sounds of the gongs resounding in both places merge with the sounds of the gongs resounding in between.
The sound of the gong resounding in Kalyāṇī is likewise [heard] in Nāgadīpa.
The commentary on the Kaliṅgara Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Nāga Sutta 231. *Atikkantavelam*: "Past the time" means past the time for the discourse seated after the expression of thanks for the meal (*bhattānumodana*). *Asambhinnehi*:

"With unbroken [vocal cords]" means by way of the excellence of the voice; the meaning is that one does not neglect the excellence of the pronunciation of the voice. Due to the impurity of one's intention...
It is neither by way of praise for virtues nor by way of the power of knowledge. "That" refers to that consumption of conditions, that wrong practice.
The commentary on the Nāga Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Biḷārasutta* (The Cat Sutta) 232.
“The junction of houses” (*gharānaṃ sandhi*) means the place where one house is connected to another. “Accompanied by filth” (*samalaṃ*) means it exists together with dirt.
It is the place for the dust-heap used when departing from a house or a village. “A rubbish heap” (*saṅkāraṭṭhānaṃ*) means a mound of refuse. Some [say...]
They say it is "the place where the heap of defilements is joined. "Emergence" (vuṭṭhāna) means emergence from the offense committed, not emergence from the defilement;
it is the resolution upon the state of purity. However, since that is simply called "confession" (desanā) regarding the offense as it was committed, he said, "confession is made known."
The commentary on the *Biḷārasutta* is finished.
11. Commentary on the *Siṅgālasutta* 233.

By the phrase "even this much," it is meant that this old jackal will not obtain even a mere measure of mental satisfaction for the duration of an entire *kappa*, because he will be in a state of constant suffering and affliction due to being incessantly scorched by the flames of the Avīci hell in every respect.
The commentary on the *Siṅgālasutta* is finished.
12. Commentary on the Second *Siṅgālasutta* 234.

"Knowing what has been done" means knowing the service rendered. "Recognizing what has been done" is precisely that same knowledge, but by way of making it manifest to others. "Only the conduct" refers specifically to the offense committed.
The commentary on the Second Siṅgāla Sutta is finished.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Simile Saṃyutta of the Sāratthappakāsinī,
the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya, is completed.
10. Bhikkhu-saṃyutta 1.
Kolita-sutta Commentary 235.
"Conversation among disciples" means conversation concerning fellow practitioners of the holy life (sabrahmacārī) among the disciples. [They thought: "May we not be like the Buddhas."
It is the practice customary among Buddhas that disciples do not address one another as "Friend, monks.
When addressed thus, the monks reply "Friend," and not "Venerable Sir. In the second jhāna, applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) cease;
for that jhāna must be brought about precisely by their cessation. As for the phrase "of which there is the cessation": of which...

Through the cessation and thorough suppression of verbal formations—namely, applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)—the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*) comes to non-occurrence because its cause has been pacified from afar.
"Noble" (*ariya*) means faultless. The intended meaning is that this silence is utterly pure, unlike the impure adoption of a vow of dumbness by the followers of other sects.
"The first jhāna and so forth... [refers to the stages of meditative absorption].
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the third jhāna and so forth are included.

It is said that they are "accompanied by applied thought" (vitakkasahagata) because they proceed together with the applied thought that serves as their object; thus he says, "having applied thought as their object.
And the state of having applied thought as their object should be understood in terms of perception and attention grasping a subtle object. Therefore he said:
“They did not appear continuously”: because mastery had not been properly attained, they were not well-mastered.
“Even perceptions and acts of attention” means that even the perceptions and acts of attention occurring for the attainment of the third jhāna were conducive only to decline, not to distinction.
“Place it rightly”: having abandoned outward distraction, place the mind rightly within itself. One-pointed.
"Make it one-pointed": by means of that very same warding off of distraction, make the mind one-pointed through the settling of consciousness (cittasamādhāna) by way of an undisturbed state of mind.
"Place it": having ensured that it does not fall away even slightly or much at all, place it upon the object of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).

Regarding the phrase "the state of great direct knowledge" (*mahābhiññatanti*), he said "the state of the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiññatanti*) because the Venerable One was a possessor of great direct knowledge (*mahābhiñño*) through the fulfillment of the level of the second chief disciple, and not merely as one who is so by chance.
"By this means" means by the means described as "Then, friends... and so forth.
"Having increased" means having repeatedly developed and expanded both concentration and wisdom by bringing them to ever higher states of distinction.
The commentary on the Koliya Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Upatissa Sutta 236.

This was said with reference to an exceedingly sublime being or formation, because desire and lust have been completely abandoned in every respect and in all things. He asks for the sake of knowledge, due to the state of the Teacher’s qualities being supremely sublime.
The commentary on the Upatissa Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Ghaṭa Sutta 237. *Pariveṇaggena*: by way of the respective cells. Some say: "In a single dwelling" means in one residence under one roof.
*Te*: those two elders. *Pāṭiyekkesu ṭhānesu*: in separate places. *Nisīdanti*: they sit.
They sit for their midday rest. It is called "gross" because its object is a limited dhamma. "They" refers to the Elder and the Blessed One.

"One whose energy is fulfilled" means one whose energy is complete by way of accomplishing the four tasks. "One whose energy is exerted" means one whose energy has been set in motion without falling into even the slightest contraction. "Merely for the purpose of placing near" means merely for the purpose of setting it down in proximity.
Because it is found among the dhammas of the four planes, it is said [of wisdom] that it "stands having entered into the dhammas of the four planes."

It has been stated. Concentration itself, in the sense of being that which is characterized, is the characteristic of concentration (*samādhilakkhaṇa*). In this way, the characteristic of insight (*vipassanālakkhaṇa*) is to be understood.

"Of each other" (*aññamaññassa*) should be understood as "of various different characteristics. "Of the other" (*aññassa*) means of the second one. "The yoke" (*dhuraṃ*) refers to the burden to be carried.
Regarding both of these—the characteristic of concentration and the characteristic of insight—the Perfectly Enlightened One has reached their fulfillment.
The commentary on the Ghaṭa Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Nava Sutta: 238.
"Abhicetasika" means based on the higher mind (*abhicetasi*). It is a mind that has become preeminent through the destruction of its opposites.
Higher consciousness (*abhicitta*). Because the jhānas indeed have as their condition the consciousness associated with them, it is therefore said, "of those dependent [on it].
"One who gains at will" means one who gains according to his desire. "According to the limit" means according to the time-limit established.
"One who gains abundantly" means one who gains immeasurably. For "slight" (*kasira*) is said to mean limited; by its opposite—
It is not difficult and is immeasurable. Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'mastery in jhāna'.
Regarding "having undertaken laxly," he said "having exercised lax energy," the meaning being that one has made a lax effort.
The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished.
5. Sujātasutta Commentary 239.
“Other forms” means the forms of others. “One whose form surpasses” means one who stands surpassing [all] by virtue of his own excellence of form and beauty of form;
he brings satisfaction even to one looking at him for a very long time. Of the seeing—that is, of the eye—...

"Hitā" means beautiful to behold. "Pāsādikaṃ" means inspiring confidence. "By way of the excellence of the complexion of the skin and the beauty of the bodily form" means by way of the loveliness of both the skin's complexion and the configuration of the body.
The commentary on the Sujāta Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya Sutta 240.
“Of ugly bodily appearance” means both an unattractive complexion and an unattractive physical form. “By way of size” means by way of the body’s dimensions.
“Whatever he desired” means whatever he himself wished for. “Great embarrassment” means a great state of shame or humiliation.
"Having adverted to the qualities" means having adverted to and attended to the Teacher’s bodily qualities and his conduct-qualities according to the measure of one's own knowledge.
"A circle of a league" means a circumference of a league.

It is stated as "kāyasmiṃ" (in the body) with the nasal vowel dropped for the sake of metrical ease in the verse; thus it is said "kāyasmiṃ. "The measure of the body is not the cause" means that what is called the measure of the physical frame is no measure at all; the intention is that only qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth are the true measure.
The commentary on the Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Visākha Sutta 241.

That which belongs to a city (*pura*) is *porī*; it refers to being endowed with urbanity. Therefore he said, “of the city-dwellers,” and so forth. Furthermore, that [urbanity] is characterized by the absence of haste, slowness, and stumbling.
It is free from defects such as lack of confidence or harshness; thus he says, "pur... pe... vācāya. "Asandiddhāya" means speech that is not loose.
Therefore he says, "apalibuddhāya," and so forth. It does not flow with the fault of *ela*; thus it is *anelagalā*, speech that is non-contradictory. Therefore he says, "niddosāya.
It reveals the Four Noble Truths and is never divorced from the truth; thus he says, "catusaccapariyāpannāya."
For these [truths] bring about, establish, and set in motion the four truths by means of delimitation. Therefore he said: "proceeding without abandoning the four truths.
A "banner" (dhaja) is so called in the sense of being raised up above all phenomena.
The commentary on the Visākha Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Nanda Sutta 242.

Regarding the terms "forest-dweller" (*āraññika*) and so forth: by the heading of the discourse on the forest, there are the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) connected with lodgings; by the heading of the discourse on alms-food, those connected with alms-gathering;
and by the heading of the rag-robe-wearer (*paṃsukūlika*), those connected with robes. By the inclusion of these very terms, [the other practices are also implied].

It should be understood that the undertaking and practice of the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) dependent on energy have been explained. This was spoken by the Blessed One at a later time after he had arrived [at Rājagaha].
The commentary on the Nanda Sutta is finished.

9. Commentary on the Tissa Sutta 243. "Bhaṇḍaka" means the bowl and robes. He sat down because he had not trained in proper conduct. Or, since speech has the sense of "striking," it is called "spears"; thus he said, "with the spears of speech.

"With the prodding of speech" means with that which is termed speech, by way of constant and all-around poking; hence the term "sannitodaka. This designation is formed by the elision of a grammatical case ending. Therefore he said, "with the goad of words."
“Born into a high clan” means one who possesses noble birth; thus, the seer was of Brahmin birth. “Mātaṅga” means a caṇḍāla.
“Therein” means in the potter’s workshop. He requested space from the potter. Seeing that it was large, he said: “A renunciant entered first.
“Right there” means near the door of that very workshop, by the doorway. “Me” means by me. “Forgive me.”
“Forgive my transgression. *Tena* means “by you. Again, *te* means “your. “He seized” refers to seizing by way of not allowing him to rise.
Therefore he said, “He did not give him leave to rise. “They woke” means they woke from sleep because the time for waking naturally had arrived.
*Chavo* means base. *Anantamāyo* means a master of illusion possessing manifold illusions.
“Sā” means that lump of clay. Regarding the phrase “it split into seven parts,” this is the intended meaning:

when that ascetic directed harsh words—what is termed a curse—toward the Great Being, the Bodhisatta, who was a Noble One (Ariya), whose mental continuum was well-composed through the perfection of virtue, view, and so forth, which were brought to fulfillment by various dwellings and attainments perfected by the cultivation of the perfections (pāramitās), and who was suffused with great compassion; [that speech was directed toward him].
Because that [kamma] was directed toward the excellence of the Great Being’s field and because of the harshness of his own intention, it became something to be experienced in this very life;
yet, had he not asked the Great Being for forgiveness, it would have become harsh and attained the nature of ripening.

However, once the Great Being was asked for forgiveness, it reached a state of non-ripening due to being obstructed by the perfection of the means employed, because it became an *ahosi-kamma* (a deed whose result has passed away).
For this is the natural law regarding the evil of slandering the Noble Ones, which is to be experienced in this very life:
that the means perceived by the Bodhisatta was the prevention of the rising of the sun.
Oppressed by that [darkness], the people brought the ascetic into the presence of the Bodhisatta and asked for his forgiveness; he too, having recognized the virtues of the Great Being...
He felt confidence in that [Buddha]. As for the placing of a lump of clay upon his head, its being split into seven pieces was done for the sake of protecting the minds of the people;

otherwise, thinking, "These, though having gone forth as renunciants, have fallen under the sway of their own minds and do not bring their minds under their own control," they might have harmed even the Great Being because of that.
"If they were to take it after making it similar, that would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. "Patirūpaṃ" means "suitable" or "proper.
The commentary on the Tissa-sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Theranāmaka-sutta.
244. "In the past five aggregates" means in a past personal existence (*attabhāva*). "By the abandoning of desire and lust" means by the absolute relinquishing of desire and lust.
It is said to be "abandoned" because of its relinquishment without regard [for it]. It is said to be "renounced" because of its being discarded in every respect.
By the phrase "the three states of existence" (*bhava*), there is the grasping of only those phenomena that are clung to (*upādiṇṇaka*). All...

By the phrase "the aggregates, bases, and elements," worldly phenomena—which function in two ways, both as appropriated (*upādiṇṇa*) and unappropriated (*anupādiṇṇa*)—are included without distinction.
It is "known" because it stands made manifest through the penetration of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*).
"In those very [phenomena]" means precisely within the phenomena of the three planes. It is "unstained," "unsoiled," and "undefiled" due to the absence of the defilements of craving and views.
"All that" refers to the cycle of existence belonging to the three planes, which was previously included under the term "all" in the three preceding sections.

"Having abandoned" means by way of the clear realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*). "Liberated in Nibbāna, known as the exhaustion of craving" means liberated in that which is called Nibbāna, where craving is exhausted.
"I call him the supreme person dwelling alone" because of the absence of craving as a companion.

And here, by the mention of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of full understanding (*pariññā*) and abandoning (*pahāna*), it should be understood that the other clear realizations are also effectively explained by implication.
The commentary on the *Theranaṃaka-sutta* is concluded.
11. Commentary on the *Mahākappina-sutta*.
245. *Mahākappina* is a term of honor, just as *Mahāmoggallāna* is.
*Tathārūpaṃ* refers to that which is connected with specific qualities, such as "the Buddha," "the Dhamma," and so forth. *Sāsanaṃ* means a message arrived from another region.
*Jaṅghavāṇijā* means merchants who travel on foot. He asked for some message—some words indicating news not previously circulated.

Rapture arose in him, as it does for one whose knowledge has reached maturity through long-continued application. It should be said that [the Buddha] is immeasurable because his qualities are immeasurable;

because he manifests the qualities of omniscience; because he demonstrates the state of leading to liberation in the other two Jewels; and because he demonstrates the state of being unified through the commonality of right view and virtue.
For those who practice according to his instructions, [he protects them] from the suffering of the woeful states and from the suffering of saṃsāra.
It is called *dhamma* because it holds [beings] back from falling away. It is called *saṅgha* because it is united by the commonality of perfectly pure view and virtue.
As for the meaning of "jewel," it is the same for all three.

"The queen gave nine hundred thousand" means she gave that amount. He addresses her with the plural form "you" (*tumhe*) out of respect for the queen. "Passion" (*rāga*) refers to the passion that follows after [an object].
"Produced" (*janita*) means brought forth by karma and the defilements. Because it is born from karma and the defilements, the word *pajā* (progeny) has the same meaning as the word *janita*;
thus he said: "The meaning is 'produced,' [that is,] 'born'. "By the eight knowledges" (*vijjā*) refers to the method set forth in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta.

For there, the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), together with the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and the mind-made power (*manomaya-iddhi*), are recorded as the "eight knowledges. It shines.
It shines by dispelling its opposites; thus, regarding that radiance of the sun, he said: “It ‘shines’ (tapati) means it ‘radiates’ (virocati).
Having entered jhāna, with a concentrated mind having increased insight, and having entered the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), he sat;
thus he said: “Meditating with twofold jhāna. “The verses on all blessings” (sabbamaṅgalagāthā) means those which are not in conflict with any blessing.
They call it a verse (gāthā). For they say thus:
"The Blessed One, the Buddha, is an auspicious sign; the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are also auspicious signs;
and for all sentient beings, that merit is an auspicious sign."
Having performed the worship, he spoke to a lay devotee who was a householder Dhamma-preacher:
"In this context, by the phrase 'the meditator shines,' the Jewel of the Dhamma is indeed included because it encompasses both the meditation upon the object and the meditation that follows from it.
By the word 'Brahmin,' the Jewel of the Saṅgha is likewise included. However, the Jewel of the Buddha is included in its own specific form."
The commentary on the Mahākappina Sutta is finished.
12. Commentary on the Sahāyaka Sutta: 246.
It is called *sameti* because it comes together (*eti*) by way of being correctly joined (*sammā saṃsandanavasena*); [this refers to] right view and so forth. Rightly, for a long time...
“Those that meet for a long time” (*cirarattasaṃketikā*) means those whose meeting lasts for a long duration; thus he said, “for a long time,” and so forth.

Now, “of these” (*imesaṃ*) refers to those of the present. This Dhamma of the Dispensation accords and meets perfectly both with their underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) and their application (*payoga*);
therefore, it is exactly the same as if it were divided in the middle, not dissimilar. And for that very reason, by the Buddha—
The meaning is that within the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Blessed One, the teaching on their practice shines and radiates.
"Proclaimed by the Noble One" means in the Noble Dhamma correctly manifested by the Noble One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"Correctly" means well-disciplined by way of the disciplining through eradication and pacification, through the subsiding of all the distress and fever of the defilements.
The commentary on the Sahāyaka-sutta is finished.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Bhikkhu-saṃyutta within the *Sāratthappakāsinī*,
the commentary on the Saṃyutta-nikāya, is completed.
The commentary on the Nidāna-vagga of the Saṃyutta-nikāya-aṭṭhakathā, known as the Sāratthappakāsinī, is hereby completed.
